title: Students who attended Miami-Dade public school pre-K outperformed peers in 18-year study
authors: Charles Bleiker, Associate Professor of Early Childhood Education, Florida International University; Adam Winsler, Professor of Applied Developmental Psychology, George Mason University; Kaitlyn Mumma, Researcher, Applied Developmental Psychology, George Mason University
content:
Choosing a preschool is a difficult and important decision. Parents are weighing cost, proximity and convenience with how each program meets the needs of the child and matches the goals and values of their family and cultural community.

This choice makes a difference. Research in early education clearly shows that children who attend high-quality preschool programs – those with smaller class sizes, a developmentally appropriate curriculum, warm teacher-child interactions and established, efficient routines – are [better prepared for kindergarten](https://www.fcd-us.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/04/Evidence-Base-on-Preschool-Education-FINAL.pdf).

We are [researchers](https://case.fiu.edu/about/directory/profiles/bleiker-charles.html) [who study](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=_Ekthu4AAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao) [early childhood education](https://www.linkedin.com/in/kaitlynmumma/), and we conducted an 18-year study [tracking the academic progress](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2026.03.004) of 27,814 students who attended different types of prekindergarten in Miami and then went on to attend the Miami-Dade County Public Schools system from kindergarten through high school. We found that the type of pre-K program the children attended made a difference for their overall educational outcomes.

## How we did our study

From 2002 to 2007, we partnered with Miami-Dade County Public Schools, early childcare providers across the county and the [Early Learning Coalition of Miami-Dade](https://www.elcmdm.org/), a nonprofit that works with childcare providers and communities to promote school readiness, with the goal of assessing five cohorts of about 10,000 students per year.

School readiness takes into consideration the children’s cognitive, language, motor and social skills, as well as behavior problems. During the study, we shared the data we collected with parents, teachers and center directors to inform interventions for struggling kids and improvements to their pre-K programs.

Some of the students in these five cohorts attended taxpayer-funded, public school pre-K programs, while some received federal subsidies administered through the state of Florida to attend center-based or family childcare at age 4.

Center-based programs, like a Kiddie Academy, for example, can be nonprofit or for-profit centers in the community. They operate either in a freestanding location or as part of a corporate or faith-based building. Family or home-based childcare programs are generally smaller and operate out of private residences.

After the children had moved through pre-K, we continued to receive their anonymized academic records each year, as long as they stayed in the public school system. The last cohort of students completed 12th grade in spring 2020.

## Outcomes in later grades

We found that children who attended public school pre-K programs at age 4 [achieved the strongest third-grade outcomes](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2026.03.004) on standardized reading and math test scores and GPA. These children outperformed those who attended center-based care, who in turn generally performed better than children who were enrolled in family childcare. Kids who attended public school pre-K were 35% less likely to be held back in third grade compared with the other groups.

Further, we found that kids who attended higher-quality elementary schools – as [measured by the Florida Department of Education](https://www.fldoe.org/accountability/accountability-reporting/school-grades/) – did better on average.

However, the quality of the elementary school that students went on to attend didn’t change the differences we observed across the early childhood education types, except when it came to reading skills. Students who attended center-based care and went on to attend higher-quality schools were better able to catch up to the public school pre-K kids by third grade in reading.

Our findings are consistent with most previous studies of public pre-K. Students who attended public pre-K [programs in Boston](https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13308); [Tulsa, Oklahoma](https://doi.org/10.1002/pam.22023); and [North Carolina](https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.12645) have shown better results on standardized test scores, lower absenteeism and better grade retention when compared with children who attended other programs, even as late as eighth grade.

However, there are outliers. Children who attended the publicly funded voluntary pre-K program in Tennessee did not perform any better than other children on [third](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecresq.2018.03.005) or [sixth grade outcomes](https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001301) – and in some cases, they performed worse.

Previous findings are also mixed on whether these effects [persist past the third grade](https://doi.org/10.1177/1529100620915848).

In our study, it appears that the long-term benefits of public school pre-K extend through eighth grade, but this conclusion is still in peer review and has not been published yet. We are currently examining whether benefits persist throughout high school.

## Collective resources

Why did kids in public school pre-K programs do better compared to center-based and family childcare? We believe that the answer likely lies in the quality and organizational differences between the three different types of early care and education.

The public school pre-K programs in our study benefited from the collective resources of the fourth-largest public school system in the country. This matters for everything from the quality of teachers they are able to hire to the facilities and curriculum.

Miami-Dade public schools require teachers to have at minimum a bachelor’s degree and a teaching credential, whereas the others required less education at the time of our study. Public pre-K teachers’ certification allows them to teach from pre-K to third grade, so they typically bring their experience of teaching in kindergarten and the early elementary grades to the pre-K classroom.

These programs also used a developmentally appropriate curriculum, while the others used a variety of materials and approaches. When we began this study, the center-based programs were mostly independent, unaffiliated sites, although some for-profits had more than one center in the study, and some nonprofit organizations such as Catholic Charities or the YMCA oversaw multiple centers.

Many of the children in the study moved from one school to another within the same district. Because Miami-Dade’s public schools are part of a countywide system, the children’s academic records moved with them easily, so their new teacher could see their progress. And since the curriculum was the same across the district, the students were able to pick up at their new school where they’d left off.

This continuity could also explain why children who entered the public school system in pre-K performed better than those outside it. The majority of the children in the study went on to attend public elementary school. The kids in public school preschool and their parents were therefore already familiar with the schools that they would be attending the following year. It’s not hard to see how this would be an advantage for a child transitioning from preschool to kindergarten.

## Better than ever

Our findings do not indicate to us, however, that every child must attend public school pre-K in order to succeed in school later on. The reality in Miami-Dade County – and in most communities – is that we need all forms of early care and education, and each setting serves important needs for families.

Indeed, students in all three types of programs made excellent school readiness gains from the beginning to the end of the age-4 academic year. It was just that the children in the public school preschools made stronger gains.

Center- and home-based care in Miami-Dade County is much higher quality across the board today than when we began our study back in 2002. Many more centers are accredited, and teacher education levels have improved. In fact, in our assessment, the quality of early education in Miami-Dade County [has never been better](https://www.elcmdm.org/article/3043765).

Still, the cohesive system offered by public schools remains the gold standard for preschool when serving most children and families. In terms of teacher preparation and qualifications, standardized curriculum, oversight and alignment with the kindergarten curriculum, public school pre-k for low-income families in Miami still offers the best hope of long-term academic success.

*Read more of [our stories about Florida](https://theconversation.com/us/south-florida-miami-news).*

*Charles Bleiker has received in the past funding from The Children's Trust, Head Start, The Early Learning Coalition of Miami-Dade and Monroe Counties.*

*Adam Winsler has received funding in the past from National Endowment for the Arts, the Institute of Education Sciences, The Children's Trust, and the Early Learning Coalition of Miami-Dade/Monroe.*

*Kaitlyn Mumma works on several projects that are funded by the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, the Institute of Education Sciences, and the Administration for Children and Families. She is employed by Abt Global. Any opinions stated in the article represent her own perspectives and do not necessarily reflect those of Abt Global or any of the State or Federal Government Agencies for whom she may perform work.*
description: A new longitudinal study followed kids from pre-K through grade 12 and found that those who attended public school pre-K programs had an academic advantage.

title: Spending in-person time with friends is the biggest predictor of whether college students flourish
authors: Roxanne Prichard, Professor of Psychology, University of St. Thomas
content:
Exercise, avoiding alcohol or even getting enough sleep aren’t the factors most connected to college students’ well-being.

Spending face-to-face time with friends and other people is the strongest predictor of their mental health, according to a [2026 study](https://doi.org/10.1080/07448481.2026.2721429) of nearly 80,000 students that I conducted with the help of my students.

This finding matters because young people are spending [less time together in person](https://doi.org/10.1177/0265407519836170) and more time communicating through screens.

Between 2010 and 2022, the percentage of U.S. high school seniors who reported seeing friends face-to-face almost every day [declined from 44% to 32%](https://thehill.com/blogs/blog-briefing-room/4037619-teens-are-spending-less-time-than-ever-with-friends/).

Against this backdrop, mental health challenges among young people have become an increasing [public health concern](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2024.1517533).

Suicide remains the [second-leading cause of death](https://afsp.org/suicide-statistics/) among Americans ages 15 to 34.

But mental health is about more than the absence of mental illness. My student researchers [and I wanted](https://cas.stthomas.edu/departments/faculty/roxanne-prichard/) to ask a somewhat different question: What helps young people flourish?

To answer that question, we created a broad measure of well-being that captured more than the lack of mental health problems, such as psychological distress. It also included positive aspects of life, such as having supportive relationships, hobbies and a sense of meaning and purpose.

## A range of measures to determine well-being

Our [research team](https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=YFciXrYAAAAJ&view_op=list_works&sortby=pubdate&inst=2827903154962173952) analyzed responses from 79,246 college students across the United States and Canada.

We examined 51 aspects of students’ lives, including their substance use, the discrimination they encountered, their financial stress, any sleep problems and different relationship challenges.

We also examined how students spent their free time, whether that meant exercising, studying, socializing, meditating, playing video games or scrolling on social media.

We used statistical methods that allowed us to compare dozens of potential influences on student well-being simultaneously, helping us identify which factors were most strongly associated with flourishing.

Among the dozens of factors we examined, six stood out as the most important and influential.

## Time spent with others pays off

The strongest factor connected to student flourishing was remarkably ordinary: spending time with other people. Students who spent more hours socializing with friends, attending student organizations and participating in cultural events tended to report feeling an overall sense of well-being.

The second most important factor surprised us. Students who spent more time on obligations, including paid work and unpaid family responsibilities, also tended to report a greater sense of well-being.

Our results raise an intriguing possibility: Well-being may come not only from leisure and self-care but also from contributing to something larger than oneself.

While problematic substance use, passive screen time and sleep problems tended to compromise well-being, these factors weren’t the biggest detriment. It was difficulty navigating interpersonal relationships, including problems with friends, romantic partners and roommates.

Making friends, maintaining healthy relationships and working through conflicts requires practice, and some of that practice time now competes with [communication mediated by screens](https://www.norc.org/content/dam/norc-org/pdf2023/snap-inc-norc-report_08012024.pdf).

Notably, the contributors to student flourishing were similar among students diagnosed with anxiety or depression and those without these diagnoses. That suggests these everyday experiences may matter across a broad spectrum of mental health.

## Helping students thrive

Supporting students’ mental and emotional health is not simply a matter of reducing screen time. It also means making it easier for young people to spend time together in person, whether through clubs, recreation programs, community events or other welcoming spaces.

Counseling and educational programs can likewise help students build friendships, communicate effectively and navigate conflict in healthy ways.

None of this means mental illness can be solved by telling a struggling young person to put down their phone, join a club or get more sleep. Mental health conditions are complex, and people experiencing them need access to effective professional care.

But our findings suggest that helping young people thrive requires more than treating symptoms. It also requires cultivating supportive relationships, healthy sleep and meaningful engagement in work, school and family life.

*Roxanne Prichard receives funding from the National Science Foundation.*
description: Helping young people thrive involves supporting healthy relationships, as well as being engaged in work, school and family life.

title: Students take up to 88 standardized tests before high school, but more testing doesn’t improve learning
authors: Liza Bondurant, Associate Professor of Secondary Math Education, Mississippi State University
content:
The public K-12 school system in the United States has become pervasively shaped by standardized testing.

I began [teaching mathematics](https://www.teal.msstate.edu/directory/lb2206) in 2005, four years after the federal law [No Child Left Behind](https://www.nea.org/professional-excellence/student-engagement/tools-tips/history-standardized-testing-united-states) was enacted. This law expanded state testing and tied test results to school performance.

Most districts changed their curricula to focus more on the content and skills covered on state tests.

Many school districts increased their instructional weekly time for English and mathematics, with average increases of [47% for English and 37% for mathematics](https://www.schoolinfosystem.org/pdf/2008/artsed.pdf) from 2001 to 2007.

To make room for additional time spent on these subjects, [44% of school districts](https://www.schoolinfosystem.org/pdf/2008/artsed.pdf) cut time from other subjects or activities, such as the arts.

A [2026 study](https://www.education-first.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Final-Local-Assessments-Landscape-Report_February-2026.pdf) of 67 school districts across 38 states found that, before high school, students take a median of 57 state- and district-required assessments.

## A short-lived law with lasting effects

[No Child Left Behind](https://www.congress.gov/bill/107th-congress/house-bill/1/text) [was replaced](https://www.edweek.org/policy-politics/why-cant-we-leave-no-child-left-behind-behind/2025/01) by another law, the [Every Student Succeeds Act](https://www.ed.gov/laws-and-policy/laws-preschool-grade-12-education/every-student-succeeds-act-essa), in 2015.

Although the Every Student Succeeds Act aimed to reduce the role of testing in classrooms, standardized tests continue to shape what teachers teach, how they use instructional time and how schools define success.

All U.S. [public schools are required](https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/34/200.5?) to administer standardized tests in reading and math annually to students in grades three through eight and at least once in high school. [These tests](https://bipartisanpolicy.org/explainer/federal-education-policy-101-state-assessments/) measure whether students are reading and understanding mathematics at, above or below the average, when compared to other students across the state.

[Students’ scores on these tests](https://www.ecs.org/50-state-comparison-school-accountability-systems-2024/) can affect schools’ ratings and rankings, and can also [determine whether states](https://www.ed.gov/teaching-and-administration/lead-and-manage-my-school/state-support-network/ssn-resources/module-4-comprehensive-support-and-improvement-csi-schools) monitor or take over public school districts that are not performing well.

## Too much time

The [exact number of tests](https://www.education-first.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Final-Local-Assessments-Landscape-Report_February-2026.pdf) students take each year before high school ranges from 35 to 88 tests. The study also found no relationship between the number of assessments students took and their proficiency or growth in English or mathematics.

The [National Association of State Boards of Education](https://www.nasbe.org/time-to-rethink-the-test-pile/) also reports that some districts give students seven assessments per grade, with most tests administered one to three times a year.

Older research also documents the time teachers spend preparing students for state tests.

[A 2016 survey](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED568172.pdf) found that 62% of K-12 public school teachers reported spending too much time preparing students for state-mandated tests. Teachers estimated spending an average of 14 out of 180 school days preparing students for these exams, whether it be reviewing the question formats students see on tests or teaching test-taking strategies.

In the same 2016 national survey, [29% of teachers](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED568172.pdf) reported spending more than a month preparing students in grades K-12 for state-mandated tests.

## Costly in other ways

Teachers also feel the effects of spending so much time preparing students for standardized tests.

[Research on](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tate.2017.03.016) [teacher turnover](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-turnover-brief) has found that teachers’ dissatisfaction with standardized testing was a key reason they left the profession.

Other [research from 2026](https://learningpolicyinstitute.org/product/teacher-turnover-united-states-report) found that teachers who worried about job consequences tied to test results reported lower job satisfaction.

These numbers tell a larger story. The costs of standardized testing do not simply appear in the amount printed on contracts with testing companies.

They are also reflected in lesson plans, teachers’ workloads, classroom time, professional autonomy and the opportunities that disappear when preparing for a test becomes a central purpose of schooling.

A test can measure learning. But when some students take as many as 88 assessments before high school and teachers report spending weeks preparing students for state exams, it’s important to ask whether it’s the best use of their limited time.

I work in Mississippi, where many communities are rural and agriculture is a major industry. Recently, I lamented to a local farmer about the time and money spent on standardized testing. He offered a simple response: “You don’t get a pig to grow by measuring it more.” His words capture the question at the heart of this debate: Does more testing help students learn, or does it take time away from learning?

*Liza Bondurant does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Students’ scores on standardized tests can affect schools’ ratings, adding to the pressure teachers experience in preparing their students for the assessments.

title: Students air their frustrations anonymously online as emigration tempts many young people in North Macedonia
authors: Daria Dergacheva · Global Voices
content:
*‘Students don’t have to be members of a political party to create change,’ says founder of online media platform*

*This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the*[*Digital Spark*](https://ddidigitalspark.org/news/)*granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the*[*Metamorphosis Foundation*](https://metamorphosis.org.mk/en/)*and*[*TechSoup*](https://www.techsoup.org/?srsltid=AfmBOoqgPtm0Yk6HG-hTECkCqfPFl9-HyRjojpYFAhrHKdM_Z419qEaW)*, in partnership with*[*CIVICUS*](https://www.civicus.org/)*and under the*[*Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI)*](https://digitaldemocracyinitiative.net/)*that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.*

Students in North Macedonia are not the happiest group: a[2026 survey](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1254227)suggests that over 76 percent of current students are thinking of emigrating. The main reasons for this [being cited are](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1254227) “quality of life” and “finding employment suitable to professional qualifications.”

However, what if students themselves could change that? North Macedonia, luckily, has people who decided to take their fate into their own hands and help students achieve a better quality of life, not only for themselves, but for many young people.

At first, [Goshe Nikolov](https://www.linkedin.com/in/goshe-nikolov/), at the time a student himself, founded Instagram-based student media, [Studentarija](https://www.instagram.com/studentarijamk/), as an entertainment resource, where students from all over the country shared memes about studies and current events. [This outlet](https://www.instagram.com/studentarijamk/) now has over 65,000 subscribers, which is a significant number for a country with [53,000 students](https://www.stat.mk/en/stat/population-and-living-conditions/education/enrolled-students-at-higher-schools-and-faculties/enrolled-students-in-the-first-cycle-of-studies-academic-year-20242025/).

As he comes to the Zoom interview with Global Voices, Nikolov already has nine years of experience running the most successful student media in the country, and with the help of his team of three, has launched a Digital Student Voice, an[online platform](https://studentskiglas.com/) that enables students across North Macedonia to anonymously report problems related to higher education and student life. They were able to do it with the help of the Digital Democracy Initiative grant.

Nikolov has a wide smile and a confident attitude; he answers questions with the clarity that could only be gained by years of hands-on experience.

We start with the history of[Studenjaria](https://www.instagram.com/studentarijamk/).

**Global Voices (GV): Could you tell us a little about your student media outlet? How did it start? How did you manage to gain so many followers and so much engagement? Is it only on Instagram?**

> **Goshe Nikolov (GN):**Studentarija started in 2017, when I was still a student. I created it from my room in a student dormitory in Skopje. At that time, Instagram was becoming increasingly popular among students in North Macedonia, but there was no Macedonian Instagram page specifically for students. So I decided to create one, and quite spontaneously, in the end it got the name Studentarija, which it still has today. In the beginning, the idea was very simple. It was a place where students could share funny and relatable content. For example, memes, funny videos, everyday posts and situations from student life. So I could never have imagined that one day it would become what it is today. Over time, the audience kept growing, and I think that demonstrated that there was a real need for such a space.
> At the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic, in 2020, I started focusing more on the real problems and challenges faced by students in North Macedonia. Students started coming to us with questions, asking for information and sharing their problems, because they often could not get the information or support they needed elsewhere.
> That was when I really understood that Studentarija could play a much bigger role in the lives of students and young people in our country.
> So I think the main reasons young people have stayed with us over the years are our openness, transparency, creativity, consistency and, of course, accessibility. Students in North Macedonia know that they can come directly to us, that we listen to them, and that Studentarija is genuinely built around their experiences and their needs.

**GV: So do you think it will remain only on Instagram, or are you planning to use other platforms for further development?**

> **GN**: At the moment, we exist only on Instagram because Instagram is the main platform where young people and our target audience spend their time. But yes, at the moment we are planning to expand our presence. We are already building our website, and we have already developed a digital platform for students where they can report problems.

**GV: Whose idea was it to create such a platform?**

> **GN:** I would say that the idea of creating a digital student voice system came naturally from the students themselves. Students began to see Studentarija as a safe space because they came to our DMs and Instagram inbox and told us about problems they were experiencing at universities, in student dormitories, with textbooks, public services and many other aspects of student life. And as a student myself, I couldn’t simply ignore those messages when I saw that something important was happening.
> We tried to make these issues public, start conversations, ask universities for answers, or simply give students a place where their voices could be heard.
> So, over the years, all these reports were coming into our Instagram inbox. That is one of the main ways we communicate with students daily. But at some point, we realized we needed a much more organized way of collecting, categorizing and following up on students’ problems in North Macedonia. And that is how the idea for Digital Student Voice emerged.

**GV: I assume that students’ problems are more or less similar across different countries, but could you give us a few examples of the ones that stand out most in your memory?**

> **GN:**Digital Student Voice has existed since April this year, and among the most common problems reported over the last few months, I would say that many were related to delays in state student payments and poor living conditions in student dormitories across the country.
> Students have reported, for example, dormitories without hot water and sometimes even without electricity, as well as problems with rodents and insects.
> We have also received reports about improper or unfair treatment by professors, problems with grades and examination procedures, and problems with transport in Skopje. So I would say the reports cover a very broad range of issues — from everyday living conditions to much broader questions about the quality of higher education in North Macedonia and the way institutions treat students.

**GV: What happens when these problems appear on the platform, when students submit them? What happens to them afterwards? Do we see them being resolved, or not being resolved? Do solutions emerge? Please explain the whole mechanism to us**.

> **GN:** I’ll try to explain the process as quickly as possible.
> First, we share the link on our Instagram page, because that is our main way of communicating with students.
> When students report problems through Digital Student Voice, they first select a category. The problem might be related to discrimination, scholarships or textbooks, student issues, or transport. Then they describe what happened and where it happened, and the report reaches us through a secure anonymous platform.
> Every few days, our team checks the reports, organizes and categorizes them, and then looks for patterns. After that, we consider what we can do with them. Depending on the problem, this can mean publishing it on our Instagram page and raising public awareness, contacting the responsible institution, asking for an official response, or drawing attention to a larger problem affecting many students.
> Our idea is not simply to collect complaints, but to transform individual students’ experiences into evidence that can be used for advocacy and for creating change. If you want, I can share some examples of what we have done in recent months, if you think that would be useful.

**GC: Yes, please do**

> **GN**: There is one very interesting example, which demonstrates the potential of this approach. There was a student dormitory in Ohrid. Ohrid is a city in North Macedonia.
> Students from Ohrid reported that they had been living without electricity in their dormitory for several days. Imagine being a student, living and studying in a dormitory, and having no electricity for several days.
> Without electricity, they didn’t even have hot water, and the food they were receiving was absolutely inadequate. When we learned about this through Digital Student Voice, we started publishing information about the situation and calling for institutional accountability.
> After our posts, the story was picked up by major media outlets, television stations, radio stations and online media. That created broad public pressure and eventually led to institutional accountability. Following this case, the director of the student dormitory in Ohrid resigned.
> So yes, for me this example shows why it is important to connect students’ individual experiences with media attention and, of course, institutional accountability.

**GV: I assume you don’t have many people working on your team. How do you manage to handle all these requests? And have you also tried to influence or engage other democratic institutions, such as political parties or, for example, municipal representatives or something similar?**

> **GN**: Yes, regarding the team behind Digital Student Voices, actually, there are currently three of us on the Studentarija team. But yes, we involve institutions, including democratic institutions, when we see that students are experiencing particular problems. We have already contacted various institutions, for example, the Ministry of Education and Science, the National Assembly, Parliament, as well as student dormitory authorities, such as those responsible for the student dormitories in Ohrid.
> I would say it is difficult, but we know what we are doing helps a large number of students. That motivates us and keeps us moving forward.

**GV:** **What are your plans for the media outlet and the platform?**

> **GN**: Studentarija will continue to exist for students and together with students. At the moment, I am the editor-in-chief of our platform, but we work with students all the time. What it has become today was not built by me alone. It was built together with countless students in North Macedonia over the nine years Studentarija has existed.
> At the same time, as I said at the beginning, Instagram is our main platform and, in my opinion, our comfort zone, because it is also the comfort zone of students and of our audience. But we are definitely exploring other formats and spaces where Studentarija can develop both as a media platform and as a way of communicating information and fostering responsible, socially engaged young people.
> I have to be honest: since we developed Digital Student Voice, considering the number of reports students have been sending us, I must say that, unfortunately, I have been negatively surprised, because I had not realized that students’ problems in North Macedonia were so much greater than I had assumed.
> From what we see every day, from what I read every day, there is a very long road ahead. And of course, we plan to remain here, to push for change and to demand change in the country.

**GV: Do you think you are transforming a media organization into a civil society organization: an NGO advocating for students’ rights, or perhaps into a political party?**

> **GN:** In terms of the way Studentarija functions today, I think we are a mix of an Instagram platform, a media platform and a civil society organization.
> You know, we are not formally registered as a civil society organization, but what we do actually touches on the work of journalists, the work of activists and even the work of institutions.
> So, you know, there are different ways in which a young person can be active in society: in a political party, within institutions, as an activist, through a civil society organization, or as a journalist in a media organization. I think we found our voice on Instagram.
> You don’t have to be part of a political party to create change in the country. That is something I have learned from my experience so far.

**GV: Thank you very much for taking the time to speak with us. All the best to you personally, to your team and to your organization. And to the students in North Macedonia.**

**Written by [Daria Dergacheva](https://globalvoices.org/author/daria-dergacheva/)**
description: “Our idea is not simply to collect complaints, but to transform individual students’ experiences into evidence that can be used for advocacy and for creating change.”

title: Do you think teachers are similar to coaches, pastors or something else? It depends on where you live
authors: Gustavo E. Fischman, Professor of Education Policies and Comparative Studies, Arizona State University; Eric Haas, Professor of Educational Leadership, California State University, East Bay; Margarita Pivovarova, Associate Professor of Education Policy, Arizona State University
content:
Three answers, three countries, one open-ended question: “Teaching is similar to what other occupation or activity?”

We asked this question to more than 3,000 people across the United States, England and Australia between May 2025 and March 2026.

Coaching was the front-runner across all three countries. But the similarities partially diverged there.

Respondents in England and Australia more often compared teaching with professional roles such as nursing and social work. U.S. respondents, meanwhile, more often likened teaching to being a parent and religious roles, such as a cleric or pastor.

In the three countries, however, one other idea stood out: Teaching was primarily associated with a caring relationship.

We have previously [examined how](https://theconversation.com/what-makes-a-good-teacher-ask-a-republican-and-a-democrat-and-they-are-likely-to-agree-282130) Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. find common ground on what makes a good teacher, despite the polarization in the [country on education](https://www.carnegiehighered.com/higher-educations-role-in-polarized-america/) and many other issues.

This time, [we wanted](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ClEsE9QAAAAJ&hl=en) [to know](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=STy3ZAEAAAAJ&hl=en) [whether people across countries](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=dXpvMgIAAAAJ&hl=en) had similar ideas of teachers.

## Common ground

In all three countries, respondents most often described teaching as centered in the relationship between teacher and student: a form of coaching, caregiving, parenting and other types of personal support.

Coaching was the most common answer in each country, but its prominence varied.

Coaching was named by 30% of U.S. respondents, compared with 23% in England and 23% in Australia.

The differences became more pronounced when participants named other occupations and activities.

Respondents in England and Australia were more likely to associate teaching with institutional, credentialed and paid professional roles, such as nursing, lecturing and social work.

“Nursing. They care for and look after people whilst they are at their most vulnerable. Teachers do a similar thing by caring and teaching young people some of the skills they will need later in life,” a 39-year-old Australian man told us.

“A lecturer, you are passing on knowledge to people, usually the younger generation,” another 32-year-old man in England said.

Compared with respondents in those countries, U.S. respondents were more likely to describe teaching through caregiving roles, such as parenting, and through religious figures, such as priests, pastors or rabbis.

“Being a parent, you are caring for young minds and shaping them through learning,” a 33-year-old woman in the U.S. told us.

“As a preacher, he teaches the word of God. How they deliver the word determines how well the people will understand it,” a 23-year-old woman in the U.S. said.

While international comparisons are informative, they do not represent a single view of teaching. Instead, they suggest that respondents in three countries likely drew on somewhat different cultural repertoires when describing the profession.

We were surprised by just how much agreement we found.

Despite differences in schooling models and cultural norms, people in the United States, England and Australia had remarkably similar ideas about how relationships are at the heart of teaching, closely echoing our other work showing that Republicans and Democrats view teachers similarly.

## AI is not at the center of people’s thinking

In September 2026, [The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/upshot/ideas-fixing-schools-ranked.html) conducted an informal survey of 37 education researchers who gave 30 ideas about how to fix schools.

Their list consists primarily of interventions such as more per-pupil funding, banning cellphones and restricting artificial intelligence in the classroom. These ideas appeared far less often in our participants’ explanations of what teaching resembles.

In fact, out of more than 3,000 responses to our survey, AI came up only a handful of times and never as the reason teaching and another occupation were said to be alike.

Given how central [AI has become](https://theconversation.com/we-asked-teachers-about-their-experiences-with-ai-in-the-classroom-heres-what-they-said-265241) to political and [academic debates](https://theconversation.com/ai-can-help-with-academic-research-but-doesnt-always-get-it-right-here-are-some-tips-to-check-the-information-you-receive-292865) about the [future of education](https://theconversation.com/when-it-comes-to-developing-policies-on-ai-in-k-12-schools-are-largely-on-their-own-268272), its near-total absence in these public descriptions of teaching is notable.

At the same time, experts and citizens agree that what separates very good teaching from poor execution is likely the quality of the relationship between educators and children.

We think that serious conversation about student achievement must include clear descriptions of very good teachers: the practices they use to encourage and enable students to learn. Our research shows that teaching should make room for both the transmission of knowledge and the meaningful and caring relationships that make learning possible.

*The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Across three countries, people agree that teaching is centered on the teacher-student relationship. But they don’t agree on which profession teaching most resembles.

title: Why it’s more important than ever to jump-start entrepreneurial careers from the college classroom
authors: Raghupathy Sivakumar, Vice President of Commercialization and Chief Commercialization Officer, Georgia Institute of Technology
content:
Recent college graduates are facing a job market that’s only getting tougher. Their [unemployment rate hit 5.7%](https://www.newyorkfed.org/research/college-labor-market#--:explore:unemployment), compared to 4.1% for all workers, in June 2026. That may not sound like much, but it’s [one of the worst](https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/americans-without-college-degrees-are-having-one-of-the-best-job-markets-in-years-5f37d00e) rates in the past 20 years.

Meanwhile, [roughly 4 in 10](https://www.forbes.com/sites/michaeltnietzel/2026/02/23/unemployment-and-underemployment-rates-among-recent-college-graduates/) graduates are underemployed, which means they work in jobs that typically don’t require a college degree. That’s the highest rate since the COVID-19 pandemic.

As an [educator](https://ece.gatech.edu/directory/raghupathy-sivakumar) for more than 25 years, I see the growing anxiety every day. In a change from years past, parents are now peppering me with questions: How can their kids leverage their college education in such a fast-changing world? Will they learn skills in school that will soon be antiquated once they graduate?

What’s essential to understand is that technology adoption cycles have accelerated at a breathtaking rate over the past few years. While the telephone and television took decades to reach 100 million users, ChatGPT and TikTok [attained that threshold](https://www.reuters.com/technology/chatgpt-sets-record-fastest-growing-user-base-analyst-note-2023-02-01/) in a matter of months. Colleges need to adapt their curricula accordingly.

Georgia Tech, where I teach engineering, has focused on pushing entrepreneurship across our campus since 2014. We’re seeing encouraging signs from our follow-ups with graduating students that it’s helping their early careers.

I believe one of the best ways to adjust to these changes is to embed entrepreneurial experiences throughout college. Such hands-on learning, in turn, develops versatile, adaptable talent, producing graduates who can pivot across jobs as industries, technologies and opportunities evolve. And this needn’t be confined to business students – young people in all majors can benefit.

## 3 core lessons

The educational value of entrepreneurship isn’t principally that every student will be able to start a company. It’s that entrepreneurial experiences [develop the capabilities](https://create-x.gatech.edu/about-us) students need in a rapidly changing economy – and ultimately build more resilient careers.

Here are some ways educators can future-proof the college experience, based on what I’ve learned and applied at Georgia Tech.

**Making adaptability a core skill:** Students need to learn [how to be nimble](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/223125). This means recognizing important changes in the landscape, identifying new problems and the opportunities they create, articulating a response and mobilizing the necessary resources. Ultimately, this approach will help students be prepared for the real world.

To impart these lessons, I believe colleges should provide hands-on opportunities to help students learn through experience before they enter the workforce. For example, they could encourage students to develop a business venture idea that addresses a newly created opportunity in the marketplace through accelerators, or short-term “boot camps” for young companies to help them grown quickly. One example is Greptile, a startup that came out of the [Georgia Tech CREATE-X accelerator](https://www.greptile.com/).

The goal isn’t that a startup will be launched – that depends on several factors coming together – but that the student gains the experience to understand a changing landscape.

**Understanding customer value:** Colleges can also teach students how to think about customer value – namely, why the solution they’re working on matters to the consumers buying it. This isn’t just for business students. All students can gain from learning to think about the customers or clients they will deal with in their careers. In fact, students from 38 majors have participated in the [entrepreneurship programs at Georgia Tech](https://create-x.gatech.edu/about-us).

Through on-the-ground experience that requires them to find customers, students can learn about the real-world impact of the products and services they create. When students spend hundreds of hours selling their young startup to the outside world, they learn to understand value at a deep level.

**Emphasizing fundamentals:** Fundamental skills are key because they outlast the technology underpinning the business. In fact, the more quickly specific technologies change, the more important a strong grounding in fundamentals becomes. This means it’s a smarter investment to offer, say, a fundamental course on wireless networking or deep learning concepts over a course that teaches specific wireless technologies or emphasizes the use of a specific model. A strong foundation gives students the tools to adapt to technologies that may not yet exist when they graduate.

## The many paths toward entrepreneurship

Another great advantage of entrepreneurial experiences is that they force students to deal with uncertainty, recognize opportunities, work around resource constraints and learn how to create value.

But other strategies work as well. A few examples are project-based learning, internships and interdisciplinary capstone classes that let students pursue independent research projects as their final course.

That said, entrepreneurial experiences provide an unusually concentrated and effective environment that requires students to solve problems, engage with customers and mobilize resources they don’t directly control – all while getting real-world feedback.

More and more universities and colleges understand this point and have ramped up support for entrepreneurial activity for their students, [such as Cornell](https://eship.cornell.edu/) and the [University of Washington](https://www.washington.edu/innovation/programs/). At Georgia Tech, we have a [playbook that we have developed](https://www.wipo.int/documents/d/global-innovation-index/docs-en-2026-gii-2026-contributors-disrupting-the-disruptors.pdf) through our experiences that follows the following principles:

**Embed entrepreneurship into the curriculum:** One simple way for colleges to incorporate entrepreneurial experiences into their coursework is to offer an entrepreneurship minor to all students, regardless of major. This would offer the opportunity to a broader range of students who otherwise might miss out.

**Build a pathway to business creation:** Entrepreneurial education is most effective when it leads to something bigger. To that end, many colleges are now offering a startup accelerator, [including MIT](https://entrepreneurship.mit.edu/accelerator/program/), [Rice University](https://entrepreneurship.rice.edu/rice-startup-accelerator) and the [University of Texas](https://undergraduates.utexas.edu/launchpad/seal).

But more is needed: A startup pathway that caters to students at all stages can substantially broaden participation and impact, regardless of whether a business results. At Georgia Tech, we have a [learn/make/launch/scale pathway](https://commercialization.gatech.edu/) that offers programs and resources for learning about entrepreneurship, building solutions, launching new ventures and eventually scaling them.

**Offer real venture experience:** A successful model combines theoretical learning with hands-on experience. The confidence that students gain through that experience may be at least as important an educational outcome as the viability of the startups they launch. After all, since most startups [tend to fail](https://hbr.org/2021/05/why-start-ups-fail), confidence is a value that successful entrepreneurs have to sustain.

## Transferring skills to the workforce

There’s another important element that’s needed: private sector partnerships. Fortunately, entrepreneurial education is well aligned with the interests of universities’ traditional corporate partners.

These companies, especially those with established, successful business models, [are eager](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/399057037) to hire students with a strong understanding of fundamentals and entrepreneurial confidence. This next generation can help the companies navigate the future.

Companies can also offer industry know-how, mentorship opportunities and financial and in-kind support. And they understand that students building a startup have to think [beyond their own discipline](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/386104454_Startups_can_offer_student_interns_real-life_advantages) to succeed. For example, an engineering student will need to understand customers, pricing, finance, sales, operations, intellectual property and team building. That broader perspective can make them more effective when they enter a corporate environment full time.

The same capabilities can also translate into venture creation itself: The value of entrepreneurial education can be seen across both traditional workforce pathways and startup outcomes. Our experience at Georgia Tech offers evidence of both.

Startups launched by Georgia Tech students over the past decade have crossed [US$4.5 billion](https://create-x.gatech.edu/) in aggregate total valuation and have created thousands of jobs. We’ve also found encouraging early evidence that students who gain confidence through these experiences have [stronger career outcomes](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/404299375_Entrepreneurship_Education_Shapes_Career_Trajectories_beyond_Entrepreneurial_Intentions).

Georgia Tech isn’t alone. The University System of Georgia has recently created a new role: a [chief innovation and entrepreneurial strategies officer](https://costasspirou.com/) to lead an initiative across all of the state’s public colleges and universities.

Other universities are pursuing similar paths, including the [University of Virginia](https://www.cavalierdaily.com/article/2025/11/paul-cherukuri-leads-uvas-entrepreneurship-strategy-as-its-first-chief-innovation-officer), [Rice University](https://profiles.rice.edu/staff/adrian-tromel) and [Cornell University](https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2026/06/matt-marx-named-vice-provost-entrepreneurship-innovation-and-external-engagement). All now have an institutionwide leadership position focused on entrepreneurship.

Taken together, these developments suggest that educators increasingly view entrepreneurship as more than just support for students who want to start companies. These steps will help ensure that when students walk across the stage to receive their diplomas, they can meet the challenges ahead of them.

*Raghupathy Sivakumar does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Hands-on learning about building a business is something students of all majors can benefit from.

title: Friendship is built over time, through ordinary moments – I teach lonely college students to notice them
authors: Justin Vaughn, Professor of Political Science and Director of the Center for Applied Civic Leadership, Coastal Carolina University
content:
The first skill I learned when [I became a political science professor](https://www.coastal.edu/academics/facultyprofiles/educationandsocialsciences/politics/justinvaughn/) nearly 20 years ago was how to quiet a room full of chatty undergraduates.

These days, I often walk into a silent room, with students staring at their phones and barely acknowledging the classmates beside them.

As I read more about the United States’ [loneliness crisis](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf), I began noticing a version of it among my students.

In a 2026 [national survey of over 40,000 college students](https://www.trellisstrategies.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Research-Brief_TSFEB26_Loneliness.pdf), nearly 6 in 10 said they felt lonely sometimes or always. At the same time, [federal time-use data](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/pdf/atus.pdf) show that the share of Americans who socialized in person with family, friends or others on an average day fell from 38% in 2015 to 30% in 2025.

Those and [similar other studies](https://www.coastal.edu/honorscollege/centerforappliedcivicleadership/friendship/) capture a familiar contradiction seen on college campuses like my own: Many new students want close relationships, but feel anxious about initiating them and have had little practice sustaining them.

I realized that my students rarely spoke to one another, and went entire semesters without learning their classmates’ names. Many students seemed unsure how to cross the few feet between them and their peers and make the social connection they craved.

I [designed a freshman honors seminar](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/why-friendship-belongs-college-classroom-justin-vaughn-ycbme?trk=public_post_feed-article-content), “Friendship & Society,” around this uncertainty, combining the academic study of friendship with practical exercises in forming and sustaining it.

## Understanding friendship

In this course, students examine how an [initial exchange can develop](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/platonic-love/202604/how-to-talk-to-strangers) into friendship through [repeated contact and shared time](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/brain-waves/201803/how-do-you-make-or-maintain-friends-put-in-the-time), and why many potential connections never progress into a lasting friendship.

They consider how friends help shape identity and memory, whether old friends are owed continued loyalty after their lives diverge and whether a friendship can remain meaningful after it ends.

Students also look at how friendship can have strong effects on physical and mental health, making it what I believe is an [overlooked public health issue](https://doi.org/10.1177/23727322251404386). Friendships can also help shape people’s broader sense of belonging in a community, building the social trust that [civic life depends on](https://www.abigailadamsinstitute.org/seeking-the-good-american-democracys-forgotten-institution).

Students test those questions through 10 “Friendship Practices,” a series of experiential activities I designed. Students are asked to share a meal with classmates or visit a public gathering place like a café or lounge to see how these settings can encourage conversation. During a “friendship safari,” small groups walk across campus, noting where conversations begin and where students pass one another without speaking.

In private journal entries and submitted reflections, students record what they expected from each situation, and what happened when they tried to form connections. They make a short film telling a story of friendship on campus and end with a friendship memoir tracing how their own relationships and expectations changed during their first semester of college.

## Diving into friendship

Students read “[Stay True](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/688054/stay-true-by-hua-hsu/),” a memoir about a friendship between author Hua Hsu and his classmate Ken that shapes Hsu’s sense of himself long after his friend’s death.

Neuroscientist Ben Rein’s book “[Why Brains Need Friends](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/761227/why-brains-need-friends-by-ben-rein-phd/)” explains the biology of connection and isolation, and shows how positive interactions activate the brain’s reward system while isolation triggers a stress response.

Students also read [longform journalism](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2025/02/american-loneliness-personality-politics/681091/), [social science research](https://www.coastal.edu/honorscollege/centerforappliedcivicleadership/friendship/), [public health reports](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf) and [political philosophy](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/T/bo3636037.html) on aspects of loneliness. They also watch [TED Talks](https://www.ted.com/talks/kio_stark_why_you_should_talk_to_strangers) and [films that explore how a brief encounter](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0374900/) with a stranger can, over time, become a friendship.

## Lessons learned

Students learn that a friendship is built from countless moments that may feel meaningless while they are happening. An unremarkable meal, or a conversation that fills 10 spare minutes rarely feels consequential on its own.

Over time, those moments build relational capital, meaning the shared trust and history friends can draw on when life becomes difficult or a disagreement needs repairing.

That reserve reaches beyond a single relationship. Communities become more connected when people have accumulated enough ordinary experience together to trust one another and keep showing up.

By the end of the course, students can weigh different kinds of evidence about how friendships form, develop and sometimes fade. They also become better able to start a conversation, recognize which public spaces make it easier to meet and spend time with others, and identify habits that help relationships deepen over time.

They finish with a clearer sense of how relationships take shape and how their own choices contribute to the communities forming around them.

*[Uncommon Courses](https://theconversation.com/topics/uncommon-courses-130908) is an occasional series from The Conversation U.S. highlighting unconventional approaches to teaching.*

*Justin Vaughn does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Students in this course learn about the biology and sociology of friendship, but also put their studies to the test by going to eat a meal with a peer, and tracking their experience.

title: From DMs to data: How an anonymous platform is turning students’ stories into fuel for change in North Macedonia
authors: Global Voices Central & Eastern Europe · Global Voices
content:
*The creators of Digital Student Voice asked ‘What if these individual stories could become evidence of systemic problems?’*

*This article was produced by the informal group Studentarija from North Macedonia through the [Digital Spark](https://ddidigitalspark.org/news/) granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by [Metamorphosis Foundation](https://metamorphosis.org.mk/en/) and [TechSoup](https://www.techsoup.org/?srsltid=AfmBOoqgPtm0Yk6HG-hTECkCqfPFl9-HyRjojpYFAhrHKdM_Z419qEaW), in partnership with [CIVICUS](https://www.civicus.org/) and under the [Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI)](https://digitaldemocracyinitiative.net/) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.*

For nine years, [Studentarija](https://www.instagram.com/studentarijamk/), an Instagram-based youth-led media outlet, has published daily information about student life in North Macedonia: from application deadlines and scholarships to public transport, accommodation, and higher education policies. But beyond providing information, it has increasingly become something else: A place where students feel safe enough to speak about problems they are unwilling to report elsewhere.

For years, the messages have arrived one after another.

A student who didn’t receive the government scholarship they were promised. Another describing cockroaches in their dormitory. Someone else reported that their subsidized student meal was suddenly terminated without explanation. A student convinced they were treated unfairly during an exam, but too afraid to speak publicly.

Most of these stories were never formally reported to the relevant institutions. Instead, they landed in Studentarija’s Instagram inbox. As thousands of messages accumulated over the years, one question became impossible to ignore: What if these individual stories could become evidence of systemic problems?

That question led to the creation of Digital Student Voice, an[online platform](https://studentskiglas.com/) that enables students across North Macedonia to anonymously report problems related to higher education and student life.

Rather than collecting complaints for their own sake, the platform aims to identify recurring patterns, document structural challenges, and transform scattered experiences into organized evidence that can inform public discussion and institutional action.

“Students trust Studentarija, and that is reflected in the large number of messages we receive every day,” says [Goshe Nikolov](https://www.linkedin.com/in/goshe-nikolov/), founder of Studentarija.

“While that trust is extremely high, we have also noticed that many students are afraid to speak publicly about the problems they face because they fear potential consequences. This became especially clear when a student dormitory in the city of [Ohrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohrid)was left [without electricity for more than 30 hours](https://www.instagram.com/p/DUjR81PCPii/?img_index=1). Students informed us about the situation, but they were afraid of being identified and facing retaliation from the dormitory management, including the possibility of losing their accommodation.”

Fear of speaking openly is not unique to one institution. For many students, publicly criticizing university staff, dormitory administrators, or government institutions can feel risky, particularly in a relatively small academic community where anonymity is difficult to preserve.

Digital Student Voice was designed with that reality in mind.

Through a [secure online form](https://studentskiglas.com/prijavi-problem), students can anonymously report issues ranging from delays in scholarships and financial aid to deteriorating living conditions in student dormitories, violations of student rights, transportation problems, discrimination, or administrative obstacles during their studies.

The objective extends beyond simply collecting reports.

The platform seeks to create a structured database of student experiences, allowing recurring problems to be identified, categorized, and monitored over time. By doing so, isolated incidents become measurable trends rather than individual anecdotes.

“The Studentarija team carefully reviews every submission, analyzes the reports, and identifies the most frequently reported issues so that we can detect recurring patterns,” says [Aleksandar Nikolovski](https://www.linkedin.com/in/aleksandarnikolovski1508/), a member of the Studentarija team.

“Our goal is to organize these findings and publicly present them to the relevant institutions. Through public communication, evidence-based reporting, and formal correspondence with decision-makers, we want to highlight what students are consistently experiencing and encourage institutions to respond. We believe that transparency and public accountability can become important drivers for positive change.”

The first results suggest that students were waiting for exactly this kind of platform.

During its first month, Digital Student Voice [received](https://www.instagram.com/p/DZYGjRQChZv/?img_index=1)around 100 reports. By the third month, that number had nearly tripled, with approximately 300 students submitting reports.

For a country with roughly [53,000 university students](https://www.stat.mk/en/stat/population-and-living-conditions/education/enrolled-students-at-higher-schools-and-faculties/enrolled-students-in-the-first-cycle-of-studies-academic-year-20242025/), that volume is significant. More importantly, the reports reveal striking similarities, regardless of where students study.

“Based on the reports we have received so far, we are already identifying clear patterns,” says [Ana Shopovska](https://www.linkedin.com/in/anashopovska/), a member of the Studentarija team.

“For example, students have repeatedly reported delays in the payment of state scholarships, as well as unjustified interruptions to the subsidized student meal program — a government measure that provides students with financial support for one meal each day. We are also continuously receiving reports about extremely poor living conditions in student dormitories, including rodents and insect infestations, prolonged periods without hot water, and even electricity outages. When the same issues keep appearing across different reports, it becomes evident that these are not isolated incidents, but systemic challenges that deserve institutional attention.”

For Studentarija, identifying these recurring themes is only the beginning.

The team regularly analyzes incoming reports, groups them into categories, and [publishes](https://www.instagram.com/p/DZYGjRQChZv/?img_index=1)summaries of the most frequently reported problems. In addition, public polls invite students to rank which issues they consider most urgent, creating another layer of community participation.

These findings are then shared with the relevant public institutions through official correspondence, media coverage, and [public communication campaigns](https://www.instagram.com/p/DavSo-QihDk/?img_index=1)aimed at encouraging concrete responses.

The approach represents a shift from reactive reporting toward evidence-based civic participation.

Instead of focusing solely on individual stories, Digital Student Voice attempts to demonstrate when multiple reports indicate a systemic issue requiring institutional attention.

In this sense, the platform serves not only as a reporting mechanism but also as a source of grassroots data about the everyday realities of higher education in North Macedonia.

The initiative also reflects a broader trend in civic technology: Using digital tools to reduce barriers to participation for groups that may otherwise remain unheard.

For students who fear retaliation, anonymity lowers the threshold for speaking out. For journalists and civil society organizations, aggregated reports provide stronger evidence than isolated testimonies. For institutions, recurring patterns can offer valuable insight into problems that might otherwise remain invisible.

Studentarija emphasizes that Digital Student Voice is not intended to replace official complaint procedures.

Instead, it complements them by documenting what students collectively experience, identifying issues that repeatedly emerge, and ensuring that these concerns are not lost among thousands of private messages.

As the platform continues to grow, the team hopes it will become a long-term mechanism for monitoring student life, strengthening dialogue between students and institutions, and encouraging evidence-based policy discussions.

After years of receiving individual messages in an Instagram inbox, Studentarija is now building something more permanent, which might actually lead to structural changes in students’ lives in North Macedonia

**Written by [Global Voices Central & Eastern Europe](https://globalvoices.org/author/cee/)**
description: Digital Student Voice is an online platform where students can anonymously report issues ranging from delays in scholarships to deteriorating living conditions in student dormitories and violations of student rights.

title: What working-class boys need to succeed at school: respect and open conversations
authors: Jon Rainford, Lecturer in Education, The Open University; Alex Blower, Research Fellow, Arts University Bournemouth
content:
Across the UK, working‑class boys are navigating an unprecedented convergence of pressures. There are [entrenched gaps](https://www.tes.com/magazine/teaching-learning/secondary/improving-school-engagement-for-disadvantaged-boys) between working-class boys and their peers in their levels of attainment at [every stage](https://www.instituteforgovernment.org.uk/publication/policy-making-left-behind-groups-boys-low-income-families) of education.

Often, however, the solutions for addressing this gap in attainment have roots in assumptions and stereotypes. These tend towards positioning working-class boys as somehow suffering from an innate [deficiency](https://policy.bristoluniversitypress.co.uk/lost-boys): apathy, laziness or a lack of ambition for their future careers and employment. The evidence does not back these stereotypes up.

Our research has focused on understanding the experiences of these boys. In 2023, we [carried out research](https://doi.org/10.3167/bhs.2023.160207) that used creative activities to explore what being a young man meant for them. We found that some of the young men felt the need to create protective identities linked to aggression, emotional suppression and educational disinterest at school to avoid harm. For them, being a boy who expressed themselves was a risky enterprise. One boy said:

> I feel like you know the bullying and torment would definitely go up quite a bit for, I guess, you know, something stupid like writing how I feel on a page.

We [worked with young men](https://bristoluniversitypressdigital.com/monobook/book/9781447370277/9781447370277.xml?tab_body=abstract-excerpt) who were open and able to engage in challenging and complex discussions, but who made it clear to us that doing this in their own educational environments would potentially lead to social, emotional and potentially even physical harm.

We saw young men with deep rooted aspirations they were often afraid to express. We did not see [problematic boys](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c246l4mdg3jo) in need of disciplining, but a need to understand and address the relational and structural conditions which shape their behaviour.

## Lacking resources – and evidence

In almost every public debate about boys, whether it be attainment gaps, misogyny or youth violence, teachers are positioned as society’s key defence. The government’s recent [violence against women and girls strategy](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/vawg-strategy-to-better-protect-children-from-misogyny-and-abuse), for instance, foregrounds the role of educators in shaping boys’ attitudes and preventing future harm.

But it assumes that schools possess the frameworks, training, and relational bandwidth to meet these challenges. Crucially, it also assumes that we truly understand the daily dynamics between teachers and working‑class boys.

The reality is that we don’t. The last major study of teacher perceptions was over [20 years ago](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/0142569042000252044). This decades-wide gap in evidence and understanding is a void which, our findings demonstrate, has been filled by stereotype and assumption. Rather than a focus on what boys need to achieve at school, there’s a risk that they are seen, both within schools and by the general public, [as perpetrators](https://theconversation.com/adolescence-in-schools-tv-shows-portrayal-of-one-boyhood-may-do-more-harm-than-good-when-used-as-a-teaching-tool-253158) of misogyny and violent behaviour in waiting – that they are an issue that [needs to be targeted](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c246l4mdg3jo).

We’ve recently carried out [a national survey](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/657178a3f8a237185d075437/t/6981ba0142cd5c0c77876448/1770109441897/Dignity+Respect+and+Meaningful+Engagement+in+the+Classroom.pdf) of over 500 teachers, exploring their perceptions of boys and young men in the classroom. It was followed up with in-depth focus groups with 40 working-class boys aged from 12 to 16, as well as 17 teachers.

We found that teachers showed a high level of confidence in their ability to model dignity, respect and active listening in the classroom. However, the perspectives of young men painted a far more inconsistent picture. It pointed toward two significant disconnects.

First, that respect is defined very differently by educators and the boys and young men they taught. Around 90% of teachers reported that they consistently modelled dignity and respect in the classroom. But when speaking with the boys, often they described the respect they received from teachers as conditional, inconsistent or transactional. The expectation was that respect for teachers came from their position of authority and respect was only paid to the young men in return for theirs.

Second, that masculinity, emotion and online influence are poorly understood and rarely discussed. When asked, [just a third of the educators we surveyed](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/657178a3f8a237185d075437/t/6874b7983b90cf4a5fc19f42/1752479643832/boysreport_V3_080625_digital.pdf) could recall a meaningful conversation with a male student about masculinity. Many felt uncomfortable and unprepared to have conversations like this. From the boys’ side, they described significant emotional needs which were often unmet, limited safe spaces to discuss feelings, and punitive responses to distress.

How teachers perceive working-class boys, and the opportunities they have to discuss masculinity at school, aren’t the only factors affecting academic attainment for these young men. Poverty, for instance, has a significant impact on early attainment and a [lasting impact on educational success](https://blogs.lse.ac.uk/inequalities/2025/05/21/the-chronic-miseducation-of-working-class-children/). But our research showed that when reflective, safe, judgement-free conversations occurred, the boys and young men responded positively. It demonstrates that working‑class boys engage, reflect and thrive in educational contexts where they feel respected, listened to and understood.

On the other hand, though, the research suggests that teachers are influenced by wider societal narratives. Within the study many educators defaulted to talking about misogyny or Andrew Tate even when not asked directly. This suggests a narrow lens of focus on issues related to masculinity, shaped by wider social anxieties.

The boys and young men consistently faced contradictory expectations about who they should be. They reported being told to “open up”, yet faced being penalised or ridiculed when they did. They were told to avoid harmful online content, yet weren’t provided any space to engage in critical, deliberate conversations about what they had seen.

Without that space for conversation on which to build, it is our fear that efforts to tackle misogyny, disengagement or disparities in educational outcomes will continue to fall short.

*Jon Rainford conducts research for Boys Impact*

*Alex Blower is affiliated with Arts University Bournemouth and Boys' Impact.*
description: Being a boy who expresses themselves can be a risky enterprise.

title: Distance learning changes lives, but comes with its own challenges
authors: Ashley Gunter, Professor, University of South Africa
content:
Across Africa, distance education has become one of the most powerful forces for expanding access to higher learning. Open and distance learning institutions such as the Open University of Tanzania, the Zimbabwe Open University and the National Open University of Nigeria have joined long-standing providers like the University of South Africa in offering flexible study opportunities to millions of students who would otherwise be excluded from higher education.

These institutions are reimagining what it means to go to university in contexts where geography, cost and social responsibilities often keep young people out of the classroom.

***Read more: [How place of birth shapes chances of going to university: evidence from 7 African countries](https://theconversation.com/how-place-of-birth-shapes-chances-of-going-to-university-evidence-from-7-african-countries-172442)***

The value of distance education is undeniable. It allows working adults to continue their studies without leaving employment, gives rural youth the chance to stay in their communities while earning qualifications, and provides people with opportunities to balance learning alongside family responsibilities. During crises such as the COVID-19 pandemic, distance education proved to be a lifeline when face-to-face teaching was impossible.

Across the continent, it is not simply an alternative to traditional universities; for many, it is the only route into higher education.

The World Bank has [reported](https://www.worldbank.org/en/topic/education/publication/steering-tertiary-education-toward-resilient-systems-that-deliver-for-all) that only 9% of the African population in the five years after secondary school is enrolled in tertiary education – the lowest rate in the world.

My [own research](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03736245.2025.2472653#abstract) takes the University of South Africa (Unisa) as a case study to dig deeper into how geography and inequality shape students’ experiences of distance learning: their access, participation, and outcomes. With over 370,000 students in South Africa and other countries, [Unisa](https://www.unisa.ac.za/sites/corporate/default) is the continent’s largest provider. It’s an ideal lens through which to understand both the promise and the challenges of this educational model.

I’m a [geographer](https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=pB1hZ4sAAAAJ&view_op=list_works&sortby=pubdate) with an interest in international education and economic development. For the Unisa case study, I took a qualitative research approach, interviewing 28 Unisa postgraduate students from different regions of Africa. I chose them to reflect the diversity of students enrolled at Unisa and because they already had experience of studying.

The study found that although distance education can meet educational needs where people can’t access face-to-face learning, it’s not a perfect solution.
