There are still challenges which make it hard for some people to study, like inadequate infrastructure (poor internet connectivity and electricity supply), financial constraints, and language and cultural barriers. There’s a need for interventions to improve the effectiveness and equity of distance education.

## Experiences of distance education

My interviews with postgraduate students across Africa showed a complex picture. For the 18 students based in cities, distance education can be genuinely empowering. Internet connections, though costly, are usually accessible in cities. Electricity supply is more stable, and digital platforms are within reach. Students in urban areas spoke of the freedom and flexibility they gained, describing distance education as the only way to balance work, family life and study.

But geography matters. For students in rural or marginalised regions, participation in distance learning can become a daily [struggle](https://theconversation.com/psychological-grit-is-over-rated-as-the-key-to-retention-in-distance-education-a-south-african-study-debunks-the-myth-199022).

Downloading a file may take hours. Travelling long distances to internet cafés eats into scarce time and resources. A student in Zimbabwe explained how he missed deadlines simply because the university portal would not load in his village. Another said:

> Some days I feel like I’m learning less and figuring out how to connect more.

Another, in Kenya, described travelling to Nairobi every two weeks to collect academic materials. She felt the sacrifice was worth it because she knew education could change her life. For others:

> I begin to wonder if it’s really worth it.

These obstacles, however, underline rather than diminish the value of distance education. Students are willing to endure enormous effort and cost to access learning because they believe in its power to transform their futures. Their determination is itself evidence of the demand for and importance of this model of education.

Still, the barriers are real. High data prices, unstable internet, and unreliable electricity continue to limit access. Women in rural areas often face additional responsibilities that leave them with little time or energy to study.

> It’s hard to keep up with my guy classmates who don’t face the same rules at home.

And the flexibility that makes distance education attractive can sometimes turn into a sense of isolation when students don’t have peer support.

> I feel alone a lot. Even when I try to share, they don’t seem to understand what I’m facing.

## Persistent inequities in distance education

Distance education can actually keep existing inequities in place, because students from wealthier, urban backgrounds are better positioned to succeed than rural students are.

My study also revealed how the realities of students’ lives not only affect their ability to use digital tools but also their sense of belonging to the academic community. There is a growing digital divide within distance education itself.

The task ahead is to make sure that these challenges do not undercut the progress distance education has already made. Over the past decade, distance education has expanded access, increased enrolment far beyond the capacity of traditional campuses, and improved the quality of digital teaching, learner support, and flexible study pathways.

Investment in affordable broadband and electricity is essential, particularly in rural and underserved regions. Financial aid needs to cover the hidden costs of learning, from devices to data. Outreach centres should be located closer to marginalised communities, and policies must explicitly address the gendered realities that shape women’s access to higher education.

***Read more: [Hunger among South African students: study shows those studying remotely need financial aid for food](https://theconversation.com/hunger-among-south-african-students-study-shows-those-studying-remotely-need-financial-aid-for-food-264542)***

Across Africa, open universities have already demonstrated how distance education can [widen participation](https://theconversation.com/how-class-and-social-capital-affect-university-students-92602) and build [inclusive](https://theconversation.com/online-learning-can-be-hard-for-students-with-disabilities-how-to-help-158650) futures. Unisa’s story, and the experiences of its students, highlight both the opportunities and the work still to be done.

Geography continues to shape who can learn, but it does not have to decide who gets left behind. With the right investments and policies, distance education can move closer to fulfilling its full promise: to provide equitable, life-changing access to higher learning for all.

*Ashley Gunter receives funding from, The Arts and Humanities Research Council UK, British Academy UK, National Research Foundation, Newton Fund UK.*
description: For rural students, distance education can keep existing inequities in place.

title: DreamWorks’ Forgotten Island is a joyous, painful love letter to the Filipino diaspora
authors: Kristine Aquino, Senior Lecturer, University of Technology Sydney
content:
It is fitting that DreamWorks’ Forgotten Island carries a title that evokes memory and loss. The film, released globally in September, is on the surface a coming-of-age adventure about friendship.

Look a little closer and it is a poignant meditation on separation, a theme that speaks deeply to the Philippines and its diaspora, whose culture for the first time takes centre stage in a major Hollywood animation.

The film, co-directed by Filipino-American Januel Mercado and Joel Crawford, centres on best friends Raissa (Liza Soberano) and Jo (H.E.R.), who grow up together in the Philippines. After graduating from high school, they reach a crossroads: Raissa, a bright and nerdy student, has been accepted into a prestigious university in the United States and will migrate, while her more carefree (but secretly devastated) friend Jo will stay behind.

But before they can say goodbye, the pair fall through a magical portal onto the fantastical island of Nakalimutan. There, they must evade mythical creatures inspired by Filipino folklore, including a terrifying *manananggal* (Lea Salonga): a shape-shifting ghoul that preys on sleeping humans.

In order to escape the island, Raissa and Jo are forced to bargain with an even more frightening foe: a “memory demon” (Jenny Slate) that demands their most precious memories as the price for the passage home.

As a Filipino-Australian and a mother, I felt both joy and pangs of sadness watching the story unfold. Seeing Filipino culture rendered on such a scale was moving, especially through the eyes of my seven-year-old daughter, who delighted in the film’s references to [jeepney vehicles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeepney), karaoke, Tagalog phrases, Filipino music and mythology.

The cast also celebrates performers with Filipino background, including H.E.R., Soberano, Salonga, Dolly de Leon and Jo Koy.

Yet beyond this celebration of Filipino culture lies a more bittersweet story. As an academic who has spent two decades researching the Filipino diaspora, I was struck by the film’s underlying anxieties about memory, separation and return – concerns that echo with one of the world’s largest diasporas.

## A story for a scattered people

What do we carry with us when we leave home and what is at risk of being lost? These are the questions that animate Forgotten Island. It also speaks to the experience of migration that has become so deeply embedded in Philippine society.

In search of work and a better life, close to 11 million Filipinos [live outside of the Philippines](https://pia.gov.ph/news/filipino-migration-bouncing-back-to-pre-pandemic-level-cfo/). This makes the Filipino diaspora among the [top ten largest in the world](https://www.un.org/en/desa/international-migration-2020-highlights), spread across [more than 100 countries](https://www.rappler.com/moveph/60705-filipinos-ofws-world-infographic/).

Filipinos have long migrated to North America as permanent settlers, reflecting the Philippines’ colonial ties to the US. But since the 1970s, migration destinations have expanded to the United Kingdom, Europe and Australia. In Australia, Filipinos are the [fifth-largest migrant group](https://www.homeaffairs.gov.au/research-and-statistics/statistics/country-profiles/profiles/philippines) and third-largest Asian community after those born in India and China.

Large numbers are also temporary migrant workers in the Persian Gulf states and across Asia.

Among the most prominent migrants are Overseas Filipino Workers (OFWs), as they are known in the Philippines, who number [around 2.5 million globally](https://psa.gov.ph/statistics/survey/labor-and-employment/survey-overseas-filipinos) and continue to increase each year. Remittances from these migrants contribute tens of billions of dollars annually to the Philippine economy, amounting to around [8.5% of the country’s GDP in 2025](https://data.worldbank.org/indicator/BX.TRF.PWKR.DT.GD.ZS?locations=PH).

Raissa’s departure for the US reflects a deeply familiar trajectory for many Filipinos, for whom migration has become both an aspiration and a necessity. For a large number of Filipino youth, the question is not whether they will migrate, but where.

## The toll of migration

The fear of forgetting that drives Forgotten Island echoes the social and emotional costs of migration.

Many Filipino children grow up with one or both parents working and living overseas, and families sustain their relationships across borders through phone calls, video chats and periodic reunions. In the film, Jo is a daughter of a migrant father working overseas, left behind for her *lola* (grandmother) to raise.

For some Filipino families, migration has fractured relationships. Children come to know their mothers and fathers primarily through the money they send home. While financial support may have become a proxy for care, it has not been able to replace the physical affection and intimacy lost through separation.

Forgotten Island captures this tension with unusual sensitivity. Beneath its humour and frenetic adventure, it deals with the fragility of human connection. And as the film’s lead song, [BRB](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vtZgwKb5Bkw&list=RDvtZgwKb5Bkw&start_radio=1), puts it:

> If you’ve lost all the memories and can’t find your way / I might be gone tomorrow but I’ll be right back, it’s okay / I’ll never forget you / I’ll never forget you.

It’s a promise familiar to many Filipino families – even when return and reunion are uncertain.

## A cultural milestone

Growing up in Australia in the 1990s, I never saw Filipino stories reflected on screen like this. I’m glad my daughter is seeing it in her time.

Whatever its [commercial fate](https://www.thewrap.com/creative-content/movies/forgotten-island-box-office-bomb-what-happened/), Forgotten Island has achieved something significant. In a story about remembering, loss and what survives across distance, the film becomes part of the collective memory of a diaspora connected across generations and continents.

*Forgotten Island is in cinemas now.*

*Kristine Aquino receives funding from the Australian Research Council.*
description: The first major Hollywood animation centred on Filipino culture speaks to the experience of migration that has become so deeply embedded in Philippine society.

title: How high is current immigration to the United States in historical perspective?
authors: Hannah Ritchie
content:
Ask Americans about the top concerns for the United States, and immigration is [rarely far](https://news.gallup.com/poll/642887/inflation-immigration-rank-among-top-issue-concerns.aspx) from the top of the list. It’s a topic that dominates election cycles and divides public opinion.

That raises a broader historical question: how high are current immigration levels compared to what the United States has experienced before?

This article looks at [Census Bureau data](https://www.census.gov/library/working-papers/2006/demo/POP-twps0081.html) stretching back to 1850 to explore that question. We first look at what the data captures, then explore how the number of immigrants and their share of the US population have changed over time.

As is often the case, the data shows that the answer depends on what you’re comparing and how far back in time you go.

# Tracking immigration with long-run US census data

One way to understand the scale of immigration is to look at how many immigrants live in the US. The Census Bureau calls this the “foreign-born population”: people living in the US who were not US citizens at birth. This is the demographic we look at in this article.

Under the Census Bureau’s definition, someone who moved to the US decades ago and has since become a citizen is still included in this foreign-born category.1

The Census Bureau also aims to include immigrants regardless of their legal status, so these totals cover both legal and illegal immigration, without separating the two.2

To put these numbers in perspective, we also need to account for the growth of the overall US population. A larger country can have more immigrant residents without immigrants making up a larger share of the population. So we examine the foreign-born population both in absolute numbers and in relative terms, as a share of the total population.

Let’s look at what the historical data shows from these two perspectives.

# The US immigrant population is much larger today than at any point in the 19th and 20th centuries

In 2024, 50 million people born outside of the United States were living there.

As the chart below shows, the increase to this level was not steady. The foreign-born population grew from around 2 million in 1850 to 10 million in 1900 and continued to rise until 1930. It then declined for four decades, reaching a low in 1970. After that, there has been a large, sustained rise.

You can explore the [year-to-year changes](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/annual-change-foreign-born-us?time=2006..latest) or [compare average annual changes across decades](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/decadal-change-foreign-born-us) in our companion interactive charts.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/foreign-born-population-of-the-united-states.png)

On this measure, the 2024 figure is an all-time high in the series. But the United States is also a much larger country than it was in the 19th and 20th centuries. To understand how the immigrant population fits into that wider change, we can look at its share of the total population.

# Relative to the total population, immigration is close to its 19th-century peak

When we look at immigrant numbers relative to the total US population, we get a different picture.

In the late 1800s, immigrants made up roughly 13% to 15% of the US population. Through the early 20th century, this share fell dramatically, reaching a low of just under 5% in 1970. After that, the share rose steadily, reaching around 15% by 2024, approximately the same as the 19th-century peak.

If we looked only at the trend for the last 100 years, we would conclude that today’s share is unprecedented. But looking further back in time shows that the US has had a similarly large share of immigrants before.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/share-of-the-united-states-population-born-in-another-country.png)

Tracking immigrants’ origins over timeWhere immigrants were born has changedImmigrants made up roughly the same share of the US population in 2024 as in 1890. But behind these similar shares are differences in where immigrants were born.At the turn of the 20th century, most immigrants living in the US were from Europe. As the immigrant population grew again after 1970, much of that growth came from people born in Latin America and Asia. Our [chart of US immigrants by region of birth](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/share-of-the-united-states-population-born-in-another-country-by-place-of-birth) shows how each region’s share of the overall immigrant population has changed over time.Looking at individual countries adds more detail. [In 1900](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/foreign-born-population-of-the-united-states-by-country-of-birth?tab=discrete-bar&time=1900&country=DEU~ITA~IRL~MEX~CAN~GBR~SWE~POL~NOR~AUT), many immigrants were born in Germany and Ireland, while Canada was the largest source outside Europe. [By 2024](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/foreign-born-population-of-the-united-states-by-country-of-birth?tab=discrete-bar&time=2024&country=MEX~IND~CHN~PHL~CUB~SLV~VNM~GTM~DOM~COL), Mexico was the most common country of birth by far, followed by India and China.

# Conclusion

Where does this leave us on the original question: how high is current immigration to the US in historical perspective? Is it unprecedented?

If we look at the number of foreign-born residents, the 2024 estimate was the highest in the Census Bureau’s series, which stretches back to 1850. So, on that measure, the 2024 figure was unprecedented.

> Immigrants made up roughly the same share of the US population in 2024 as in 1890.

But the population of the United States has also grown. Relative to the total population, the share of immigrants in 2024 was approximately the same as in 1890. If we only look at the last few decades, we miss this historical perspective — there have been periods where immigrants made up a similarly large share of the country.

Of course, migration patterns have changed substantially in other ways. One example is where immigrants were born. At the turn of the 20th century, most of the foreign-born population came from European countries. Today, Latin America and Asia account for much larger shares.

You can read more about where migrants come from, where they live, and how migration is changing in the US and around the world on our [Migration topic page](https://ourworldindata.org/migration).
description: We use long-run census data to understand the scale of recent US migration trends, and how these compare to previous centuries.

title: The ethical cases for immigration as a human right
authors: J. Toby Reiner, Professor of Political Science, Dickinson College
content:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement [arrested roughly 50,000 immigrants](https://thehill.com/homenews/administration/6072318-ice-arrests-surge-non-criminals/) in July and August 2026; almost 80% of those migrants did not have a criminal record. Until the end of the Biden administration, federal authorities did not expect migrants to leave the country while their [visa renewal was pending](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/07/28/us/ice-arrests-airports-visa-overstay.html). The Trump administration has changed that policy.

ICE has defended itself for the overall scale of detentions by saying that [it is simply enforcing federal immigration law](https://www.foxnews.com/video/6376522353112). However, immigrant rights advocates are skeptical about this claim and wary [about the lack of oversight of ICE agents](https://www.americanimmigrationcouncil.org/fact-sheet/ice-cbp-legal-analysis/).

This scale of immigration enforcement raises fundamental philosophical questions: What ethical obligations do governments have to prospective migrants? And what claims to admission do migrants have?

As a [scholar of migration ethics](https://doi.org/10.1080/16544951.2026.2618874), I have studied the arguments philosophers make about migration. Many philosophers claim that immigration should be understood as a human right. From their perspective, governments have an important responsibility to tread carefully when denying entry to migrants and especially when deporting them.

## Freedom of movement as a human right

To consider the moral foundations of criticisms of ICE, it is useful to first examine the arguments in favor of freedom of movement.

Several philosophers have argued for freedom of movement, often on the grounds that migration should be [understood as a human right](https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199676606.003.0003). For example, the philosopher [Kieran Oberman](https://www.lse.ac.uk/people/kieran-oberman) argues that people have a basic interest in being able to move to any country in which they have core attachments, such as a job or close family members. This argument follows the claim, developed by philosophers such as John Stuart Mill and John Rawls, [that individuals](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctvjf9z6v) [should be free to pursue their own life plans](https://www.gutenberg.org/files/34901/34901-h/34901-h.htm). They hold that this pursuit is essential to achieving self-realization.

The argument for freedom of movement often involves a comparison to movement within a nation-state. At least in liberal democracies, citizens are entitled to move anywhere they wish within state borders. Political philosopher [Joseph Carens](https://www.politics.utoronto.ca/people/directories/all-faculty/joseph-carens) uses this claim when he argues that freedom of international movement is justified as an [extension of internal freedom of movement](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ethics-of-immigration-9780199933839?cc=us&lang=en&).

Citizens may move where they wish within state borders because this protects freedom. This includes both the freedom to pursue important personal projects and goals, and to pursue [joint projects such as business endeavors](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ethics-of-immigration-9780199933839?cc=us&lang=en&).

The freedom-based argument for migration maintains that the same considerations that apply within a country also [do so internationally](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-ethics-of-immigration-9780199933839?cc=us&lang=en&). For example, immigration restrictions can prevent people from marrying their preferred partner or from pursuing the job of their dreams.

If we value freedom, we have a reason to allow people to work, study and live wherever they wish because doing so may be integral to a fulfilling life.

If migration were a human right, then any state-imposed restriction on movement across borders would constitute an unjust violation of rights. According to this perspective, then, [states do not have the right to control immigration](https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/20452610.pdf).

Underlying this view is a conception of human rights in which rights [take precedence over other values](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/rights/#RigTru), such as social welfare, because they protect vital human interests.

## Migration and cultural cohesion

Against this view, other philosophers hold that societies rely for their cohesion on [some degree of cultural commonality](https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674986787). In this view – echoed by many political critics of mass migration – unless political communities have shared values, [they will be unstable](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/15/opinion/europe-immigration-ceuta-far-right.html).

A related argument made by philosophers such as [Sarah Song](https://polisci.berkeley.edu/people/person/sarah-song) and [Michael Walzer](https://www.ias.edu/sss/faculty/walzer) is that [control over migration](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/immigration-and-democracy-9780190909222?cc=us&lang=en&) is integral to self-determination. Without it, states cannot be sovereign entities that decide for themselves what shape their society should take. They cannot produce “communities of character”: social groups that share a way of life that they [wish to pass on to their descendants](https://books.google.com/books/about/Spheres_Of_Justice.html?id=2ndITi80AcsC).

## Migration and global equality

But some philosophers argue national sovereignty cannot override people’s equality of opportunity – a key goal of liberal democracies. Migration [could serve a way](https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.3366/j.ctvxcrk89) to expand opportunities across borders.

In this view, restrictions on migration render citizenship a form of feudal privilege in an unequal world; they deny people from poorer countries the chance to access opportunities and resources [in wealthier economies](https://www.jstor.org/stable/1407506?seq=1).

This argument holds, then, that restrictions on migration fix a global hierarchy in place, reduce social mobility and give people unearned advantages based on where they happened to be born. Moreover, they do this using [all the tools of violence](https://www.versobooks.com/products/228-violent-borders?srsltid=AfmBOoosoO9Ac7ugHlPfw09misdi8x1jWQQ5mSS-Ep6l9Rk14sYSX4EV) at the state’s disposal.

As with the freedom argument, this claim hopes to appeal to both the left and the right, for equality of opportunity is a bipartisan political value.

## Migration restriction and its impact on opportunities

In addition, scholars such as the political geographer [Reece Jones](https://www.reecejonesauthor.com/) argue that migration restrictions [reinforce global racial inequalities](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/676268/white-borders-by-reece-jones/). As Jones notes, the migrants who are denied admission to the U.S., and to Western European countries, are predominantly from countries in the Global South that are majority nonwhite.

Advocates of the equality argument often hold that migration will not merely promote equality of opportunity but also reduce economic inequality. This is because opportunities to access social welfare, healthcare and other important social goods are often greater in wealthier economies.

For example, the philosopher [Darrel Moellendorf](https://philpeople.org/profiles/darrel-frank-moellendorf) argues that children should have the same opportunity [to become a banker wherever in the world they are born](https://www.routledge.com/Cosmopolitan-Justice/Moellendorf/p/book/9780813365565). Moellendorf holds that, if there were global equality of opportunity, a child born in Mozambique would have the same chance of becoming an investment banker as would one born in Switzerland. Migration is thus a crucial means of enabling people born in the Global South to [access lucrative jobs](https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/24439454.pdf).

There are [many objections to this proposal](https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780190909222.003.0005). For example, Song points out that different societies regard different opportunities as important. It therefore might not be possible to come up with a global list of opportunities [that should be equal](https://dissentmagazine.org/article/achieving-global-and-local-justice/).

Yet the equality of opportunity argument gets to the core of the dispute about migration. Liberal democracies understand themselves to be committed to meritocracy. This requires that individuals rise and fall based on their own talents.

As migration restrictions deny people opportunities based on where they were born, they may be in tension with fundamental democratic principles.

*J. Toby Reiner does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: A political philosopher explains the ethical arguments in favor of free movement.

title: The story of Little Italy’s Feast of San Gennaro is the story of how Italian immigrants became American
authors: Clare Whitton, PhD Candidate in Medieval History, University of Oxford
content:
For two weeks in September, everyone wants to be Italian – at least judging by the crowds at the annual [Feast of San Gennaro](https://sangennaronyc.org/) in New York City’s Little Italy.

Founded in 1926, the largest and longest-running Italian festival in the United States celebrates its 100th anniversary this year, with locals and tourists alike descending upon Mulberry Street in Manhattan to celebrate Italian American culture.

To be sure, there’s plenty that’s commercialized: Frank Sinatra impersonators croon “New York, New York,” while vendors hawk shirts with quotes from “The Godfather” and “The Sopranos” at astronomical prices. Classic Italian American fare like chicken parm subs and sausage and peppers fly off food carts.

And yet in my work [as a medievalist](https://www.history.ox.ac.uk/people/clare-whitton), I’ve explored how this festival champions traditions that go back thousands of years.

If anything, the fact that centuries-old rituals coexist with sweet Italian sausages and big, floppy pizza slices speaks to a lengthy, strenuous and beautiful process of cultural assimilation.

## From the Bay of Naples to Little Italy

Between 1881 and 1920, over [4.5 million Italians](https://www.routledge.com/The-Routledge-History-of-Italian-Americans/Connell-Pugliese/p/book/9780367230937) immigrated to America. Thousands, most of whom hailed from southern Italy, settled on Manhattan’s Lower East Side to form what became [Little Italy](https://www.digitalgreensboro.org/record/15655?p=%28+%28subject%3A%28cultural+%2B+identity%29%29%29&v=pdf).

These “[huddled masses](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poems/46550/the-new-colossus)” faced all sorts of difficulties: overcrowded tenements, trouble finding work, racial discrimination and [suspicion of their southern Italian Catholic practices](https://doi.org/10.1057/9780230115323_4), particularly from Irish Catholics. The Italian procession of religious statues and the street parties that followed, the Irish argued, looked far too pagan and idolatrous to be considered “real” Catholicism. Irish suspicion of such practices were also shared by local Protestants.

But by the early 20th century, Italian communities had grown so large that they could [fund their own Italian-speaking churches](https://services.publishing.umich.edu/Books/T/The-Ruin-of-Souls2).

One such parish was the [Church of the Most Precious Blood](https://oldcathedral.org/shrine-church-of-the-most-precious-blood), built in 1904 on Baxter Street. In 1926, a group of parishioners led by [Alexander Tisi](https://www.nydailynews.com/2010/07/17/how-street-it-is-for-kings-of-the-fair-as-producers-get-lions-share-from-cookie-cutter-fests/) organized a tribute to one of the most popular holy figures from southern Italy: St. Januarius, known in Italian as San Gennaro.

An early Christian bishop, Gennaro [was brutally beheaded](https://gallica.bnf.fr/ark:/12148/bpt6k314988h/f3.item) outside of Naples on Sept. 19 in AD 305 on account of his faith. His execution was one of several that took place during the [Diocletian Persecutions](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/religion-and-philosophy/diocletianic-persecution), a systematic campaign against Christians by the Roman Empire.

Since then, southern Italians have attributed [all sorts of miracles](https://www.nytimes.com/2009/09/21/world/europe/21iht-naples.html) to his intercession, including extinguishing [the volcanic fires of Mount Vesuvius](https://repositori.udl.cat/server/api/core/bitstreams/3a649f23-e6d4-473a-8147-2e7f84cb3860/content) in 1631.

He is also seen as something of a prophet. [Since at least 1389](https://www.routledge.com/The-Natural-History-of-a-Neapolitan-Miracle-The-Secret-of-San-Gennaros-Blood/deCeglia/p/book/9781032442617), two vials purportedly containing the [saint’s blood](https://theconversation.com/what-makes-religious-relics-like-pieces-of-the-true-cross-and-hair-of-saints-sacred-to-christians-181699) have been venerated in Naples because of their inexplicable [ability to liquefy](https://www.jstor.org/stable/1479851) on his feast days. [The liquefaction has long been interpreted](https://italoamericano.org/curiosities-san-gennaro/) as a sign of the saint’s protection. On the other hand, Italians viewed the blood staying solid as the sign of a looming catastrophe. The [Allied bombings of Naples in 1943](https://historiamag.com/the-liberation-of-naples-in-1943-and-its-dire-consequences/), for example, occurred after the blood failed to liquefy.

Since the later Middle Ages, Gennaro’s feast on Sept. 19 has been [one of the most important dates](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781108779555.004) on Naples’ calendar.

During medieval and Renaissance celebrations, [pork was the meal of choice](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781805432456), with pigs often awarded to the winners of street games. Young men might [wrestle a greased-up pig](https://brill.com/display/book/9789004251830/B9789004251830_014.xml) inside the Naples Cathedral, with the victor cooking the animal for supper.

## The road to cultural assimilation

Centuries of devotion transformed San Gennaro into a symbol of Neapolitan identity. New York’s festival was designed to preserve those traditions.

That first Feast of San Gennaro in 1926 gave Italian immigrants a rare opportunity to publicly profess the cultural identity they had left behind in Italy.

It began with a procession featuring a 3-foot statue of San Gennaro. Hoisted upon men’s shoulders, the saint traveled around the church and the surrounding streets. While en route, [devotees tacked dollar bills to his body](https://www.instagram.com/p/DWmW_2njeUZ/), as many still do today. There was no blood relic, but there was a purported bone fragment of Gennaro’s specifically donated for the occasion. The chip of bone was placed in a circular container [called a reliquary](https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/distributed/R/bo25041081.html) and hung around the saint’s neck. Afterward, the Italians of Little Italy gathered around plates of roasted chicken to toast to their shared heritage and traditions.

The event was a big success. Just two years later, in 1928, [The New York Times reported](https://www.nytimes.com/1928/09/23/archives/upsets-police-ban-on-parade-images-justice-callahan-finds-warren.html) that thousands of ex-Neapolitans were congregating for a festival that had already extended from one day to a full week.

But with triumph came trouble. That same year, New York Police Commissioner Joseph Warren prohibited the procession, arguing that the dollar bills pinned to the statue represented the “[profanation of sacred religious symbols](https://www.nytimes.com/1928/09/23/archives/upsets-police-ban-on-parade-images-justice-callahan-finds-warren.html).” The decision was ultimately reversed by a New York Supreme Court judge, on the grounds that Warren violated the populace’s religious liberties.

Warren’s attempt to suppress the procession exemplifies the sort of religious prejudices plaguing Italian communities during that period. But it was not the only form of discrimination Italians faced.

The darkness of southern Italians’ skin subjected them to discrimination, birthing [derogatory slurs](https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2019/10/12/opinion/columbus-day-italian-american-racism.html) like “guinea” or “swarthy.” The suspicion that Italian immigrants were [prone to criminal behavior](https://online.ucpress.edu/currenthistory/article-abstract/15/1/23/169598/Italy-s-Criminals-in-the-United-States?redirectedFrom=fulltext) was reinforced by real [mafia organizations](https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=2eCPAgAAQBAJ&printsec=frontcover#v=onepage&q&f=false), such as the infamous Black Hand.

These prejudices, combined with the establishment of Italian churches and feasts, led to the belief that Italian immigrants clung too strongly to the traditions of their homeland and refused to assimilate into American culture.

## Non-Italians join the party

It was not until after World War II that outsiders no longer hesitated to participate in Italian culture and festivities.

[In 1949](https://www.nytimes.com/1949/09/19/archives/gay-little-italy-dances-in-street-fiesta-of-san-gennaro-draws.html), local newspapers reported that thousands of people of various ethnic backgrounds attended the riotous feast, where they watched Italians dance to folk songs in the streets and symphonic bands parade through the neighborhood beneath a new innovation: colored string lights casting pops of green, white and red along the city streets. [Food played a big role](https://www.nytimes.com/1956/09/11/archives/food-little-italy-feast-of-san-gennaro-provides-excuse-to-visit.html): Stalls piled high with fresh clams, pasta and pastries promised non-Italians an authentic taste of Italy.

From there, attendance ballooned. [In the 1960s](https://www.nytimes.com/1962/09/15/archives/little-italy-begins-san-gennaro-fete-buses-chartered-booths-open.html), chartered buses ushered in Italians from states as far away as Maine and Ohio. [By the 1970s](https://www.nytimes.com/1979/09/14/archives/san-gennaro-is-on-all-weekend.html), the feast had some 3 million visitors a year. Many locals today still recall how, in the 1960s and 1970s, young men [climbed greased-up steel poles](https://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20120917/little-italy/groups-want-revive-gambling-grease-pole-at-san-gennaro-fest/) set out in the street in hopes of claiming a cash prize. The oily affair was squashed over safety concerns in the 1980s.

Over the years, the feast has faced its [own challenges](https://www.nytimes.com/1996/01/02/nyregion/for-little-italy-group-famine-after-the-feast.html) from within the Italian community.

[In 2007](https://nypost.com/2011/02/28/san-gennaro-throws-no-dough-around/), some inhabitants of Little Italy petitioned Mayor Michael Bloomberg to cancel the festival, citing [the strain](https://www.nytimes.com/2002/03/17/nyregion/neighborhood-report-little-italy-mulberry-street-residents-grow-weary-living.html) that tourists placed on the local neighborhood and [mafia interference](https://openroadmedia.com/ebook/the-italians-of-new-york/9781955835275). In 1996, for example, [19 members of the Genovese crime family](https://www.nytimes.com/1996/06/12/nyregion/19-indicted-in-blow-to-genovese-mob.html) were arrested for gambling, collecting dues from vendors and even stealing money off Gennaro’s statue.

Nevertheless, Bloomberg declined to interfere. The event, [he said](https://www.nydailynews.com/2007/03/28/san-gennaros-a-pizza-ny-says-bloomberg/), was a part of New York itself.

No one understands this more than the organizers of this year’s feast. When discussing [the plans for 2026](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=LLJjTHly1BQ&list=OLCvbfU0SOw0sci86fxt2mMpWhSgzn2Xw4A&index=2), the committee declared that this event was not just an Italian festival, but a tribute to New York’s cultural melting pot.

The 100th festival is dedicated to the Italian Americans who contributed to the city’s birth, an honor that arrives at a moment of controversy. Two months prior, Mayor Zohran Mamdani omitted Little Italy from a map of the city’s immigrant enclaves, [sparking immediate backlash](https://abc7ny.com/post/mamdani-says-he-will-change-map-immigrant-neighborhoods-backlash-leaving-several-communities/19482161/). While Mamdani vowed to reinsert the neighborhood, [some argued](https://www.thenation.com/article/society/little-italy-mamdani-map-italian-immigration/) that the omission accurately reflected the [dwindling number](https://www.nytimes.com/2020/03/13/nyregion/arthur-avenue-bronx-little-italy.html) of Italians living along Mulberry Street.

The controversy underscores the question fueling the centenary: How should the immigrants who built the city of New York be honored, even as the descendants of many of those immigrants [have left their old neighborhoods](https://www.nytimes.com/2018/02/19/nyregion/little-italy-manhattan-fire.html) for different parts of the country?

Perhaps the answer is this year’s grand marshal, San Gennaro himself, who continues to serve as a bridge between the children of the Italian diaspora and their forefathers, just as he did in 1926.

*Clare Whitton receives funding from Blackfriars Hall, The University of Oxford.*
description: Italian immigrants used to be accused of clinging too tightly to the Old World. Today, millions gather in Little Italy to celebrate the food, faith and traditions they brought with them.

title: Around 90% of refugee kids live in poverty in their first year in Australia: report
authors: Melissa Wong, Research Fellow at the Social Policy Research Centre, UNSW; Yuvisthi Naidoo, Senior Research Fellow, Social Policy Research Centre, UNSW
content:
Almost a third of people living in Australia were born overseas, and almost half have at least one overseas-born parent. Migrant and refugee communities have been central to the nation’s economic, social and cultural life for generations.

But there has been remarkably little quantitative evidence on the living standards of different groups of migrants once they settle in Australia.

A new [report](https://povertyandinequality.acoss.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Employmentincomespoverty_migrantsrefugees_2026.pdf) has found an alarming number of refugees spend their first decade in Australia in poverty.

The report, produced by our team and published in partnership with Australian Council of Social Service (ACOSS), analyses two Australian Bureau of Statistics datasets that link settlement records to the 2021 census. The two datasets covered permanent migrants and temporary residents who arrived in the last ten years.

Together, this allowed comparison of the outcomes of people across visa pathways against the general Australian population for the first time.

## Three in five refugees arrive into poverty

Between 2011 and 2021, around 1.3 million people arrived as permanent migrants into Australia.

The report shows just over half came on skilled visas, 35% on family visas and about 11% – roughly 140,000 people – on humanitarian visas.

People who arrive on a humanitarian visa have usually fled conflict or persecution. Many have been displaced for years.

So it’s not surprising the early years in Australia are difficult. What startled us, however, was the extent of hardship.

In the first year after arrival, the research shows that for humanitarian entrants:

- on average, around three in five (59%) live in households with A$400 or less a week
- 73% live in households with $500 or less a week
- 75% of men and 80% of women were not in the labour force (meaning they’re not employed and not looking for work)
- around nine in ten (almost 90%) refugee children under 15 live in households with $500 or less a week in their first year of arrival.

This is concerning. [Research](https://melbourneinstitute.unimelb.edu.au/research/reports/breaking-down-barriers/research-report-pages/report-2) shows sustained poverty in early childhood impacts health, education and later life chances.

## Hardship eases with time – but slowly

Living standards improve as families establish themselves by finding work, securing housing, enrolling children in school, and building communities. But the change is slow and marked by gender.

For men aged 25–44 years, entry into workforce participation is relatively quick. By the third year, the rate of those not in the labour force fell to 32%, and full-time/part-time work increased to 58%. By the tenth year, full-time employment alone had steadily increased to 50%.

Women tend to enter the workforce more slowly, largely due to caring responsibilities; the report found 40% were in full-time and part-time work by the tenth year.

Among humanitarian entrants aged 25 to 44, 13% of men and 17% of women provided unpaid care. This compared with 8% and 12%, respectively, across Australia.

Larger family sizes, language barriers, employment skills, location and limited access to informal labour markets are also likely contributors.

Overall, 33% of humanitarian entrants remain in poverty, living with incomes below $500 a week at the ten-year mark. This affects half of all children from refugee backgrounds.

These findings show people often make substantial progress over time but also highlight the need for employment and settlement support, particularly for women.

## Other migrants fare better, but hardship persists

[Australia’s skilled migration program](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/what-we-do/skilled-migration-program) is designed to attract people with the qualifications and experience needed in the Australian labour market. On the whole, it succeeds.

Around 59% of the skilled migrants who arrived in the decade to 2021 are in full-time work and about 20% are in part-time work.

Gender still shapes the pattern: 51% of women aged 25-44 work full-time compared with 82% of men (though both rates are above the Australian averages for their gender).

Family migrants, on the other hand, face more hardship.

On average, between 2011 and 2021, 17% were in poverty, living on less than $500 income per week. About 6% were unemployed, and 27% of family-migrant women aged 25–44 were not in the labour force.

Crucially, the report highlights the many skilled and family migrants aged 25–44 years (more than 85,000 people between 2011 and 2021) who were unemployed and affected during this time by the [Newly Arrived Resident Waiting Period policy](https://www.servicesaustralia.gov.au/newly-arrived-residents-waiting-period).

Under this policy, which is still in place, people are only granted access to the social security system four years after they have been granted permanent residency, even if they have already lived, worked and paid taxes in Australia.

Outcomes for temporary visa holders are linked to and limited by whether or not they have the right to work.

This includes people on bridging visas who may be seeking asylum and may have to wait years for their claims to be heard.

Until then, they have limited work rights and no access to mainstream income support, and must rely on low payments via the [Status Resolution Support Service](https://immi.homeaffairs.gov.au/what-we-do/status-resolution-service/status-resolution-support-services).

## What would help?

The new report recommends Australia:

- reduce number of years in the Newly Arrived Resident Waiting Period
- increase funding to the Status Resolution Support Services program
- invest further in settlement support, especially in areas such as employment, health, education, housing and social connection.

This builds on similar recommendations from the [Workforce Australia inquiry](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/committees/reportrep/RB000017/toc_pdf/RebuildingEmploymentServices.pdf), the [Accelerating Settlement Outcomes report by the Settlement Council of Australia](https://scoa.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/scoa_deloitte_report_accelerating_settlement_outcomes.pdf) and [reports](https://activateaustralia.org.au/resources/reports/) by Settlement Services International.

The new report shows that with adequate amounts of support, migrants are, by and large, able to successfully improve their employment outcomes, establish their families and provide opportunities for their children in decades to come.

*Melissa Wong received funding for this report from the ACOSS/UNSW Sydney Poverty and Inequality Partnership, which is co-funded by UNSW and ACOSS members.*

*Yuvisthi Naidoo received funding for this report from the ACOSS/UNSW Sydney Poverty and Inequality Partnership, which is co-funded by UNSW and ACOSS members.*
description: New research reveals how the visa someone arrives on shapes whether their first ten years are secure or spent in poverty.

title: Millions of Africans are displaced without crossing a border – and their needs are often overlooked
authors: David James Cantor, Director of the Refugee Law Initiative, School of Advanced Study, University of London
content:
The eruption of the [Bundibugyo strain of Ebola](https://www.who.int/news/item/17-05-2026-epidemic-of-ebola-disease-in-the-democratic-republic-of-the-congo-and-uganda-determined-a-public-health-emergency-of-international-concern) in the eastern region of the Democratic Republic of Congo in May 2026 sparked a major crisis.

Transmissions and deaths are [skyrocketing, and no vaccine is currently available](https://www.who.int/emergencies/disease-outbreak-news/item/2026-DON614).

This virus is [notably prevalent](https://www.un.org/sustainabledevelopment/blog/2026/08/ebola-virus-reaches-displacement-camps-in-dr-congo/) in settlements and communities for internally displaced persons (IDPs) and communities. This happened too with the [Mpox outbreak](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(25%2902100-2/fulltext) that started in the Congo in 2025 and spread to the rest of the world.

But who are “internally displaced persons”? And why are they [disproportionately affected](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40890976/) by disease outbreaks such as Ebola and mpox?

Across Africa, there were estimated to be [31.7 million people](https://api.internal-displacement.org/sites/default/files/publications/documents/IDMC-GRID-2026-Global-Report-on-Internal-Displacement.pdf?_gl=1*uwcp7m*_ga*MTg3NTg5MTEwLjE3ODMzMjI4NDU.*_ga_PKVS5L6N8V*czE3ODY3MDIxODkkbzckZzAkdDE3ODY3MDIxODkkajYwJGwwJGgw#page=7) living in internal displacement camps as of the end of 2025. More than 29 million of them were displaced due to conflict and violence.

Sudan hosted the largest number of internally displaced people of any country in the world – [approximately 9.1 million](https://www.unhcr.org/media/global-trends-2025-report) of its total population of around [52 million](https://www.unfpa.org/data/world-population/SD). Another 2.8 million remained displaced outside the country as refugees.

Over [20 years ago](https://rli.sas.ac.uk/people/professor-david-james-cantor), I began doctoral research in Colombia with more than 40 displaced communities living in conflict-affected regions. This has since extended to include research on Mexico, central America and Yemen. I then helped set up networks to support researchers and policymakers working on internal displacement in Africa, Latin America and the Middle East. This work led to the recently published [Handbook of Internal Displacement](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-oxford-handbook-of-internal-displacement-9780198928775?cc=gb&lang=en&).

Based on this work, it’s become clear that the issue of “internal displacement” remains poorly understood despite the very large number of people involved and their significant role in shaping social trends.

This may be about to change. The [Handbook](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-oxford-handbook-of-internal-displacement-9780198928775?cc=gb&lang=en&) includes expert input from over 70 researchers globally. Its 45 thematic chapters offer a comprehensive reference point for work across many different fields. These include sociology, politics, economics, history and law, as well as development, humanitarian, migration and conflict studies.

The Handbook opens up new ways of thinking and engaging with the consequences of internal displacement in Africa and beyond.

It also offers a crucial resource. It highlights the fact that internally displaced people – rather than refugees – make up the bulk of displacement globally. This points to the need for resources to be allocated to the challenges that come in the wake of displacement.

## Internally displaced people

Global policy [describes](https://docs.un.org/en/E/CN.4/1998/53/Add.2) internally displaced people as those

> who have been forced (…) to flee or to leave their homes (…) and who have not crossed an internationally recognized State border.

The term is a convenient policy label to distinguish them from cross-border refugees. But, within their own countries, IDPs are really just “the displaced”.

Africa records the highest levels of war-related internal displacement of any region globally. In 2025, even with the [new wars](https://acleddata.com/update/middle-east-overview-january-2025) raging in the Middle East, Africa remained the epicentre with [14.5 million new internal displacements](https://api.internal-displacement.org/sites/default/files/publications/documents/IDMC-GRID-2026-Global-Report-on-Internal-Displacement.pdf?_gl=1*1mn6uvn*_ga*MTg3NTg5MTEwLjE3ODMzMjI4NDU.*_ga_PKVS5L6N8V*czE3ODU3NjQ2NzEkbzQkZzEkdDE3ODU3NjQ2NzckajU0JGwwJGgw#page=16).

In 2024, it saw [vastly more displaced people (11.5 million) than every other region combined (8.5 million)](https://api.internal-displacement.org/sites/default/files/publications/documents/idmc-grid-2025-global-report-on-internal-displacement.pdf?_gl=1*12864vg*_ga*MTg3NTg5MTEwLjE3ODMzMjI4NDU.*_ga_PKVS5L6N8V*czE3ODU3NjQ2NzEkbzQkZzEkdDE3ODU3NjQ3MTckajE0JGwwJGgw#page=15).

The scale of displacement reflects the high number of countries in Africa that are in conflict, as well as the large, protracted wars that displace huge numbers of people each year. This includes the DRC, which [reported 9.7 million war-related internal displacements in 2025](https://api.internal-displacement.org/sites/default/files/publications/documents/IDMC-GRID-2026-Global-Report-on-Internal-Displacement.pdf?_gl=1*1mn6uvn*_ga*MTg3NTg5MTEwLjE3ODMzMjI4NDU.*_ga_PKVS5L6N8V*czE3ODU3NjQ2NzEkbzQkZzEkdDE3ODU3NjQ2NzckajU0JGwwJGgw#page=16).

Yet war is just one driver of displacement.

## What’s driving displacement

In Africa, a multitude of climate-related hazards – such as cyclones, flooding and drought – generate cascading risks. In 2025 alone, they pushed [an additional 2.9 million internal displacements](https://api.internal-displacement.org/sites/default/files/publications/documents/IDMC-GRID-2026-Global-Report-on-Internal-Displacement.pdf?_gl=1*1mn6uvn*_ga*MTg3NTg5MTEwLjE3ODMzMjI4NDU.*_ga_PKVS5L6N8V*czE3ODU3NjQ2NzEkbzQkZzEkdDE3ODU3NjQ2NzckajU0JGwwJGgw).

Other displacement drivers in Africa include [criminal, extremist and terrorist violence](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/62537/chapter-abstract/559702114?redirectedFrom=fulltext) and [large-scale development projects](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/62537/chapter-abstract/559702251?redirectedFrom=fulltext).

Each driver further weakens people’s ability to cope, while displacement itself creates additional pressures. In many African nations, [war and disasters occur simultaneously](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/62537/chapter-abstract/559702307?redirectedFrom=fulltext) and can interact in ways that intensify internal displacement.

## The impact

Internal displacement can disrupt lives to a shocking extent.

It has wide-ranging effects on society, affecting the communities that host IDPs, the places they pass through and the home communities to which some eventually return.

Unlike refugees, IDPs stay within their country and remain exposed to the dangers and devastation caused by the conflicts and disasters they fled.

Although they may be citizens, they are often [treated with suspicion](https://issafrica.org/iss-today/displacement-as-a-weapon-of-war-targeting-africa-s-most-vulnerable) and end up marginalised and hidden in local populations. Where they lose access to land, housing, work, and social and family support networks, they often experience high levels of poverty.

These accumulated disadvantages often make IDPs, such as those in the DRC, [more vulnerable to illness and death](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/62537/chapter-abstract/559702881?redirectedFrom=fulltext) than other war-affected populations (including refugees).

African countries have traditionally relied on settlements and camps as a way of responding to displacement.

The “[protected villages](https://www.thenewhumanitarian.org/news/1998/12/29/protected-villages-policy-%E2%80%9Cnot-working%E2%80%9D)” policy in Uganda was an early example of encampment, resettling displaced people into villages ostensibly removed from the conflict between the [government and the Lord’s Resistance Army](https://theconversation.com/who-is-joseph-kony-the-altar-boy-who-became-africas-most-wanted-man-200361) in the 1990s. More recently, the majority of the 4 million displaced Ethiopians in 2023 lived in [camps or camp-like settlements](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/62537/chapter-abstract/559702394?redirectedFrom=fulltext).

Internal displacement in Africa is increasingly an [urban phenomenon](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/62537/chapter-abstract/559702394?redirectedFrom=fulltext), and feeds into wider trends towards urbanisation.

As a result, cities and towns, such as [Mogadishu and Baidoa in Somalia](https://www.euaa.europa.eu/publications/coi-report-somalia-displacement-mogadishu), now host many displaced people. This creates a whole new set of development challenges.

The losses caused by displacement can undermine development. National development plans can also be thrown off course when people are no longer where those plans expect (or want) them to be.

In cities, heightened pressure on local services also [creates a need for flexible and imaginative urban planning](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/62537/chapter-abstract/559704130?redirectedFrom=fulltext).

## What needs to change

Africa is the [only region globally where governments have created regional legal treaties for protecting IDPs](https://academic.oup.com/edited-volume/62537/chapter-abstract/559703806?redirectedFrom=fulltext).

For example, in 2006, countries in central Africa created a pioneering [Protocol on the Protection and Assistance to Internally Displaced Persons](https://icglr.org/ova_doc/protocol-on-the-protection-and-assistance-to-internally-displaced-persons-2/). The African Union then spearheaded the [Convention for the Protection and Assistance of Internally Displaced Persons in Africa](https://au.int/en/treaties/african-union-convention-protection-and-assistance-internally-displaced-persons-africa) in 2009.

But IDPs still attract relatively little political interest or funding from the wider international community. Unlike refugees, they are too often seen by donors as a faraway problem confined to poorer parts of the world.

This is wrong. Disasters create many IDPs each year, even in countries like the US. What is more, the low profile of internal displacement has real-life consequences for IDPs in regions like Africa. [One study found](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2666623522000137?via%3Dihub) that between 2010 and 2019, per capita health aid to people displaced by conflict was less than one-seventh of that provided to refugees.

Aid cuts by major donors like the US, the UK and Germany in the 2020s have exacerbated the problem. This has forced aid agencies into [“hyper-prioritisation”](https://researchinginternaldisplacement.org/short_pieces/internal-displacement-in-the-context-of-hyper-prioritisation/) – using scarce resources only for the most urgent needs – since 2025.

Across its many chapters, the research in the [Handbook of Internal Displacement](https://global.oup.com/academic/product/the-oxford-handbook-of-internal-displacement-9780198928775?cc=gb&lang=en&) underlines that internal displacement – and the vulnerabilities it creates and worsens – cannot be ignored. The needs of internally displaced people (and host communities) must be properly factored into social assistance, humanitarian and development interventions.

The Handbook offers detailed guidance on how this can be done, while supporting the efforts of displaced people to protect themselves during crises and overcome displacement-related vulnerabilities.

*David James Cantor has received funding for research on internal displacement from the Leverhulme Trust, UK Economic and Social Research Council, UK Arts and Humanities Research Council, UNHCR and UNDP. He was previously a senior advisor on issues including internal displacement for UNHCR Americas Bureau. He is a Trustee for Refugee Legal Support, a UK charity.*
description: The issue of internal displacement remains poorly understood despite the very large number of people involved.

title: South Africans are far less tolerant of migrants than before – hotspots, drivers and solutions
authors: Steven Gordon, Chief Research Specialist., Human Sciences Research Council
content:
[Anti-immigrant marches](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c7v9572ne0lo) in several major South African cities (such as Tshwane and Johannesburg) in early May 2026 once again led to questions being asked about xenophobia in post-apartheid South Africa.

In the wake of the protests President Cyril Ramaphosa [called](https://www.ewn.co.za/ramaphosa-says-illegal-immigration-concerns-shouldn-t-give-rise-to-xenophobia/) on South Africans to embrace solidarity with their African neighbours. For their part, [foreign governments](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-05-04-escalating-xenophobia-in-sa-sparks-diplomatic-protests-by-african-nations/) lodged their protests while [police](https://iol.co.za/news/politics/2026-05-02-south-africa-on-edge-as-anti-migrant-protests-surge-and-police-warn-of-no-mercy/) sought to curtail violence.

The tension in the country was palpable.

Are the recent outbreaks of anti-immigrant activism a harbinger of a wider uptick in anti-migrant sentiment amongst South Africans? Recent [public opinion data](https://hsrc.ac.za/special-projects/sasas/) from the Human Sciences Research Council (HSRC) suggests that this might be the case.

The HSRC’s South African Social Attitudes Survey is an important source of information on what ordinary South Africans think about international migration. The survey series consists of nationally representative, repeated cross-sectional surveys that have been conducted annually by the HSRC since 2003.

The [latest data](https://hsrc.ac.za/news/research-outputs/going-from-bad-to-worse-a-rise-in-anti-immigrant-sentiment-in-south-africa/), from the 2025 survey, show that South Africans are more hostile towards immigrants than at any other time before since the survey began in 2003. An important dimension of the change has been an attitudinal shift and hardening of attitudes towards migrants among poorer and working-class adults. In addition, the recent growth of anti-immigrant sentiment has been geographically concentrated in four provinces: Mpumalanga, Gauteng, Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal.

***Read more: [What research reveals about drivers of anti-immigrant hate crime in South Africa](https://theconversation.com/what-research-reveals-about-drivers-of-anti-immigrant-hate-crime-in-south-africa-123097)***

The rise in anti-immigrant sentiment is particularly concerning given that the country is due to hold local government elections [on 4 November 2026](https://www.elections.org.za/pw/News-And-Media/News-List/News/News-Article/Electoral-Commission-welcomes-announcement-of-4-November-2026-as-Local-Government-Elections-date?a=AISDGvpz75ps1usOfX7oijDmyJafW5sb/d+cisS2zzc=). Aspirant political parties, in an attempt to maintain or gain power, may seek to exploit anti-immigrant sentiment for their own ends. In this way elections can provide a potential accelerant for xenophobia.

Growing hostility may even provoke xenophobic violence in a country that [has a long history of collective anti-immigrant hate crime.](https://theconversation.com/what-research-reveals-about-drivers-of-anti-immigrant-hate-crime-in-south-africa-123097) and is home to more than [two million international migrants](https://www.statssa.gov.za/publications/03-09-17/03-09-172023.pdf).

## Declining Hospitality

South African Social Attitudes Survey has included the following in its questionnaire since 2003:

> Please indicate which of the following statements applies to you? I generally welcome to South Africa… (i) All immigrants; (ii) Some immigrants; (iii) No immigrants; and (iv) Uncertain.

In 2003 about a third (34%) of the South African adult population said that they would welcome all immigrants. The remainder indicated that they would accept either none (32%) or some (35%).

The proportion of the public that would be prepared to welcome foreigners tended to fluctuate within a narrow band over the 2003-2017 period.

But around the time of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020, the research data began to show an upswing in anti-immigrant sentiment.

***Read more: [Xenophobia is on the rise in South Africa: scholars weigh in on the migrant question](https://theconversation.com/xenophobia-is-on-the-rise-in-south-africa-scholars-weigh-in-on-the-migrant-question-181288)***

About a quarter (26%) of those surveyed said that they would welcome all immigrants during the [2021 survey round](https://hsrc.ac.za/news/research-outputs/going-from-bad-to-worse-a-rise-in-anti-immigrant-sentiment-in-south-africa/). This was similar to figures in the [mid-2010s](https://hsrc.ac.za/news/research-outputs/going-from-bad-to-worse-a-rise-in-anti-immigrant-sentiment-in-south-africa/).

But the share that held this hospitable attitude fell in subsequent survey rounds. In 2025 15% of adults said that they would welcome all foreigners.

Conversely, the proportion of the public adopting a hostile position (in other words ‘welcome no immigrants’) increased from 30% in 2021 to 42% in 2025.

## Geography and class

The provinces with the highest growth in anti-immigrant sentiment – Mpumalanga, Gauteng, Limpopo and KwaZulu-Natal – are ones through which most [immigrants](https://www.statssa.gov.za/publications/03-09-17/03-09-172023.pdf) travel and often settle.

The situation has become particularly delicate in KwaZulu-Natal. The share of adults in the province who said that they would welcome no immigrants grew from 23% in 2021 to 45% in 2023 and then again to 60% in 2025.

The upsurge in hostility in KwaZulu-Natal could be linked to growing [popular anger](https://www.citizen.co.za/news/iec-democracy-failing-kzn-satisfaction-collapses-from-54-to-6/) against the current economic and political status quo. A staggering 88% of provincial residents are unhappy with present economic conditions, and an equal proportion expect conditions to worsen over the next five years.

The notable attitudinal shift among poor people is also concerning.

South Africa is a [highly unequal nation](https://theconversation.com/south-africa-has-a-huge-gap-between-the-rich-and-poor-4-urgent-reasons-to-tackle-inequality-236595) characterised by stark economic divisions. Most citizens can be found on the wrong side of these divides and could be classified as economically disadvantaged.

Historically, [as research has shown](https://mg.co.za/article/2019-09-05-prejudice-against-immigrants-cuts-across-class-and-race/), anti-immigrant sentiment in the country tended to cut across class divisions. But in the years following the COVID-19 pandemic, something changed.

Before the pandemic, South African Social Attitudes Survey data showed a linear relationship between economic disadvantage and anti-immigrant sentiment. In the years following the pandemic, however, a clear pattern emerged. As the lockdowns ended and the post-pandemic recovery began, most socioeconomic groups in South Africa became more and more hostile towards immigrants. But antipathy grew at a much more aggressive rate for the low and lower middle socioeconomic groups.

During the 2025 survey round, adults in these groups were much more hostile towards foreigners than those in the upper middle and high socio-economic groups.

## The drivers

What could have caused the economically disadvantaged to become more antagonistic towards immigrants over the last five years or so?

It could be argued that the poor have become more likely to scapegoat foreigners for the failures and inequalities of the post-pandemic economic recovery. Poor people have been badly affected by [a cost of living crisis](https://specialprojects.news24.com/south-africas-cost-of-living-crisis/index.html) and persistent [deindustrialisation](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-03-10-sa-economy-stuck-in-the-slow-lane-grows-a-pathetic-11-in-2025/). They need someone to blame and foreigners have long provided a handy scapegoat.

The South African economy has struggled in the last few years, dealing with doggedly [high unemployment](https://mg.co.za/business/2026-02-17-south-africas-unemployment-rate-eases-to-31-4/). The country also has notoriously high [crime rates](https://www.dailymaverick.co.za/article/2026-02-22-crime-levels-still-unacceptably-high-desh-despite-decrease-in-murders-and-sexual/). Such problems, as experts have argued [again](https://theconversation.com/xenophobia-is-on-the-rise-in-south-africa-scholars-weigh-in-on-the-migrant-question-181288) and [again](https://theconversation.com/5-xenophobic-myths-about-immigrants-in-south-africa-debunked-by-researchers-191194), cannot be directly laid at the feet of immigrants living in the country. But it would appear that they are getting blamed anyway.

## What should be done?

The South African government has a [National Action Plan](https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/201903/national-action-plan.pdf) to Combat Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance.

Implemented in March 2019, one of its goals was to reduce public hostility towards migrants. Clearly, whether because of a lack of resources or government coordination, the plan has not succeeded.

The country needs to reinvigorate it and its associated processes. What’s needed is political, civic and community leaders to address legitimate socio-economic grievances without allowing immigrants to become scapegoats for deeper structural failures in society.

Efforts to strengthen social cohesion, improve economic inclusion, enhance public trust in governance and promote responsible political leadership are also crucial.

Well-provisioned and effective anti-xenophobia strategies are urgently required to address the worsening situation. The alternative is to allow hatred to flourish.

*Steven Gordon has received funding from South Africa's National Research Foundation. He is affiliated with the University of Johannesburg.*
description: Data show that South Africans have become more hostile towards immigrants.

title: Diaspora distress: When geopolitical conflict follows immigrant workers into the office
authors: Amir Bahman Radnejad, Chair and Associate Professor of Innovation and Marketing, Mount Royal University; Brenda Nguyen, Associate Professor, University of Lethbridge
content:
Rostam does not sleep through the night anymore. At 2 a.m., when his phone buzzes, he’s awake before the sound finishes. It might be his parents calling from Tehran, on a connection that is unreliable, sporadic and sometimes cut off mid-sentence. He has learned not to miss those calls, because the next one may not come for days.

Rostam is a pseudonym for a participant in our ongoing research study on diaspora workers, but his experience is one that many workers across Canada will recognize.

Rostam checks the news constantly, piecing together what is happening. Since [the United States and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran](https://theconversation.com/what-is-the-strait-of-hormuz-and-why-does-its-closure-matter-so-much-to-the-global-economy-277364) in late February, the conflict has escalated rapidly. By 4 a.m., he has been awake for two hours. [This is hypervigilance](https://health.clevelandclinic.org/hypervigilance): the body monitoring a threat it cannot act on and refusing to stand down.

When the call does come through, the relief is physical. They are alive. They speak carefully, partly to protect him and partly because the call may be monitored. He hears his father’s voice and thinks this could be the last time.

In the morning, he will go to work. He will sit in meetings, contribute to agendas and make sure his face doesn’t betray what he’s feeling — a competency that has always served him well.

He doesn’t speak about any of this at work. To talk about it risks being regarded as a representative of a country he has complicated feelings about or as importing politics into a space that doesn’t want them. So he says nothing. That silence is the problem.

## The invisible cost at work

Decades of research have established that [code-switching](https://hbr.org/2019/11/the-costs-of-codeswitching) — the constant calibration of self-presentation across cultural contexts — carries a real psychological toll on workers. It can contribute to stress, anxiety, burnout and costly errors in judgment at work.

These impacts often remain invisible to employers until the damage has already been done to both the individual and the organization.

Diaspora employees who are struggling don’t signal it in ways that trigger organizational concern. [They manage, but at considerable personal cost](https://www.jstor.org/stable/259200?origin=crossref). These costs accumulate in ways that surface slowly and are almost always misattributed. [Declining engagement is read as a shift in attitude, and withdrawal is interpreted as a personality change](https://doi.org/10.5465/amj.2007.26279183).

In some cases, [employees do not withdraw at all](https://doi.org/10.1556/JBA.2.2013.017/). Instead, they bury themselves in work and appear by every visible metric to be thriving. Managers have no reason to look closer until the break happens.

This isn’t a problem that diversity, equity and inclusion programs can solve as they exist, because it’s not about inclusion or diversity. It’s a perceptual problem: leaders don’t see what diaspora employees are managing and therefore cannot respond to it.

***Read more: [Diaspora communities carry the burden of watching war from afar](https://theconversation.com/diaspora-communities-carry-the-burden-of-watching-war-from-afar-278968)***

## A condition without a name

This challenge extends well beyond Canada’s Iranian community, which numbered [approximately 200,000 people in the 2021 census](https://thecanadianencyclopedia.ca/en/article/iranians). Many other diaspora communities, including Ukrainians, Palestinians, Sudanese, Afghans and Syrians, are navigating similar terrain.

A [2025 study found](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jad.2024.10.075) higher rates of severe depression, anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder among diaspora Tigrayans in Australia than among people inside the war zone itself.

People inside a conflict zone often suppress their own fear to protect family members living through it with them. Members of the diaspora, by contrast, often cannot meaningfully assist those in immediate danger, which creates a profound sense of helplessness. At the same time, those around them may not recognize the fear and distress they’re concealing.

Aitak Sorahi, an Iranian Canadian, tried to explain what she was living through to a [reporter at The Canadian Press in April](https://www.cp24.com/news/canada/2026/04/07/war-crimes-iranian-canadians-horrified-by-trumps-latest-threat-to-destroy-iran/) as U.S. President Donald Trump threatened to destroy Iran unless it agreed to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. She could not find the words. “I don’t even know how to describe my feeling,” she said, “because I don’t have a name for it.”

We propose one: diaspora distress, a framework emerging from our ongoing research and organizational practice.

## Diaspora distress

Diaspora distress is the psychological burden carried by people living in one country while their homeland — and the family, friends and memories embedded there — are under active geopolitical threat. Often, this burden is compounded by the policies or rhetoric of their host country’s own government.

The feeling sits closest to grief, but the comparison only goes so far. Grief has a fixed point — a death, a diagnosis, a loss that has occurred and can be named. It comes with a recognized social script: people sit together and are able to share memories of the deceased. Diaspora distress offers no comparable ritual because the loss one is anticipating may or may not arrive.

In addition, [diaspora communities are not monolithic](https://doi.org/10.1017/sus.2024.1). Outsiders often assume a shared solidarity, but geopolitical crises tend to deepen existing internal divisions about what intervention means, who is to blame and what liberation looks like. The people who should be each other’s community of grief often find themselves on opposite sides of an argument.

The result is that diaspora employees are frequently alone with this in every environment they occupy: at work, at home and within communities that might otherwise support them. That isolation is the specific nature of diaspora distress.

## What organizations should do

Developing the capacity to recognize diaspora distress does not require expertise in geopolitics or new policy infrastructure. It requires language: the organizational decision to name what some employees are carrying as a recognized condition.

Institutional acknowledgement works differently than other supports because it removes the requirement that employees claim what they’re carrying. It gives them a name for what they have been living with.

In practice, this can take three forms: a leadership message acknowledging that some colleagues are carrying weight from events in their home regions; a line added to standard manager check-in prompts asking whether anything outside work is affecting employees; or an addition to existing employee assistance programs and benefits communications that names diaspora distress explicitly.

Rostam will open his phone again tonight at 2 a.m. In the morning, he will code-switch from the person who spent the night reading the news into the person his organization knows. What remains is whether his organization will adopt the language to see it, and whether his leaders will decide that seeing it is part of their job.

*Amir Bahman Radnejad is affiliated with Canadian Global Affairs Institute.*

*Brenda Nguyen is affiliated with the Strategic Capability Network.*
description: Millions of employees are living in two worlds. Researchers are only beginning to understand what that costs.

title: Politicians have scapegoated immigration for decades. It’s time to flip the script
authors: Jane McAdam, Scientia Professor and ARC Laureate Fellow, Kaldor Centre for International Refugee Law, UNSW
content:
For decades now, public discourse about refugees and immigrants has become increasingly fractured, ugly and untrue.

From John Howard’s “we will decide who comes to this country” [mantra](https://www.howardlibrary.unsw.edu.au/explore/tampa-controversy), to Kevin Rudd’s “if you come by boat you will never permanently live in Australia” [in 2013](https://pmtranscripts.pmc.gov.au/release/transcript-22762), through to Tony Abbott’s “stop the boats” election victory that same year, it has been a prominent feature of Australia’s recent political landscape.

For the Coalition, it was about stopping so-called “[illegals](https://www.smh.com.au/opinion/are-they-illegals-no-and-scott-morrison-should-know-better-20131022-2vz6a.html)”.

For Labor, it was framed as “[saving lives at sea](https://www.smh.com.au/politics/federal/saving-lives-trumps-politics-says-gillard-20120819-24g0i.html)”.

For both, it was about keeping people seeking asylum out of contact with the Australian community, demonised and dehumanised, called by [numbers, not names](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2013/oct/30/officer-disciplined-for-calling-asylum-seekers-by-numbers-instead-of-names).

Against this backdrop, it’s perhaps unsurprising Australians turned out [in the thousands](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-09-01/weekend-anti-immigration-rallies/105718340) to rally against immigration this weekend. It could be seen as the culmination of years of MPs using immigration issues for [short-term political gain](https://theconversation.com/population-panic-how-demography-is-used-for-political-gain-230409).

But just as government messaging has partly contributed to this situation, it could also help get us out of it.

## Not always ‘sinister invaders’
