Political language about immigration wasn’t always so negative.

At the end of the second world war, then-Prime Minister Ben Chifley welcomed [170,000](https://www.naa.gov.au/students-and-teachers/student-research-portal/learning-resource-themes/society-and-culture/migration-and-multiculturalism/prime-minister-ben-chifley-and-immigration-minister-greet-postwar-migrants) refugees and other displaced people from Europe.

In the 1970s, when the first boats of Vietnamese asylum seekers arrived in Australia’s north, Prime Minister Malcolm Fraser [insisted](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:%22library/prspub/3859964%22) they be treated humanely and processed fairly.

As writer Thomas Keneally [recalled](https://www.smh.com.au/opinion/politicians-must-stop-using-language-to-strip-refugees-of-their-humanity-20150610-ghknq7.html):

> there was no long-term mandatory detention involved. The newcomers were not depicted as sinister invaders \[…\] language was not misused and neither were human souls.

And as former Immigration Minister Andrew Giles [said](https://minister.homeaffairs.gov.au/AndrewGiles/Pages/speech-to-refugee-legal-21042023.aspx) in 2023:

> Seventy years ago, of course, we embarked on a migration journey that has transformed our nation into a diverse and dynamic multicultural society \[…\] in very large part \[…\] shaped by the nearly one million refugees who have come to Australia since the end of WWII. We should take great pride in this.

## ‘Real people, real families’

The threatening thuggery on display at the weekend’s anti-immigration marches has been rightly called out by Australian politicians on both sides.

In a change from her predecessor’s hardline approach, Federal Opposition Leader Sussan Ley [said](https://www.smh.com.au/politics/federal/australia-belongs-to-all-of-us-ley-calls-for-calm-ahead-of-anti-immigration-march-20250830-p5mr3k.html) while “strong borders keep us safe, they also allow us to be generous and compassionate to those fleeing conflict”.

Meanwhile, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke [reiterated](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/czjmre371l1o) “there is no place in our country for people who seek to divide and undermine our social cohesion”.

At the same time, we can’t simply ignore concerns people have about the impact of immigration on housing, cost of living and infrastructure – much of which is based on misinformation which feeds a far-right agenda, [according to](https://www.abc.net.au/listen/programs/radionational-breakfast/neo-nazis-used-anti-immigration-rallies-aly/105718364) Multicultural Affairs Minister Anne Aly.

When misinformation spreads, it [impedes](https://www.unsw.edu.au/content/dam/pdfs/law/kaldor/resource/2025-03-countering-misinformation-refugees.pdf) evidence-based decision-making and results in poor laws and policies.

The positive role of immigration is something the opposition’s new immigration spokesman, Senator Paul Scarr, wants to [stress](https://www.couriermail.com.au/news/queensland/federal-coalition-dumps-duttonera-stance-on-migration/news-story/24f42d059dd1eacb4eb0a5eb69f34743).

He seems to be setting a new tone based on empathy, not division, drawing on his deep “respect and admiration” for migrant and refugee communities who are making “an outstanding contribution”.

When “we talk about immigration”, he [says](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/2025/jun/29/real-people-real-families-coalition-signals-dramatic-shift-away-from-anti-immigration-rhetoric-of-dutton-era), “we should never forget that we’re actually talking about real people, real families”.

When Prime Minister Anthony Albanese came to office in 2022, he [stressed](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2022-05-22/anthony-albanese-acceptance-speech-full-transcript/101088736) the importance of a vision for Australia that promotes “unity and optimism, not fear and division”.

For the first time in a long while, there does seem to be bipartisan support for this approach.

## Walking the walk

The dissonance, though, is that the broader architecture of Australia’s asylum policies remains squarely in place. It’s largely about deterrence, interception and offshoring.

And this week, parliament is expected to progress a bill that would facilitate the swift removal of around 350 [non-citizens](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/article/2024/jun/03/the-deportation-debate-is-toxic-politics-if-the-system-is-truly-broken-we-need-more-than-kneejerk-solutions) to Nauru.

In 2023, the High Court of Australia [ruled](https://theconversation.com/high-court-reasons-on-immigration-ruling-pave-way-for-further-legislation-218699) it was unlawful to hold people in immigration detention indefinitely, so for the [extraordinary sum](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2025-08-30/federal-government-inks-400m-deal-for-nauru/105716134) of A$408 million up-front, and $70 million a year, Australia will pay Nauru to take them.

While the deal may solve a [political problem](https://www.smh.com.au/national/secret-refugee-deal-with-nauru-just-moves-the-problem-out-of-sight-20250831-p5mr6e.html) for the government, it does so at great financial and moral cost.

As Australia’s Race Discrimination Commissioner, Giridharan Sivaraman, has [warned](https://humanrights.gov.au/about/news/media-releases/race-commissioner-says-anti-migration-rhetoric-distracts-real-causes):

> economic inequality, housing stress, and job insecurity are real and urgent challenges, including for people from migrant backgrounds. We need genuine solutions to these challenges – not dangerous, exploitative, anti-migrant rhetoric.

## Telling a new story

The more positive public statements we have seen in recent days and months will remain hollow unless we start to see real policy change.

[Governments can](https://www.kaldorcentre.unsw.edu.au/sites/kaldorcentre.unsw.edu.au/files/Kaldor_Centre_Principles_for_Australian_Refugee_Policy_Summary_Mar22.pdf), and should, help people around the world who are struggling most.

***Read more: [Think curbing overseas migration will end the housing crisis? It won’t – and we can’t afford to do it](https://theconversation.com/think-curbing-overseas-migration-will-end-the-housing-crisis-it-wont-and-we-cant-afford-to-do-it-211120)***

This doesn’t mean shying away from people’s legitimate concerns about housing, infrastructure and cost-of-living pressures.

But it does mean explaining migrants are [not the cause](https://australiainstitute.org.au/post/migrants-are-not-to-blame-for-soaring-house-prices/) of these challenges, and that reducing immigration could in fact be [counterproductive](https://www.theguardian.com/news/datablog/article/2024/may/30/migration-has-been-blamed-for-the-housing-crisis-but-its-not-that-simple).

While the evidence shows immigration [isn’t behind](https://theconversation.com/cutting-migrant-numbers-wont-help-housing-the-real-immigration-problems-not-being-tackled-this-election-250646) Australia’s housing woes, for instance, there’s [plenty of proof](https://www.oecd.org/en/topics/sub-issues/migration-regional-and-local-development/migration-in-australia.html) migrants are crucial for the country’s economic development.

The latter is the story politicians should be telling. Some have started to, but counteracting decades of messaging to the contrary will take time.

*Jane McAdam receives funding from the Australian Research Council. In 2024-25, she served as a member of the Ministerial Advisory Council on Skilled Migration's Expert Sub-Committee.*
description: Anti-immigration rallies across Australia are the culmination of years of political scaremongering. But better immigration messaging could change the trajectory.

title: What an exhibition by artists of the Vietnamese diaspora says about home and belonging
authors: Anh Khoi Nguyen, Postdoctoral Research Associate in Linguistics, University of Manchester
content:
Which objects create a feeling of home for you? A particular chair, a table, a teacup from your childhood kitchen?

Visitors to the current exhibition at London’s Museum of the Home are asked to bear this question in mind. Entitled [No Place Like Home (A Vietnamese Exhibition) Part II](https://www.museumofthehome.org.uk/whats-on/exhibitions-and-installations/no-place-like-home/), the show brings together eight artists, born and raised all over the world, who share roots in Vietnam.

Many layers of memory can be derived from a single object. For me, a UK-based German-Vietnamese linguist, Vietnamese artist Duong Thuy Nguyen’s pile of rice bowls (entitled *Chúng ta là một thể hợp nhất* / We Are An Unmistakable Fusion) immediately recalls meals shared with family or friends. For Nguyen herself, however, that plaster crockery stack also evokes the layered high-rise architecture of her native Hanoi.

At the entrance to the show, KV Duong and Hoa Dung Clerget’s installation – entitled The Cityscape – recreates an urban skyline with white plastic chairs. At its highest points, these are stacked seven high, weighted down at their bases with sandwich bags full of dry rice.

Plastic chairs, Vietnamese food – even the word “Vietnamese” itself – will, for many visitors, signify expensive holidays, beaches and islands. They will bring up memories of the safe taste of street life from the elected discomfort of a plastic chair, enjoying ice coffee or a bowl of soup to the soundtrack of motorcycle engines.

But for those in the Vietnamese diaspora, these same signifiers can conjure up far more complicated memories. [My research](https://doi.org/10.1075/ll.21004.ngu) into public Vietnamese writing and imagery used by Vietnamese immigrants and their descendants in Manchester speaks to the experience of having to leave one home far away and make a new one elsewhere.

## Hidden histories

[I have studied](https://doi.org/10.1075/ll.21004.ngu) Mancunian store signs and menus of establishments run by Vietnamese immigrants, in which Chinese writing can often be found alongside English and Vietnamese. This multilingualism references a hidden layer of meaning to which many customers with no Vietnamese connection will be oblivious.

It is tied to the [traumatic displacement](https://doi.org/10.1080/1369183X.2020.1724414) of the Chinese minority of Vietnam during the [third Indochina war](https://research.aston.ac.uk/en/publications/asean-and-the-dynamics-of-resistance-to-sovereignty-violation-the) (between 1978 and 1991) and to the contacts Vietnamese refugees made with Chinese communities in the host countries to which they fled.

No Place Like Home features a series of sculptures by the artist KV Duong, who was born in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam to Chinese-Vietnamese parents and grew up in a mixed neighbourhood of Vietnamese and Chinese families in Canada. He renders these hidden layers of meaning visible by transferring a childhood family photograph, taken when he was six, on to the surface of a moon-shaped vase from the [Chinese Ming dynasty](https://www.jstor.org/stable/25165269?seq=1#page_scan_tab_contents), the last to rule Vietnam.

Elsewhere, in a bake of clay, concrete, wire and found candles, and painted with acrylic, Duong recalls his first memory of a birthday celebration – a memory set in Canada, the year he turned seven.

Within Asian diasporas, differences can lose their significance when it comes to carving out a place of their own. From the outside, Chineseness and Vietnameseness seem self-evidently separate; different foods, countries and languages.

This separation, however, collapses when you consider the [complex stories](https://doi.org/10.1080/01434632.2020.1744614) I have encountered in my research. Stories like that of an ethnically Chinese woman who fled Vietnam and opened a Vietnamese restaurant and store in England and whose shop is now managed by a British-born man who speaks Cantonese with his family but who learned Vietnamese through his work.

Things are blurred even further in the case of the barbershop next door, which features English, Vietnamese and Chinese on its storefront, and is run by a Vietnamese refugee who was told by his uncle to learn Cantonese before coming to England and who is now married to a British Chinese woman.

## Diasporic placemaking

Diasporic [placemaking](https://opendocs.ids.ac.uk/opendocs/handle/20.500.12413/17493) is often a story of connection. But it is also a complicated story about who owns public spaces and decides who gets to use them.

At the exhibition opening, the French artist Carô Gervay told me that this was the first time Vietnamese diasporic artists had been given space by a publicly funded institution in the UK. The ambivalence she felt at this is further elaborated on in the work she has made in collaboration with the UK artist Cường Minh Bá Phạm.

Entitled No Place Like Home: a Metastory, this handbound book, printed on recycled paper and packaged in glassine, details the decision-making process that led to the Museum of the Home commissioning this exhibition.

Told through a mixture of text and photography, the story illustrates how those who own public spaces can strategically dole it out to play groups against another – or for the purpose of optics. Those on the margins have to constantly negotiate visibility and navigate the complex terms under which they can achieve it.

As a child growing up in Munich, Germany, the Lunar New Year was the one time in the year when I would be surrounded by people who looked like me and my family, when I would eat food like my mother cooked.

It was the one time in the year I heard the language of my parents and grandparents – in spirited conversations, in late-night karaoke sessions, in children’s voices as they wished adults a prosperous New Year in return for a small red envelope of money, *lì xì*, decorated with golden Chinese characters.

One step outside, though, and I would be back in front of an inconspicuous residential building on a German street, with “Asia-Restaurant” inscribed on a sign above the door. Back then, Vietnamese restaurants were often concealed behind the innocuous word “Asia”, so all-encompassing as to be rendered meaningless. They would be disguised as a “China-Restaurant”, or a Japanese sushi bar. These were places hidden to all except a select few.

For the Vietnamese diaspora, home is composed of such hidden places. A neighbourhood or a street, the inside of a restaurant, a family dinner table; pockets of Vietnameseness in France, Germany, Canada, the US or the UK.

Being part of the diaspora means being able to read a place’s hidden meanings, hidden histories of being on the outside, of journeys and goodbyes. But it also means making new and often unexpected connections with other cultures as well as with others with shared roots from all around the world.

More than any artwork, object or place, to my mind, what creates a sense of home is seeing such talented artists, their friends and family in tow – each with a unique background, each having grown up in their own little pockets of Vietnameseness – all come together in the same room to share their stories.

*Anh Khoi Nguyen does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Diasporic placemaking is often a story of connections and hidden stories. It is also a complicated story about who owns public spaces and who decides who gets to use it.

title: How your body clock affects your mental health and ways to keep it in sync
authors: Sarah Chellappa, Associate Professor, Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience, University of Southampton
content:
Ever wondered why a bad night’s sleep can leave you irritable, anxious or sad? Poor sleep affects our emotions, but its timing also plays a role.

Our [circadian rhythms](https://theconversation.com/topics/circadian-rhythms-94) are nearly 24-hour cycles that regulate alertness, hormones, body temperature and digestion.

Deep inside the brain, a cluster of nerve cells called the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) acts as the body’s master clock. It uses light signals from the eyes to coordinate clocks in other organs, including the brain, liver, heart and gut.

When daily routines fall out of sync with this clock, mood can suffer. Research suggests circadian disruption may contribute to mental health challenges.

Our internal clock helps regulate hormones, including melatonin and cortisol. Melatonin helps regulate the sleep-wake cycle. Levels stay low during the day, rise in the evening as darkness falls (signalling to the brain that it is time to rest), peak in the middle of the night, and drop off in the morning. Cortisol, which helps us respond to stress, typically rises towards morning.

These changes prepare the body for activity and rest, while influencing emotional wellbeing.

In a [2024 laboratory study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37648646/), my colleagues and I investigated whether our internal clocks influence mood independently of everyday activities.

We studied 19 healthy adults over 32 hours, measuring mood while minimising changes in their surroundings and behaviour.

We found that anxiety-like and depression-like mood were highest at around 8am to 9am, while participants reported greater mental fatigue and lower physical comfort between approximately 6am and 8am. These patterns were linked to their internal biological clocks, suggesting that mood can fluctuate according to biological time, independently of everyday routines.

Circadian disruption has also been [linked to depression](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38394243/) and bipolar disorder, a condition involving episodes of depression and elevated or irritable mood.

The relationship also works in both directions. Mental health difficulties can disrupt sleep and circadian rhythms, potentially creating a cycle in which low quality sleep and psychological distress reinforce one another.

## What happens when our clocks fall out of sync

Night shift workers may need to stay awake when their bodies are preparing for sleep and rest when their internal clocks promote alertness.

This mismatch is known as circadian misalignment.

In a [2020 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33122670/), we investigated how this misalignment affected mood in two controlled laboratory experiments involving people with and without shift-work experience.

Participants followed schedules designed to simulate day and night shifts while all other behavioural and environmental factors were controlled for, including light exposure, physical activity, food intake and opportunities for sleep.

We found that mood and wellbeing reduced when participants’ sleeping and waking schedules were misaligned with their internal body clock. The effects were observed in non-shift workers as well as shift workers.

These findings suggest circadian misalignment can influence mood, although larger studies are needed to establish the long-term consequences.

Outside the laboratory, many people experience a mismatch known as [social jetlag](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27218855/). This occurs when people’s sleep and waking times differ substantially between working days and days off.

Artificial light can also affect our internal clocks. Bright light in the evening, including light from electronic screens, can suppress melatonin and delay our sleep time.

My [research on light sensitivity](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33049062/) has highlighted differences between individuals. Some people’s circadian rhythms are much more sensitive to evening light than others, meaning the same exposure may have different effects.

## Could changing meal times help?

Light is the strongest environmental signal for the master clock, but eating also influences the timing of biological processes in other organs.

In a [2022 study](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36095195/), my colleagues and I investigated whether changing meal times could reduce the effects of simulated night work on mood.

Nineteen healthy volunteers followed carefully controlled schedules designed to mimic night shifts. One group ate during both the day and night, while the other ate only during the daytime.

Among participants who ate during both periods, ratings of depression-like mood increased by 26.2% and anxiety-like mood by 16.1% compared with their baseline measurements.

We did not observe significant increases in either measure among those who ate only during the daytime.

These findings suggest that the timing of meals may influence how circadian disruption affects mood. However, the study involved a small group of healthy volunteers under laboratory conditions. Further research involving shift workers is needed to establish whether eating only during the daytime can help reduce symptoms of anxiety and depression.

## How to support your body clock

Although we may not control our working hours or sleep schedules, some daily habits may help keep our internal clocks aligned.

1. [Get morning daylight](https://theconversation.com/why-morning-blue-light-therapy-could-improve-sleep-and-daily-activity-in-older-adults-251576). Light is the most powerful environmental signal for the master clock. Spending time outdoors after waking can support alertness and help regulate the timing of sleep later. The amount of light needed varies between people.

***Read more: [Tired, irritable and craving carbs? Why darker days affect our bodies and brains](https://theconversation.com/tired-irritable-and-craving-carbs-why-darker-days-affect-our-bodies-and-brains-295124)***

1. Reduce bright light before bed. Dimming household lights and limiting screen use in the evening/night-time may help the body prepare for sleep. The [NHS recommends](https://www.nhs.uk/every-mind-matters/mental-wellbeing-tips/how-to-fall-asleep-faster-and-sleep-better/) avoiding electronic screens for at least an hour before bedtime.
2. Keep a regular sleep-wake schedule. Going to bed and waking up at reasonably consistent times can help reinforce circadian rhythms. A [systematic review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33054339/) associated regular sleep patterns with better health outcomes, including diabetes, heart diseases and depression.
3. Consider food and exercise timing. Consistent and earlier food times may help support the body’s daily rhythms for physical health, although research is needed to establish the best eating schedules for mental health. Regular physical activity can also benefit sleep. A [review of studies](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30374942/) found that evening exercise generally did not interfere with sleep, although vigorous exercise ending very close to bedtime sometimes did.

## Protecting sleep and mental health

Research suggests that the timing of sleep and daily activities can influence mood, although more evidence is needed to establish whether changing these routines can help prevent or treat mental health conditions.

Maintaining consistent routines and getting enough sleep may support emotional wellbeing, but these habits cannot replace appropriate treatment. Anyone experiencing persistent sleep or mood problems should seek medical advice. Understanding how our internal clocks influence mood may eventually offer new ways to support mental health.

*Sarah Chellappa does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Research shows that disrupted body clocks can affect mood. A circadian rhythms researcher explains how sleep, light and meal timing influence mental health.

title: Around half of people will experience a mental health issue in their lifetime
authors: Hannah Ritchie
content:
How common are mental health issues? International health statistics often publish estimates on the share of people who have a mental health disorder at a given point in time. For example, the Global Burden of Disease study [estimates that](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/mental-illnesses-prevalence?country=~USA) in 2023, 5% of people in the United States had depression.

But people can develop a mental health issue at any stage of their life, or experience recurring episodes over their lifetime.

These statistics don’t tell us anything about what share of people will *ever* experience a mental health problem. That’s the question I want to answer in this article.

To do this, I’ll use data from a 2023 study by John McGrath and colleagues, which drew on data from 29 countries to model what share of people develop mental disorders over their lives.1

This data came from World Mental Health Surveys, conducted between 2001 and 2022. In these surveys, more than 150,000 people are asked in face-to-face interviews about their history of specific mental health disorders. These are structured diagnostic interviews, and from there, researchers can understand the prevalence of these disorders and when they tend to begin in someone’s life.

As these interviews include people at very different stages in their lives, they can help build up a model of how the cumulative risk of a mental illness develops with age. For example, what share of people have experienced depression by the age of 15, 30, or 50?

For many, their first experience is young — in childhood, adolescence, or early adulthood. In [a previous article](https://ourworldindata.org/when-do-people-experience-mental-health-conditions-for-the-first-time), I looked at the age at which people tend to develop mental health issues for the first time.

In the chart below, you can see these cumulative risk curves for men and women across four mental health disorders: depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, and alcohol dependence and abuse. Age is shown on the horizontal axis, and the cumulative risk on the vertical axis.

![Four line charts of the cumulative share of men and women who develop depression, anxiety disorders, bipolar disorder, and alcohol dependence/abuse by age, where the visualization compares lifetime ri](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/b50fb4bb-3541-43cd-740e-1776a8e0c800/w=2550)

In the first panel, for example, you can see that by the age of 75, one in three women has experienced depression at some point in their lives. One in five men has.

By age 30, it’s only around half as many, which tells us that roughly half of those who will ever experience depression have their first episode before 30, and half after.

From this chart, you can also see clear sex differences. Depression and anxiety are more common in women than in men, but alcohol dependence and abuse are the opposite. Men and women are equally likely to experience bipolar disorder.

# How likely is someone to experience a mental health disorder in their lifetime?

With these cumulative risk curves, we can return to our original question: what share of people will develop a particular mental health disorder in their lifetime?

The chart below answers this question, showing the share of men and women who will experience different mental health disorders by the age of 75.

Anxiety disorders encapsulate a range of conditions, including generalized anxiety, phobias, panic disorder, social anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). Almost one in three women and nearly one in five men will experience at least one of these in their lifetime.

Mood disorders include both depression and bipolar disorder. More than one in three women and one in four men will experience at least one of these. The sex gap here is explained by differences in rates of depression, rather than bipolar disorder.

> Depression and anxiety are more common in women than in men, but alcohol dependence and abuse are the opposite.

Finally, we see that substance use disorders — whether that’s alcohol or other drugs — are the opposite. They’re more common among men. Alcohol or drug abuse has a much less stringent definition, so its rates are far higher than dependence on a particular substance.

![Horizontal grouped bar charts of the share of men and women who develop different mental health disorders by age 75, where it compares lifetime risk by sex across 11 disorders grouped into anxiety, mo](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/0d23ae4f-5161-42df-9038-d444f158e900/w=2550)

People can often experience multiple mental health disorders in their lifetime. It’s fairly common that someone with depression also experiences anxiety, or that someone with an addiction to alcohol has a history of depression or PTSD. So, to estimate the share of people who will experience *any*mental health disorder in their lifetime, we can’t just add all of these shares together.

The authors do provide a separate estimate, though, and conclude that around **half of people can expect to develop*****at least one*****of the mental health disorders** studied in this article by the time they’re 75.2

Additional informationWhy these estimates of lifetime risk might be conservativeThe main takeaway from this article is that mental health issues are incredibly common. Around half will develop at least one of these disorders by the age of 75. Even for specific issues, such as depression or anxiety, one in three women will experience it at some stage.But there’s reason to expect that these figures are actually conservative, and the true lifetime risk could be even higher.This is because these studies rely on people recalling previous mental health episodes. Most people can do this reasonably well, particularly in structured diagnostic interviews. But in older generations, in particular, recall can be an issue.My colleague Saloni Dattani [wrote about this](https://ourworldindata.org/depression-lifetime-risk) in detail for the lifetime risk of depression. She presents the headline result that around one in three women and one in five men in the United States experience depression by the age of 65. But she also highlights various studies in other high-income countries that find even higher figures, particularly when they attempt to adjust for this “recall bias”.John McGrath and colleagues — the authors of the meta-analysis used in this article — also flag this as a limitation in our understanding of lifetime risk.It therefore seems fair to frame these results as conservative. The true share could be higher.
description: What is someone’s risk of developing depression, anxiety, or other mental health issues at some point in their life?

title: How the body clock could help personalise depression treatment
authors: Timothy Hearn, Lecturer, University of Cambridge; Anglia Ruskin University
content:
A person with depression might sleep much longer than usual and still wake feeling exhausted. Later that evening, when they want to go to bed, they may find themselves wide awake. Researchers are investigating whether patterns like these could help explain why antidepressants work better for some people than others.

The clue may lie in the [body’s internal clock](https://theconversation.com/topics/body-clock-2947), which helps regulate when someone sleeps, wakes and feels alert.

An [Australian study](https://doi.org/10.1192/bjp.2026.10798) examined 11,380 people, predominantly with severe or recurring depression. About 23% met the researchers’ criteria for a proposed subtype called “circadian depression”, named after the body’s roughly 24-hour internal clock.

Participants needed at least three of six features, including being a night owl, sleeping longer during depression, morning tiredness and seasonal changes in mood or behaviour. The other features involved habitually sleeping and waking later, and having different sleep schedules on working days and days off.

Compared with other participants, this group reported [less benefit and more side-effects](https://doi.org/10.1192/bjp.2026.10798) from two common types of antidepressants, SSRIs and SNRIs, which affect how brain cells communicate through chemical messengers. However, some people with these sleep patterns still reported benefiting from these medicines.

The researchers also found genetic associations with later sleep timing, reduced sensitivity to insulin, the hormone that helps regulate blood sugar, and a protein involved in inflammation, the immune system’s response to injury or infection. These associations reflect inherited tendencies, rather than evidence that participants actually had blood-sugar problems or inflammation.

[The findings are preliminary](https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-observational-study-on-circadian-subtype-of-depression/). Participants recalled their symptoms and medication experiences, and those in the proposed group generally had more severe depression. The researchers did not measure their internal clocks or establish cause and effect.

Some features overlap with [recognised forms of depression](https://www.sciencemediacentre.org/expert-reaction-to-observational-study-on-circadian-subtype-of-depression/), so it remains unclear whether this is a distinct subtype. All participants had European genetic ancestry, limiting how widely the findings can be applied. The 23% figure therefore cannot be assumed to represent everyone with depression.

## How the body clock affects mood

The body clock coordinates roughly [24-hour cycles](https://www.nigms.nih.gov/education/fact-sheets/Pages/circadian-rhythms), known as circadian rhythms, which affect sleepiness, body temperature and hormones, the chemical messengers that help regulate the body. Light reaching the eyes helps keep this clock aligned with day and night. Meals and physical activity also provide timing cues.

When [internal timing clashes with daily demands](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/circadian-rhythm-disorders), sleep can suffer. Someone whose clock runs late may feel alert at midnight but have to get up for work while their body is still expecting sleep. Being a night owl is not necessarily a problem. Persistent disruption is the concern.

Sleep and mental health can [reinforce one another](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2214756121). Disrupted sleep may worsen depression, while depression and stress can disturb sleep and daily routines.

One possible link involves [brain systems that regulate emotion and reward](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2214756121), including the ability to enjoy pleasurable experiences. Animal experiments suggest that disrupting the body clock can affect these systems and produce depression-like behaviour.

In [small laboratory experiments](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33122670/), researchers altered the sleep schedules of shift workers and people who did not work shifts. When their sleep and waking times were out of step with their internal clocks, participants reported worse mood. They had not been recruited because they had depression, and temporary low mood is different from clinical depression.

Conventional antidepressants might leave a timing problem untreated, but that remains a hypothesis. The Australian study did not test body-clock treatments, and its findings cannot establish whether someone with disrupted rhythms would benefit more from an alternative medication.

## Could light therapy help?

[Light therapy](https://www.nimh.nih.gov/health/publications/seasonal-affective-disorder) involves sitting near a specially designed bright-light box at a scheduled time, often in the morning. Morning light can [shift a late-running body clock earlier](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/circadian-rhythm-disorders/treatment), helping someone feel sleepy and wake earlier.

***Read more: [Why morning blue light therapy could improve sleep and daily activity in older adults](https://theconversation.com/why-morning-blue-light-therapy-could-improve-sleep-and-daily-activity-in-older-adults-251576)***

The treatment is used for seasonal affective disorder, depression that follows a seasonal pattern, often during darker months. Evidence suggests it can also help with depression that has no seasonal pattern.

A [review of 11 clinical trials](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39356500/) involving 858 people examined bright-light therapy for non-seasonal depression, including bipolar depression. Bipolar disorder involves depression alongside episodes of unusually elevated or irritable mood and increased energy.

In trials reporting remission, about 41% of people receiving bright light improved enough to fall below the threshold for depression, compared with 24% receiving dim light or treatment without bright light.

But these trials did not select people with the proposed circadian subtype, so they cannot tell us whether that group benefits more. Light may also influence mood through [brain pathways separate from the body clock](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2214756121).

Timing and medical guidance matter. Light can shift the clock earlier or later depending on when it is used. People with bipolar disorder need [particular supervision](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40705857/) because light therapy can sometimes trigger unusually elevated or irritable mood.

Regular waking times, daytime activity and meals may also [support daily rhythms](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/circadian-rhythm-disorders/treatment). Melatonin, a hormone that rises in the evening and signals biological night, can help shift a delayed clock when carefully timed. However, studies have [not established melatonin supplements](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8968118/) as an effective depression treatment.

## Towards more personalised treatment

Could measuring someone’s internal clock help doctors choose treatments? [Wrist-worn activity monitors](https://www.nhlbi.nih.gov/health/circadian-rhythm-disorders/diagnosis) can estimate sleep patterns, while saliva samples taken throughout an evening can show when melatonin starts rising, offering a more direct measure of internal timing.

Researchers need to establish whether the proposed group really has distinct biological rhythms, then test whether choosing treatment based on those measurements helps people recover sooner.

For now, sleep patterns cannot reliably predict which antidepressant will work best, and the findings provide no reason to change prescribed medication without medical advice.

If future trials confirm a benefit, a prescription for depression might one day specify when to receive light as carefully as which medicine to take.

*Timothy Hearn does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: A new study suggests that sleep patterns may be linked to how people respond to antidepressants, raising the possibility of more personalised treatment.

title: Would subsidising weight loss drugs make health care fairer?
authors: Lauren Ball, Professor of Community Health and Wellbeing, The University of Queensland; Emily Burch, Accredited Practising Dietitian and Lecturer, Southern Cross University
content:
GLP-1 medicines such as Ozempic, Wegovy and Mounjaro have transformed the treatment of obesity, but access to them in Australia increasingly depends on something much less medical: whether you can afford them.

Around [half a million](https://doi.org/10.1002/bcp.70715) Australians are now using GLP-1 medicines. Nearly half access these medicines privately, paying between [A$200 and $700](https://www1.racgp.org.au/newsgp/clinical/price-talks-continue-as-health-minister-pushes-for) a month out of pocket.

***Read more: [Mounjaro is more effective for weight loss than Ozempic. So how does it work? And why does it cost so much?](https://theconversation.com/mounjaro-is-more-effective-for-weight-loss-than-ozempic-so-how-does-it-work-and-why-does-it-cost-so-much-239185)***

Calls are becoming [louder](https://www.theaustralian.com.au/health/medical/the-cost-and-value-of-listing-ozempiclike-drugs-for-obesity-on-pbs/news-story/33ad17d95c9070a023d4d0e8dcfd9f99) for the Australian government to subsidise GLP-1 medicines for people living with obesity who do not have diabetes. This is because obesity costs the Australian economy [billions](https://www.obesityevidencehub.org.au/collections/impacts/cost-impacts-of-obesity-and-of-obesity-prevention-measures) of dollars each year.

But would subsidising GLP-1 medicines make health care in Australia fairer? Or would that money be better invested in the environments that shape health, such as affordable nutritious food, access to health care and better opportunities for physical activity?

## GLP-1 medicines work – while you take them

A 2025 [review](https://www.cochrane.org/about-us/news/glp-1-drugs-effective-weight-loss-more-independent-studies-needed) involving almost 28,000 people found that semaglutide (the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy) led to an average weight loss of [around 11% of body weight](https://doi.org/10.1002/14651858.CD015092.pub2) compared with placebo. Importantly, most people maintained that weight loss for up to two years if they continued taking the medication.

But there’s a catch.

Like many treatments for chronic conditions, GLP-1 medicines appear to work best while people continue taking them. Clinical trials show people generally [maintain](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.57349) their weight loss during treatment. But they are not paying hundreds of dollars a month out of pocket.

In the real world, cost is one of the biggest barriers to ongoing use. Some [research](https://doi.org/10.1002/oby.70058) suggests more than half of users stop treatment within six months, most commonly because they can no longer afford it.

Stopping the medication often means some weight returns. A recent [analysis](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eclinm.2026.103796) estimated that people regained around 60% of the weight they had lost within a year of stopping GLP-1 medicines, although weight regain slowed over time.

Even so, people were projected to maintain around 25% of their original weight loss in the longer term. For someone who lost 20 kilograms, that would mean regaining 15kgs, but remaining 5kgs lighter than when they started.

This suggests GLP-1 medicines may need to be viewed less as a short-term weight loss aid and more as a long-term treatment for a chronic condition.

But that raises an important question: if people need ongoing treatment to maintain the benefits, what happens when ongoing access depends on their ability to pay?

## The burden of obesity isn’t shared equally

Obesity and type 2 diabetes are not distributed evenly across the Australian population. Rates are consistently [higher](https://www.aihw.gov.au/reports/overweight-obesity/overweight-and-obesity/contents/population-groups#remoteness) among people experiencing socioeconomic disadvantage, in many regional and remote communities, and among Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people.

This matters when we talk about who should pay for treatment. Obesity isn’t simply a matter of personal responsibility. Our [health](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13679-020-00398-7) is shaped by income, housing, education, access to health care, transport and the cost of healthy foods.

***Read more: [No, taking drugs like Ozempic isn’t ‘cheating’ at weight loss or the ‘easy way out’](https://theconversation.com/no-taking-drugs-like-ozempic-isnt-cheating-at-weight-loss-or-the-easy-way-out-219116)***

Two people can receive exactly the same advice about healthy eating and physical activity, but have very different opportunities to follow it.

Someone with secure housing, predictable working hours, reliable transport and access to affordable, nutritious food starts from a very different position to someone experiencing financial stress, working multiple jobs, or living a long way from health services.

This means those people most likely to experience obesity and obesity-related complications are often the Australians least able to access effective treatment.

This creates a paradox. The Australians carrying the greatest burden of obesity and its complications may be among the least able to afford one of the most effective treatments now available.

When effective treatment is financially out of reach, people may look for alternatives. Current access to GLP-1 medicines is increasingly influenced by commercial [telehealth](https://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/medical-weight-loss-promotion-under-scrutiny-australia-2026a10001qb?form=fpf) providers focused on weight loss and [reports](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2024-05-22/compound-pharmacies-banned-weight-loss-drugs-replica-ozempic/103861108) of black-market access through unregulated sources have also emerged. These pathways may not provide the medical, nutritional and psychological support needed to use these medicines safely.

## The bottom line

Wider access to GLP-1 medicines could make effective obesity treatment available to Australians who currently can’t afford it.

But, subsidising medicines won’t change the social and environmental conditions that contribute to unequal rates of obesity in the first place. Australia still needs investment in affordable, nutritious food, prevention, primary health care, and environments that support physical activity.

Making treatment fairer is important. So is reducing the need for the treatment in the first place.

*Lauren Ball receives funding from the National Health and Medical Research Council, Health and Wellbeing Queensland, Heart Foundation, Gallipoli Medical Research and Mater Health, Springfield City Group. She is a director of Dietitians Australia, a director of the Darling Downs and West Moreton Primary Health Network and an associate member of the Australian Academy of Health and Medical Sciences.*

*Emily Burch does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Those carrying the greatest burden of obesity and its complications may be among the least able to afford one of the most effective treatments now available.

title: When do people experience mental health conditions for the first time?
authors: Hannah Ritchie
content:
Mental health conditions can begin at almost any age. For many people, they develop in the early stages of life.

Around a third of people who will ever experience a mental health disorder do so by the age of 14.1 Two-thirds do by the age of 25.

But this varies a lot by condition. Some are much more common in childhood or adolescence, while others are more evenly distributed across adulthood. Knowing the age at which people might be particularly vulnerable to the onset of a mental health condition is important. It helps societies offer support — whether that’s an assessment of risk factors, screening, or preventive interventions — at the right time to make a difference.

The chart below shows how this age distribution looks for nine different mental health disorders. Each curve shows, among people who will ever develop that condition, the share who first do so at any given age.

The data behind this comes from a large meta-analysis of 192 studies by Marco Solmi and colleagues.1

> Around a third of people who will ever experience a mental health disorder do so by the age of 14.

I’ve sorted these conditions into three groups.

First, those that **commonly develop at any point in someone’s life**. This includes generalized anxiety disorder, depression, and bipolar disorder (the latter two are often referred to as mood disorders).

Second, those that tend to **develop earlier in life, with a very strong age peak around early adolescence**. Social anxiety tends to first develop in childhood, and almost 80% of those who will experience it at some point in their lives do so before the age of 18. Eating disorders tend to begin during someone’s teenage years, with a peak age of 16 and a median age of 18.2

And third, those that tend to **peak around age 20 but will often develop for the first time throughout adulthood**. This includes substance use (alcohol and cannabis) disorders and schizophrenia, which commonly develop in someone’s twenties.

![Density plots of age of onset for a range of mental health disorders where the visualization compares when different conditions typically first appear across the lifespan, grouped into disorders that ](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/412d02ec-0ffc-4ffb-8cf3-8272156c3300/w=2550)

Additional informationSome notes on the data used in this visualizationThe chart above uses smoothed curves from [the meta-analysis](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41380-021-01161-7) published by Marco Solmi and colleagues in *Molecular Psychiatry*.Here are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting this data.First, the definition of onset age varied among the underlying studies in the meta-analysis. In some, it meant the age at which someone first experienced symptoms. In others, the age of diagnosis or first hospitalization. Differences in this definition can, of course, affect these results; someone may experience symptoms long before they receive a diagnosis. This could shift the median age of onset significantly. The authors did test the sensitivity of their results to different definitions and found, for example, that shifting from symptoms to diagnosis for depression changed the median age from 26 to 31 years.Second, these curves do not tell us anything about how prevalent these conditions are across the entire population. They are scaled by the proportion of people who will ever develop a given condition. The depression curve, for example, is far lower than the schizophrenia curve, even though depression is much more common in the general population.Third, this data only tells us about the age of onset. It does not tell us about the age distribution of people experiencing the condition at any given time. Many people will have recurring episodes — or very long periods — with a given mental health disorder, which isn’t reflected in the chart.Finally, these curves are limited by the number of high-quality studies of different conditions. In particular, geographical diversity is limited, with most studies coming from high-income countries in North America, Europe, or Australia.
description: Knowing when people are most at risk allows us to offer support when it might make the biggest difference.

title: Can social media bans protect young people’s mental health? Early research suggests that bans aren’t the answer
authors: Ari Lightman, Professor of Digital Media and Marketing, Carnegie Mellon University
content:
The year 2026 has been an expensive one for social media platforms.

Since March, YouTube and Meta, the parent company of Instagram and Facebook, have settled or paid out in multiple lawsuits to the tune of more than US$17 billion for allegedly [acting negligently](https://www.nbcnews.com/tech/tech-news/verdict-reached-landmark-social-media-addiction-trial-rcna263421), deliberately designing their platforms [to hook kids](https://www.npr.org/2026/08/26/nx-s1-5944781/meta-settlement-child-safety-lawsuit) and [misleading the public](https://www.courthousenews.com/facebook-faced-with-massive-penalties-after-new-mexico-privacy-verdict/) about safety and privacy. If these suits are any indication of how states and the public are starting to view social media platforms, more may follow.

On top of these lawsuits, social media platforms are facing a loss of business as [bans for minors](https://theconversation.com/is-australias-social-media-ban-for-under-16s-working-285518) are accelerating and spreading worldwide. [Australia was one of the first](https://theconversation.com/australias-social-media-ban-is-now-in-force-other-countries-are-closely-watching-what-happens-271407) with a ban on kids under 16 on social media starting in December 2025, [followed soon after by the U.K.](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fact-sheet-new-rules-to-protect-children-online/fact-sheet-new-rules-to-protect-children-online) with a similar prohibition.

The current list of countries looking to ban minors from these platforms tops [more than 20](https://www.reuters.com/legal/government/australia-europe-countries-move-curb-childrens-social-media-access-2026-09-17/), from Greece to the United Arab Emirates to Canada. The proposed and enacted bans around the world vary in terms of [age restriction](https://social-media-age-tracker.onrender.com/), parental consent rules and [age verification methods](https://facephi.com/observatory/en/age-verification-laws-by-country/). Different countries are looking at restricting different platforms, but most include a mix of Snapchat, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and X.

These bans [aren’t necessarily for mental health reasons only](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/28/technology/social-media-bans-meta.html) – some are motivated by political concerns about foreign-owned platforms, and others aim to protect young people’s privacy. But nearly every government banning social media platforms for young people [mentions their mental health as a reason](https://builtin.com/articles/social-media-bans-children).

The question is, are these bans the solution to the [mental health problems young people are facing](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/adolescent-mental-health)? I [research digital media and marketing](https://www.heinz.cmu.edu/faculty-research/profiles/lightman-ari) and measure the impact of new technologies, and I’m skeptical about whether prohibiting access to these platforms will actually improve young people’s mental health.

## Mental health concerns

Since Jonathan Haidt’s 2024 book “[The Anxious Generation](https://www.anxiousgeneration.com/)” critics of social media have increasingly focused on young people’s mental health. Haidt argues that social media disrupts kids’ social and neurological development, contributing to rising anxiety and depression through [sleep loss](https://theconversation.com/social-media-before-bedtime-wreaks-havoc-on-our-sleep-a-sleep-researcher-explains-why-screens-alone-arent-the-main-culprit-251453), fragmented attention, [addiction](https://theconversation.com/it-is-hijacking-my-brain-a-team-of-experts-found-ways-to-help-young-people-addicted-to-social-media-to-cut-the-craving-219954), loneliness, social comparison and [perfectionism](https://theconversation.com/social-media-teenage-girls-with-perfectionist-tendencies-need-to-take-extra-care-heres-how-95479).

A 2026 study found that young people between 14 and 20 are more than [100% more likely to experience mental illness](https://doi.org/10.1503/cmaj.250926) than 14- to 20-year-olds 50 years ago.

Increased use of social media and screen time is compounding an already precarious time for minors. In 2021 it was estimated that 20.5% of young people [experienced elevated symptoms of anxiety](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapediatrics.2021.2482), and 25.2% of youth reported elevated symptoms of depression globally.

Many factors contribute to this, including [better screening and awareness of kids’ mental health problems](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.4605), as well as societal disruptions as a [result of the COVID-19 pandemic](https://theconversation.com/students-are-returning-to-school-with-anxiety-grief-and-gaps-in-social-skills-will-there-be-enough-school-mental-health-resources-165279). As the world sheltered in place and moved online for work, school and social interactions, there was an [increase in isolation and loneliness](https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2022/05/covid-19-increase-loneliness).

## Not all bad

In light of these concerns, [some researchers argue](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2026-721073) that bans on social media platforms are like putting an age restriction on buying alcohol or cigarettes.

But unlike these addictive and potentially harmful substances, there are [benefits to social media](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40124-025-00357-7), especially for teens who feel disconnected from their local communities and [want to build relationships](https://theconversation.com/screen-time-guidelines-for-kids-and-adolescents-have-shifted-as-research-paints-a-more-nuanced-picture-281300) with others who feel similarly.

Social media platforms allow for global connectivity and community-building with like-minded groups. They also provide a place for [self-expression and civic engagement](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40124-025-00357-7).

In a Pew survey of U.S. teens, 80% said [social media helps them stay connected](https://www.pewresearch.org/internet/2022/11/16/connection-creativity-and-drama-teen-life-on-social-media-in-2022/) to what’s happening in their friends’ lives.

## Show me the money

One place where the comparison with tobacco is actually quite apt is in relation to the money from lawsuit settlements.

In 1998, states [settled a lawsuit against the major tobacco companies](https://www.naag.org/our-work/naag-center-for-tobacco-and-public-health/the-master-settlement-agreement/) to recover smoking-related healthcare costs. Part of the settlement was allocated to programs aimed at reducing youth smoking. In 2026, total state funding for these programs amounts to [just 3.4% of the $21.7 billion](https://www.tobaccofreekids.org/state-report) in revenue states will collect from tobacco settlement payments and tobacco taxes.

Similarly, some money from an [August 2026 Meta settlement with a group of states](https://www.npr.org/2026/08/26/nx-s1-5944781/meta-settlement-child-safety-lawsuit) for $17 billion is slated for [state-based programs focusing on mental health infrastructure](https://apnews.com/article/meta-trial-instagram-settlement-97d342f2a33d835eda2356c5e1af9e37), school and community programs, and public health campaigns.

However, there is no oversight or direction as to how states should use the funds, nor is there a mechanism to report how that money has improved kids’ mental health care, safety and well-being.

## Is it even possible?

Early evidence from the Australian social media ban shows that kids are finding work-arounds: Roughly 61% of kids ages 12–15 [continue to access platforms using false IDs](https://mollyrosefoundation.org/more-than-60-of-australian-children-still-using-social-media-despite-ban-for-under-16s-research-shows/), altered appearances or virtual private networks, or VPNs, even though [millions of accounts were disabled](https://www.cato.org/blog/policymakers-should-stop-going-after-vpns-enforce-internet-age-restrictions). In fact, this has become so common that U.K. lawmakers are debating restricting consumer VPN access.

Some countries, such as Australia, require the platforms themselves to develop ways of verifying a user’s age. Some minors have [bypassed scans](https://www.bitdefender.com/en-us/blog/hotforsecurity/kids-bypass-age-verification) from [biometric age estimation technology](https://www.eff.org/deeplinks/2025/12/age-assurance-methods-explained) by using photo manipulation software, substituting celebrity photos, [using clever makeup](https://fortune.com/2026/05/05/gen-alpha-using-makeup-to-pass-age-verification-tech-online/) and even utilizing older friends and parents to pass the “selfie tests” on their behalf. Others simply manipulate their birth years during registration or rely on [existing adult-verified accounts](https://www.bbc.com/news/technology-63204605) managed by family members.

And all of these age-verification methods, whether developed by a government or a social media platform, rely on [collecting sensitive data to estimate age](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/mar/02/ban-children-social-media-biometic-data-surveilled) accurately, which creates privacy concerns.

Australia is currently [seeking to raise fines](https://www.npr.org/2026/06/29/nx-s1-5874576/australia-fines-child-social-media-accounts) on social media platforms that fail to comply with its requirements. The Australian safety commissioner, charged with enforcing the ban, issued a compliance update that showed 7 in 10 children who held accounts in restricted platforms [remained on those platforms](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/most-australian-teens-still-social-media-three-months-after-under-16-ban-began-2026-07-31/), and more than 80% of Australian teens ages 10-15 still use social media frequently.

Beyond concerns about enacting and enforcing these restrictions, some policymakers also worry that total bans could push some kids to [migrate to even riskier online spaces](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2022.101339).

## What could work

Based on the evidence, I’m not convinced that banning social media platforms will be an effective solution to the mental health crisis among young people today.

So what could work?

Supporting young people’s mental health is a complex endeavor that will require a combination of people, organizations and resources coming together.

I believe kids’ mental health would be better served by governments enforcing [safety by default standards](https://hateaid.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/safety-by-design-report-pathways-to-safer-social-media-platforms-hateaid.pdf) on social media platforms rather than outright bans. This means that the highest security and privacy options are in place by default so that minors still on a platform are protected. For instance, accounts would be unsearchable by default, so users would have to intentionally make a profile change to be found by people they don’t know in real life.

Safety by default standards also place limits on the manipulation, algorithmic restraint and other addictive mechanisms that may lead to psychological harm in vulnerable populations such as young people.

Educating kids on digital literacy and online safety as well as ensuring [some screen-free time](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/articles/parents-ultimate-guide-to-social-media) are also going to help support kids’ mental health.

It’s also important for parents and other caregivers to recognize changes in behavior as a result of [addiction to social platforms and screens](https://theconversation.com/how-much-time-do-kids-spend-on-devices-playing-games-watching-videos-texting-and-using-the-phone-210118). And when adults start seeing signs of a problem, they need clear, easy and affordable ways to connect their kids to mental health support, which is not available in most places right now.

And finally, the United Nations recommends [bringing kids into the conversation](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/05/1167608) about what’s best for them online. Obviously, this does not mean putting 12-year-olds in charge of regulatory agencies. But feedback from young people about what they care about, what they get out of being online and what makes it hard for them to look away from their screens could inform changes to social media platforms and education programs that could help young people engage online more safely and maintain a healthy balance.

*Ari Lightman is affiliated with Jewish Healthcare Foundation*
description: Kids have found ways around most of the safeguards meant to keep them off social media platforms.

title: Nicotine pouches, vaping or cigarettes: Which nicotine product is actually the least harmful?
authors: Emma Fenske, Assistant Professor of Medicine, Addiction Medicine, University of Colorado Anschutz; Oregon Health & Science University
content:
“Do you smoke cigarettes?” I asked my patient succinctly in a recent clinic appointment.

He matter-of-factly responded, “Not anymore, I use Zyn pouches now.”

As with any patient, I gauged his readiness – or reluctance, in some instances – to disrupt his use of nicotine.

I asked about his interest in trying nicotine replacement therapy, a medical [treatment that provides low, controlled amounts of nicotine](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/want-quit-smoking-fda-approved-and-fda-cleared-cessation-products-can-help). Initially, his response caught me by surprise.

“Aren’t I already using nicotine replacement products?” he asked astutely.

I gathered my thoughts and explained that while nicotine pouches are indeed a form of nicotine replacement, there are important caveats. Actual nicotine replacement therapy products are regulated by the [Food and Drug Administration](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/want-quit-smoking-fda-approved-and-fda-cleared-cessation-products-can-help) to help people quit smoking. In contrast, I explained that Zyn and other nicotine pouches are [commercial tobacco products](https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/nicotine-pouches/) that are regulated by the FDA but are not FDA-approved smoking cessation medications.

My patient was surprised, because he had not realized there was a difference, which is a common misunderstanding. This encounter proved pivotal in the direction I would take in my subsequent clinical encounters.

As an [addiction medicine physician](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Gb7borIAAAAJ&hl=en), I often talk with patients who use nicotine in various forms.

Understanding how these products differ and what we know about their relative risks can help people make more informed choices.

## Doing away with good/bad thinking

One of the most important distinctions I make when I talk to patients is distinguishing between the harms caused by nicotine itself and the harms caused by the way it is delivered.

Combustible tobacco products such as cigarettes expose users to [thousands of chemicals](https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/tobacco-products-ingredients-components/chemicals-every-puff-cigarette-smoke) produced by burning tobacco, while newer products such as vapes deliver nicotine without combustion.

But the lack of combustion does not make the newer products inherently safe. [Nicotine remains addictive](https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/health-effects-tobacco-use/nicotine-why-tobacco-products-are-addictive), and [studies have raised concerns about its cardiovascular effects](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms241914570), including changes in heart rate, blood pressure and underlying vascular function.

The long-term health effects of newer nicotine products – particularly nicotine pouches – are not yet well established.

As a result, discussions about which nicotine product is appropriate for a given person do not fall into categories of “good” or “bad.” Rather, they involve nuanced conversations with patients to help them reach their goals and reduce overall harm.

What’s more, the health implications of a nicotine product depend not only on what is in it, but also on who is using it, how they use it and what it replaces. Relative harms vary significantly when talking about a current tobacco smoker who switches to an e-cigarette compared with a nonsmoker who starts vaping. The same distinction matters for nicotine pouches: Their lower exposure to many toxic chemicals does not make them risk-free, particularly for adolescents and other nonsmokers who have not previously used nicotine.

## Relative harms

In 1965, 42.4% of the U.S. population smoked. By 2022, that [figure had dropped to 11.6%](https://www.lung.org/research/trends-in-lung-disease/tobacco-trends-brief/overall-smoking-trends).

This dramatic decline did not happen because of a single intervention, but through decades of [accumulating scientific evidence](https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco-surgeon-general-reports/about/history.html), [public education campaigns](https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/campaign/tips/about/impact/campaign-impact-results.html), [warning labels](https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/labeling-and-warning-statements-tobacco-products/cigarette-labeling-and-health-warning-requirements), restrictions on advertising, smoke-free policies, higher tobacco taxes and shifts in social norms. At the same time, the tobacco landscape has evolved, with noncombustible nicotine products such as e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches becoming increasingly prominent.

In the U.S., 6.5% of adults [reported using e-cigarettes](https://www.cdc.gov/nchs/products/databriefs/db524.htm) in 2023, while [past-year nicotine pouch use](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.amepre.2026.108393) rose from 3.4% in 2023 to 5.9% in 2024. This fast-growing trend makes it clear that the public is in need of a better understanding of the relative harms of nicotine products.

To be clear, the major source of cigarette-related harm is [burning tobacco](https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/tobacco-products-ingredients-components/chemicals-every-puff-cigarette-smoke), not simply the presence of nicotine.

Tobacco smoke contains thousands of chemicals, many of which are [toxic and carcinogenic](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41568-021-00423-4), culminating in [approximately 2.5 million cancer deaths](https://iarc2026conf.iarc.who.int/data/onglet27/module0/modalPreview.php?langue=fr&paramProjet=22269) per year worldwide.

Patients also often land in the hospital with complications related to tobacco use, including [chronic obstructive pulmonary disease](https://theconversation.com/more-than-140-000-americans-die-from-copd-each-year-heres-why-survival-depends-on-more-than-avoiding-smoking-277475) and cardiovascular disease.

While nicotine itself is the reason for dependence, the toxic mixture generated by burning tobacco leaves is what makes cigarette smoking so extraordinarily harmful.

## Nicotine products compared

So, where do vaping, [heated tobacco](https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/other-tobacco-products/heated-tobacco-products.html) – also known as “heat-not-burn products” – cigarettes and oral nicotine fall on the spectrum of safety?

- Electronic cigarettes – or vapes – generally contain fewer and lower levels of many toxic chemicals compared with cigarette smoke. However, inhaled aerosols can still contain harmful substances such as propylene glycol, which is often found in [certain medicines, cosmetics and food products](https://wwwn.cdc.gov/tsp/substances/ToxSubstance.aspx?toxid=240). While propylene glycol is classified as “generally safe” by the FDA for use in food, that designation does not establish that it is safe to inhale. The lungs process substances differently from the digestive system, and the health effects of chronic inhalation of propylene glycol through e-cigarette aerosol remain incompletely understood.
- [Heated tobacco products](https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/other-tobacco-products/heated-tobacco-products.html) such as processed tobacco sticks, loose-leaf chambers, tobacco capsules and pods, or carbon-tipped pods typically heat tobacco to lower temperatures as opposed to burning it. This can lead to lower exposure to harmful substances compared with conventional cigarettes. However, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention [considers any tobacco product harmful](https://www.cdc.gov/tobacco/other-tobacco-products/heated-tobacco-products.html), given that these products still deliver tobacco-derived nicotine and other toxins.
- An increasingly prominent product is the nicotine pouch, such as the brand-name product Zyn. Sales of nicotine pouches in the U.S. have increased substantially in recent years, [particularly since 2023](https://tobaccomonitoring.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/Nicotine-Pouch-Sales-Data-Brief_8.10.2025.pdf). Unlike traditional smokeless tobacco, nicotine pouches contain no tobacco leaf; instead, they contain nicotine, flavorings and other ingredients. Users typically place a pouch between the upper lip and gum, where nicotine is absorbed through the tissues of the mouth.

Nicotine pouches generally result in lower exposure to many toxic substances, given that there is no combustion or inhaled aerosols. However, they can deliver substantial amounts of nicotine. Depending on the product, a [single pouch may contain several milligrams of nicotine](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13318-021-00742-9) – comparable to or exceeding the amount of nicotine you would otherwise get from a cigarette. These products therefore [remain addictive](https://www.fda.gov/tobacco-products/health-effects-tobacco-use/nicotine-why-tobacco-products-are-addictive).

With all nicotine products, the relevant comparison is not “safe” versus “dangerous,” but rather “more harmful” versus “less harmful.

## FDA-approved nicotine replacement therapy

Nicotine replacement therapy, on the other hand, is an [FDA-approved medical treatment](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/consumer-updates/want-quit-smoking-fda-approved-and-fda-cleared-cessation-products-can-help) that delivers controlled, low amounts of nicotine without the many carcinogens and toxic chemicals found in tobacco smoke. These products come in the form of patches, gum, lozenges, nasal sprays and inhalers, intended to reduce cravings and withdrawal while helping people gradually move away from tobacco use.

Unlike nicotine replacement therapies, which are FDA-approved and supported by strong [evidence](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2022.0395) of effectiveness for smoking cessation, e-cigarettes are not FDA-approved cessation treatments, despite evidence that they can help some people quit smoking. Evidence for nicotine pouches as a cessation aid remains limited, and they have not been FDA-approved for this purpose.

Patterns of nicotine and tobacco use [also vary considerably across countries and populations](https://www.who.int/publications/b/81238), reflecting differences in culture, tobacco-control policies, product availability and patterns of use.

Similarly, access to smoking-cessation treatment and harm-reduction resources [varies substantially from country to country](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/7x18m7f9). In the U.K., for example, cessation services are integrated into the country’s National Health Service, while Australia provides [state-based "Quit” line services](https://www.quit.org.au/en) and permits regulated access to some nicotine vaping products through pharmacies. Many countries have limited or no comprehensive services focused on smoking cessation, and access to medications such as nicotine replacement therapy remains uneven.

## Putting nicotine risk in perspective

For people who do not use nicotine, there is little reason to start. For people who smoke, quitting remains the best option. But if quitting is not immediately achievable, moving away from combustible tobacco may reduce exposure to harmful chemicals in cigarette smoke.

The goal is not to label every nicotine product “good” or “bad,” but to help people understand the trade-offs – and to make choices that move them toward less harm and, ultimately, away from nicotine dependence.

*Emma Fenske does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Not all nicotine products are equally harmful. An addiction medicine physician explains how to parse the science.

title: In a culture obsessed with staying young, we ignore the many benefits of ageing
authors: Olivia Maurice, Cognitive Neuroscientist, Western Sydney University; University of Sydney
content:
Every morning, millions of people wake up hoping to look, think and feel younger than they did yesterday.

The [anti-ageing industry is worth hundreds of billions of dollars](https://www.forbes.com/sites/laiafarrangraves/2026/04/13/longevity-beauty-how-2026-is-redefining-skincare/), promising everything from “miracle” supplements to gene therapies. Few people embody this pursuit more visibly than entrepreneur Bryan Johnson, [whose quest to slow ageing and achieve “immortality”](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-30/biohacker-bryan-johnson-kate-tolo-living-forever/107089326) has gained global fascination.

Johnson has meticulously documented countless treatments in his biohacking regimen, including cosmetic enhancements, stem cell therapies, a total plasma replacement and, most recently, even cloning his own cells.

The message is clear: [ageing is something to defeat](https://www.theguardian.com/wellness/2026/jul/14/anti-ageing-science-longevity-culture).

But science tells a more complicated story.

While [some aspects of functioning become less efficient with age](https://www.racgp.org.au/getattachment/241138d1-7067-49e7-8844-916afdb5ba2c/attachment.aspx), others remain remarkably resilient. Some even improve. Far from being a period of inevitable decline, research shows later life can bring a variety of unexpected strengths.

## Ageing is not a linear process

Much of what we hear about ageing focuses on what becomes harder.

[Older adults often experience reductions](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cger.2013.07.002) in processing speed, working memory capacity, episodic memory retrieval and aspects of learning.

These changes are real and important, particularly when they affect everyday independence or signal neurodegenerative disease, such as dementia.

However, ageing research increasingly shows that cognitive ageing is not a one-size-fits-all. [Different abilities change at different rates](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cger.2013.07.002), while some remain stable or improve well into later life.

## The emotional advantages of ageing

One of the clearest examples of beneficial change is [the positivity effect](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00339). Research shows that older adults often pay more attention to, and remember, positive information compared to negative information.

This is not because they have poorer memory of negative events. Rather, this pattern of remembering [seems to be linked to changes in motivation and priorities](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cobeha.2017.07.009). As [some psychologists suggest](https://doi.org/10.1093/geront/gnab116), older people become more focused on emotionally meaningful experiences because they perceive time as more limited.

This shift can have benefits.

Healthy older adults often report [greater emotional stability](https://doi.org/10.1037/emo0000734), [improved ability to self-regulate](https://doi.org/10.1080/13607860902989661), [stronger focus on meaningful relationships](https://doi.org/10.1177/0265407510391362), and even [increased life satisfaction](https://doi.org/10.3390/bs13040293).

In other words, ageing can bring a greater ability to prioritise what matters.

## Experience creates cognitive strengths

Although some aspects of cognition do decline with age, others remain stable. These aspects of cognition can become relative strengths as we accumulate knowledge, learn new strategies and gain experience over our lifetime.

Research shows [ageing is associated with changes in emotional strategy use](https://doi.org/10.1093/geronb/gbad021). This includes a greater ability to accept events and to take perspective, such as when dealing with something sad or stressful.

[Ageing is also associated](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13423-026-02968-7) with changes in [metacognition](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-021-00089-5) – our ability to monitor, evaluate and regulate our own thinking.

Decades of experience can help people improve awareness of their strengths and limitations on certain tasks. As a result, we get more efficient at selecting the right strategy, compensating for what we find challenging, and adapting our approach when circumstances change.
