In everyday life, this ability to “[know how we think](https://www.bbc.co.uk/bitesize/articles/zjgs3qt)” may be just as important as speed or accuracy on a test measured in a lab. A younger brain may be faster, but an older brain can be wiser.

## Ageing and self-regulation

Another often overlooked aspect of ageing is the potential for improvements in how we self-regulate.

Healthy older people show relative strengths in [managing emotions](https://doi.org/10.1080/07317115.2022.2128706), [socially and emotionally meaningful decision-making](https://doi.org/10.20900/agmr20230003) and [adaptive goal prioritisation](https://doi.org/10.2190/AG.74.2.a).

This means that as we age, goals start to change. Rather than having expansive, future-oriented goals, older people optimise available resources to prioritise wellbeing, independence and core relationships.

My own doctoral research examined whether lifelong experiences, [such as multilingualism](https://researchers.westernsydney.edu.au/en/studentTheses/the-costs-and-benefits-of-multilingual-experience-across-sensory-/), contribute to these adaptive changes. Across adulthood, multilingual experience was not associated with a universal advantage.

However, the findings suggested more specific patterns. We found that multilingual experience had certain benefits for working memory, executive function and self-regulating behaviour and emotions, particularly later in life.

***Read more: [If AI can translate instantly, why learn another language?](https://theconversation.com/if-ai-can-translate-instantly-why-learn-another-language-280310)***

## Rethinking ‘successful ageing’

There’s a growing view in research of [ageing as a process of selective adaptation](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-32091-x). The idea is that some of our cognitive abilities decline while others are maintained or even get stronger.

The goal of healthy ageing should not be to restore youth.

The longevity movement often frames ageing as a biological enemy – something to slow or reverse. But a more realistic goal is supporting “[healthspan](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-77302-0_10)”: maintaining physical health, independence, cognition and quality of life through later adulthood.

There are [evidence-based approaches to support healthy ageing](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0140-6736(24%2901296-0), and they won’t surprise you:

- regular physical activity
- lifelong learning, such as languages or new skills
- social connection
- good sleep
- healthy diet
- cardiovascular health
- managing sensory health such as hearing and vision.

These strategies don’t stop ageing, but they help people age better.

Ageing certainly changes the brain. But many of the qualities we value most – perspective, emotional stability, resilience and wisdom – often emerge precisely because we’ve lived for more years.

The question isn’t how we can live *longer*. What we really should be asking is: how do we age *well*?

*Olivia Maurice does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Ageing isn’t all downhill – science shows we gain more than wrinkles.

title: How studying astronauts could help tackle ageing on Earth
authors: Samantha Jones, Postdoctoral Research Associate in Musculoskeletal and Ageing Science, Faculty of Health and Life Sciences, University of Liverpool; Anne McArdle, Professor of Musculoskeletal and Ageing Science, University of Liverpool
content:
Astronauts who undergo long-duration spaceflight aboard the International Space Station often return with health problems that resemble some age-related conditions in people on Earth.

Remarkably, [some of this decline reverses](https://faseb.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1096/fj.201801625r) within months of their return but others persist. This raises an intriguing question: what can be learned from these rapid changes and could they help prevent or reverse aspects of [age-related decline](https://theconversation.com/topics/age-related-decline-33683) on Earth?

That question has turned space into a laboratory for ageing research. Spaceflight reproduces many features of ageing. Astronauts also experience unusual conditions, including very low gravity, increased radiation and disrupted sleep. Even so, changes that usually develop over decades on Earth can appear within weeks or months in space, giving scientists an opportunity to observe some ageing-related processes in fast-forward.

A [2026 study](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/acel.70360), which tracked four astronauts during the nine-day Axiom-2 mission, examined chemical markers attached to DNA that can be used to estimate biological age. This is an estimate of how old the body appears to be based on molecular changes, rather than the number of years a person has lived.

The astronauts’ estimated biological age increased during the mission and began to fall after they returned to Earth. This does not mean that they physically aged by years in a matter of days. With only four participants, the study cannot provide firm conclusions, but it shows how rapidly the body can respond to the conditions of spaceflight.

Why would leaving gravity behind affect the body in ways that resemble ageing? On Earth, muscles, bones, and the cardiovascular system and other organs are adapted to function under the constant pull of gravity. That continual mechanical load helps keep these systems healthy, although their function often declines later in life. In space, many of those demands disappear.

## When muscles age in fast-forward

Skeletal muscle provides one of the clearest examples. Astronauts lose muscle mass and strength at a startling rate in very low gravity, even while exercising for around two hours a day to attempt to limit the effects.

Some of the biological processes involved may overlap with those associated with [sarcopenia](https://academic.oup.com/ageing/article/48/1/16/5126243), the age-related loss of muscle strength and mass that increases the risk of frailty, falls and loss of independence.

Scientists are still working out how closely muscle loss in space resembles sarcopenia, because similar effects can arise through different biological processes. The crucial difference is timescale. That compression is exactly what drew our team to space.

Through our UK Space Agency-funded [MicroAge mission](https://www.liverpool.ac.uk/life-course-and-medical-sciences/research/microage-in-partnership-with-the-uk-space-agency/), we sent lab-grown human muscle constructs to the International Space Station.

These miniature muscles, roughly the size of a grain of rice, were engineered from human muscle stem cells. Using lab-grown tissue, rather than relying solely on the limited number of astronauts available for study, allowed us to compare muscle adaptations in very low gravity with those seen during ageing on Earth. It also allowed us to carry out early tests of possible ways to protect muscle. If some of the same mechanisms are involved in both settings, space could provide a useful opportunity to study years of biological change over the course of months for a single mission.

Our follow-up mission, [MicroAge II](https://www.liverpool.ac.uk/life-course-and-medical-sciences/research/microage-in-partnership-with-the-uk-space-agency/microage-ii/), will explore the biology of this decline in greater detail. It focuses on mitochondria, the structures inside cells that produce most of the energy those cells need. Problems with mitochondria are recognised as one process involved in muscle ageing on Earth.

MicroAge II will investigate whether similar changes to their structure and function also contribute to rapid muscle loss in space. Why does any of this have significance beyond the space station?

Loss of muscle mass and function is one of the most consequential aspects of growing older. It underlies frailty, falls and the loss of independence that many people fear, [yet effective treatments remain limited](https://theconversation.com/what-happens-to-strength-balance-stamina-and-reflexes-as-you-age-and-what-you-can-do-about-it-289004). Testing potential interventions in populations that age over decades is inevitably slow. Space research will hopefully help scientists identify relevant biological processes and test early ideas more rapidly.

Experiments in space cannot replace final clinical studies involving older people, however. Any treatment suggested by this work would still require extensive testing on Earth to establish whether it is safe and effective but would identify potential drug candidates far more quickly.

*Samantha Jones receives funding from UK Space Agency.*

*Anne McArdle currently receives research funding from the Medical Research Council, the Biotechnology and Biological Sciences Research Council and UK Space Agency.*
description: Spaceflight can reproduce some changes associated with later life within weeks, offering clues about muscle loss, frailty and recovery.

title: A never-ending childhood of malaria
authors: Hannah Ritchie
content:
I’ve never had malaria, but I know several people who have. They describe it as one of the worst experiences of their life.

What starts out feeling like the flu — which is bad enough — can quickly progress into something far worse. The body swings from intense fever and sweats to chills deep enough to make you shake uncontrollably. Everything aches, from your muscles and joints to the pounding headache that makes it impossible to think clearly. Your body is so fatigued that it’s a battle to make it to the bathroom when the nausea and vomiting arrive.

That’s what a pretty standard infection feels like. For some, it goes much further. Here is how [one account](https://www.gatesnotes.com/what-malaria-feels-like-mosquito-week) describes it:

> “I awoke to what felt like lightning going through my legs, and then spreading through my body and in my head. Probably the worst headache, body aches, and chills you could possibly imagine. It felt like I was being stung repeatedly by an electric shock gun and could barely control my movements. The pain was so intense; I actually believed I was dying, literally crying out in pain so bad that I was taken to a 24-hour clinic that night at 3am.”

Imagine (or remember) what a bout of this pain feels like. Then imagine having to suffer through that more than 100 times. That’s the reality for some children in the world.

I often donate to the [Against Malaria Foundation](https://www.againstmalaria.com/). When I do so, I become obsessed with one single metric: the number of lives my money might save. That’s because malaria kills a lot of people: over 600,000 every year, and [most of them are children](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/malaria-deaths-by-age).

While focusing on deaths, I gloss over the number of *infections* that donated bed nets might prevent. Donating £10,000 saves around four lives and prevents 2,500 infections.1 Saving four lives is great. But so, too, is sparing 2,500 people from the awful experiences described above. That suffering is what these donations are protecting against.

Before digging into the data, I didn’t quite grasp how brutal the non-fatal side of this illness is. It’s estimated that there are around [280 million cases](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/estimated-number-of-malaria-cases) of malaria every year. That means one case for roughly every 30 people.

In some parts of the world, though, those rates are much, much higher.

![Choropleth world map of new malaria cases per 100 people in 2023 where the highest rates are concentrated in central and eastern sub‑Saharan Africa while Europe, North America, Australia and much of S](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/2d4f1142-e4e2-488b-4e9a-be288bc0ab00/w=906)

Click to explore

The map shows how concentrated malaria is. It is still a significant problem across much of the tropics — including South and Southeast Asia, and South America — but its focal point is Africa.

We also get this perspective from the chart below. In countries like Benin, Mozambique, Nigeria, and Sierra Leone, there are roughly 30 new cases of malaria for every 100 people, every year.

That’s around 100 times higher than in high-burden countries in other regions, such as India or Colombia.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/new-cases-of-malaria-per-100-people.png?tab=discrete-bar&time=latest&country=BEN~CAF~MOZ~COD~NGA~SLE~CIV~UGA~PAK~IDN~IND~COL~PER~BRA~TZA~GHA&mapSelect=BEN~CAF~MOZ~COD~NGA~SLE~CIV~UGA)

When I first saw this data, my initial thought was: if there are 30 cases per 100 people, that means around one-third of Nigerians or Beninese must be infected *every year*. That in itself is quite staggering.

Yet that is quite far from the truth. Looking at this data by age group, we see that malaria infections are incredibly common among children; much less so among adults, who have built up immunity.

In Benin, there are 98 cases for every 100 children under five years old. In Nigeria, 79 cases. Almost one case for every child.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/malaria-cases-per-100-by-age.png?tab=discrete-bar&time=latest&country=~BEN)

But again, this doesn’t mean that every child in Benin gets malaria once a year. It’s an average: some regions see much less transmission of the disease, while children living in very high-burden areas will often be infected five or six times over.

Studies in high-transmission areas of Burkina Faso find that the number of episodes among children reaches up to six per year.2 In parts of Uganda, the median was more than 5 infections per year.3 That’s roughly once every two months. You’ve barely recovered from the previous infection before you’re floored with another one.

> In Benin, there are 98 cases for every 100 children under five years old.

One of the most extensive (and tragic) studies I’ve seen followed 111 children in Senegal over an average span of 17 years.4 The children were monitored almost daily for malaria infection. The median child experienced 43 attacks of malaria over the course of their childhood.5

In the chart, you can see the number of malaria infections each child experienced over that period, with one bar representing one child.

What’s staggering is that four children were infected 100 times or more. The highest suffered through 112 episodes. Even the boy who experienced the fewest was still infected 11 times.

![Bar chart of the number of malaria infections recorded in 111 children in the Dielmo cohort in Senegal where bars are ranked from highest to lowest to show the wide variation in lifetime infections — ](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/a20566dd-0ed5-4104-c6bb-25d14f6acd00/w=2550)

This level of suffering is hard for me to get my head around. For most children growing up in areas with very high rates of malaria, their childhood is a constant and relentless series of malaria episodes. The symptoms themselves must be hard to deal with. But the toll this takes on the body is extreme, too. It is not surprising that so many [become malnourished](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/share-of-children-younger-than-5-who-suffer-from-stunting) and have their development hindered.

> The median child experienced 43 attacks of malaria over the course of their childhood.

This extensive study spanned decades, from 1990 to 2015. Many living there didn’t have access to insecticide-treated bed nets or other preventive measures. Over the course of those 25 years, people did start to get them. Infection rates fell 25-fold as a result. Clearly, this is a problem we can do something about. As it turns out, it can be done fairly cheaply, too. An insecticide-treated bed net costs just $2.

Many children and families in the world still lack this basic tool. That is why I’m happy to donate to organizations trying to change that.

I would love to see humanity beat malaria in my lifetime. Not just to stop the 600,000 deaths that happen every year, but to give millions of kids something back that no chart can capture: their childhood.
description: How often do people in high-burden areas get malaria? Studies suggest that many children can experience five or more malaria infections a year.

title: Eating less protein may ‘slow’ ageing. But here’s why the evidence isn’t clear-cut
authors: Sharayah Carter, Lecturer Human Biosciences (Nutrition and Dietetics), RMIT University
content:
Protein powders. Protein yoghurt. Protein snack bars. Protein is everywhere. Supermarket shelves and social media are full of messages encouraging us to eat more of this nutrient.

But now, a [new review](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpblue.2026.100079) of over 350 studies suggests eating less protein may be linked to healthier ageing, by slowing down the biological process of ageing in cells.

These messages can sometimes feel confusing. How much protein should you eat?

Importantly, most of the evidence in the new review comes from animal studies, not humans. So let’s take a look at what it actually means for you.

## First, how much protein do you need?

Protein is a nutrient made up of amino acids, and found in a wide range of foods. It is [essential](https://dietitiansaustralia.org.au/health-advice/protein) for maintaining muscles, repairing tissues and supporting overall health.

Australian dietary guidelines [recommend](https://www.eatforhealth.gov.au/nutrient-reference-values/chronic-disease/macronutrient-balance) around 15–25% of our daily energy comes from protein. Good sources include legumes, nuts, fish, eggs, dairy and lean meat.

Data shows most Australians already meet these [recommendations](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/health/food-and-nutrition/usual-nutrient-intakes/latest-release).

***Read more: [What happens if I eat too much protein?](https://theconversation.com/what-happens-if-i-eat-too-much-protein-261849)***

## What the new study looked at

The [new research](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpblue.2026.100079) brings together evidence from animal and some human studies to better understand how restricting protein (and specific amino acids) influences the biology of ageing.

Overall, the evidence suggests eating less protein changes the way the body uses energy, helps cells remove damaged components, and reduces the build-up of ageing cells. Together, these biological changes are associated with healthier ageing and longer lifespan in animal studies.

However, it’s still not clear exactly why these benefits occur. They may be due to eating less protein overall, less animal protein, or fewer specific amino acids – or simply eating a healthier diet.

Importantly, the review was designed to understand the biology of ageing, not whether people should change how much protein they eat.

## The strongest evidence comes from laboratory animals

The most convincing findings came from studies in mice, rats, flies and yeast. Animals with lower-protein diets often lived longer and showed signs of healthier ageing.

But laboratory animals live in tightly controlled environments where researchers can precisely manipulate diets over their entire lifespan. That level of control simply isn’t possible in humans.

Human biology is also far more complex, meaning findings in mice and rats do not always translate directly to people.

The review also suggests total protein may not be the whole story. Restricting specific amino acids, the building blocks of protein – particularly methionine, isoleucine and valine – produced many of the same benefits in animal studies as reducing total protein.

## Studying humans is much harder

Human evidence remains limited. The review discusses intervention studies in which low-protein diets were compared with participants’ usual diets. However, these studies lasted only a few weeks, making it impossible to know whether restricting protein influenced people’s lifespan or healthy ageing.

And the picture becomes much more complicated in humans. Higher-protein diets can help preserve muscle mass, particularly in older adults, and when combined with resistance exercise, can reduce the risk of frailty and [sarcopenia](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.metabol.2023.155637) (loss of muscle mass and strength as we age).

***Read more: [How much protein do I need as I get older? And do I need supplements to get enough?](https://theconversation.com/how-much-protein-do-i-need-as-i-get-older-and-do-i-need-supplements-to-get-enough-215695)***

Eating more [protein](https://doi.org/10.3389/fendo.2018.00443) can also help people feel fuller for longer, making it useful for managing weight in those who are living with obesity.

But people don’t eat protein in isolation. They eat food.

For example, eating a lot of legumes and nuts will give you protein alongside fibre, healthy fats and other nutrients. But if you have a high-protein diet that comes mainly from red and processed meat, you may also be eating a lot of saturated fats and salt.

Large studies have linked eating a lot of animal protein – particularly red and processed meat – with [worse health](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-76357-2) and [early death](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.2790). But these studies can’t prove protein itself is responsible.

This is why it’s difficult to separate the effects of protein itself from the foods providing it, or someone’s overall diet. The other factors may explain why some findings about protein seem to conflict.

## Longevity is about more than protein

Research into long-living populations also shows why we should be cautious about focusing on one nutrient alone.

The [Mediterranean diet](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnphys.2026.100015) has the strongest evidence for healthy ageing – but it isn’t low in protein. It contains moderate amounts of protein from legumes, fish and nuts, alongside plenty of vegetables, fruits, wholegrains and olive oil, while limiting red and processed meat.

By comparison, the traditional [Okinawan diet](https://glycemicindex.com/2022/05/the-okinawan-diet-japanese-equivalent-to-the-mediterranean-diet/) from Japan – which is also associated with healthy ageing – contains relatively little protein. But it emphasises plant foods (such as sweet potato and tofu) and is low in calories.

Both diets are associated with living longer. They show that isolating protein alone may miss the bigger picture.

Longevity is shaped by much more than diet. Regular [physical activity, good sleep](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eclinm.2025.103741), strong [social connections](https://doi.org/10.1002/lim2.91), managing stress and not smoking all reduce our risk of dying early.

Diet is one important piece of the puzzle, but longevity also depends on who you are, your stage of life, your overall diet, the source of your protein and your general health.

## So should you eat less protein?

Not based on this review.

This review explains how protein restriction might affect ageing in laboratory animals. But it highlights how much we still don’t know about how this might translate into dietary advice for humans.

The relationship between protein and longevity is far more nuanced than simply “less is better”.

For now, the strongest evidence still supports meeting current protein recommendations, particularly as we age. Rather than chasing the latest nutrition headline, aim to choose mostly minimally processed protein foods as part of an overall healthy diet.

*Sharayah Carter does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: A new review links eating less protein to longer lifespans and improved metabolism. But lots of this evidence comes from animals, not humans.

title: Another benefit of regular sleep
authors: Tianyi Huang · eLife
content:
Benjamin Franklin’s famous quotation – “Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise” – underscores the importance of sleep-wake patterns to our health and well-being. Of all the phenomena that are influenced by the 24 hour light-dark cycle, the sleep-wake cycle is the best known, but many other biological processes central to health are also influenced. However, empirical evidence about the impact that disruptions to sleep-wake patterns have on human health remains sparse and is mostly limited to studies on shift workers, despite an increase in other forms of disruption (notably higher levels of artificial light at night and increased use of mobile media in bed).

In recent years, an increasing number of studies have looked at the impact of sleep regularity (and irregularity) on aspects of health besides sleep quantity and quality, often made possible by the availability of wearable technology that is able to monitor rest-activity cycles in large numbers of people. Studies have found evidence that sleep irregularity is associated with a higher incidence of obesity (Patel et al., 2014), depression (Fang et al., 2021), cardiovascular disease (Huang et al., 2020) and other chronic disease outcomes.

Now, in eLife, Matthew Pase, Andree-Ann Baril and colleagues – including Lachlan Cribb, Ramon Sha and Stephanie Yiallourou, all of Monash University, as joint first authors – go one step further by linking sleep regularity with all-cause and cause-specific mortality in a large UK population (Cribb et al., 2023). Between 2013 and 2015, a total of more than 106,000 participants in the UK wore a watch-like device called an accelerometer over seven consecutive days. Based on the signals from this device it was possible to tell when the participants were asleep, sedentary, or active. Cribb et al. then derived a novel metric called the Sleep Regularity Index (SRI) to quantify day-to-day consistency in sleep-wake schedules. This metric is an estimate of how likely it is that a person is in the same state (that is, either awake or asleep) at any two time points 24 hours apart, with higher SRI values indicating higher sleep regularity. The researchers also noted how many of the participants subsequently died (via data from the UK national death register).

Over a median follow-up of 7.1 years, some 3,010 participants died, with 1,701 of these deaths being due to cancers and 616 being due to cardiovascular disease. Compared with those who had a medium SRI value, the top 5% (that is, the most regular sleepers) had 10% lower all-cause mortality, and the bottom 5% (that is, the most irregular sleepers) had 53% higher mortality. The association appeared nonlinear, with stronger associations observed for the increased mortality with more irregular sleep. Similar nonlinear patterns were observed when Cribb et al. examined cancer mortality and cardiovascular disease mortality separately.

The work by Cribb et al. is consistent with recent studies on sleep regularity and mortality from the US and Japan, although these findings are based on a smaller sample size (Chung et al., 2023a) or on self-reported sleep regularity (Omichi et al., 2022). Other studies found that sleep regularity was a stronger predictor for mortality than sleep duration or sleep apnea (Chung et al., 2023b; Windred et al., 2023). Interestingly, a genome-wide association study for sleep traits (Jones et al., 2019) reported a heritability estimate of 2.8% for sleep regularity, compared with 19.0% for sleep duration and 22.3% for fragmented sleep: this suggests that it may be easier to modify sleep regularity via interventions than it would be to modify other sleep traits because sleep regularity is less genetically determined.

Promoting sleep regularity is not a new idea in the area of ‘sleep hygiene’, and encouraging regular sleep schedules is also an essential component in cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (Sletten et al., 2023). From the behavioral perspective, promoting sleep regularity may also enhance the time-of-day effect of other behaviors, such as time-restricted eating and exercise. However, promoting sleep regularity for broader health promotion and disease prevention has not been tested in intervention studies and requires additional evidence from future investigations.

In summary, the study by Cribb et al. adds to the emerging evidence for the potential benefits of sleep regularity on chronic disease risk and mortality. The findings, in conjunction with prior evidence, provide a strong foundation to answer the following question: would public health interventions to improve sleep regularity causally lead to reductions in chronic disease and premature deaths at the population level?
description: A large observational study has found that irregular sleep-wake patterns are associated with a higher risk of overall mortality, and also mortality from cancers and cardiovascular disease.

title: Where humans build, mosquitoes follow – bringing dengue, West Nile and other diseases with them
authors: Kylee Rae Noel, Postdoctoral Research Associate in Entomology, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Sadie Jane Ryan, Professor of Medical Geography, University of Florida
content:
A mosquito buzzing in your backyard may seem like a minor annoyance. But these tiny insects, with their taste for human blood, are increasingly appearing in areas where they were once rare or absent, and that’s raising concerns about the spread of mosquito-borne diseases, including [West Nile](https://theconversation.com/west-nile-virus-season-returns-a-medical-epidemiologist-explains-how-its-transmitted-and-how-you-can-avoid-it-236382), [Zika](https://www.cdc.gov/zika/about/index.html) and [dengue fever](https://theconversation.com/dengue-carrying-mosquitoes-expand-their-reach-into-new-territories-including-florida-291837).

Florida’s struggles with dengue fever in 2026 should be a warning.

Hillsborough County, home to Tampa, had seen [more than 350 dengue cases](https://www.cdc.gov/dengue/data-research/facts-stats/current-data.html), at least [one of them fatal](https://www.cidrap.umn.edu/dengue/tampa-woman-dies-dengue-florida-fights-surge-cases), by late October. Miami-Dade County had reported [more than 200 cases](https://www.cdc.gov/dengue/data-research/facts-stats/current-data.html), and the statewide number was still rising in what has been described as the [largest dengue outbreak in modern Florida history](https://www.wtsp.com/article/news/health/hillsborough-county-dengue-fever-outbreak/67-fbba8479-4f32-49aa-9b9f-088f8ef700d1). More than 400 of the over 700 Florida cases, including many of those in Hillsborough County and at least seven in the Orlando area, were listed as locally acquired from mosquitoes in the area.

Climate change is part of the reason people in many parts of the country are seeing more mosquitoes. Rising global temperatures and [shorter winters](https://theconversation.com/why-winter-cold-spells-are-getting-milder-288038) expand the [area suitable for mosquitoes](https://doi.org/10.1093/jme/tjaa135) to live in and transmit viruses that cause diseases. [Climate change also brings](https://theconversation.com/trumps-epa-decides-climate-change-doesnt-endanger-public-health-the-evidence-says-otherwise-275619) increasingly erratic storm systems, heat and rainfall patterns that leave standing water, creating [conditions ideal for mosquitoes](https://www.tampabay.com/news/health/2026/10/09/dengue-fever-cases-florida-hillsborough-tampa/) to breed.

The other major factor shaping where mosquitoes live, often overlooked, is humans themselves.

We study [entomology](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=_AglZHgAAAAJ&hl=en) and [medical geography](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=pPLqtm0AAAAJ&hl=en), including the spread of mosquito-borne diseases. To understand why you may be seeing more mosquitoes, and why communities like Hillsborough County are [spending millions of dollars](https://floridapolitics.com/archives/823787-dengue-response-costs-surge-past-6m-in-hillsborough-county/) on attempts to control them, start by looking close to home.

## Mosquitoes follow when humans move in

Mosquitoes such as *Aedes aegypti* – the primary transmitter of pathogens that cause dengue fever, [yellow fever](https://www.cdc.gov/yellow-fever/causes-and-spread/index.html), [Chikungunya](https://www.cdc.gov/chikungunya/about/index.html) and Zika in the Americas – likely [arrived in the U.S. with the slave trade](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pntd.0012110). Both *Aedes aegypti* and *Aedes albopictus*, a transmitter of many of the same diseases but a more recent arrival in the U.S., are moved by the global shipping network, which can take them to new locations and reintroduce them in parts of their ranges where they may have been controlled in the past.

*Aedes aegypti’s* habits, including its ability to [use household environments](https://hcfl.gov/newsroom/2026/10/20/hillsborough-county-treating-for-mosquitoes-by-air-week-of-oct-20-23) for living and breeding, have made it a very successful and established invader where climate conditions permit.

A flowerpot saucer, clogged gutter, discarded tire, birdbath or even a bottle cap can collect enough water for mosquito larvae to develop. A single *Aedes aegypti* mosquito can lay more than [100 eggs at a time](https://www.denguevirusnet.com/life-cycle-of-aedes-aegypti.html) up to five times during its lifespan, which is only about a month.

As suburban neighborhoods expand, so do opportunities for mosquitoes to breed and find humans for their meals.

Across the United States, new housing developments create thousands of these small water-holding containers and bring together the two things these mosquitoes need: standing water and people.

This combination allows them to spread through transportation networks, establishing populations far from their original ranges, and explains why mosquito expansion is often linked to patterns of human movement and development.

*Aedes albopictus*, originally native to Southeast Asia and [now found in all habitable continents](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13071-022-05413-5), provides a striking example of this spread. These mosquitoes [arrived in the U.S.](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/00001699.htm) mostly [because of human actions](https://doi.org/10.1186/s13071-022-05413-5). They stowed away on boats and other vehicles, often riding in used tires or lucky bamboo.

Their early dispersal in the U.S. has been linked to the [interstate highway system](https://doi.org/10.3201/eid0303.970309). By 2017, *Aedes albopictus* was documented in [1,368 counties across 40 states](https://doi.org/10.1093/jme/tjx088), and it has continued to expand across much of the eastern and central U.S.

One of Iowa’s first established *Aedes albopictus* populations, for example, appeared in the [Des Moines metropolitan area](https://doi.org/10.1093/jme/tjag052), where it has continued to grow and expand to other communities.

Its spread from southeast Asia all the way to the U.S. Midwest demonstrates how globalization and suburban growth can create opportunities for mosquitoes.

## US’s most common mosquito threat: West Nile

[West Nile virus](https://www.cdc.gov/west-nile-virus/about/index.html) remains the most widespread mosquito-borne disease in the continental United States. It is primarily transmitted by [*Culex* mosquitoes](https://www.cdc.gov/mosquitoes/about/culex-mosquitoes.html), including common house mosquitoes, which are found in much of the country.

*Culex* mosquitoes can breed in a wide range of habitats, including storm drains, roadside ditches, retention ponds, wetlands and other standing water. Their ability to thrive in both urban and rural environments has helped make West Nile virus an enduring public health concern in many states.

Because *Culex* mosquitoes are already established across much of the country, climate change may not necessarily introduce them to new regions. Instead, research is increasingly focused on how changing temperatures and precipitation patterns could influence their abundance, seasonal activity and ability to transmit disease.

Researchers found that New York state’s season with temperatures suitable for mosquitoes to transmit West Nile virus [lengthened by an average of 20 days](https://doi.org/10.1101/2025.08.01.667982) between 1999 and 2024.

A study conducted by one of us, Sadie Ryan, showed that in Florida, all 67 counties had a [suitable season for mosquitoes spreading West Nile virus](http://doi.org/10.1177/15303667261426902) for five or more months in 2000, and 2.33 million people in Florida experienced a nine-month-long season. By the 2030s, as temperatures warm, the study projects that around 70% of Florida’s population is likely to have a chance of getting West Nile nine months out of the year.

In 2025, for example, Florida took longer to cool down in the fall than usual, leaving moderate temperatures and enough standing water that *Aedes* mosquitoes could [remain active late into the year](https://www.fpren.org/2025-10-21/how-floridas-weather-swings-are-shaping-mosquito-season). Florida saw a rise in dengue cases.

Longer warm seasons means mosquitoes will become a growing public health issue, and controlling them will become increasingly crucial.

*Sadie Jane Ryan receives funding from The National Science Foundation (NSF), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and Wellcome Trust.*

*Kylee Rae Noel does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Disease-carrying mosquitoes are moving deeper into the US. Climate change is only part of the problem.

title: How much development aid is spent on climate change?
authors: Hannah Ritchie
content:
This is a question I’ve had for a while. I care a lot about climate change. I also care a lot about basic health and development programs in the world’s poorest countries — vitamin supplementation, nutrition programs, antiretroviral treatment for HIV, and bed nets treated against malaria.

These two priorities could easily come into conflict. With a fixed aid budget, every dollar spent on climate programs is one less dollar for everything else. And with [large cuts](https://ourworldindata.org/data-insights/foreign-aid-contributions-fell-in-2025-amongst-almost-all-of-the-top-10-donors) to foreign aid in the last few years, that budget is shrinking.

For a long time, I didn’t have good data to see whether this tension was real. But someone recently pointed me to the [RioMarkers database](https://data-explorer.oecd.org/vis?lc=en&df[ds]=dsDisseminateFinalDMZ&df[id]=DSD_RIOMRKR%40DF_RIOMARKERS&df[ag]=OECD.DCD.FSD&dq=DAC_EC..1000..2.10...Q._T..&lom=LASTNPERIODS&lo=2&to[TIME_PERIOD]=false), which tags aid projects according to whether they target environmental outcomes under the Rio Conventions (which include biodiversity, climate change mitigation, climate change adaptation, and desertification).1

Using it, we’ve constructed data on the amount of development aid allocated to climate-related projects, and how that compares with aid for other causes.

The headline statistic is that around one-fifth of development aid is now coded as climate-related.2

But the “climate-related” label is not as straightforward as it might seem. Some of these projects look like ones that would have happened regardless of climate change. Untangling how many matters for anyone concerned about where aid is being spent, regardless of whether their focus is on health, development, or climate.

# How much foreign aid is climate-related?

Development aid comes in two forms. *Bilateral* aid flows from one country directly to another. *Multilateral* aid has a middleman; donors pool money with international organizations such as the World Bank or the World Health Organization, which then run programs themselves.

The RioMarkers database covers only **bilateral aid**, which makes up around **90% of global development aid**. That’s what I’ll focus on here.

In 2024, donors committed around $210 billion as bilateral aid.

Around 31% of that went to things that aren’t specific to a project, such as hosting refugees in donor countries, administration, budget support, and debt relief. These can’t be coded as climate or non-climate-related projects, and are termed “non-allocable aid”. This is shown in the chart.

The remaining 69%, around $145 billion, went to specific projects. The second bar breaks this down into climate- and non-climate-related projects.

![Stacked bar chart of 2024 bilateral development aid where about a third of allocable aid, $50 billion of $145 billion, goes to climate-related projects. Of the $210 billion total, $65 billion is non-a](https://ourworldindata.org/cdn-cgi/imagedelivery/qLq-8BTgXU8yG0N6HnOy8g/89f8a1db-ad3e-45a8-bcdc-d8d26cd9c600/w=1620)

Around **one-third** of this funding — $50 billion — was committed to climate-related projects in 2024.

These projects can fall into two categories. **Mitigation** aims to reduce or avoid greenhouse gas emissions; think investments in clean energy, stopping deforestation, or low-carbon transport. **Adaptation** helps countries deal with the impacts of climate change: flood defenses, drought-resilient crops, or more reliable water supplies.

> The headline statistic is that around one-fifth of development aid is now coded as climate-related.

Many projects count as both; they make communities more resilient to disasters while reducing emissions at the same time. Restoring mangroves, for example, can protect coastlines during storms, but also store carbon.

The second bar shows the split between mitigation-only, adaptation-only, and both. It’s roughly even, with mitigation-only projects making up slightly more than the others.

Putting all of this together, in 2024, climate-related projects made up:

- a third of bilateral, project-specific aid;
- almost one-quarter of all bilateral aid (including the non-allocable parts);
- around one-fifth of all development aid.

This last number assumes that no multilateral aid is given to climate projects, which seems unlikely. So the true share is probably slightly higher.

# How has the amount spent on climate aid changed over time?

The RioMarkers data goes back to 2010. Then, around $22 billion globally was committed to climate-related projects. It’s worth noting that a significant share — around a third — of allocable aid wasn’t screened for being climate-related, so this is likely to be an underestimate.

The share of allocable aid that wasn’t screened declined substantially in the early 2010s and has remained below 10% since 2014.

By 2024, climate-related aid had increased to $50 billion.

You can see this in the chart below, which again breaks global bilateral project aid into climate and non-climate-related projects.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/aid-climate-mitigation-adaptation.png)

Total development aid, though, has also increased over this period. What if we look at the *share* of aid going to climate programs?

You can see this relative breakdown in the chart below. In 2010, around 18% went to climate-related projects (which, again, might be an underestimate for the reason above). By 2024, it had grown to 34%.

The type of projects has also changed. In 2010, most climate funding was allocated to mitigation projects. But over time, adaptation has become more prominent, and today, programs that include *some* form of adaptation outspend those focused solely on mitigation.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/aid-climate-mitigation-adaptation.png?stackMode=relative)

# What counts as climate-related aid?

What does this 34% figure for 2024 actually include?

The RioMarkers database not only codes a project as mitigation or adaptation, but also as having climate change as its primary or secondary objective. A project with climate as its main objective probably wouldn’t exist in a world without climate change. One with it as secondary might still go ahead for other reasons; the climate benefits are a bonus.

As you can see in the chart, more than half of climate-related funding goes to projects where it’s only a secondary objective. All funding for these projects is counted in its full value, not just the share we might attribute to climate.

It’s hard to know the counterfactual, but many of these programs would probably have gone ahead regardless. If we only counted projects with climate as their main objective, climate’s share of bilateral project aid would fall from 34% to 13%.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/foreign-aid-climate-main-secondary.png)

Looking at individual projects in the database, we started to see why drawing this line is complicated.

Japan committed around $310 million to Iraq for its Samawah Water Supply Improvement Project, which is building climate-resilient water infrastructure in a drought-prone area. It’s tagged as an adaptation project, with climate as the main objective. But basic water supplies in a region prone to drought seem like a core development need. Perhaps it would have been funded anyway.

France provided $122 million to Tanzania to build its Kakono hydroelectric power plant. It provides low-carbon electricity, which has an obvious link to climate. In the database, climate is coded as a primary objective. But access to energy is a development goal in and of itself. High-income countries were funding energy infrastructure projects in low- and middle-income countries, long before aid statistics had a climate tag attached.

Finally, South Korea provided $163 million for a hospital and training center in Tanzania. Building a hospital and healthcare facilities is a fairly standard development aid project. But because it’s built with energy efficiency and low-carbon design in mind, it’s counted as mitigation as a secondary objective. It doesn’t exist to tackle climate change, but all of this $163 million counts as climate-related aid.

There are many similar cases where it’s hard to disentangle whether climate change is *the* reason aid was given, or it’s just a label put on a project that would have gone ahead anyway.

# What’s still not clear

Ideally, all of this climate funding would be additional: funding for everything else could stay the same, and new money would be available for climate change. But that scenario seems unlikely. Many countries view climate finance as part of their overseas commitments, not as something on top.

That leaves two concerns, which pull in opposite directions.

The first is **displacement**: climate projects could divert funding from more traditional ones. Clean energy infrastructure could crowd out antimalarial bed nets, or anti-deforestation projects could divert money from maternal nutrition programs.

The second is **relabeling**: traditional aid programs with a climate code attached. Donor countries have often committed to climate finance in addition to their aid spending, not instead of it. If this is simply an exercise in relabeling, they are ticking off these commitments without providing any new money.

For example, when a new hospital gets a climate tag for being energy efficient, no bed nets are lost, but no new climate money is generated either.

My guess is that both are happening. That more than half of climate funding has it as a secondary objective gives some evidence of this. But this data can’t tell us how much of each is happening.

Answering that would need a detailed analysis of historical aid projects: how they compare with modern ones, and how aid allocations to non-climate sectors, such as health, infrastructure, and humanitarian response, have changed as the climate’s share has grown.

If anyone is interested in taking this on, please do. With so much aid now tagged with a climate label, and global budgets shrinking, it’s a question with an important answer.

Which countries give and receive climate-related aid?Some more data that might help us understand changes in aid allocation.If you want to dig deeper into answering this question, looking at country-specific data can be useful. It allows us to see who is giving aid to climate-related projects, and who is receiving it.One way to understand how much relabeling is happening is to look at the full history of aid projects in one or two individual countries. Were the same types of projects — hydroelectric plants or railway lines — being built in the 1970s and 1980s, just without a climate finance label attached? Or have the types of projects genuinely changed?Here, I’ll present only the summary statistics at a country level. This may raise more questions than it answers, but I think it is still a useful entry point for further analysis.Below, you can see, for a range of donor countries, the share of the development aid they provide that is climate-related. In recent years, South Korea’s share has risen sharply, sometimes to more than 60% to climate projects. In Japan, it ranges from around 50% to as much as 80%. France also gives more than 40%.Contrast that with the United States and Canada, which tend to allocate less than a fifth.One question that would need detailed project-by-project analysis is whether this reflects genuine differences in their aid portfolios, or whether the latter countries are just less likely to flag infrastructure or clean energy projects as climate finance.

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/foreign-aid-given-climate.png)

Look at which countries *receive* aid for climate-related projects, and what stands out is how many are middle-income countries, rather than the poorest. Climate-related projects dominate aid spending in Brazil and India, for example. You can see this in the chart below.Climate-related finance accounts for a smaller share of development spending in low-income countries, but it’s not insignificant: in Uganda, for example, it has increased to almost 50%. In Madagascar, too.Again, it’s worth digging into these examples at a project-specific level. As we saw earlier, a new hospital in Tanzania was coded as climate-related because it was built with a low-carbon design. If this is common across low- or lower-middle-income countries, traditional health and development projects may still dominate, with little displacement by climate finance.That raises two important questions. First, tensions between countries: how much aid for the poorest countries might be crowded out by spending on climate projects in middle-income ones? Second, tensions within a given country: are climate and other development projects really in conflict, or are the same projects still going ahead, just with a climate label?

![](https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/share-foreign-aid-received-climate.png?country=IND~PHL~BGD~IDN~BRA~SLE~SEN~UGA~MDG)
description: Around one-fifth of development aid is spent on climate-related projects. But what does climate-related mean, and does it crowd out other aid projects?

title: For centuries, bird migration was a mystery – a tech revolution is changing that, and could help save these amazing creatures
authors: Peter P. Marra, Dean of The Earth Commons, Professor of Biology and the Environment, Georgetown University; Amy L. Scarpignato, Senior Species Recovery Specialist, Road to Recovery, The Earth Commons, Georgetown University
content:
For [more than 2,000 years](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aristotle/histanimals8.html), scientists have scratched their heads over one of the most basic mysteries of the natural world: Where do birds go?

[Billions of birds](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-018-0666-4) appear and disappear with the seasons every year. Early naturalists offered explanations for the disappearances that today seem fantastical: Birds [transformed into other species](https://penelope.uchicago.edu/aristotle/histanimals8.html), one theory went. Others suggested they [hibernated underwater](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/news/swallow-debate-america-mud-winter-hibernate/) or even [migrated to the moon](https://thereader.mitpress.mit.edu/when-birds-migrated-to-the-moon/).

The truth, that these small animals were traveling thousands of miles across the planet, must once have seemed just as improbable.

Then, in the early 1800s, dramatic evidence emerged supporting the theory of migration. White storks began appearing in Germany with African arrows embedded in their bodies. These birds became known as [*pfeilstörche*, or “arrow storks](https://www.audubon.org/magazine/what-gruesome-stork-taught-us-about-bird-migration).” They provided compelling evidence that birds disappearing from Europe were traveling all the way to Africa and back.

Almost two centuries later, scientists are still asking the same question, but our ability to answer it has been transformed.

For most of ornithological history, scientists understood migration through brief glimpses of a bird, a specimen collected somewhere else, or the rare instance of a banded bird recovered hundreds or thousands of miles from where it had been marked. From these fragments of intelligence, scientists reconstructed journeys that took place largely beyond their view.

Today, it’s possible to see the journeys themselves, almost in real time.

## A century of following birds

Bird banding was [the first tool](https://www.nature.com/scitable/knowledge/library/bird-banding-83032042/) used to attempt a systematic approach to connect these fragments of information. Since the early 1900s, researchers have [placed uniquely numbered metal bands](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=y4-HxZFJF8Y) on birds and hoped someone, somewhere, would encounter them again.

Of [more than 79 million birds banded, only about 6.5 million have been recovered](https://www.pwrc.usgs.gov/BBL/Bander_Portal/login/howmany.php). That generally told scientists just two things: where a bird was banded and where it was encountered again. Everything between them remained invisible.

Over the past quarter-century or so, the tools used to determine where birds go have changed dramatically.

Tracking devices can now be carried by increasingly smaller birds, [recording their movements](https://doi.org/10.1038/srep11069) and communicating with land-based receivers or satellites orbiting the earth. Testing [stable isotopes](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00442-005-0071-y) in feathers and other tissues can reveal where a bird originated. [Genetic testing](https://doi.org/10.1111/mec.12977) can distinguish populations.

At the same time, the extraordinary [growth of bird-watching and citizen science](https://www.fws.gov/sites/default/files/documents/2024-11/2022-birding-in-the-us-demographic-and-economic-analysis.pdf) has created another revolution.

Millions of observations by bird-watchers submitted to [eBird](https://ebird.org/home), an online database to record the birds they see, [show the distribution and abundance of birds](https://science.ebird.org/status-and-trends) across a continent throughout the year in ways early ornithologists could scarcely have imagined.

Collectively, these methods open an extraordinary new window into migratory birds and one of nature’s most remarkable behaviors: migration.

## Discovering unknown migrations

More than [70% of North American bird species](https://ace-eco.org/vol19/iss2/art13/) are migratory. Yet scientists have known surprisingly little about where specific populations go.

A species like the [American robin](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/American_Robin/overview) may breed across thousands of miles of North America, with different breeding populations migrating to entirely different places for the winter. Birds breeding in one part of the continent may travel one route and encounter one set of environmental conditions, while members of the same species experience a completely different set of conditions along another route.

These connections between where a bird breeds and where it spends the winter is called [migratory connectivity](https://repository.si.edu/server/api/core/bitstreams/51a5d839-0ecc-4f44-ab3a-1371ef88261a/content). They are critical for understanding everything from the consequences of climate change on birds to how avian pathogens and diseases spread, to a species’ basic ecology.

We are [ornithologists](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=qi-EePYAAAAJ&hl=en) and [conservation scientists](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=NbFDyzcAAAAJ&hl=en) who have spent almost 15 years along with a team of contributors compiling this rapidly expanding knowledge on bird movement into [The Atlas of North America’s Migratory Birds](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691163185/the-atlas-of-north-americas-migratory-birds). It is being published Nov. 3, 2026, by Princeton University Press, with all profits going to bird conservation and research in Latin America and the Caribbean. The atlas covers the latest information on seasonal movements for nearly 600 species and combines a century of bird-banding data with eBird observations, tracking studies, stable isotope testing, genetics and other sources of information.

What emerges is a picture of migratory birds that is both more complicated and more remarkable than the simple arrows pointing between breeding and wintering ranges on a map.

Consider the [yellow-billed cuckoo](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Yellow-billed_Cuckoo/overview). These birds breed over a wide range of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. but migrate to a relatively small wintering area in the [Gran Chaco region](https://www.worldwildlife.org/places/gran-chaco/) of northern Argentina, Paraguay and southern Bolivia.

In contrast, [peregrine falcons](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Peregrine_Falcon/overview) that breed in Alaska migrate almost directly south, dispersing across the Americas to wintering grounds that extend as far as southern South America.

Discoveries like these are accumulating rapidly. Collectively, they amount to a renaissance in our understanding of animal movement never before imagined.

## Living masterpieces

The more clearly scientists can follow individual birds and populations across the planet, the more extraordinary these species can seem.

Migratory birds such as the [arctic tern](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Arctic_Tern/overview) and [northern wheatear](https://doi.org/10.1098/rsbl.2011.1223) cross oceans, deserts and mountain ranges. Some, like the [bar-tailed godwits, fly thousands of miles without stopping](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2008.1142). Others, like the American redstart, return year after year to [remarkably precise breeding](https://doi.org/10.1139/z96-254) and [wintering](https://doi.org/10.1093/auk/118.1.92) locations.

They navigate landscapes and respond to winds, weather, food and environmental conditions across enormous geographic scales.

We see these species and their migrations as among evolution’s great living masterpieces. That’s why we combined science with natural history and artist [John Anderton’s](https://alchetron.com/John-C-Anderton) extraordinary illustrations of the birds themselves. The maps allow us to see where birds travel, and the art brings the species to life.

Together, they make visible something that humans could only imagine for most of our history.

## A map for conservation

North America has [lost about 3 billion birds](https://www.birds.cornell.edu/home/bring-birds-back/) during the past half-century, and many migratory species continue to decline.

To understand why a population is declining and help save it, researchers need to understand the species’ entire annual cycle: its critical stopover habitats, wintering grounds and threats along its migration routes.

For much of the history of ornithology, scientists studied birds primarily during their breeding season. That made practical sense. [Birds are conspicuous then](https://afonet.org/2022/07/peterson-reference-guide-to-bird-behavior/) – singing, defending territories, building nests and raising young.

But a migratory bird may spend only a few months of its life in its breeding grounds. Conditions such as weather, food availability and habitat quality encountered during migration can [determine whether an individual survives to breed again](https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.1854).

Drought thousands of miles away can affect a bird’s condition months later. [American redstarts](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/American_Redstart/overview) depart [later after dry winters](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.282.5395.1884) and [produce fewer young](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2660976/). Declining horseshoe crab populations in Delaware Bay have reduced food availability for migrating [red knots](https://www.allaboutbirds.org/guide/Red_Knot/overview), contributing to [lower survival](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspb.2003.2663).

## The power of people

All of this knowledge has accumulated because people value birds and have devoted enormous time and effort to understanding them.

For more than a century, thousands of bird-banders have woken up before the crack of dawn to set traps, carefully place bands on birds’ legs and release them, often knowing the chances of ever learning what happened to those individuals were exceedingly small.

More recently, tracking technology has allowed researchers to [follow individual birds across continents and oceans](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0603715103). Those tracks exist because scientists, students, technicians and others have spent countless hours attaching and recovering tags, and contributing and sharing their data.

Today, millions of bird-watchers contribute observations that, thanks to advances in data science, allow us to [watch migration unfold](https://science.ebird.org/status-and-trends/abundance-animations) across an entire continent.

We have spent much of our careers [documenting the decline of birds](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44358-026-00177-7), and we know the challenges facing migratory species are formidable. But we also have hope for these creatures’ survival.

Scientists today know more about where migratory birds go, how populations are connected and what they encounter along the way than at any previous point in history. That knowledge is helping to identify where conservation efforts can make a difference for the future.

*The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: An early clue came from storks found in Europe with African arrows in their bodies. Today, an atlas reveals hundreds of bird migration routes that are both complicated and remarkable.

title: How much rain can a hurricane make, and does the storm size matter?
authors: Zachary Handlos, Atmospheric Science Educator, Georgia Institute of Technology
content:
*[Curious Kids](https://theconversation.com/us/topics/curious-kids-us-74795) is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.*

> **How much rain can a hurricane make, and how much do big versus small hurricanes make? – Naarah, age 8, Pittsburgh**

Hurricanes can produce enormous amounts of rain, adding up to [trillions of gallons of water](https://www.noaa.gov/explainers/explainer-understanding-hurricane-hazards). But the big risk isn’t their total amount – it’s how much rain falls on each location.

One town in Texas got [over 60 inches (152 centimeters) of rain](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/AL092017_Harvey.pdf) from Hurricane Harvey over five days in 2017. That means empty swimming pools there would have filled with rainwater 5 feet (1.5 meters) deep. Hurricane Lane [dumped 58 inches (147 centimeters) of rain on Kahuna Falls, Hawaii](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/EP142018_Lane.pdf), the following year.

So, what causes that much rain, and does the size of the storm matter?

I’m an [atmospheric scientist who teaches](https://handlos.eas.gatech.edu/about-me-2/) college students about weather at Georgia Tech. Let’s take a look at where a hurricane’s rainfall comes from and some of the questions about hurricanes and their rainfall that scientists are still trying to answer.

## First, what goes into creating a hurricane?

A few ingredients are needed [for a hurricane to form](https://oceanservice.noaa.gov/facts/how-hurricanes-form.html): A tropical thunderstorm complex, lots of moisture in the air, [winds that don’t change speed much with height](https://theconversation.com/what-is-wind-shear-an-atmospheric-scientist-explains-how-it-can-tear-apart-hurricanes-and-why-el-nino-ramps-it-up-213527), and warm sea surface waters below.

The water temperature is very important.

The magic number for surface water temperature to be able to fuel a hurricane is [at least 80 degrees Fahrenheit](https://oceantoday.noaa.gov/fuelforthestorm/) (26.5 degrees Celsius). At that temperature and above, the [warm ocean water evaporates into the air](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wPDoIrGUrEc), changing from liquid to vapor. As it makes that change, it provides energy to fuel the storm and also adds moisture to the atmosphere that eventually falls as rain.

When a hurricane moves over warm water, especially when the warm water extends many feet below the surface, the storm [pulls in even more energy and moisture](https://ocean.si.edu/planet-ocean/waves-storms-tsunamis/where-do-hurricanes-get-their-strength).

## What affects hurricane size and rainfall?

This is one of the many questions about hurricanes that atmospheric scientists are working on.

The average hurricane is [about 300 miles (482 kilometers) wide](https://www.weather.gov/source/zhu/ZHU_Training_Page/tropical_stuff/hurricane_anatomy/hurricane_anatomy.html), but hurricanes – or typhoons, as they’re called in the western Pacific of the Northern Hemisphere – can be much bigger or smaller.

[Super Typhoon Tip](https://www.britannica.com/event/Typhoon-Tip) in 1979 grew to half the size of the lower 48 U.S. states. It had a radius of about 690 miles (1,110 kilometers), measured from the center of the storm to its outer edges, meaning it was 1,380 miles (2,222 kilometers) wide. Tropical Storm Marco’s gale-force winds in 2008, in comparison, had a radius of 11.5 miles (18.5 kilometers), meaning it was about 23 miles (37 kilometers) across – not much larger than New York City.

In 2025, scientists published a study showing that hurricane size appears to be [influenced by how warm the ocean water is](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2424385122) compared to its usual temperature that time of year. So, if a hurricane moves over water that is much warmer than normal, it tends to grow in size rapidly as well as growing in strength.

A recent hurricane that was very large in size was the extremely destructive [Hurricane Helene in 2024](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/AL092024_Helene.pdf). As Helene moved over water near Florida that was [much warmer than normal for late September](https://www.earthdata.nasa.gov/learn/data-in-action/warm-waters-gulf-america-helped-fuel-hurricane-helene), it picked up lots of moisture that it carried all the way to the mountains of North Carolina. Several days of rain from the storm caused [catastrophic flooding](https://theconversation.com/how-hurricane-helene-became-a-deadly-disaster-across-six-states-240522) there.

But don’t count the small hurricanes out.

Just because a hurricane is small, that does not mean that it won’t have a big impact.

[Hurricane Andrew in 1992](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/1992andrew.html) was destructive yet small. Its [strongest winds extended](https://www.nps.gov/articles/tropical-storms.htm) only about 90 miles (150 km) from its center when it reached Miami and the Everglades. But that Category 5 hurricane is still known as one of the strongest hurricanes to hit the United States. It [destroyed more than 25,000 homes](https://www.weather.gov/lmk/HurricaneAndrew30Years).

A strong storm isn’t necessary for a lot of rain to fall. [Tropical Storm Allison in 2001](https://www.wpc.ncep.noaa.gov/tropical/rain/allison2001.html) is still one of the wettest tropical weather events in U.S. history. It caused over US$4 billion in damage in Texas alone, and it didn’t even develop into a hurricane!

## So, what really leads to the highest rainfall totals?

Hurricanes that move slowly or nearly stop along their path usually cause the biggest rainfall problems because their rain keeps falling over the same location. The rain may be just as intense in a fast-moving hurricane, but it doesn’t stick around as long.

An example is [Hurricane Harvey](https://www.climate.gov/news-features/event-tracker/reviewing-hurricane-harveys-catastrophic-rain-and-flooding), which hit southeastern Texas in late August 2017. The storm dropped an estimated [27 trillion gallons](https://tdem.texas.gov/disasters/hurricane-harvey) of water over the state – that’s enough to fill about 40 million [Olympic-size swimming pools](https://sports.yahoo.com/deep-olympic-swimming-pool-everything-125603914.html).

When Harvey stalled over the Houston area, the storm kept drawing moisture from the warm waters of the Gulf. Over four days, it brought precipitation that totals as high as [60.58 inches (1.54 meters) of rain over Nederland, Texas](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/AL092017_Harvey.pdf). The extreme rainfall overran the town’s drainage and [transformed Nederland into an island](https://bayoubulletinnews.com/60-inches-of-rain-what-hurricane-harvey-taught-nederland-texas/).

If a storm moves fast, like [Hurricane Michael did in 2018](https://www.weather.gov/tae/hurricanemichael2018) when it hit the Florida Panhandle, its winds and storm surge can make a big mess, but its rainfall totals will be lower.

Michael was a Category 5 hurricane – more powerful than Harvey and Helene – but its [rainfall totals for locations along its path ranged from 6 to 10 inches](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/AL142018_Michael.pdf) (15 to 25 centimeters) because it was moving so fast. That’s still a lot of rain, but not compared to Harvey or to Helene, which dumped [30 inches (76 centimeters) of rain](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/data/tcr/AL092024_Helene.pdf) on Busick, N.C., over a few days.

So, a hurricane can be large or small in size and still have a big impact, depending on how slowly it’s moving.

There is still a lot to learn about hurricanes. Some big questions involve what’s known as [rapid intensification](https://www.nhc.noaa.gov/aboutgloss.shtml#r). That occurs when a tropical storm’s maximum wind speed increases quickly, by 30 knots (about 34.5 miles per hour or 55 kilometers per hour) or more within 24 hours.

When rapid intensification occurs, as happened with hurricanes Harvey, Michael and Helene before they hit land, the storm can surprise coastal residents and become catastrophic.

Hurricanes of all sizes can be dangerous, so accurate forecasting well before they reach land is crucial to help people prepare for their impacts. One very important area of research that today’s scientists – and future scientists – can work on is [improving forecasting](https://news.ucar.edu/133083/predicting-hurricane-rapid-intensification-further-advance) so coastal residents know what’s coming and have time to prepare.

*Hello, curious kids! Do you have a question you’d like an expert to answer? Ask an adult to send your question to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com. Please tell us your name, age and the city where you live.*

*And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.*

*Dr. Zachary Handlos is the Director of the Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences undergraduate degree program and is a Senior Academic Professional within the School of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences at the Georgia Institute of Technology. He receives funding from the U.S. National Science Foundation, and is currently finishing his 2-year term as chair of the American Meteorological Society Board on Higher Education.*
description: Storms big and small can produce a lot of rain. What matters most is how fast they’re moving, as an atmospheric scientist and educator explains.

title: Why fall yard care could start with doing less – but not nothing
authors: Manjot Kaur Sidhu, Assistant Extension Professor of Horticulture and Ornamental Horticulture Specialist, University of Maine
content:
Every autumn, homeowners and gardeners tend to engage in a familiar ritual. As trees shed their leaves, people drag out rakes, leaf blowers and lawn bags to strip their yards bare before winter arrives.

It is a tidy habit rooted in aesthetics, but ecologically, clearing away fallen leaves strips the very foundation of local ecosystems. Far from dead debris requiring disposal, this fallen foliage forms a dynamic layer and a biological interface that drives nutrient cycling and is [essential for soil health and the environment, including biodiversity](https://extension.illinois.edu/blogs/garden-scoop/2017-11-08-fall-garden-cleanup-and-wildlife).

As a [researcher of plant growth](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=eQAsesUAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao) in yards and gardens, I would recommend leaving leaves on the ground. There, they can provide essential [winter habitat for native pollinators](https://extension.psu.edu/programs/master-gardener/counties/lackawanna/news/how-to-support-our-pollinators-insects-and-birds-during-the-winter-months) – even in places that don’t have freezing temperatures. And they act as a [nutrient-dense, natural mulch](https://www.lsuagcenter.com/articles/page1669123105183) for the soil.

Here is the science behind why the first step of fall yard care could simply be doing less – along with practical ways to keep your yard looking neat while nourishing the ecosystem underneath.

## A winter sanctuary for native pollinators

To understand why leaf litter matters, it helps to look closely at what happens beneath the surface as temperatures drop. While honeybees pass the winter in [sheltered hives](https://environmentamerica.org/massachusetts/articles/what-do-bees-do-in-the-winter/), the vast majority of North America’s native pollinators do not.

Up to 70% of native bee species, including many insects’ cocoons and larvae, [nest in the ground](https://xerces.org/pollinator-conservation/nesting-resources). Fertilized queen bumblebees burrow [just a few inches into the soil or hide under dense leaf mulch](https://xerces.org/pollinator-conservation/nesting-resources) to survive the freezing months ahead, to lay eggs in the following spring.

Raking, bagging and blowing leaves away destroys this crucial winter nursery.

Many other insects depend on the shelter of fallen foliage:

- Moths and butterflies: Species such as the [luna moth (*Actias luna*)](https://www.inaturalist.org/taxa/47916-Actias-luna) and the Isabella tiger moth, whose [caterpillar form is the woolly bear](https://www.keystone.edu/2026/10/07/woolly-bears-on-campus-folklore-fall-and-the-facts/), spin cocoons or roll themselves directly inside fallen leaves. Raking or shredding those leaves destroys the next generation.
- Fireflies: Adult fireflies lay eggs in moist soil, and their larvae spend up to two years hunting for their food, [soft-bodied invertebrates under damp leaf litter](https://blog.nwf.org/2024/09/leave-the-leaves-to-save-fireflies/). Raking deprives them of moisture and habitat.
- [Predatory ground beetles](https://ipm.ucanr.edu/natural-enemies/predaceous-ground-beetles/#gsc.tab=0): These beneficial predators [spend the winter under leaves](https://www.lsuagcenter.com/%7E/media/system/b/8/4/b/b84bc30880b73ecdd797defdedd2cec7/p3949%20maintainingleaflitter_rh924pdf.pdf), emerging in spring to feed on common garden pests such as aphids, slugs and mites.

## Nature’s engineered soil insulator and fertilizer

In addition to being a shelter, [fallen leaves are an evolved biological mechanism for nutrient cycling](https://njaes.rutgers.edu/fs1369/). Trees actively pump vital elements, including calcium, magnesium, potassium and nitrogen from deep subsoils, into their foliage. When autumn comes and leaves drop, these stored nutrients are deposited back into the soil.

Leaving leaves in place triggers fundamental ecological benefits.

A thick blanket of intact leaves acts as a natural insulator for the ground. Air pockets trapped between overlapping leaves moderate the soil temperature and slow heat transfer, [buffering against the freeze-thaw cycles that heave soil](https://yardandgarden.extension.iastate.edu/faq/what-frost-heaving-and-how-do-i-prevent-it), fracture plant roots and expose beneficial soil microbes to lethal cold. The intact leaf blanket also conserves moisture and prevents soil from drying out over the winter.

As fungi, earthworms and micro-arthropods digest fallen leaves through late fall and spring, they [break down organic matter into a rich material called humus](https://education.nationalgeographic.org/resource/humus/). This slow-release organic fertilizer boosts soil structure, improves water retention in sandy soils, and [prevents erosion and runoff in heavy rains](https://wcsoilworks.com/humus-versatile-and-close-to-nature/).

Decaying leaves feed beneficial mycorrhizal fungi in the soil. Those fungi form [symbiotic relationships with plant and tree roots](https://njaes.rutgers.edu/FS1384/), helping the roots collect water and nutrients from the soil to nourish the plants above. A natural layer of leaves also [suppresses spring weed seeds](https://extension.colostate.edu/resource/using-leaves-in-the-landscape/) organically without needing synthetic chemical herbicides. And the moist, insulated microclimate under leaf litter is also critical for [terrestrial amphibians, including frogs and salamanders](https://njaes.rutgers.edu/fs1369/), to survive freezing temperatures.

## How to ‘leave the leaves’

Adopting a softer approach to fall cleanup does not mean your yard has to look completely untamed or that you have to [risk killing your lawn](https://www.southernliving.com/hidden-dangers-leaves-lawn-12129619). Here is how to balance suburban expectations with sound ecological science:

- Move, don’t remove: Move the leaves from lawns and sidewalks, rake them into garden beds, around ornamental plants or into vegetable plots, using manual rakes or electric leaf blowers. Aim for a layer 2 to 3 inches deep. Leaving leaves in grassy areas can [help ticks hide there too](https://www.capecod.gov/2025/11/25/leave-the-leaves-cape-cod/), but if you move the leaves to garden beds or spots that are used less, the ticks will be less likely to nest in the grass. Establishing [pollinator zones](https://tickfreenh.org/reduce-ticks-while-supporting-pollinators-in-your-yard/) on the property can also help reduce tick populations.
- Skip the leaf shredder: Mowing over leaves with a mulching mower is better than sending them to landfills, but high-velocity mower blades still kill overwintering insect eggs, chrysalises and larvae. Leave leaves intact wherever possible in plant beds.
- Wait for spring to clean up: Do not cut back hollow-stemmed perennials or clear leaf beds during early, warm spring days.
