description: We know how cities move, but policy and organizational changes are needed before algorithms can actually improve mobility.

title: Dog parks are an antidote to the isolation and divisions that social media can fuel
authors: Kevin B. Johnson, Professor  of Pediatrics, Biomedical Informatics and Science Communication, University of Pennsylvania
content:
The case against social media has gotten so well rehearsed that most people can easily merge it into ordinary conversation: It makes people lonely. It sorts them into camps. It hands them a room full of people who already agree with them and calls that a community.

I’ve given this speech myself, with feeling, having read my phone notifications in the host’s powder room 11 minutes earlier.

I am a [pediatrician, health communicator and researcher](https://ldi.upenn.edu/fellows/fellows-directory/kevin-b-johnson-md-ms/) at the University of Pennsylvania, and diagnosing is in my blood. [Two decades of research](https://www.nationalacademies.org/projects/HMD-BPH-21-14/publication/27396), a [surgeon general’s advisory on loneliness](https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf) and [Meta’s recent settlement of up to US$17 billion](https://ag.ny.gov/press-release/2026/attorney-general-james-secures-171-billion-and-groundbreaking-reforms-meta), pending court approval, all describe the same thing. What we recite are the symptoms. The more interesting question is what these symptoms diagnose.

Simply put, our dependency on social media creates a deficiency disease. It’s not something toxic we’re ingesting; it is something our lives online have stopped us from receiving.

I figured out that cost while standing in a field in Harford Park with a dog leash wrapped around my ankles.

## A corner bar without the alcohol

Harford Park in Wayne, Pennsylvania, is 30 acres of rolling grass and mature trees the township [designated for off-leash dogs in 1997](https://www.radnor.com/Home/Components/FacilityDirectory/FacilityDirectory/22/33).

I go most afternoons. So do the same 15 or 20 people, which is how I ended up tangled in someone else’s very long leash on a Tuesday, concentrating hard enough on my own feet that I stopped talking and just listened.

Two conversations were running at once. In one, a regular who is having a rough year was getting gently harassed about the weight he’d put on against his doctors’ advice — first by me, then by three other people who piled on uninvited. In the other, someone was arguing about Dr. Anthony Fauci, and the regulars chimed in on both sides. Gossip, complaints and dogs greeting dogs became the backdrop.

As I worked to free my ankles, it clicked: The dog park, like the local knitting club or the Saturday pickleball group, does the job a corner bar used to do. There are regulars and running jokes, and once a person is known, a spot in the conversation is reserved for them.

What makes these places work is that a shared focus on one small part of a life opens into something fuller. Regulars may share a taste in dog breeds or beer, but they are not colleagues, political soulmates or relatives. They differ on favorite restaurants, income, age, religion, values and beliefs. They are together because a golden retriever and a nervous rescue mutt need to run in the morning, and there is a field nearby.

## Chance encounters can increase empathy

Sociologist Ray Oldenburg called places like this [third places](https://www.hachettebookgroup.com/titles/ray-oldenburg-phd/the-great-good-place/9780786752416/) and defined them as “public places that host the regular, voluntary, informal, and happily anticipated gatherings of individuals beyond the realms of home and work.” Oldenburg noted the erosion of places that once manufactured accidental encounters, such as main streets, neighborhood pubs, general stores and even the drugstore soda fountain.

Off-leash parks have been [among the fastest-growing amenities in U.S. city park systems](https://www.tpl.org/media-room/dog-parks-lead-growth-us-city-parks) for two decades. A study in the [Journal of Urban Affairs](https://doi.org/10.1080/07352166.2017.1343634) found dog park users reported higher social capital and neighborhood cohesion.

The park is not a utopia. It’s a corner bar without the booze.

Thomas Pettigrew and Linda Tropp’s [meta-analysis of 515 studies](https://doi.org/10.1037/0022-3514.90.5.751) provides the best evidence for why these accidental connections matter. They found that contact between groups generally reduces prejudice, but the quality and circumstances of that contact matter. The more interesting finding came later, when they [tested how it works](https://doi.org/10.1002/ejsp.504): The effect runs less through learning facts about the other group than through reduced anxiety, more empathy and more perspective.

That is exactly what the park does. The man I disagree with about nearly everything hasn’t changed his mind, and neither have I. What changed is that his politics is now maybe the eighth thing I know and appreciate about him, behind his dog’s bad hip, his sense of humor, the awful year he had and his love of what Philadelphians call “wooder ice.”

That shift, from opinions to a person, is why “just show people the other side” keeps failing online. When sociologist Christopher Bail and colleagues paid Republicans and Democrats to [follow bots representing the views of the opposite party](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1804840115) on Twitter, the Republicans came out substantially more conservative than they went in. Democrats shifted slightly left, though not significantly. Exposure to opinions is not the same thing as exposure to a person. The feed gave people arguments. The corner bar gives people other people.

## Making room for tolerance and trust

If [the places people gather shape their health](https://doi.org/10.1177/02750740251346805), as a growing body of research suggests, then the shift from communities set by geography to communities assembled by algorithm creates a slow burn of intolerance and mistrust.

There are now [decades of research on social media and anxiety](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0329466), and a growing body of experimental work about what algorithmic curation does to what people see. Almost none of it treats the encounter pattern as a health exposure.

Social platforms have mastered what German American sociologist Herbert Gans called [selective homogeneity](https://doi.org/10.7312/gans17884). They sort people by interests, identities, tastes and grievances, then make it easy to stay among people who feel familiar.

They are like virtual Levittowns – the postwar suburban developments outside Philadelphia, among other places in the Northeast, where thousands of identical houses went up on farmland and were sold to buyers screened by price. In early Levittowns, covenants [barred Black families outright](https://doi.org/10.1093/oso/9780195314748.003.0002).

In 1958, [Gans moved into a Levittown](https://doi.org/10.7312/gans17884-014) in New Jersey and stayed two years doing research on its residents. He found that although original settlers and those who moved in by choice were happy, their rebellious teenage offspring, who had the fewest places to go and the least to do in those communities, were not.

This was an early, real-life sorting of the type that algorithms would make all too common 60 years later.

By contrast, repeated, low-stakes, in-person contact like the interactions between regulars at a dog park or corner bar creates room for tolerance and trust. People come back. They notice an absence. They share attention around a task, a place or a dog, rather than around presenting themselves or defending a position.

Deficiency diseases are easily treatable. Nothing has to be taken away; instead, something has to be given back.

*Read more of our stories about [Philadelphia and Pennsylvania](https://theconversation.com/us/philadelphia-pennsylvania-news), or sign up for our Philadelphia [newsletter on Substack](https://tcphilly.substack.com/).*

*Kevin B. Johnson receives funding from the National Institutes of Health.*
description: The people who stretch a person’s sense of humanity may be the ones no algorithm currently selects.

title: Many cities buried urban streams. Here’s how to bring them back
authors: Luna Khirfan, Associate professor, School of Planning, University of Waterloo
content:
As many cities developed, streams that once flowed on the surface were buried underground to make way for growing infrastructure. However, as heavier rainfall, extreme weather and aging infrastructure place growing pressure on cities, these buried streams could become part of the solution.

Restoring streams to the surface — a practice known as stream daylighting — can help manage stormwater, restore habitats and create greener, more walkable public spaces. But recognizing these benefits is easier than delivering a successful project.

Municipalities must find feasible sites, co-ordinate across departments, secure funding and plan for long-term maintenance. But they must also ensure that environmental improvements benefit existing residents rather than contribute to displacement.

[My research on stream daylighting](https://doi.org/10.1080/09640568.2025.2526614) compares two contrasting approaches in Seoul, South Korea, and Zürich, Switzerland. The findings suggest that municipalities don’t need to choose between a single large project and many small interventions. They need flexible programs that can identify the right approach for each site and apply lessons from one project to the next.

## Two cities, two approaches

Between 2003 and 2005, Seoul restored the [Cheonggyecheon stream](https://www.koreajoongangdaily.com/korea/a-tale-of-two-streams-from-seoul-to-wellingtonnbsp/12726130) through a rapid, centralized and costly project along one major downtown corridor. The city removed an elevated motorway and integrated the restored stream with public transit, cycling infrastructure, pedestrian bridges, walkways and public spaces.

The example shows what stream daylighting can accomplish when political leadership, infrastructure renewal and major public investment align. It also exposes the risks associated with large flagship projects. The project required substantial capital investment and continues to incur maintenance costs.

Critics have questioned its ecological integrity because [pumps supply water to the channel](https://doi.org/10.1080/10630732.2013.855511). Redevelopment around the corridor also increased land values and displaced some smaller businesses.

[Zürich’s Bachkonzept](https://www.theguardian.com/cities/2017/aug/29/river-runs-global-movement-daylight-urban-rivers), or stream concept, took a different approach. The city began with pilot projects in the 1980s and restored numerous smaller stream segments over several decades.

Zürich linked the projects to sewer management, infrastructure renewal, ecological restoration and neighbourhood planning. Daylighted streams now pass through residential areas, parks and public spaces. Paths, small bridges, seating, playgrounds and recreational areas accompany many of them.

No single project in Zürich has the public profile of Seoul’s Cheonggyecheon. Together, however, the projects form a distributed network that improves watershed function, connects habitats and gives neighbourhoods greater access to water.

This incremental approach may be more practical for many smaller municipalities. Cities can begin with manageable sites, monitor their performance and pursue new projects as infrastructure renewal or redevelopment creates opportunities.

## Find opportunities before they disappear

The first step is not construction. It is mapping.

Municipalities can combine culvert inventories and [historical watercourse maps](https://www.lostrivers.ca/disappearing.html) with data on flood and heat risks, social vulnerability, public land, parks, planned infrastructure projects and major redevelopment sites.

Mapping does not imply that every buried stream should return to the surface. It gives municipalities a consistent way to identify sites that deserve technical study before other land-use and infrastructure decisions make daylighting difficult or impossible.

Toronto illustrates this challenge. The city recognizes [historical watercourses and supports their restoration where feasible](https://newsinteractives.cbc.ca/features/2024/daylighting-rivers/). But that support fails to identify what sites should receive priority, who should assess them or how a project would be funded and maintained.

Research on [flood risks in Toronto](https://doi.org/10.3389/frsc.2022.919724) identifies Black Creek and Flemingdon Park among the neighbourhoods where flood exposure intersects with social vulnerability and limited capacity to adapt. Combining this evidence with lost-stream mapping, public land ownership and capital plans could help the city identify equitable pilot opportunities.

## Choose the right delivery pathway

Stream daylighting generally enters municipal practice through one of two routes.

The first is public capital works. Culvert replacement, sewer separation, road reconstruction, park renewal, ravine restoration and flood-control projects give municipalities opportunities to examine whether a stream should remain underground. This pathway is especially promising on public land, where a municipality has greater control over design, public access and maintenance.

The second route is private redevelopment. Large industrial, commercial, brownfield or transit-area sites may provide enough space to restore a stream channel, accommodate floodwater and establish vegetation.

Timing matters. Once buildings, roads and development densities are set in place, restoring a waterway becomes much more difficult. Municipalities should screen large sites early and make decisions about land dedication, development rights, public access, construction costs and maintenance transparent.

[Vancouver’s Still Creek](https://vancouver.ca/home-property-development/still-creek-enhancement.aspx) shows how municipal investment, redevelopment opportunities, watershed planning and community stewardship can support gradual restoration rather than one defining project.

Over more than two decades, the city and its partners have delivered site-specific projects involving habitat restoration, rainwater management and public access, including a developer-funded daylighting project completed in 2009.

Updated plans now connect future restoration to redevelopment and flood management, while community organizations contribute through stewardship and salmon monitoring.

## Build a program that learns

A daylighting project doesn’t end when construction finishes. Vegetation becomes established, water conditions change and communities use new public spaces in unexpected ways. Municipalities should therefore follow an adaptive cycle: map, assess, co-design, implement, monitor, learn, adjust and scale.

Monitoring should cover flood performance, water quality, habitat, public use, accessibility, maintenance costs and equity. Municipalities should then use the findings to manage completed sites and improve the selection and design of future projects.

Equity also requires sustained attention. Attractive public spaces can increase neighbourhood desirability and development pressure. Affordable housing measures, community benefits and ongoing monitoring can help ensure that existing residents share in the gains.

Scaling a daylighting program does not necessarily mean constructing a larger project. It can mean building a connected portfolio of smaller interventions that gradually restores watershed function.

Stream daylighting will not be feasible everywhere. Without a clear program, however, municipalities may never identify where it could work.

The central lesson from Seoul and Zürich is that cities should treat buried streams not simply as forgotten natural features. They are ecological systems, climate infrastructure and, if developed with care, public spaces all residents can enjoy.

*Luna Khirfan has received funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.*
description: Stream daylighting can help manage stormwater, restore habitats and create greener, more walkable public spaces.

title: From nightlife to life at night: cities must stay open later to beat the rising heat
authors: Andreina Seijas, Lecturer, Urban School, Sciences Po
content:
Summer in Europe is normally cause for celebration. Not this one, however, which will rank as one of the [hottest on record](https://apnews.com/article/heat-wave-france-europe-climate-change-record-81c341900166135de6cbc0f49156477b). Wildfires have broken out everywhere from France to Greece, while intense drought [has turned](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-08-08/britain-green-pastures-turn-brown-amid-drought/107011800) the grass in London’s famous Hyde Park brown. This week, much of Europe is sweltering through [yet another heatwave](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/8/13/europe-swelters-in-latest-wave-of-extreme-heat).

Most European cities are designed to weather cold, not intense heat. But temperatures are now regularly climbing over 35°C. Prolonged, damaging heat is forcing rapid change. Rather than abandoning normal life, urban residents put it on hold until cooler conditions arrive in the evening.

These changes are already measurable. In our [recent research](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42949-025-00297-7), we analysed two years of bank card transaction data from three Australian cities to see what happened when the temperature rose over 35°C. We found overall spending fell 7% during heatwaves. Consumers spent less between midday and early evening, before spending stabilised after sunset.

As extreme heat becomes more common, it will affect businesses and organisations in more cities. More of life will have to happen at night.

## People stay home when extreme heat arrives

We used anonymised, large-scale bank card transaction data and daily temperature records from Melbourne, Sydney and Adelaide between January 2023 and December 2024. Temperatures reached 35°C or higher on 62 days over this period – 27 in Adelaide, 20 in Melbourne and 15 in Sydney. The dataset captures virtually all point-of-sale spending in three-hour intervals.

When temperatures rose above 35°C, daytime spending fell sharply, especially during the hottest part of the day – 12pm to 6pm. Some spending shifted to cooler periods, such as evenings or the days before, or after extreme heat.

Department and variety stores were among the hardest hit: despite being air-conditioned, spending was 35% lower between 3pm and 6pm on extremely hot days.

Spending on eating out, entertainment and shopping dropped off during the afternoon before recovering in the evening. Spending at convenience stores proved more resilient. Overall, some purchases were postponed but others were lost altogether.

## The shift to cooler hours

Heat is no stranger to many cities around the world. But even these places are now finding it [too hot](https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/how-heat-changes-sleep-work-shopping-d3efe4d8).

The daily rhythm of urban life is changing in cities such as Dubai, where summer temperatures can now push past 50°C. The Middle East is [warming faster](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024JD041625) than the global average. In response, authorities have opened [floodlit public beaches](https://www.rfi.fr/en/middle-east/20241006-too-hot-by-day-dubai-s-floodlit-beaches-are-packed-at-night), which remain open overnight.

In France, [Paris](https://www.adaptaville.fr/horaires-d-ouvertures-des-lieux-de-fraicheur) and Toulouse have begun keeping parks, gardens and swimming areas open into the night. In Italy and Spain, tourists are increasingly exploring Rome and Seville [after sunset](https://www.bbc.com/travel/article/20260605-siesta-then-fiesta-enjoy-europe-like-the-locals). In Seoul, South Korea, more than 120 public libraries [now stay open](https://english.seoul.go.kr/122-seoul-public-libraries-extend-hours-to-10-pm-transforming-into-climate-shelters) until 10pm to act as climate shelters.

Despite these examples, there’s [little evidence](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-024-02117-9) of a wider shift. Authorities in many cities are not yet actively planning for a future where extreme temperatures make afternoons unpleasant or dangerous.

Most cities are still organised around a daytime model. Public transport becomes less frequent after the commuter rush in early evening, while community centres, childcare facilities and public buildings tend to close early. Parks [often lack](https://www.theguardian.com/australia-news/article/2024/sep/08/not-safe-to-run-in-the-dark-how-inadequate-lighting-in-public-spaces-is-creating-barriers-for-women) adequate lighting or safety measures to make it possible to visit in cooler evenings.

Efforts to make cities more resilient to climate change [often focus](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.nbsj.2025.100245) on redesigning streets, cooling buildings and expanding tree plantings and other green infrastructure. These are essential. But they are only part of the story.

Cities will have to adapt not only through modifying spaces, but also by modifying times. Climate resilience is more than just what infrastructure cities provide – it’s when it is available.

## Rethinking the city after dark

To keep cities open later, authorities will need to strengthen [social infrastructure](https://www.gehlpeople.com/knowledge-hub/publications/social-infrastructure-is-essential-infrastructure/) – the network of public spaces, cultural institutions, libraries, sports facilities, community centres and other neighbourhood amenities crucial to everyday life in a city.

Public libraries are well-known heat refuges. But if they close before temperatures fall, it leaves people exposed.

Creating night cities doesn’t have to mean large-scale redevelopment. Often, it’s about changing existing patterns.

Sensible measures include:

- boosting frequency and reliability of public transport in evenings, especially during heatwaves
- extending opening hours for libraries and other community facilities
- installing better lighting along pedestrian routes
- ensuring public spaces remain safe and comfortable after dark.

It’s hard for some people to shift schedules to avoid the worst of the heat. Workers with fixed hours cannot simply move their working day, while carers and parents are constrained by school and care schedules. Older adults and people with limited mobility may also depend on public transport and services that become less available after dark.

That means time-shifting will have to be accompanied by investment in accessible evening infrastructure, as well as protections for the workers needed to keep cities running later.

## Nightlife – or life at night?

As extreme heat reshapes daily life in more cities, authorities must plan ahead. We will need more research on how cities can best adapt their daily rhythms to rising temperatures.

It’s common to think of a city’s nightlife as revellers visiting bars or watching performances.

But in the very near future, nightlife may come to mean something else: normal life lived at night to avoid broiling by day.

*Acknowledgements: Shashi Karunanethy and Dean Magee contributed to the Australian research.*

*Andreina Seijas does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: From floodlit beaches to late-night libraries, city life has to change to beat the heat.

title: Beyond the 15-minute city: What really makes people want to walk
authors: Paula Negron-Poblete, Professeure agrégée à l’École d’urbanisme et d’architecture de paysage, Université de Montréal
content:
A sedentary lifestyle is a trap lurking around every corner, and adopting [more active lifestyles](https://montrealgazette.com/entertainment-life/fitness-want-to-boost-your-daily-step-count-consider-location-location-location/) is an increasing priority. But what really motivates people to walk? A neighbourhood may offer excellent opportunities to walk to many destinations, but only a few specific routes will actually be perceived as conducive to walking.

As a professor at the School of Urban Planning and Landscape Architecture at the Université de Montréal, I am seeing significant disparities in walkability across different areas. While accessibility to shops and services is necessary to create healthy living environments, it’s not enough. The safety, comfort and appeal of walking routes are more likely to encourage people to walk.

## Accessibility and walkability

Walking is often a convenient way to get to a grocery store or a bus stop, for example. A destination is considered accessible on foot if it is no more than 800 metres away.

The [Walk Score](https://www.walkscore.com/methodology.shtml) indicator allows you to determine the walkability of any address based on the availability of services and shops within walking distance. The term “[15-minute city](https://www.mdpi.com/953594)” is also used to refer to environments where people can reach multiple destinations on foot (about one kilometre) or by bike (just under five kilometres) within that time frame.

But the decision to walk also depends on the safety, comfort and the appeal of the route, factors that vary depending on the urban community, its landscape and individuals themselves. These factors are particularly important when walking is an activity in and of itself. This is referred to as [walkability or walking potential](https://www.sfu.ca/inclusive-environments-lab/core-projects/swan-project.html).

## Ensuring safe routes

A neighbourhood with an abundance of retail options along busy boulevards or in shopping centres surrounded by large parking lots can offer several destinations within a 15-minute walk. But walking there is unsafe, since pedestrians constantly share the space with cars. Safety conditions along the route are therefore poor due to the increased risk of accidents.

The poor condition of sidewalks can also hinder walking. For people with limited mobility, broken surfaces or raised concrete slabs increase the risk of falls. For [people who use wheelchairs](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/montreal-pedestrian-accessibility-1.6476400), the transitions between the sidewalk and the street at intersections are often problematic.

[Safety levels can also vary by season](https://doi.org/10.71781/2782). For example, snow-covered or icy sidewalks can create barriers to walking for many people, including older adults. If they have no other means of getting around, they run the risk of becoming isolated.

Features of the built environment can undermine the perceived safety of walking routes. Damaged, neglected buildings with few windows convey a sense of danger. In contrast, In contrast, routes through areas that are active throughout the day help create a [sense of safety](https://www.marshalls.co.uk/landscaping/blog/eyes-on-the-street-creating-safer-spaces). A recent survey conducted in the United States showed that pedestrians [avoid busy streets](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pmedr.2022.102003), but in many neighbourhoods, stores are located along these routes, which forces people to use them.

The perception of safety is particularly important for encouraging children to walk. Even if their school is close to home, the presence of cars in the vicinity and high traffic speeds reduce the safety of the routes to school.

From policies like Toronto’s [Vision Zero Road Safety Plan](https://www.toronto.ca/services-payments/streets-parking-transportation/road-safety/vision-zero/vision-zero-plan-overview/) to the creation of [school streets](https://greencommunitiescanada.org/action-project/montreal-school-streets/), numerous initiatives have been implemented in recent years to ensure safe and pleasant journeys for pedestrians, especially children.

***À lire aussi : [Cars versus kids: How resistance to change limits children’s right to the city](https://theconversation.com/cars-versus-kids-how-resistance-to-change-limits-childrens-right-to-the-city-263254)***

## Comfortable routes

A clear separation between the sidewalk and vehicle lanes enhances safety for pedestrians. Adding greenery also improves the comfort and appeal of the route. Street furniture plays a similar role: the regular placement of benches, for example, gives older adults the opportunity to take a break during their walk. Finally, lighting designed with pedestrians (and not just drivers) in mind makes it easier to spot potential obstacles along the way and to walk safely after dark.

At intersections, the installation of curb cuts or raised crossings allows pedestrians to cross the street at the same level as the sidewalk, improving comfort and the continuity of movement. Sidewalks wider than two metres also make walking smoother: they allow pedestrians to avoid obstacles (parked bicycles, curbside recycling bins), walk in groups or navigate more easily in a wheelchair.

Conversely, some infrastructure features hinder walking because they increase risks for pedestrians. This is the case with driveways used by cars to access off-street parking. These features are common in areas that are more car-dependent, where off-street parking is ubiquitous.

## The joy of walking

The opportunity to encounter other people on the street is also highly valued. Outdoor dining areas, green spaces and public art all help to enhance walking experiences. Canadian cities like [Montréal](https://artpublicmontreal.ca/en/tours/), [Vancouver](https://vancouvermurals.ca/) and [Toronto](https://www.streetartoronto.ca/) offer walking routes that showcase urban murals.

It’s important to go beyond simple functional improvements aimed at making walking routes safer. When designing or redesigning a space, it’s also an opportunity to enhance the enjoyment that walking can provide.

For example, an intersection near a school can be transformed with creatively designed pavement markings, making the walk to school more fun and enjoyable for children.

The promotion of walking has to be a collective effort that involves different urban planning professionals.

*Paula Negron-Poblete has received funding from the Fonds de recherche du Québec and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.*
description: A sedentary lifestyle lurks in every neighbourhood. So what motivates people to walk?

title: Why finance jobs are widening income inequality in cities around the world
authors: Marta M. Elvira, Profesora Ordinaria de Direccion  Estrategica y Dirección de Personas, IESE Business School (Universidad de Navarra); Nils Neumann, Graduate student, sociology, University of Michigan; Olivier Godechot, Professor in sociology, Sciences Po
content:
Try to imagine the history of New York without Wall Street, or London without the City. It’s not easy.

Hosting a country’s main financial markets shapes a city’s identity, raises its profile and creates jobs. But there are trade-offs. By acting as a magnet for high-paying finance jobs and related professions, many financial cities suffer from particularly high levels of income inequality.

In fact, alongside globalisation and the clustering of highly skilled workers, our research has found that the presence of a financial market is a major driver of the growing concentration of top earners and earnings inequality in select cities.

In a [study conducted by two dozen researchers](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44284-026-00407-1), we examined top earnings in cities in 10 countries across Europe, North America and Asia, analysing two decades of linked employer-employee data.

For every country studied, we compare two cities: the financial hub housing the main national markets and related industries, and a second, comparison city that is closest in terms of population, employment and share of GDP.

In the US, for instance, we compared New York to Los Angeles. In Spain, we compared Madrid to Barcelona, in Japan it was Tokyo and Osaka, in France, Paris and Lyon, the Netherlands, Amsterdam and Rotterdam, and so on.

We wanted to understand whether the earnings of the top 1% were increasing, whether higher earners were clustered in certain cities, and what role the finance sector plays in determining income inequality.

***Leer más: [Top earners are increasingly isolated at work – here’s why it matters](https://theconversation.com/top-earners-are-increasingly-isolated-at-work-heres-why-it-matters-250861)***

## A richer, more concentrated top 1%

Across all 10 countries, the earnings share of the top 1% (i.e. how much of the total income went to those one percenters) increased over time, growing by an average of 0.17% per year. Countries such as Denmark and Sweden experienced the smallest rises, while the US posted the largest.

That is the aggregate for top earners: already high incomes increasing year after year. Our findings that are consistent with [data documenting the global increase in income inequality](https://wid.world/world/#sptinc_p99p100_z/US;FR;DE;CN;ZA;GB;WO-PPP/last/eu/k/p/yearly/s/false/3.87/30/curve/false/country). But where do these high-flyers live and work?

In all of the countries we studied, the highest earners nationwide were more concentrated in financial cities than in the second cities. In 1990, earnings in financial cities were on average 1.7 times more likely to be in the national top 1% than those in comparison cities. Nearly two decades later, they are 2.4 times more likely.

Financial hubs were consistently responsible for an outsized percentage of the income growth among very top earners. On average, financial cities accounted for 65% of the increase in their countries’ top 1% earnings shares. In France, Spain and Sweden, financial cities accounted for more than 100% of the increase, meaning that earnings in other cities actually declined.

The growing gap between financial and comparison cities is mainly driven by the surge in earnings in the financial sector. We estimate that this sector accounts for 30% of the divergence between the two types of cities.

***Leer más: [‘We got lazy and complacent’: Swedish pensioners explain how abolishing the wealth tax changed their country](https://theconversation.com/we-got-lazy-and-complacent-swedish-pensioners-explain-how-abolishing-the-wealth-tax-changed-their-country-272041)***

## Centralised economies

The research’s two-decade-long timeframe helps interpret the trend. In the 1990s, many finance firms distributed ballooning profits among their employees, pushing salaries skyward.

As [another of our studies](https://www.iese.edu/insight/articles/salaries-finance-income-inequality-crisis/) has shown, even when banking profits took a hit – during the 2008 crisis and its aftermath, for instance – salaries remained high. This was even the case when countries enacted specific regulations like capping bonuses to curb salaries in the sector and discourage risk taking.

Broader national contexts – including overall income inequality levels and how centralised and diversified economies are – also make a difference.

In countries such as Spain, Sweden and Denmark, financial cities contributed substantially to relatively modest increases in overall top 1% earnings shares. In contrast, in Germany, the US and Canada, financial cities played a smaller role in much larger aggregate increases in national top earnings.

Sweden, Norway and Spain are generally more centralised economies than Germany, Canada or the US, so their financial hubs naturally play a larger role.

Additionally, in North America, finance’s wage-setting practices have spread to other sectors such as tech. Meanwhile in Scandinavian countries, finance has remained a niche sector, with exceptionally high wages but limited spillover into other sectors.

## Financialisation, globalisation and skills

Some [75% of European Union citizens live in cities and urban areas](https://europa.eu/eurobarometer/surveys/detail/3368), a figure set to rise to 78% by 2050. Around the world, cities are expanding.

This makes it vital to understand what makes them the way they are. Globalisation is often blamed for income inequality in cities because cities provide the high-paying professional infrastructure ⎯ the consultants and lawyers as well as the bankers ⎯ for global business. Our research shows that some of the cities with the largest surge in earnings concentration are places like Stockholm and Madrid ⎯ important European capitals but not centres of global commerce.

Another suggested cause for income inequality is that highly educated workers and productive firms cluster in amenities-rich cities. But our research carefully paired cities with similar amenities and skill levels. In every case, the financial city contributed disproportionately to top earnings, and the other did not.

It is therefore safe to say that the presence of a financial sector is the determining factor in income inequality. This finding has profound implications for the sorts of cities, and societies, we want to create.

title: How heatwaves make life harder for homeless people
authors: Will Haynes, Leverhulme Early Career Research Fellow, Cultural Geography, Lancaster University
content:
Cities are getting hotter. Building materials like concrete or asphalt trap and radiate heat. Heat emissions from vehicles and air conditioning units are concentrated in urban areas, and there’s less of a breeze in built-up places.

Alongside [fewer trees or the absence of cooling rivers](https://www.bbc.co.uk/weather/articles/cednp88vpxqo), heatwaves can feel harsher in urban areas, where homeless people are among the [most vulnerable to extreme heat](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/climate-change-and-health).

Researchers like me don’t yet know enough about how [high temperatures](https://theconversation.com/topics/heatwave-4853) affect those experiencing homelessness, or what exactly should be done to protect them as [the effects of climate change become more severe](https://doi.org/10.1177/17579139231224690).

But we do already know that [cities in the UK are not well adapted](https://www.redcross.org.uk/get-help/prepare-for-emergencies/heatwaves-uk/why-uk-heat-bad) to high temperatures. Making matters worse, many people don’t have access to reliable and safe resources.

In central Manchester, for example, there are few public toilets to access and free drinking water is not easy to find. In June 2026, [reports](https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/someone-could-die-weather-how-34196056) have highlighted multiple instances of homeless people in the city suffering illness and sunburn from high temperatures. This summer, some charities and organisations have handed out provisions in hot weather, like cold drinks or suncream.

***Read more: [How turning front gardens into driveways has added to night-time heat](https://theconversation.com/how-turning-front-gardens-into-driveways-has-added-to-night-time-heat-287338)***

[Alongside other vulnerable groups](https://gmintegratedcare.org.uk/healthy-living/heatwave-health-warning/), Greater Manchester Combined Authority has [recognised](https://www.greatermanchester-ca.gov.uk/what-we-do/resilience/prepare-yourself/hot-weather-and-heatwave/) that people experiencing homeless face acute challenges from hot weather. But for those sleeping rough, advising people to avoid the heat can be unhelpful. Some people simply can’t escape the heat.

This is not just an environmental problem. Homeless people are at higher risk of various health problems. A [report](https://homelesshub.ca/resource/beating-heat-street/) from a Canadian organisation called The Homeless Hub outlines some heat-related emergencies that those experiencing homelessness are exposed to including heat cramps, exhaustion, heat stroke, as well as factors that can endanger health like insomnia or the ability to store food safely.

Heatwaves also bring risks that come from sheltering or keeping cool by canals or rivers, as many homeless people do. [Sadly, drowning is a serious issue](https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/news/greater-manchester-news/man-dies-river-irwell-manchester-34341840), particularly among vulnerable people. In France, [at least 74 people have died](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn4d2vv935lo) in unsupervised bodies of water since the beginning of the June-July heatwaves.

[My research](https://www.lancaster.ac.uk/lec/about-us/people/william-haynes) is about everyday experiences of homelessness. I routinely see both the challenges from extreme weather and adaptations that are made to cope with that.

While researching homelessness in Rome, Italy, I’ve seen people carrying all their belongings and clothes even in the searing summer temperatures, or hiding them, so they aren’t stolen or damaged. Others build shaded structures out of cardboard, around park benches or hang out in cooler spaces such as parks, by fountains or near rivers.

## Removing dangerous design

During my fieldwork in Toronto, Canada, I saw people using public amenities like bus stops for shade. That’s especially commonplace because camping in green places like parks is not allowed in Toronto. In a tiring heatwave, a chance to lie down and rest is extremely valuable, and something many of us might take for granted.

[Hostile urban design](https://theconversation.com/defensive-architecture-designing-the-homeless-out-of-cities-52399), like the removal of park benches or integrating spikes into seats to discourage lying down, can be dangerous. People need more accessible public toilets and water fountains, not less. Toronto has a [heat relief network](https://www.toronto.ca/community-people/health-wellness-care/health-programs-advice/hot-weather/cool-spaces-near-you/), a citywide network of more than 500 cool spaces available all summer, signposted online – something UK cities could integrate as heatwaves become more commonplace.

The Museum of Homelessness in London has a project called [Severe Weather Emergency](https://museumofhomelessness.org/swe), where systems of care in the UK are assessed on their preparedness in facing the challenges of climate change. Council [signposts can offer helpful advice](https://heat.gov/who-is-most-at-risk-to-extreme-heat/at-risk-people-experiencing-homelessness/) to help everyone deal with the heat, like those suggested by a website called [heat.gov](https://heat.gov/who-is-most-at-risk-to-extreme-heat/at-risk-people-experiencing-homelessness/) in the US. Ending efforts to [remove the presence of homelessness through policing](https://theconversation.com/cities-are-clearing-encampments-but-this-wont-solve-homelessness-heres-a-better-way-forward-236762) should extend to all weather conditions, not just heatwaves or [extreme cold](https://www.crisis.org.uk/ending-homelessness/key-homelessness-policy-areas/rough-sleeping/what-is-swep/).

[Recent research](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2502873123) shows that future urban warming is likely underestimated. Considering the health risks, the perspectives and experiences of homeless people must be at the centre of a new urban heat strategy in Manchester and throughout the UK. These people have huge experience and appreciate the challenges they face very well.

Involving more people experiencing homelessness in research, service provision and policy encourages the development of solutions that are suitable to a certain place and inclusive to all. This “nothing about us without us” approach is already [used by some Canadian organisations](https://homelesshub.ca/resource/nothing-about-us-without-us-seven-principles-leadership-and-inclusion-people-lived-experience-homelessness/) working to support homeless people. Faced with shared environmental challenges and by listening to others, we can still make our cities fairer and cooler for everyone.

*Will Haynes does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Homeless people are at higher risk of various health problems.

title: Heat deaths are a public health crisis rooted in housing inequality
authors: Philip Broadbent, Wellcome Multimorbidity PhD Fellow & Public Health Registrar, University of Glasgow
content:
The heatwaves of late May and June killed an estimated 2,700 people in England and Wales, according to a [recent analysis](https://www.lshtm.ac.uk/newsevents/news/2026/more-2700-excess-deaths-estimated-england-and-wales-during-may-and-june) – around 550 in May, when west London hit 35.1°C, and 2,200 in June, as East Anglia reached 37°C.

Both events broke records that had stood since 1944 and 1976, and researchers estimate that 42% of the deaths were attributable to the extra heat resulting from human-induced [climate change](https://theconversation.com/topics/climate-change-27). They add to a mounting toll: [more than 10,000 people died](https://roundourway.org/latest/more-than-10-000-deaths-during-uk-heatwaves-between-2020-and-2024-new-data-finds) during UK heatwaves between 2020 and 2024, according to the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA).

Public health experts call extreme heat a [“silent killer”](https://www.theguardian.com/environment/2025/jun/27/the-silent-killer-what-you-need-to-know-about-heatwaves) that can claim anyone, even the young and fit. That is true and worth repeating. But it obscures the pattern of what is happening: heat deaths are not scattered randomly across the population. They fall predictably and measurably on particular people in particular homes.

Around 60% of the estimated deaths in May and June were among people aged over 85. But age is only part of the story, because vulnerability to heat is socially patterned. A [Government Actuary’s Department analysis](https://actuaries.blog.gov.uk/2026/06/09/heat-health-and-inequality/), published days before the June heatwave, shows that England’s most deprived communities are concentrated in dense urban areas with the least green space – places subject to the [“urban heat island”](https://theconversation.com/topics/urban-heat-islands-52917) effect. This is where concrete and tarmac absorb heat by day and release it at night, depriving residents the relief of overnight cooling that allows people to recover.

Every English neighbourhood that ranks among both the 10% most deprived and the 10% most exposed to extreme heat is in London. During the 40°C heatwave of 2022, the urban heat island effect was itself [responsible for a substantial share](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11334115/) of London’s heat-related deaths.

The common thread is housing. An analysis by the [Resolution Foundation](https://www.resolutionfoundation.org/publications/its-getting-hot-in-here/) thinktank found that 54% of the poorest fifth of English households live in homes at high risk of overheating, against 18% of the richest fifth. Two-thirds of social renters, and six out of ten households with young children, live in homes at the highest risk as the country warms.

Flats, small homes and overcrowded properties trap heat. Renters cannot fit shutters or external shading, and cooling costs money that low-income households do not have. The [English Housing Survey](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/english-housing-survey-2023-to-2024-climate-resilient-homes-fact-sheet/english-housing-survey-2023-to-2024-climate-resilient-homes-fact-sheet), carried out by the UK government, found that 2.9 million households say that their homes get uncomfortably hot.

## Year-round problem

The troubling part of this is that these are largely the same homes we already knew were dangerous in winter. Cold homes caused an estimated [4,950 excess winter deaths](https://www.endfuelpoverty.org.uk/4950-excess-winter-deaths-caused-by-cold-homes-last-winter/) across Britain in 2022-23 – around 45 people a day through the coldest months.

We have treated fuel poverty as a cold-weather problem, answered with winter fuel payments and seasonal campaigns. But a badly-insulated home is thermally incompetent all year round: it leaks heat in January and traps it in July. The same outdated, inadequate housing stock kills in both seasons; only the mechanism changes. Fuel poverty is not a winter problem that pauses in spring – it is a year-round emergency.

None of this is inevitable, as last summer proved. In 2025, UKHSA recorded [1,504 heat-associated deaths in England](https://www.gov.uk/government/statistics/heat-mortality-monitoring-report-england-2025/heat-mortality-monitoring-report-england-2025): roughly half the 3,039 its models had predicted from temperatures alone, a pattern consistent across all five heat episodes from that year. UKHSA is careful to note that causes cannot be firmly attributed, but heat-health alerts and the system-wide response across the NHS, social care and emergency services are likely to have contributed. Adaptation, in other words, saves lives at scale.

But adaptation, too, is unequal. Private adaptation – air conditioning, well-ventilated houses, leafy suburbs – all correlate with wealth. And public health advice to “keep cool” is [least effective](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5773866/) for precisely those with the least capacity to act on it: the tenant who cannot alter her flat, the pensioner who cannot afford to run a fan. As heatwaves intensify, the gap between those who can buy their way to safety and those who cannot will widen, unless policy closes it.

Heat episodes in England are predicted to become [more intense, longer and more frequent](https://www.gov.uk/guidance/health-effects-of-climate-change-hecc-report) as the climate warms. The Climate Change Committee, the government’s independent climate adviser, has proposed that heat-related deaths in 2050 should be [no higher than they are today](https://www.theccc.org.uk/publication/a-well-adapted-uk/). Achieving this will require treating heat as both a housing and an inequality issue. This includes retrofit programmes that prepare homes for summer as well as winter, more trees and green spaces in the most deprived neighbourhoods, and making sure the Decent Homes Standard – the government’s minimum standard for safe and suitable housing – includes protections against overheating. It also means targeted support for people who are already known to be most at risk from extreme heat.

What it does not mean is simply relying on more leaflets advising people to drink water and close the curtains. The deaths of May and June were tragic, but not random. Our response should not be random either. We know whose homes will be dangerous next summer – the question is whether we act before it arrives.

*Philip Broadbent receives funding from The Wellcome Trust 223499/Z/21/Z*
description: This summer’s heat deaths weren’t random. Poor, badly insulated homes are a public health hazard in summer as well as winter.

title: Why street art doesn’t always make a city better
authors: Juan Manuel Ros García, Profesor Catedrático Área de Proyectos Arquitectónicos, Universidad CEU San Pablo
content:
For years, our understanding of street art has been incomplete. Some people reduce it to [decoration](https://www.routledge.com/Art-Space-and-the-City/Miles/p/book/9780415139434), a [tourist attraction](https://doi.org/10.1177/12063312261427926), or a form of [urban cosmetic enhancement](https://doi.org/10.1177/0038026118771293). Others [eye it suspiciously](https://doi.org/10.4000/belgeo.13381), viewing it as an unsolicited aesthetic imposition. But neither of these positions tells the whole story.

The fundamental issue is not whether a particular mural is widely liked or disliked, or whether a particular sculpture looks good in photos. The real question is this: how does an artistic intervention change the everyday experience of a town or city?

We are not just talking about the urban landscape, but about how a city can become more integrated, balanced and meaningful for those who live there. In other words, we are talking about quality of life. Urban art can ([some would argue it must](https://orcid.org/0000-0003-4988-8912)) introduce everyday beauty, serenity and reflection – things that symbolically activate public space in the service of subjective wellbeing.

## Who gets to make urban art?

Well-known urban artists have never flown under the radar. Whether in informal art (such as graffiti) or more mainstream works, artists have always fervently asserted their authorship.

But what street art seeks to do above all else is generate headline-grabbing moments of surprise. Take Banksy’s Girl with Balloon, which captivated people because its simple, minimalist image, found on the street, was able to stir up a range of emotions, from loss and childhood nostalgia to hope and fragility.

Nevertheless, the presence of well-known names establishes a silent hierarchy. This means that artists like Taki 183, Keith Haring, Basquiat, Blek le Rat, Oldenburg, Banksy, OBEY and Kapoor are able to intervene in public spaces, while others are not. It is not enough to simply occupy a wall or produce any old image; it takes artistic skill, authorisation and negotiation, understanding of the context, responsibility, and the ability to create a meaningful experience.

But even among those who manage to make their mark in the public sphere, not every work succeeds in having a positive impact on the quality of shared urban life.

***Leer más: [Graffiti has undergone a massive shift in a few quick decades as street art gains social acceptance](https://theconversation.com/graffiti-has-undergone-a-massive-shift-in-a-few-quick-decades-as-street-art-gains-social-acceptance-196995)***

## A deeper question

This is the focus of [AUPART](https://investigacionusp.ceu.es/en/ipublic/item/10180533), our ongoing research project into urban art and quality of life. The project does not start from the premise that any piece of urban art automatically improves collective wellbeing; it deeply probes this assumption, and seeks to find out whether it is true at all.

Quality of life is not a simple concept, nor can it be directly attributed to a single factor. According to, for instance, the framework set out by the Spanish National Statistic Institute’s [Multidimensional Quality of Life Indicator](https://www.ine.es/en/experimental/imcv/experimental_ind_multi_calidad_vida_en.htm), it depends on material conditions, social relations, perception of the environment, safety, governance, subjective wellbeing and everyday experience of a place.

That is why, when we study urban art, we ask ourselves in what specific ways it can exert an influence, and under what conditions it might have an impact. A work of art should not be judged solely on formal quality, scale or whose signature it bears, but also on its ability to act as a mediator between public space and urban life.

## When public art succeeds or fails

Two long-running projects that have done just this are [Mural Arts of Philadelphia](https://muralarts.org/?utm_source), which features numerous works that have had an impact on the community, and the [Inside Out Project](https://www.insideoutproject.net/) led by the French street artist JR, which has an international reach.

In our study we have analysed works such as Julia, the Jaume Plensa sculpture in Madrid’s Plaza de Colón. With results currently undergoing peer review we cannot claim that it improves quality of life in absolute terms. But we can say that it plays an undeniable role in urban mediation, offering a highly visible artistic presence that can alter the experience of the surroundings, the perception of safety, the symbolic value of place, and emotional connections to the square where it is installed.

However, a work of great artistic merit can also fail socially if it does not fit in with the practical reality of the space where it is installed. This was what happened with Richard Serra’s [Tilted Arc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tilted_Arc), a solid steel plate some 36 metres long, installed in 1981 in Federal Plaza, New York.

The sculpture was criticised, not only for aesthetic reasons but also for its impact on the everyday use of the space. This was actually the artist’s intention, but it did not go down well. By dividing the square, it meant that members of the public had to alter their normal routes. It led to concerns regarding safety and traffic flow, and was [removed in 1989](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/37705386_Tilted_Arc_Controversy_Dangerous_Precedent) after a lengthy public and institutional controversy.

## Beyond aesthetics

It is often believed that street art is in itself enough to regenerate an area. For example in Wynwood, a neighbourhood in Miami, urban mural art has generated visibility and an [urban brand](https://thewynwoodwalls.com/), but the district’s evolution has led to growing commercialisation, increasingly standardised murals being commissioned, and concerns about runaway gentrification and the loss of the creative community that made the area famous in the first place. There was reputational and economic success, but that did not equate to social regeneration.

Mural Istanbul, an initiative in the Turkish capital, made similar mistakes. It addressed artistic activism from a solely aesthetic point of view, and was widely seen as a form of social alienation that only aimed to draw attention to a neglected part of the city.

Authors – such as urbanists [Malcolm Miles](https://www.routledge.com/Art-Space-and-the-City/Miles/p/book/9780415139434?utm_source), [Ann Markusen and Anne Gadwa](https://www.arts.gov/sites/default/files/CreativePlacemaking-Paper.pdf?utm_source), art historian [Miwon Kwon](https://direct.mit.edu/books/book/2621/One-Place-after-AnotherSite-Specific-Art-and?%20utm_source) and architect [Kevin Lynch](https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262620017/the-image-of-the-city/) – have all highlighted from their own perspectives that the value of public art cannot be separated from the society, institutions and territory that make it possible.

It is not enough for people to just see a work of art. It is also essential that they remember it, understand it, apply it to their own understanding of their surroundings, analyse it, evaluate it and, ultimately, feel able to draw inspiration from it.

This was the case with the [Heerlen Murals](https://urbact.eu/good-practices/street-art-murals-urban-renewal) project in the Netherlands. Following the decline of Herleen’s mining industry, the city used community murals to promote social and urban regeneration, improve the image of deprived neighbourhoods, and encourage participation among different groups of citizens.

***Leer más: [Melbourne’s love-hate relationship with being Australia’s ‘street art capital’](https://theconversation.com/melbournes-love-hate-relationship-with-being-australias-street-art-capital-78177)***

## Not just decoration

On its own, street art cannot resoundingly improve life in a city, but it can help to strengthen certain aspects of quality of life. It achieves this when it manages to create stronger bonds with place, stimulates social interaction, reinforces shared identity, helps people understand their surroundings, and manages to be accepted by locals while receiving institutional support.

When this happens, artists become more than image producers – they become somebody capable of creating bonds between their work, place and community, making public space an expression of memory, values and shared forms of belonging.

If we aspire to more liveable, inclusive and culturally vibrant cities, we have to find the conditions under which artistic interventions have positive, measurable effects on public space and community life.

This requires us to prepare each project more thoroughly, assess its social relevance, check whether the location actually needs it, and analyse the context. It means recognising that the impact of urban art is not measured solely by how it decorates the city, but by how it transforms a community’s relationship with the place it inhabits, and acknowledging the value of public space as a catalyst for social learning. If we settle for something that just looks nice, we miss out on an enormous opportunity to improve the places where we live.
