title: Kids need to play — and how cities are designed and resourced affects their access
authors: Ozlem Cankaya, Associate Professor, Early Childhood Curriculum Studies, MacEwan University; Marielle Papin, Assistant Professor in Political Science, MacEwan University; Salim Hashmi, Lecturer in Psychology, King's College London
content:
Decades of research in child development confirms that [young children’s play is linked to positive outcomes in mental health, cognitive and social development](https://theconversation.com/as-a-child-psychiatrist-i-know-its-critical-for-kindergartens-to-embrace-playful-learning-224056) as well as fewer behavioural problems.

Despite this consensus, play [is becoming hard to access in everyday life](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-016-3490-2), particularly in cities, due to a combination of [spatial or environmental](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cities.2025.106642) [and socio-cultural factors](https://doi.org/10.17269/s41997-020-00355-w).

Increased traffic, dense housing, limited or constrained access to green space and natural environments and heightened concerns about safety and risky play have [reduced children’s independent play opportunities outdoors](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41835458).

Many families rely on structured programs to compensate for these constraints, but these [often come with financial costs, scheduling pressures and limited availability](https://doi.org/10.25336/P6CW3H).

## Play is shaped by systems

Play depends on a set of conditions that must be created and maintained.

Parks and green spaces may be [available but not always](https://www.cbc.ca/player/play/video/9.7165534) accessible, safe or inviting. Community programs can be valuable, but they often require registration fees, transportation and time commitments that not all families can manage.

It’s not only up to parents to create play opportunities — [urban planning decisions, infrastructure, policy and politics](https://doi.org/10.1080/23748834.2026.2614191) have significant influence. Who gets to play, where they play and how they play are not neutral questions. They are determined by how [cities are designed, how resources are distributed and whose needs are prioritized](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11524-024-00855-x).

When these systems are uneven, opportunities for play are also uneven. Families living in [high-density housing may lack access](https://healthyplan.city/en) to nearby outdoor spaces. Neighbourhoods with fewer investments in infrastructure may have limited or poorly maintained play areas.

Caregivers working multiple jobs may have less time to facilitate or supervise play. Cultural and [social dynamics and privilege](https://theconversation.com/reopen-recreation-spaces-after-covid-19-for-the-good-of-the-public-not-the-individual-144344) can shape how safe families feel using public spaces.

[Girls, racialized children or children from ethnic minority backgrounds](https://www.unicef.org/eca/stories/importance-outdoor-play-and-how-support-it) may be less likely to participate in outdoor play. Researchers studying the [leisure experiences of African Nova Scotian children](https://doi.org/10.1080/14927713.2023.2291023) note that anti-Black racism constrains children’s access to play: Policing surveillance, under-resourced communities and scrutiny of Black families in cases of children’s potential injuries from play are identified as barriers for African Nova Scotian children.

***Read more: [Where can Black children go in summer? Black families face disparities and need equitable options](https://theconversation.com/where-can-black-children-go-in-summer-black-families-face-disparities-and-need-equitable-options-253013)***

This means play is not only a developmental issue, but also an equity issue. When access to play varies, so do opportunities for learning, exploration and social connection. Over time, these differences can accumulate, contributing to broader inequalities in development and well-being.

The central challenge is no longer about recognizing the importance of play. If we want cities where children can thrive, our societies need to create conditions where play is part of everyday life, not something that must be scheduled, supervised or purchased.

## Third places in the city

The concept of [a third place refers to](https://www.cbc.ca/radio/tapestry/searching-for-connection-third-places-may-be-the-solution-1.6680662) an environment that exists beyond home and work or school or day care, where individuals can gather, interact, spend time informally and create community.

Child-friendly third places are particularly important because they support spontaneous, self-directed play that is not constrained by rigid rules or structured programming.

In urban contexts, third places include locations such as libraries, parks, community centres, community gardens and shared public areas that are accessible, low-cost or potentially free and socially welcoming. For example, in Edmonton, StoryWalk at MacEwan University — an outdoor path where children and families can follow pages of a storybook posted sequentially along a campus path — [creates a third place at the university for young children](https://theconversation.com/how-a-downtown-university-story-walk-promotes-childrens-literacy-and-belonging-in-higher-education-231659).

When thoughtfully planned and resourced, such third places equitably allow children to explore, negotiate social interactions and engage in imaginative activity, all of which are associated with cognitive and social development.

## Nature can offer a powerful play opportunity

Natural environments represent a particularly [powerful form of third place](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13679-015-0179-2). Unlike highly structured playgrounds, which often prescribe specific actions (climb here, slide there), settings such as parks, green spaces and wooded areas [offer open-ended materials and variable conditions](https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.7721/chilyoutenvi.14.2.0021) that invite exploration, experimentation and imagination.

Children can manipulate elements such as sticks, water, sand and uneven terrain. Such elements support problem-solving, creativity and physical co-ordination in ways that fixed equipment cannot.

***Read more: [Wonder and wisdom in a children’s forest nature program](https://theconversation.com/wonder-and-wisdom-in-a-childrens-forest-nature-program-106692)***

Natural spaces tend to sustain longer and more complex play episodes because they do not limit how materials can be used. Nature-based play environments foster cognitive flexibility and social interaction, whereas structured playgrounds — while valuable for safety and accessibility — often constrain the depth and diversity of children’s play experiences.

However, inequities in the distribution of wealth within cities directly and indirectly impact how “natural” play spaces are regulated, maintained and used, influencing [children’s access to this form of outdoor play](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.healthplace.2018.11.008).

Research shows that children growing up in marginalized neighbourhoods often have the least access to safe, spontaneous and nature-based play opportunities despite potentially benefiting the most from them.

For parents or caregivers, rather than relying solely on organized programs, it is valuable to identify what third places and outdoor spaces might be available locally. Where feasible, these can be integrated into everyday routines to create consistent and equitable opportunities for play.

## Quality indoor play experiences

Another possibility for families can be offering quality indoor play experiences that don’t require expensive or highly specialized toys.

Our recent research shows that children can engage deeply [in meaningful play using everyday materials](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44271-025-00362-y), particularly versatile objects that invite exploration, experimentation and imaginative thinking.

***Read more: [How children’s play with everyday objects can encourage skills needed for STEM success](https://theconversation.com/how-childrens-play-with-everyday-objects-can-encourage-skills-needed-for-stem-success-274274)***

Recycled and scrap materials such as cardboard, fabric, containers or other household objects provide flexible opportunities for problem-solving, construction and early STEM thinking at home. Doll play provides [opportunities for children to practice](https://doi.org/10.1111/desc.13163) social skills by creating imaginary worlds and taking others’ perspectives.

Materials like [blocks similarly support reasoning, design thinking and innovation because they allow children to test ideas, revise structures and create](https://theconversation.com/mathematical-thinking-begins-in-the-early-years-with-dialogue-and-real-world-exploration-128282) without fixed outcomes. The quality of play depends less on the cost of materials and more on the possibilities they afford.

Beyond parents’ and caregivers’ own choices, creating equitable opportunities for play requires cities and communities to invest in flexible everyday environments, as well as accessible third and natural spaces where all children can explore, imagine and belong.

*Ozlem Cankaya receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada (SSHRC) and the Spencer Foundation, and is affiliated with the International Toy Research Association, Terra Centre and the Council for Early Learning and Care.*

*Marielle Papin receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.*

*Salim Hashmi has received funding for research from Mattel.*
description: If we want cities where all children can thrive, we need to create conditions where play is part of daily life, not something that must be scheduled or purchased.

title: New towns are back – but this time they must be more walkable
authors: James White, Professor of Planning and Urban Design, University of Glasgow; Hannah Hickman, Associate Professor in Planning Practice , University of the West of England
content:
The UK’s next generation of [new towns](https://theconversation.com/topics/new-towns-9508) form a central part of the government’s growth strategy, while also promising to address the housing shortage.

Unlike the low-rise, car-dependent towns built after the second world war, these proposed towns are intended to be denser, more walkable and built around public transport and active lifestyles.

But the UK does not build dense housing particularly well, and various economic, political and cultural forces are pushing new developments in the other direction.

The government [argues](https://www.gov.uk/government/speeches/mais-lecture-2026) that higher density development can help support inclusive economic growth while lowering carbon emissions and reducing dependence on private cars. Its [new towns programme](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/new-towns-draft-programme) and its [seven proposed locations](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/seven-new-towns-proposed-to-kickstart-housebuilding-push) reflect this shift in thinking.

Developments such as Leeds South Bank, Manchester Victoria North and London Thamesmead are intended to support dense urban living in locations with strong transport links and job opportunities.

Wholly new settlements, such as Tempsford in the much-vaunted Oxford to Cambridge growth corridor, will have an ill defined aim of [“ambitious density”](https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/new-towns-draft-programme/annex-a-draft-new-towns-planning-policy) and are expected to have a higher density development model than the last generation of new towns.

## What density looks like

In reality, a higher density model doesn’t necessarily mean tall shiny towers. Cities like Barcelona, Paris and Stockholm, to take just three European examples, often consist of six-storey apartment blocks arranged around grid patterns of walkable streets and public squares – yet they are [significantly denser](https://theconversation.com/think-your-country-is-crowded-these-maps-reveal-the-truth-about-population-density-across-europe-90345) than equivalent British cities.

Being “ambitous” about density, as the government intends, will require a decisive shift away from the two-storey housing estates that were developed around UK towns and cities in recent decades. Instead, there will be a move towards mid-rise neighbourhoods with housing between four and eight storeys and located close to walkable mixed use high streets.

Yet Britain’s housing system is not set up to deliver these kinds of neighbourhoods – or towns. Most housing in the UK is still built at low densities, and there appears to be little appetite within the powerful and [highly profitable](https://housingevidence.ac.uk/project/why-have-the-volume-housebuilders-been-so-profitable/) volume housebuilding industry to adapt their established business models.

Denser schemes can be more complex and expensive. Building safety regulations, alongside [rising land and material costs](https://housingforum.org.uk/reports/key-publications/the-cost-of-building-a-house/), means high-density development is less financially attractive than suburban housing. Cultural preferences also matter. Research repeatedly shows that people in the UK [prefer houses over flats](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02673037.2019.1584665#abstract), while proposals for denser development often encounter strong local opposition.

These attitudes are not universal, however. In much of Europe, there is strong support for compact living across income groups, particularly where supported by [decent local amenities and accessible green space](https://www.mdpi.com/2071-1050/11/12/3480). Even in the UK, the prevalence of three to five storey tenements and apartments in Scottish cities demonstrates that higher densities are both [acceptable and often desirable](https://blogs.ed.ac.uk/docomomoiscul/wp-content/uploads/sites/8300/2015/01/Glendinning_New-Old-Tenement_secured.pdf) places to live.

However, the horror of the Grenfell Tower fire – and the subsequent revelation that thousands of people were living in buildings with [the same unsafe cladding](https://theconversation.com/grenfell-tower-finally-the-worst-type-of-cladding-is-to-be-banned-five-years-on-185040) – have only deepened existing anxieties about higher-density urban living.

More recently, planning concepts associated with density, such as the “15-minute city” or low traffic neighbourhoods, have become politically polarising. Some have even characterised such ideas as a [government conspiracy](https://theconversation.com/15-minute-cities-how-to-separate-the-reality-from-the-conspiracy-theory-200111) to control how people live and move around cities.

Dense neighbourhoods that work well – whether in Europe or parts of the UK – typically depend on high quality urban, landscape and architectural design, a mix of tenures, land uses and amenities, and good public transport. While these are precisely the ingredients identified in the UK’s new towns policy, they are also the components of placemaking that local authorities struggle to deliver and the housebuilding industry actively resists.

If [planning deregulation](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/landmark-planning-and-infrastructure-bill-becomes-law) leads to higher density neighbourhoods being built hastily and without sufficient thought, we could quickly ended up with overcrowded places that lack shops and services and are poorly served by public transport. This outcome would only serve to strengthen local opposition to new development.

The success of the UK’s next generation of new towns will therefore depend not just on the raw number of homes built, but also on whether they can create denser places that people genuinely want to live in.

*James White receives funding from the Economic and Social Research Council.*

*Hannah Hickman receives funding from the Economic Social Research Council, National Infrastructure Planning Association*
description: But economic and cultural forces mean dense housing is harder to develop than low-rise sprawl.

title: Children who grow up in poverty are 5 times more likely to be poor young adults: new study
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Roger Wilkins, Professorial Fellow and Co-Director, HILDA Survey, Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research, The University of Melbourne; Esperanza Vera-Toscano, Honorary Fellow, The University of Melbourne; Instituto de Estudios Sociales Avanzados (IESA - CSIC)
content:
About 757,000 Australian children aged under 15 lived in poverty in 2022-23 – more than all the people living in cities of Geelong, Newcastle and Wollongong combined.

That’s about [one in six Australian children](https://povertyandinequality.acoss.org.au/poverty-in-australia-2026-who-is-affected), according to the latest estimates from the Australian Council of Social Service (ACOSS) and UNSW Sydney.

But what happens to these children as they grow older? Do the disadvantages of growing up below the poverty line disappear as they finish school, find jobs and establish their own households?

Our research, recently published in [The Economic Record](https://doi.org/10.1111/1475-4932.70074), suggests childhood poverty casts a long shadow, affecting young Australians well into their 20s and 30s.

## Lasting effects of a poor childhood

We used data from the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia ([HILDA](https://melbourneinstitute.unimelb.edu.au/hilda)) Survey, which has followed Australian households since 2001.

We examined 2,205 people whose childhood household incomes were observed in at least three years, and whose incomes were known at least once again from age 24. This allowed us to examine whether growing up in poverty was associated with an increased risk of experiencing poverty as adults, aged 24 to 35.

Australia does not have an official poverty line. So we defined poverty using a relative income measure, widely used in international research. This takes into account household disposable income (after taxes and government payments, such as family tax benefits) and is adjusted for household size.

In dollar terms, the poverty line we were looking at sits at about A$72,000 for a couple with two children, and about $55,000 for a single parent with two children.

We found children growing up below the poverty line had a 22.4 percentage points higher risk of living in poverty in their 20s and early 30s than those who grew up in households with incomes between 150% and 200% of the poverty line.

To be clear, 200% of the poverty line, the upper limit of the childhood income of the reference group, is still not even close to being wealthy. It’s simply the median income: about $144,000 for a couple with two children.

What this means is that Australians who grow up poor face a 27% risk of being in poverty in early adulthood, in contrast to just 5% in the reference group. That’s more than five times the risk.

We also looked at others who grew up in near-poverty, with household incomes between 100% and 150% of the poverty line, or roughly $72,000 to $108,000 for a couple with two children. They also had a higher poverty rate in early-adulthood: 8.7 percentage points higher than children from the reference group.

By contrast, we found no statistically significant differences in early adulthood poverty between the income group just below the median and those who grew up in households with higher incomes.

## A ‘double whammy’ for kids from single-parent families

Australia has [1.2 million single parent families](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/labour/employment-and-unemployment/labour-force-status-families/latest-release). Children in those families are especially vulnerable to poverty persisting into early adulthood.

According to [2026 ACOSS–UNSW research](https://povertyandinequality.acoss.org.au/poverty-in-australia-2026-who-is-affected/), 37% of children in sole-parent families were living in poverty in 2022–23, compared with 11% of children in partnered families.

Low-income single-parent families face compounding pressures: even beyond obvious financial pressures, one parent also has to carry out all the unpaid work of child care and household tasks.

Not only are children in single-parent families more likely to experience poverty, our research showed that poverty is more persistent into adulthood, likely because of those compounding pressures. It’s a double whammy.

In August 2025, Swinburne University researchers [surveyed 2,590 Australian single parents](https://doi.org/10.25916/sut.29757344), who were mostly women.

They found almost four out of five single mothers (78%) spent “a lot” or “almost all” of their time worrying about or planning for their family’s financial wellbeing. As one respondent said:

> I need more money. The financial stress feels untenable.

## What makes poverty persist into adulthood?

We examined several possible reasons why poverty is more likely to last into later life. These included educational attainment, reduced employment, lower rates of partnering and poorer health.

We found people who grew up in more disadvantaged households were generally less likely to complete post-school qualifications, be employed or live with a partner.

They were also more likely to be single parents. Some health measures were also associated with childhood economic circumstances.

These adult outcomes are themselves associated with poverty risk. But even when we accounted for them, the association between childhood poverty and early-adulthood poverty remained substantial.

## What can we do about it?

Our research doesn’t isolate a single cause of childhood poverty. But our findings do strongly suggest policies focused on reducing poverty in families with children can deliver lasting benefits.

To significantly reduce adult poverty, we need more focus on directly reducing economic hardship in families with children, especially those from low-income single-parent families.

In 2023, the Albanese government [boosted financial support](https://www.pm.gov.au/media/extending-financial-safety-net-single-parents) for low-income single parents, raising the age cut-off for the Parenting Payment (Single) until the youngest child turns 14. That change was expected to help at least 57,000 single primary carers, who were mostly women (91%).

But more is still required, such as targeted increases to Family Tax Benefit Part A payments.

And if we want to track the success of policy changes in reducing long-term poverty, we need better evidence. That means more long-term studies, following individuals over their lives from kids to adults.

Then we would be able to better identify the key factors keeping Australians locked into poverty for decades – or helping them escape it.

***Read more: [Many parents – mostly mothers – lose family payments from the first dollar they earn. Here’s how we could fix it](https://theconversation.com/many-parents-mostly-mothers-lose-family-payments-from-the-first-dollar-they-earn-heres-how-we-could-fix-it-262119)***

*Roger Wilkins receives funding from the Australian Research Council. Funding for this research was received from the Paul Ramsay Foundation.*

*Esperanza Vera-Toscano does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: A study shows how childhood poverty casts a long shadow, affecting young Australians well into their 20s and 30s.

title: The impossible equation of being a researcher mother, striving to make ends meet
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Marie Janot Caminade, Docteure en science politique, chercheuse à l'Institut des sciences sociales du politique (ISP), Université Paris Nanterre
content:
How can we encourage women to pursue scientific careers? In recent years, a number of mentoring or awareness campaigns have been put in place to encourage French high school students to study maths, physics or engineering sciences, while they remain underrepresented in these fields. One of the last large-scale initiatives is the [*Filles et Maths* program](https://www.education.gouv.fr/plan-filles-et-maths-pour-que-les-jeunes-filles-prennent-toute-leur-place-dans-les-metiers-de-l-462873), launched in 2025, including work on gender bias, the implementation of “role models” or timetables featuring flexible hours.

The program was nonetheless met with criticism: while women remain under-represented in some disciplines, they also remain a minority in the highest positions across the board in the academic world, from mathematics to social sciences.

In France, gender [inequalities](https://journals.openedition.org/socio-logos/7275) are therefore not limited to access to scientific studies: they cut across all university careers and make many women leave French Higher Education and Research before securing tenure. This “drain” is explained by several factors among which motherhood holds an important place. A [survey in Denmark](https://www.cbs.dk/en/articles/new-study-one-three-women-leaves-academia-after-becoming-mother) illustrates that unlike men, one in three women abandon their scientific career after the birth of their first child.

The survey I have been conducting among doctoral students and social scientists highlights the difficulties faced by women who became mothers before becoming permanent employees. Since the [1980s](https://theconversation.com/comment-la-globalisation-bouleverse-luniversite-97017), recruitment requirements have become tougher with candidates needing to have written a good PhD paper, [regularly have their work published](https://council.science/blog/publish-or-perish-mentality/), participate in scientific events and get involved in the life of research labs. Much of this work falls under [*hope labour*](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/342960498_Hope_labour_and_the_psychic_life_of_cultural_work), that is, unpaid work done in the hope of future employment.

In this context, what could be called the myth of the [“total researcher”](https://theconversation.com/how-uk-universities-are-failing-mothers-on-their-staff-268261) takes shape. This is based on the double penalty of being a productive scientist (without necessarily receiving any financial reward) and embodying the ideal of a career woman, devoted companion, and dedicated mother all rolled into one.

However, this ideal of the “total researcher” clashes with the actual conditions of scientific work and motherhood.

## Paying the motherhood penalty in academia

Becoming a full-time researcher requires mothers who aren’t tenured researchers to reorganise their lives. Some cram several days’ work into one by doing casual work, part-time teaching, unpaid scientific projects, and parental responsibilities. The pace often makes women work under pressure, sometimes at the expense of the quantity and quality of their scientific work.

Other women choose to remain unemployed or take parental leave and thus link their career to that of their spouse if they earn enough. If this strategy of linked career is favourable for scientific production when you have a child, it also creates material dependence that could lead to sexist and sexual violence within the family unit, which this testimony from Jeanne, a doctor and mother of a little girl, illustrates:

> “I sometimes feel like I have to \[‘have sex’\], telling myself that ‘I owe him’ and ‘He lets me know it’.”

In a [professional context](https://theconversation.com/luberisation-mondiale-de-lenseignement-superieur-est-elle-ethique-174310), where every moment must count, maternity, parental or sick leave become scientific working hours in themselves.

Rebecca, for example, shared that she continued writing her final thesis when her son was sent to hospital in an emergency. This situation feeds a feeling of double guilt: the respondents believe they are never up to par, neither as mothers nor as researchers. Joana explains:

> “I took parental leave from work, but I feel bad about working when I see my son next to me.”

Some non-tenured researcher dads, on the other hand, benefit from an academic paternity bonus. The gendered division of domestic and parental tasks, as well as taking paternity leave, sometimes allows them to devote more time to their research. To quote Marion’s doctor of History husband’s words: “I have completed nearly two articles in one month of paternity leave!”

## The ‘initiatory rite of passage’ rhetoric

Even when they reorganise their lives to ensure their scientific activity, non-tenured researcher mothers face disqualification mechanisms from their peers.

Some remarks that seem kind on the surface often come back to motherhood: “You should spend more time with your children,” “they must miss you”, or “where is your child?”

Other colleagues, often women incumbents, the difficulties that non-incumbents face in reconciling motherhood and scientific work seem perfectly normal, presenting them as inevitable trials. Louise reports how one female colleague explained to her:

> “What you’re going through is normal; it’s an uphill battle. We’ve all been there.”

While such pep talks are meant to be comforting, the constraints related to motherhood appear as an obligatory rite of passage to becoming a ‘total’ researcher.

## Motherhood-related constraints that become faults

Due to [increasing competition](https://www.campusmatin.com/metiers-carrieres/personnels-statuts/un-chercheur-temoigne-dans-son-livre-la-precarite-gagne-tout-le-monde-meme-les-titulaires.html) in the French Higher Education & Research system, motherhood can be used against some women as a means of sidelining them. Some respondents said they were excluded from scientific events on the basis that they now had “better things to do” with their children.

When [precarious researchers](https://theconversation.com/struggling-phd-mums-the-need-for-a-supportive-environment-for-mental-wellbeing-253258) voice their concerns at meetings, their difficulties in reconciling scientific work and motherhood are disqualified on the grounds that they “knew” what having a child meant before becoming a tenured researcher.

The constraints related to motherhood end up remaining invisible behind criticism about a supposed lack of scientific productivity, which tends to arise from pregnancy onwards, through comments on untenured researcher mothers-to-be’s physical appearance and how they supposedly mismanage stress with regards to important deadlines in their careers.

Anouk recounts that, after auditioning for a position as a lecturer when she was pregnant, a member of the jury who said she wanted to help her “reminded him” that committees were looking for “nice people to chat to at the coffee machine”, before offering her the following [advice](https://theconversation.com/advice-for-balancing-motherhood-and-a-scientific-career-7929):

> “Are you pregnant? You looked pale. Next time, apply some blush on your cheeks so you don’t make a bad impression.”

The complaints also concern the routes travelled to academia: not attending certain events organised during the school holidays, taking on casual work or failing to develop other research subjects that are unrelated to their PhD; are frequently associated with a lack of scientific commitment, thus obscuring the financial and family-related constraints these women face.

## A case of the fate of Sisyphus?

Faced with the impossibility of achieving the tenured researcher ideal, many respondents end up internalising their challenges as individual failures and gradually abandon academia.

This distance from academia is actually the result of structural constraints that make it difficult to reconcile motherhood and careers in research. Élodie expresses a sense of exhaustion with the predicament:

> “I am like [Sisyphus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisyphus)! My fate is to do work that will never be recognised, that will never lead to anything because I had a child at the end of my PhD studies.”

In this context, in Higher Education and Research, schemes like France’s *Filles et Maths* Maths program are not going to be enough to reduce inequalities. More broadly, rethinking the criteria around tenure is what needs to happen.

The current requirements favour women with sufficient material resources and time, to the detriment of people experiencing family, social or financial constraints. This marginalisation is not only unequal: it is harmful to research. By depriving people of certain talents, it also deprives them of certain knowledge.

*A weekly e-mail in English featuring expertise from scholars and researchers. It provides an introduction to the diversity of research coming out of the continent and considers some of the key issues facing European countries. [Get the newsletter!](https://theconversation.com/europe/newsletters?promoted=europe-newsletter-116)*

*Marie Janot Caminade ne travaille pas, ne conseille pas, ne possède pas de parts, ne reçoit pas de fonds d'une organisation qui pourrait tirer profit de cet article, et n'a déclaré aucune autre affiliation que son organisme de recherche.*
description: Getting into a tenured position in higher education and research can be likened to an obstacle course – this is particularly true when women add motherhood into the mix.

title: In Bosnia and Herzegovina, children with Down syndrome are using a video game to safely navigate the internet
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Nurbek Bekmurzaev · Global Voices
content:
*A virtual assistant called Sol the Owl guides kids through the game*

*This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the[Digital Spark](https://ddidigitalspark.org/news/) granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the[Metamorphosis Foundation](https://metamorphosis.org.mk/en/) and[TechSoup](https://www.techsoup.org/?srsltid=AfmBOoqgPtm0Yk6HG-hTECkCqfPFl9-HyRjojpYFAhrHKdM_Z419qEaW), in partnership with[CIVICUS](https://www.civicus.org/) and under the[Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI)](https://digitaldemocracyinitiative.net/) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.*

Like their peers, children and young people with Down syndrome are curious about technology and the internet, but there are often no suitable, dedicated tools to help them learn how to safely navigate the web. This is true in Bosnia and Herzegovina as well, where children with cognitive disabilities are underserved and tend to end up in digital isolation because of caregivers’ [concerns about digital safety](https://www.unicef.org/protection/keeping-children-safe-online) and the risks of being online.

There are approximately [550-700 children and adolescents with Down syndrome](https://www.ejog.org/article/S0301-2115(16%2930894-6/fulltext) in the country. They are supported by three specialized associations nationwide: the[Association “Life with Down Syndrome of FBiH](https://www.downsy.ba/)”, [Down Syndrome Association Mostar](https://down-sindrom.org/), and [DOWN SY I MI](https://www.facebook.com/people/Udru%C5%BEenje-Down-sy-i-mi-Banja-Luka/100067670422119/#). To teach online safety, these organizations have to rely on online safety tools that heavily feature text, abstract explanations, and complex language, which are not accessible or meaningful for children with Down syndrome.

A group of developers, IT professionals, and designers in Bosnia and Herzegovina has been working to address the lack of a digital safety tool tailored to children and adolescents with Down syndrome. Their goal is to help young people understand, practice, and feel confident making decisions online.

Global Voices conducted a written interview over email with Stefan Filipovic, a member of this group, to learn how they created a video game to teach children with the genetic condition about digital safety. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.

**Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.**

> **Stefan Filipovic (SF):** We are a group of IT professionals, developers, and designers from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Most of our work is in commercial technology, but we also have experience developing educational and socially useful video games, such as [Eureka – Edukativna videoigra](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=io.legitgaming.eureka&hl=en), an educational game for children, and [Lea & Leo](https://www.legitgaming.io/lea-and-leo/), a game about children with diabetes.
> We joined the Digital Sparks project because we wanted to use that experience for a group that, in our opinion, is often overlooked when digital products are designed. Young people with intellectual disabilities are using phones and the internet, but many digital tools are simply not designed with their needs in mind.
> The video game SafeClick ([Siguran klik](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=io.legitgaming.safeclick)) allowed us to work on something practical and useful while also learning how to design more inclusively and to involve educators and users in the process.

**GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?**

> **SF:** While working with Servis Centar “Dajte nam šansu – Zvjezdice” – an association and day center that provides free support to children, young people, and people with developmental disabilities, we saw that young people with Down syndrome were using phones and the internet, but there were very few cyber-safety resources made specifically for them.
> Most materials use a lot of text, complicated explanations, or interfaces that are difficult to follow. To our knowledge, parents and educators often end up focusing on limiting internet use rather than teaching young people how to deal with unsafe situations.
> We wanted to try something different. With SafeClick, we use simple stories, familiar situations, pictures, and game mechanics to help users practice what to do when they receive a suspicious message, meet someone online, or experience cyberbullying.

**GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?**

> **SF:**We developed the first playable version of SafeClick. The game is currently awaiting approval by the App Store and Google Play. It is designed for mobile devices, with simple, accessible interactions and visual scenarios.
> One important decision was to avoid punishing users for mistakes. Instead, the game explains what happened and gives them another chance. We worked closely with educators and parents and used their feedback to make the scenarios easier to understand.
> We are currently in the phase of arranging mentoring sessions with the mentor assigned to us through the project, with the aim of earning additional opportunities to promote the game and reach as many users as possible.

**GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.**

> **SF:** Although the game will be published soon, the initial feedback from special education teachers and parents has been highly practical. Special thanks to Jelena Zilic and her children, who provided the first useful in-game test users’ feedback. They helped us see that situations, which are difficult to explain verbally, can become much easier when they are shown visually and practiced through a game.
> For example, instead of simply telling someone not to respond to a stranger online, SafeClick lets them see the message, decide what to do, and practice blocking and reporting that individual, and reporting the situation to a caregiver. I really believe we managed to turn an abstract topic into something young people can actually practice.

**GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed?**

> **SF:** Before this project, we mostly thought about accessibility as a product and UX (interface) issue. Working on SafeClick made us look at it differently. Being able to use the internet safely is also about being able to participate in everyday life. Communicate, learn, find information, and be part of your community.
> If a person cannot understand or safely use digital services, they are left out. We also learned that privacy and accessibility should not be things added at the end of development. They need to be considered from the beginning. That is something we will take with us into our future projects.

**GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?**

> **SF:** The biggest lesson for us was that making something technically simple is actually quite difficult. With commercial products, it is easy to keep adding features. With SafeClick, we had to constantly ask ourselves whether a button, animation, sentence, or screen was really necessary.
> Our earlier experience with Eureka – Edukativna igra and Lea & Leo helped us understand the value of video games for learning, but SafeClick taught us much more about cognitive accessibility and designing with educators and users in mind.

**GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?**

> **SF:** Our immediate objective is to publish SafeClick, launch it in the media, and inform the wider community about the game’s availability. Looking ahead, we plan to build on this experience to develop a wider portfolio of digital tools tailored for marginalized groups and to continue exploring how games and other digital tools can make learning and participation easier for people who are often left out of mainstream technology. We are open to new collaborations and partnerships.

**Written by [Nurbek Bekmurzaev](https://globalvoices.org/author/nurbek-bekmurzaev/)**
description: Being able to use the internet safely is also about being able to participate in everyday life.

title: Fewer and fewer parents will smack their children – but it’s still legal. Should that change?
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Divna Haslam, Associate Professor & Clinical Psychologist, The University of Queensland
content:
A [study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chiabu.2026.108339) published this month shows many Queenslanders believe parents should not be convicted of assault for doing things such as smacking their children for misbehaviour.

I am a clinical psychologist who researches child adversity, parenting and mental health.

So what else did the study find? And what does it mean about laws around how Australians discipline their children?

## What was the research?

The study was conducted by researchers at the Australian National University and Monash University and funded by the Queensland Law Reform Commission as a part of a [review](https://www.qlrc.qld.gov.au/reviews/completed/2025/review-of-particular-criminal-defences) examining legislation that allows “reasonable discipline” of children.

Researchers surveyed 1,662 adults living in Queensland and conducted a series of focus groups. As part of the survey, participants read short stories describing a mother’s use of physical punishment in response to an 11-year-old child. In these stories, the child had kept a mobile phone in her bedroom at night against family rules. When caught by her mother, the child began swearing at her and refused to hand over the phone.

The stories differed in the type of physical punishment the mother used. This ranged from grabbing the child’s hand tightly, to hitting her thigh with a wooden spoon to the mother slapping her across the face. Participants then reported whether they believed the mother should be found guilty of assault if the case went to court.

Stories also varied if the child had a formal or suspected diagnosis of ADHD, but this did not appear to influence formal perceptions of guilt.

## What the study found

Results showed there was no clear consensus among participants on whether the mother should be found guilty or not. However the level of force the mother used did matter to those surveyed.

About 57% of respondents said the mother should be found guilty of assault for slapping the child across the face. This figure was about 47% for the scenario where the mother slapped the child on the thigh and left a bruise.

Around 37% of adults believed the mother should be found guilty for slapping the child on the thigh with a wooden spoon, followed by about 22% when the mother slapped the child on the thigh without leaving a bruise. Only about 7% believed the mother was guilty of assault in the case where she gripped the child’s hand tightly.

Overall, about 65% of participants believed the mother should be found not guilty of assault across all the examples of physical punishment.

However, it’s important to note the findings don’t necessarily mean participants believe the behaviour is acceptable. It could be they understood the behaviour in context (after all parenting is tough), or simply that they do not favour a criminal justice response.

The findings suggest even those who believe the mother was guilty favoured non-punitive educational responses rather than a criminal justice response.

## Beliefs are changing

Even so, the findings are surprising given attitudes towards physical punishment of children for misbehaviour have shifted in recent years. They are also unexpected considering hitting children is a violation of the [UN Convention on the Rights of the Child](https://www.unicef.org/child-rights-convention/convention-text).

My [2023 research](https://theconversation.com/1-in-4-adults-think-smacking-is-necessary-to-properly-raise-kids-but-attitudes-are-changing-218837) shows three in four Australians do not believe physical punishment is necessary.

This is drastically lower than 2002 [data](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1440-1754.2011.02144.x), which found three in four Australians believed it was sometimes necessary to smack a naughty child.

The 2023 data also showed 64.2% of parents aged 65 and over had used physical punishment whereas only 14.4% of parents under 24 had. This suggests a generational shift against physical discipline.

## What does the law say?

Physical punishment of children by parents and caregivers is legal in all states and territories of Australia through a variety of legal [defences](https://aifs.gov.au/resources/resource-sheets/physical-punishment-legislation). These differ across states but essentially mean parents can use a defence to avoid an assault charge if the behaviour was for discipline and was considered “reasonable”.

What is “reasonable” is open to interpretation. In part, this latest study was trying to determine whether there is consistency in what Australians viewed as reasonable. The research findings suggest there is not, and that current laws do not make it clear what behaviours are acceptable and unacceptable.

## Is smacking harmful?

There is no research demonstrating long-term benefits of smacking.

But research shows physical punishment is [associated with harms](https://doi.org/10.1037/fam0000191) similar to physical abuse. These include increased aggression and behaviour problems, poor mental health, damaged parent-child relationships, poor developmental outcomes, and increased risk of physical abuse.

These negative impacts can [follow the child into adulthood](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2011-2947) and have been linked to mood, anxiety and substance disorders, increased risk of suicide and [intimate partner violence](https://theconversation.com/evidence-shows-children-who-are-smacked-are-more-likely-to-be-involved-in-partner-violence-in-adulthood-159632).

## Should the law change?

In 2013, the [Royal Australasian College of Physicians](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2013/jul/26/doctors-campaign-smacking-children-illegal) called for smacking to be banned in Australia. Since then, similar calls have been have been made by [researchers](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.anzjph.2023.100044), a [Royal Commission into domestic family and sexual violence](https://www.agd.sa.gov.au/law-and-justice/royalcommissionDFSV), and the [World Health Organization](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/corporal-punishment-and-health).

Most recently the Queensland Law Reform Commission [recommended](https://www.qlrc.qld.gov.au/reviews/completed/2025/review-of-particular-criminal-defences/review-publications) a staged approach to removing the use of the defence for discipline. This would make it clear that parents should not use physical force to discipline children.

The commission also recommends a community awareness campaign to increase support for parents and the use of diversion, rather than prosecution for parents.

## What next?

Globally, [70 countries](https://endcorporalpunishment.org/countdown/) have banned physical punishment of children.

Many worry prohibiting physical punishment would lead to parents suddenly being convicted of assault, but data from [overseas](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c0q59q00w5wo) shows this doesn’t happen. Instead, countries see [reductions](https://doi.org/10.1002/car.1131) in this form of violence suggesting legislative change may protect children.

## What’s a better alternative?

The [American Academy of Pediatrics](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/142/6/e20183112/37452/Effective-Discipline-to-Raise-Healthy-Children?autologincheck=redirected), a key body that informs global clinical practice, suggests parents use positive parenting [techniques](https://raisingchildren.net.au/school-age/behaviour) instead of smacking.

These techniques include encouraging good behaviour, addressing emotions behind misbehaviour, using [calm non-violent](https://theconversation.com/research-shows-its-harmful-to-smack-your-child-so-what-should-parents-do-instead-186739) discipline strategies, such as time out, and parents using [evidence-based supports](https://www.health.gov.au/our-work/triple-p-positive-parenting-program?language=en) and [resources](https://raisingchildren.net.au).

*If this article has raised issues for you, you can contact: [Lifeline](https://www.lifeline.org.au/) (13 11 14); [13YARN](https://www.13yarn.org.au/) for Indigenous Australians (139 276); or [Beyond Blue](https://www.beyondblue.org.au/) (1300 224 636).*

*Divna Haslam has receieved a variety of government and non-government funding. She is a Director of the Parenting and Family Research Alliance, and a member of its "end physical punishment of Australian Children" working group. She is a former consultant for Triple P International and a member of the Queensland Family Child Commission Expert Advisory Council and the World Health Organisation technical advisory group for violence against children estimates.*
description: Some might worry prohibiting physical punishment would lead to parents suddenly being convicted of assault,. But data from overseas shows this doesn’t happen.

title: Not enjoying being a parent? You’re not alone. Here’s how to handle this complicated feeling
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Alison Fogarty, Research Fellow, Lifespan Institute and School of Psychology, Deakin University, Deakin University; Grace McMahon, Clinical Psychologist and Research Officer in the Intergenerational Health Group, Murdoch Children's Research Institute; Monique Seymour, Senior Lecturer, Clinical Psychologist, Psychology, Institute of Health and Wellbeing, Federation University Australia; Deakin University
content:
We’re often told parenting is one of the most rewarding things we’ll ever do. But as many parents will attest, it is also full of very difficult moments. And sometimes these moments seem almost constant.

While it can feel taboo to say it out loud (“I’m not enjoying being a parent”), a glance at [online parenting forums](https://www.reddit.com/r/Parenting/comments/1wxcj8o/i_dont_enjoy_parenting_right_now/) will show you, parents can feel it at many different times in their child’s lives. From the sleeplessness of newborns, to toddler tantrums, disobedient kids and grumpy teens.

What does the research say about this? And what can you do when you’re finding it really tough?

## How common is this feeling?

Feeling stretched is a normal part of raising children. Many parents [report](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0192513X18811388) finding parenting harder than they had imagined, with some not enjoying parts, or even all, of the parenting journey.

Research indicates [roughly 5-14%](https://www.cell.com/trends/cognitive-sciences/abstract/S1364-6613(26%2900029-X) of parents regret they had children, with [up to 29%](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/pdf/10.1111/fare.70088) reporting they regret parenthood sometimes.

Much of this feeling appears to come down to [regretting the circumstances](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0192513X18811388) around having children, such as making sacrifices, choice of partner, or the number of children. It is not necessarily about regretting the child themselves.

## Why it happens?

Stress and exhaustion are extremely common experiences for parents. A 2025 [survey](https://parentingtoday.net.au/) of 10,000 Australian parents of children aged 0-18 years found almost half reported tiredness got in the way of them being the parent they wanted to be.

These feelings can be heightened during [different stages of parenting](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00737-014-0494-8). For example, [two thirds of Australian mothers](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2214.2011.01333.x) report experiencing high levels of fatigue during the early parenting period, and research suggests that fatigue is also [common among fathers](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1111/cp.12016) during this time.

[Higher rates of stress](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2214.2009.01052.x) are also reported among parents of [children with disability](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/cch.13193) or chronic health conditions.

Beyond sleep deprivation, having [little time to yourself](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/birt.12210), losing your sense of who you are outside of parenting, isolation, the mental load, and [financial stress](https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/a0035444.) can also hamper enjoyment of parenting.

## Parenting is not perfect

Unrealistic expectations can [play a part too](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0747563216309104?via%3Dihub).

Social media often presents an idealised view of parenting, filled with happy children, patient parents and spotless homes. Comparing our own experiences with these portrayals can leave us feeling unsatisfied with our family life and that we aren’t good enough parents.

Support [also matters enormously](https://unsworks.unsw.edu.au/entities/publication/c77b01c8-d086-445f-a42f-8bd1629d6772). The so-called “village” isn’t a reality for many families, particularly those who live far from extended family or whose families can’t offer practical or emotional help.

## Is it OK not to enjoy it?

Enjoying parenting and loving your child are very different things. Not enjoying a particular stage of parenting (like newborn sleep deprivation, or sibling arguments) says nothing about how much you love your child or how good of a parent that you are.

It’s also OK not to love, or even like every part of parenting. For example, making school lunches every day. It doesn’t mean that you don’t love your children.

## What can I do if I am not enjoying parenting?

- **Name it.** Saying “I’m not enjoying this right now” to a partner, friend or health professional can ease the shame and remind you you’re not alone.
- **Set realistic expectations.** Aim for “[good enough](https://adc.bmj.com/content/78/4/293)” rather than perfect. Notice which expectations are really yours and which come from social media or other people. Let go of what you can.

***Read more: [Parents make mistakes. So what does ‘good enough parenting’ look like?](https://theconversation.com/parents-make-mistakes-so-what-does-good-enough-parenting-look-like-214146)***

- **Look for small moments of connection.** You don’t need to enjoy every activity. Find one or two things you do enjoy doing with your child. A bedtime story, a walk, a meal, a shared hobby or TV program you like to enjoy together.
- **Share the load and take time for yourself.** Be specific about what you need from your partner, family or friends. Even [short breaks](https://doi.org/10.1111/birt.12210) where you’re fully off duty can help.
- **Look after the basics.** Try and make sure you get sleep, movement, food, and time for the things that remind you of who you are outside of parenting.
- **Remember it’s a stage.** Children change quickly, and so does what parenting asks of you. Many parents find their enjoyment returns as their children grow and become more independent.

## When it’s more than a rough patch?

For most parents, not enjoying parenting is normal and passes. It can come and go across days, weeks or even years.

But when these feelings settle in and intensify, they may signal [parental burnout](https://www.cope.org.au/new-parents/looking-after-yourself/parental-burnout) or [depression or anxiety](https://www.panda.org.au/checklists). Signs to look out for include:

- feeling exhausted by parenting most of the time, even after rest
- feeling emotionally distant or detached from your children
- no longer getting any pleasure or meaning from being a parent
- ongoing irritability, or fantasising about escaping
- feeling low, anxious or hopeless most days
- finding it hard to respond to, play with or care for your children.

If this sounds like you, talk to your GP, maternal and child health nurse, or a psychologist.

If you’re not enjoying parenting right now, you’re not alone and it doesn’t mean you’re failing as a parent. Children don’t need parents who love every minute of parenting. They need parents who keep showing up, and who get support when they need it.

*If this article has raised issues for you, you can contact: [PANDA](https://www.panda.org.au/) (1300 726 306) who support the mental health of parents and families during pregnancy and their first year of parenthood; the [Pregnancy, Birth and Baby Helpline](https://www.pregnancybirthbaby.org.au/) (1800 882 436); [Lifelife](https://www.lifeline.org.au/) (13 11 14); [13YARN](https://www.13yarn.org.au/) for Indigenous Australians (139 276); or [Beyond Blue](https://www.beyondblue.org.au/) (1300 224 636).*

description: Enjoying parenting and loving your child are two very different things.

title: Protecting children from harm isn’t enough — welfare systems must support healing through quality mental health care
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Emmanuelle Khoury, Associate professor, School of Social Work, Université de Montréal; Rosemary R. Carlton, Associate professor, School of Social Work, Université de Montréal
content:
In Québec and across Canada, people working in child welfare do [remarkable work to protect children and youth from maltreatment](https://www.journaldemontreal.com/2026/09/04/la-dpj-et-son-role-parfois-crucial) and to support families facing complex challenges.

[But when tragedies occur, such as the recent deaths of children and youth](https://montrealgazette.com/news/children-died-batshaw-montreals-anglophone-youth-protection-agency/) receiving [child welfare services in Québec](https://montrealgazette.com/news/batshaw-deaths-youth-protection-quebec-solidaire/), public debate tends to turn to [accountability, institutional practice and systemic failure](https://montrealgazette.com/news/batshaw-deaths-youth-protection-quebec-solidaire/%20https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/batshaw-youth-protection-deaths-9.7283412).

We need to understand what happened and whether systems worked as they should have. Yet focusing on these questions alone can inadvertently narrow attention to risk, failure and responsibility. Too easily overshadowed is how well child welfare systems support the broader well-being of the young people in their care.

If child welfare systems are to keep young people safe over the long term, they must attend not only to risks of harm but also to the conditions that support mental health and well-being. Many young people involved with child welfare are living with trauma, grief and loss, family conflict and disruption, instability, discrimination, poverty and mental-health challenges.

Across our work on [youth mental-health recovery](https://doi.org/10.1111/camh.12419) and child welfare, a common theme has emerged. Young people benefit from services that foster hope, recognize their strengths, involve them actively in decisions that affect them and create meaningful opportunities for connection and participation.

These insights call for a broader understanding of protection.

## Taking young people seriously

While child welfare systems are often judged by how well they prevent harm, [young people themselves frequently describe a broader set of needs and interests](https://www.erudit.org/fr/revues/crimino/2023-v56-n1-crimino07959/). One of the most consistent findings in [youth mental-health research](https://www.un.org/youthaffairs/en/youth-mental-health-and-well-being) is that young people want their views to matter.

Young people’s right to participate in matters concerning their care is written into child welfare laws and policies. Nevertheless, a significant gap remains between listening to young people and genuinely [incorporating their knowledge into decision-making](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40271-020-00444-5).

A recent study by one of this article’s authors into [clinical encounters in youth mental-health services](https://doi.org/10.7202/1127009ar) suggests that participation can sometimes become symbolic rather than meaningful.

For example, some young people participating in the study appeared to agree with proposed care plans during therapy meetings. But they explained that they had not felt comfortable expressing disagreement or were unaware that alternative options were available to them.

When young people feel their experiences and voices are taken seriously, trust grows, engagement improves and their sense of agency increases.

In contrast, when their views were ignored or minimized, youth in the study said they felt that services were something being done to them rather than with them. This distinction is important when reflecting on how to better support youth.

***Read more: [How a failure to support youth who were once in care may be fuelling unemployment](https://theconversation.com/how-a-failure-to-support-youth-who-were-once-in-care-may-be-fuelling-unemployment-240956)***

## Relationships are a form of protection

Research shows that [supportive relationships help](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1708589) young people navigate adversity. Trusted adults can help them make sense of difficult experiences, build confidence, imagine different futures and gain access to opportunities.

Relationships are not simply an added [benefit of effective services](https://revueintervention.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/ri_154_2022.1_Khoury.pdf). They are essential to [ensuring young people’s well-being, in the context of child welfare and beyond](https://montrealgazette.com/news/provincial-news/batshaw-youth-protection-teen-girl-suicide-investigation/).

Instability and a lack of trust can contribute to worse long-term outcomes for [young people involved in child welfare](https://edjep.ca/un-tiers-des-personnes-en-situation-ditinerance-sont-passees-par-la-dpj/).

[Recent research](https://cremis.ca/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/20250815_rapportfinal_pij.pdf) captures young people’s frustration at having to constantly rebuild trust because of [worker turnover](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/montreal/2-years-laurent-report-quebec-youth-protection-dpj-1.6835661) and service disruptions. [A multi-year study](http://edjep.ca/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/rapport_instabilite_eng.pdf) found high levels of placement instability. On average, the 2,573 young people participating in the study experienced 5.89 placement moves each.

[Another recent study](https://smjaction.ca/en/%F0%9F%8C%B1-sante-mentale-et-protection-de-la-jeunesse-retour-sur-notre-projet/) suggests that many young people involved with child welfare and mental-health services go through multiple transitions throughout adolescence and early adulthood.

Each transition — whether involving a new worker or a new placement — carries the possibility of losing someone who knows the young person’s history, understands their strengths and insecurities and has earned their trust. Stability is important not only for the young people themselves but also for [the whole network of adults and relationships around them](https://www.un.org/youthaffairs/en/press-releases/new-un-report-calls-global-shift-towards-ecosystem-based-approaches-youth-mental).

## What can we learn?

Recent tragedies involving child welfare and youth mental health will rightly prompt official reviews of protection processes, standards of care and institutional accountability.

But research with young people reveals a broader lesson: quality of care cannot be measured through compliance indicators or organizational targets alone, just as protection cannot be reduced to removing or managing immediate risks of harm.

We must also listen to these young people who are asking for real opportunities to be heard, to take part in decisions made on their behalf, [to have hope](https://www.ledevoir.com/opinion/idees/910026/sante-mentale-jeunes-si-espoir-etait-droit?) and to form relationships with adults who stay long enough for trust to develop.

Young people have been saying this for years. Their message is neither complex nor controversial. But acting on it requires systems to do more than assess risk and demonstrate procedural compliance.

It requires equipping child welfare professionals with the time, training and organizational support necessary to provide relationship-based and trauma-informed care to young people. It also requires reducing disruptions caused by staff turnover and service fragmentation, and creating formal and informal opportunities for young people to contribute to the decisions, services and care plans that affect their lives.

Protection will remain incomplete as long as systems fail to listen to young people, take their experiences seriously, meaningfully incorporate their perspectives into decision-making and invest in relationships that foster connection, trust and hope. These are not alternatives to protection and well-being. They are among the conditions that make both possible.

*The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Protection must also mean building the conditions young people need like stable relationships with adults who stay and real involvement in decisions about their care.

title: Childhood adversity linked to billions in health and economic costs – new research
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Kat Ford, Research Fellow in the Public Health Collaborating Unit, Bangor University; Liverpool John Moores University; Karen Hughes, Professor of Public Health, Bangor University
content:
Childhood trauma can leave scars that last long after the experiences themselves have ended. Its effects can reach into adult life, increasing the risk of mental illness, physical health problems and other difficulties.

Our [latest research](https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/16/9/e124416) estimates that the health effects associated with adverse childhood experiences cost the equivalent of £7.8 billion in Wales and £115.6 billion in England in 2023. These figures represent 8.4% of Wales’s gross domestic product (GDP) and 5% of England’s.

These are not bills paid directly by governments. Instead, they put a monetary value on the burden of illness and premature death associated with childhood adversity, showing the scale of its potential effects on society.

[Adverse childhood experiences](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00787-021-01938-9) are traumatic or highly stressful events. They include physical, verbal and sexual abuse, as well as experiences such as domestic violence, parental separation, or living with a family member who has mental health problems, misuses alcohol or drugs, or has been in prison.

[Around half](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12889-016-2906-3) of adults in England and Wales report at least one such experience. About one in ten report four or more.

[Research](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lanpub/article/PIIS2468-2667(17%2930118-4/fulltext) has consistently linked childhood adversity to poorer health and wellbeing in adulthood. People exposed to several types of adversity face greater risks of mental illness, chronic physical conditions and health-harming behaviour, like smoking and harmful alcohol use. Childhood adversity has also been linked to poorer education and employment outcomes and a greater likelihood of involvement in violence.

These consequences can [increase demand](https://theconversation.com/childhood-trauma-linked-to-distrust-of-healthcare-professionals-new-research-229054) for healthcare and other public services. Understanding the costs helps to show the scale of the problem and the potential benefits of investing in prevention.

## Counting the costs

We combined data from 10 studies conducted across England and Wales between 2012 and 2024. These studies interviewed adults about their childhood experiences and their health as adults. In total, we analysed data from 28,449 adults.

We examined seven causes of ill health, including mental illness, cancer, heart disease and stroke, alongside four health risks: smoking, high alcohol use, drug use and high body mass index. We explored links between childhood adversity and these outcomes, then used data from [the global burden of disease study](https://www.healthdata.org/research-analysis/gbd) to estimate how much illness and premature death across the population could be associated with it.

Finally, we assigned a monetary value to these health effects using a [government estimate](https://post.parliament.uk/quality-adjusted-life-years-qalys-in-healthcare-decision-making/) of society’s willingness to pay to reduce ill health and premature death.

***Read more: [Childhood trauma linked to distrust of healthcare professionals – new research](https://theconversation.com/childhood-trauma-linked-to-distrust-of-healthcare-professionals-new-research-229054)***

Drug use and violence showed some of the strongest links with childhood adversity. Our estimates suggest it was associated with around 60% of drug use in Wales and 57% in England. It was also associated with almost half of all violence: 49% in Wales and 46% in England.

However, the largest estimated financial costs came from mental illness and smoking. This is because these affect more people and account for a greater share of ill health overall.

In Wales, the estimated costs associated with childhood adversity were £1.8 billion for mental illness and £1.8 billion for smoking. In England, the figures were £37.8 billion and £22.7 billion respectively.

We also calculated regional estimates for England for the first time. These ranged from £6.3 billion in the north east to £18 billion in the south east.

## Why prevention matters

Our findings strengthen the case for preventing childhood adversity and supporting children and families who experience it. Reducing exposure to trauma could help improve health across people’s lives, while potentially reducing the wider costs associated with illness and premature death.

There are [several ways](https://phwwhocc.co.uk/resources/tackling-adverse-childhood-experiences-aces-state-of-the-art-and-options-for-action/) to help prevent childhood adversity. These include supporting parents, building life skills, challenging harmful social norms and addressing the [social conditions](https://www.who.int/publications/b/66048) that put families under pressure.

Awareness and action to address childhood adversity has increased across the UK. [Evidence suggests](https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/15/8/e098412) that some adverse childhood experiences may be declining. But others such as verbal abuse and household mental illness have been less addressed and may even be increasing.

People affected by trauma also need effective support. Trauma-informed approaches, which recognise how past experiences can shape people’s needs and behaviour, are one way to improve that support. For example, the [Trauma-informed Wales Framework](https://www.traumaframeworkcymru.com/) sets out an approach to understanding and responding to trauma across society.

***Read more: [The consequences of childhood trauma on children’s mental health](https://theconversation.com/the-consequences-of-childhood-trauma-on-childrens-mental-health-196178)***

There are important limits to our findings. The estimates put a monetary value on health effects, including the value society places on reducing the risk of illness and premature death. They are not a direct measure of public spending or money that could automatically be saved through prevention. The study also identifies associations between childhood adversity and health outcomes, rather than proving that adversity caused every case.

Some vulnerable groups, including people in prison, were not represented in the surveys, despite being [more likely](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40352-020-00115-5) to have experienced childhood adversity. Our estimates may therefore understate the true scale of the problem.

Even with these limitations, the findings highlight the potential scale of the health and economic burden associated with childhood adversity. Preventing trauma and providing better support for those affected could bring benefits that extend well beyond childhood.

*Kat Ford receives funding from Public Health Wales NHS Trust. She is affiliated with Bangor University and Liverpool John Moores University.*

*Karen Hughes is fully employed by Public Health Wales NHS Trust and is an Honorary Professor at Bangor University.*
description: The health effects of childhood adversity carry a huge economic burden, according to new research across Wales and England.

title: Advice around children’s screen use can be overwhelming. There is no single ‘right’ approach
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Kate Mannell, Research Fellow in Digital Childhoods, Deakin University
content:
When should your child start engaging with screens? How long should they use them for? Can they watch or play alone? Should there be a gap before bed?

There is lots of advice for parents about children’s screen use – and it’s getting [more complex](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/17482798.2026.2644298).

The advice is conflicting, often prescriptive and can be stressful to navigate.

My [new research](https://www.routledge.com/Screen-Time-and-the-Impossibility-of-Modern-Parenting/Mannell/p/book/9781041112082) looks at how we talk about children and screens. How is advice changing and how can parents make sense of it?

## What is the advice around screen use?

For years, advice about young children and screens was mostly about age and time. Broadly, parents were told to avoid screens until a child is two and then limit it to two hours per day.

This messaging is [still prevalent](https://www.schn.health.nsw.gov.au/kids-health-hub/screen-time/recommended-screen-time). But it’s been widely [critiqued](https://researchonline.lse.ac.uk/id/eprint/66927/1/Policy%20Brief%2017-%20Families%20%20Screen%20Time.pdf) for assuming all screen use, and all children, are the same. It also ignores positive outcomes, such as play and social connection.

## My research shows advice is changing

My [research](https://www.routledge.com/Screen-Time-and-the-Impossibility-of-Modern-Parenting/Mannell/p/book/9781041112082) analysed public discussion about screens and young children (from birth to 8 years). I looked at official guidelines, TikTok content, Australian news reporting, online articles and marketing materials for children’s goods and services. I also interviewed 34 parents about the messaging they get and how it impacts them.

I found advice for parents about young children and screens has been expanding in two key ways.

First, it’s no longer just about age and time but when and how to use screens.

For example, parents are told to [prohibit screens](https://beststartinlife.gov.uk/screen-time-under-5s/) during meal times and before bed. They shouldn’t have screens on [in the background](https://cps.ca/uploads/tools/CPS_ScreenTime-EN.pdf) during other activities. And they should make sure content is [“slow paced” and “predicable”](https://beststartinlife.gov.uk/screen-time-under-5s/).

Second, advice is no longer just about avoiding “harms” but maximising “benefits”. Parents are told that screen use “[should be educational](https://www.health.gov.au/topics/physical-activity-and-exercise/physical-activity-and-exercise-guidelines-for-all-australians/recommendations-for-infants-toddlers-and-preschoolers-birth-to-5-years?language=en)”. That “active” screen use is better than “[passive](https://mother.ly/life/active-screen-time-benefits-for-kids/)”. And that instead of solo screen time, parents should watch and discuss content [with their child](https://www.health.gov.au/topics/physical-activity-and-exercise/physical-activity-and-exercise-guidelines-for-all-australians/recommendations-for-infants-toddlers-and-preschoolers-birth-to-5-years?language=en) – explaining things, singing along and pausing to ask questions.

This kind of advice is being issued by governments and health organisations, and is circulating in traditional media, online articles and social media content.

## How does this advice create problems for parents?

While this advice is well-intentioned, my [research](https://www.routledge.com/Screen-Time-and-the-Impossibility-of-Modern-Parenting/Mannell/p/book/9781041112082) shows it can create more pressure and uncertainty.

For starters, it’s conflicting. Advice about maximising benefits reassures parents that some screen use is okay, while other advice says any screen use will cause a [host of negative impacts](https://www.theguardian.com/society/2025/may/01/children-under-six-should-avoid-screen-time-french-medical-experts-say), from impaired brain development to motor control issues.

Even when advice seems balanced, the details quickly become confusing. For example, lots of advice currently [recommends](https://www.care.com/c/low-stimulation-shows-for-toddlers/) avoiding “high stimulation” shows in favour of “low stimulation” shows. But there’s endless debate online about what counts as high stimulation and how specific shows should be categorised ([is Bluey high stim](https://mother.ly/parenting/why-families-are-taking-a-bluey-break/)?).

My research found newer advice also makes managing kids screen use more stressful, exhausting and guilt inducing.
