Parents aren’t just told to watch the clock, but also to research the best content, converse with kids as they watch, and make sure screen use doesn’t happen in the “wrong” times and places. Some advice even tells parents to check if shows are fast-paced by [counting the seconds](https://screenwiseapp.com/guides/cocomelon-and-baby-sensory-content) between editing cuts.

## What about different family circumstances?

All this advice tells parents what to do without any knowledge of their unique circumstances.

We know kids play and engage with screen media in many different ways. And we know kids can [differ in how they respond](https://www.routledge.com/Children-Talking-Television-The-Making-Of-Television-Literacy/Buckingham/p/book/9780750701105) to the same media experiences.

Families also have different [values, lifestyles and circumstances](https://academic.oup.com/book/32086). For example, for some of the single parents I interviewed, kids watching a show by themselves was a lifesaver for everyone.

## So, what can parents do?

Here are two things that might be helpful to remember when faced with one-size-fits-all advice.

**1. There is no single “right” approach**

In my research, I spoke to two parents with similar aged toddlers. One family’s main rule was “no TV in the morning” (turning it off caused chaos). The other’s was “TV only in the morning” (this worked best for everyone). Both families figured this out through trial and error. Examples like this are a great reminder that context is everything.

**2. What works for your child?**

It might feel unhelpful to hear “there’s no right approach”, but shifting from what the advice says is right to what matters for your child can simplify the task at hand.

You don’t need to know whether Bluey is “high” or “low” stimulation – you just need to know whether it ramps your kid up (and whether or not you’re okay with that!).

You don’t need to know how much screen time the average child “should” have – you just need to know whether the time your child spends with screen media allows for other important things in their life.

You don’t need to know what screen use has the most “benefits” – you just need to know whether your child is generally playing, growing and having fun, with screens and without.

*Kate Mannell receives funding from the Australian Research Council.*
description: Advice around screens is no longer just about avoiding harms, but maximising benefits for your kid. No wonder some parents feel like their heads might explode.

title: Kids and teens are going to AI chatbots for advice. How can parents make sure this is safe?
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Amy Dawel, Clinical Psychologist and Associate Professor, School of Medicine and Psychology, Australian National University
content:
Last week, Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett [warned artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots are not a sufficient replacement](https://www.abc.net.au/news/2026-10-08/afp-warns-child-abuse-victims-turning-to-ai-chatbots/107244604) for human support for children. The comment was in response to a recent Adelaide University [study](https://icmec.org.au/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Cubitt_et_al_AI_and_non_AI_online_child-sexual_victimisation_disclosures_and_help_seeking-1.pdf) that found more than one in three Australian children turn to AI chatbots for support when they are sexually victimised online, or otherwise tell nobody at all.

While there can be [benefits](https://www.apa.org/topics/artificial-intelligence-machine-learning/health-advisory-ai-adolescent-well-being) to children using AI, such as help with [learning](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.lindif.2025.102646), or [practising social skills](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/research/talk-trust-and-trade-offs-how-and-why-teens-use-ai-companions), there is also a risk they will go to AI chatbots and assistants for emotional support over parents and other trusted adults.

In Australia, around half of children aged between 10 and 17 who use AI are turning to it for [personal and social reasons](https://www.esafety.gov.au/research/talking-to-machines-childrens-experiences-with-ai-assistants-and-companions). This includes seeking advice on sensitive topics, talking about their feelings, and just “hanging out”.

So how can parents help their children to use AI safely?

## Why are kids turning to AI chatbots over people?

One practical reason why young people are using the tech is it can provide them with [answers around the clock](https://www.commonsensemedia.org/research/talk-trust-and-trade-offs-how-and-why-teens-use-ai-companions). This means a chatbot might be a natural go-to when a child wants a quick answer and a trusted adult or friend isn’t available.

Another reason is pure [curiousity](https://www.internetmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Me-Myself-AI-Report.pdf). Like adults, young people are experimenting with AI and trying to understand what it does and how it can make their lives better.

## Seeking deeper connections

Sometimes the reason for talking to chatbots is deeper though.

It might be that a young person wants information about something they feel embarrassed about raising with their parents or friends. As teens [explore their identity](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2021.11.006), they begin to ask more sensitive questions. This may make them [more likely](https://www.esafety.gov.au/research/talking-to-machines-childrens-experiences-with-ai-assistants-and-companions) to use AI for personal reasons than younger children.

For others, the reason is an unmet need for connection. Reaching out to chatbots for personal reasons is more common for those who are [already vulnerable](https://www.internetmatters.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Me-Myself-AI-Report.pdf).

A 2025 [Danish study](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijhcs.2024.103409) found loneliness may be a precursor for high school students seeking AI companionship. Other studies suggest a [lack of connection](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3790597) to parental figures may also lead to teens talking to chatbots.

## What do kids miss out on when they choose chatbots over people?

A major concern is that, if AI use becomes excessive, it may displace real-world interactions and create [unrealistic expectations](https://www.esafety.gov.au/newsroom/blogs/ai-chatbots-and-companions-risks-to-children-and-young-people#what-are-the-risks) of human relationships.

This problem is linked to [sycophancy](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec8352) – the tendency of AI to be overly agreeable.

AI interactions lack the natural friction that happens in human relationships. This warping of social experience is a particular worry when it comes to young people because they are still forming their understanding of how relationships work. We know real-life human social interaction is [crucial](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dcn.2024.101486) to teens’ development.

## AI lacks context

Another concern is the quality of the advice AI provides. And it’s not just [its capacity to spread](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-025-02194-6) convincing [misinformation](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-025-26148-9) that’s a problem.

AI lacks the full context of a child’s life. Parents and carers are often much better placed to provide the nuanced and age-appropriate guidance their child needs.

There are also more subtle impacts. When a child poses questions to an AI chatbot over a parent, they are missing out on day-to-day moments of connection with family. While each miss may be small, the accumulation over time can truly matter.

This is especially important for children. Research [shows](http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2017.03.002) strong and secure bonds with parents in the preteen years support kids as they navigate the challenges of adolescence.

Here’s how can parents and carers can help their child experiment with AI and stay safe.

## 1. Explore AI together

Find a moment to sit down and explore AI tools on a device with your child. You might:

- engage in brainstorming ideas with the software
- test a chatbot’s ability to correctly source information
- ask the AI about itself with questions such as “do you have feelings?” and “can you think?”
- ask AI to generate and edit a short story with your child as the lead character
- ask AI to tell a joke
- play a game with an AI chatbot, such as [twenty questions](https://thegeniusofplay.org/tgop/genius/play-ideas-tips/play-ideas/20-questions.aspx).

One AI game that is both fun and educational is the “catch the AI out” game. The idea is to test AI on topics that you know or can fact check. Points are scored each time you catch the AI make an error.

## 2. Ask your child questions

While exploring these AI tools and functions with your child, ask them questions to help them think more critically about the tech such as:

- what do you think AI is good at?
- what can humans do that AI can’t?
- where do you think AI gets it’s information from?
- how often is AI wrong about something? How can you check this?
- what do you think an AI chatbot does with the information you tell it?

Their answers can open up conversations that help your child enjoy AI while understanding its limitations and how to [stay safe](https://www.esafety.gov.au/parents/issues-and-advice/online-safety-basics).

For instance, if your child says AI does everything better than humans, you can help them brainstorm all the things people have to offer – hugs, for starters.

Or, if your child isn’t sure what AI does with their information, you might talk them about [privacy risks](https://theconversation.com/more-than-half-of-children-and-teens-are-using-ai-for-personal-reasons-this-comes-with-risks-288951).

## 3. Remind your child you are there to support them

It’s important to encourage your child to come to you for advice on difficult topics instead of AI.

To help children feel more comfortable, maintain a curious mindset whenever they raise a sensitive topic with you. Research [shows](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-010-9586-6) teens who perceive their parents as more accepting tend to share more. Try to take a moment to listen to them before jumping in with advice too.

You can also ask [non-judgemental questions](https://www.esafety.gov.au/research/talking-to-machines-childrens-experiences-with-ai-assistants-and-companions) about your child’s AI use to show you’re engaged. This can be as simple as asking them how they’re feeling about a particular AI interaction, or what they’re currently using AI for.

Talking about AI with your child should be an ongoing conversation.

## 4. Keep up to date with the tech

One of the challenges for parents is that AI is rapidly evolving. Australia’s eSafety Commissioner offers [resources](https://www.esafety.gov.au/) that can help people keep up to date.

We are currently researching how children use AI chatbots and how it impacts their lives as they enter their teen years, through one-to-one conversations with them. If your child is aged between 9 and 12 years, and is chatting with AI, you can [register their interest](https://tinyurl.com/chatbot-study-EOI).

*Amy Dawel receives funding from Australian Rotary Health and the Australian Research Council.*
description: Children and teens often turn to artificial intelligence for advice on sensitive topics. But chatbots are not a substitute for human support.

title: Why adoptive families can struggle to get help until they reach crisis point
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Claire Agius, Lecturer/Researcher, Manchester Metropolitan University
content:
In a deeply personal passage of his [first Labour Party conference speech](https://labour.org.uk/updates/stories/andy-burnhams-speech-to-labour-party-conference-2026/) as UK prime minister, Andy Burnham paid tribute to the care workers who had looked after his father, Roy, who had Alzheimer’s disease and had died just two weeks earlier.

Those workers were “holding a threadbare system somehow together”, he said, yet remained “invisible to the political class of this country”. Addressing them directly, he added: “You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you.”

His words made me think about the [care](https://theconversation.com/topics/care-1365) that goes unseen within families. Why are some forms of caring recognised as care, while others become almost invisible simply because they are considered part of family life?

I research trauma and adoption, and I am also an adoptive parent. I’m familiar with the story often told about adoption: a child finds a permanent family, a new life begins and everyone lives happily ever after.

But my research focuses on what happens after that supposed happy ending, particularly when the effects of a child’s earlier trauma continue into their adoptive family. And Burnham’s words made me wonder how much of the care provided by adoptive parents goes unrecognised simply because we call it parenting.

In England and Wales, an adoption order makes adopters the [child’s legal parents](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/adoption/adoption-accessible). But a legal order cannot erase what happened beforehand.

Children adopted from care are often described as “[previously looked-after](https://explore-education-statistics.service.gov.uk/find-statistics/children-looked-after-in-england-including-adoptions/2024)”, a phrase I have long struggled with. There is nothing necessarily “previous” about the effects of their early experiences. A child may be physically safe but still struggle to feel safe. Earlier experiences can affect their development and their ability to trust the adults closest to them, since a family can be permanent in law long before a child feels secure enough to believe that permanence will last.

Adoptive parents are therefore living alongside the effects of experiences that happened before they even knew their child. This can make the parenting very different from what people usually imagine.

The relationship offering safety can also be the relationship in which fear and mistrust are expressed. For some families, this includes [child-to-parent violence and abuse](https://www.respect.org.uk/pages/114-capva). A child experiencing overwhelming distress may run away or behave in ways that put themselves or others at risk. Parents may find themselves calling the police to protect their child or another family member, or because they fear for their own safety.

Understanding the reasons behind a child’s behaviour does not protect a parent from the emotional and physical impact of living with it. A parent can see why their child is hurting and still be hurt themselves.

My colleagues and I have researched compassion fatigue among adoptive parents [raising children affected by early trauma](https://doi.org/10.1093/bjsw/bcad185). Compassion fatigue describes the emotional exhaustion and disconnection that can develop through repeated exposure to another person’s trauma.

My doctoral research also explored adoptive parents’ mental health more broadly. Parents described feeling exhausted while continuing to hold family life together. Sometimes, the very fact that they were managing made their distress harder for others to recognise.

The effects can reach beyond parents and children, affecting siblings and other family members. The adversity may belong to the child’s past, but its consequences can become part of the whole family’s present.

## When families struggle to get help

Families are also affected by what happens outside the home. At school, a frightened child may be seen simply as badly behaved. A child who cannot get through the school gates may become an attendance problem. When the reasons behind their behaviour are overlooked, attention can quickly turn to what the parents are supposedly doing wrong.

Parents described fighting for help while feeling judged or blamed, sometimes until their family reached breaking point. Professionals, meanwhile, described recognising that families needed support but working within services that could not always provide it.

This is where [Burnham’s description of a “threadbare system”](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/live/cj4zwkp2p1kt?post=asset%3A640926c8-ec4a-41d9-80ae-45faaaf61424#post) particularly resonated with me. I have often described the services surrounding adoptive families as both traumatised and traumatising. Professionals are working under enormous pressure, often without the resources needed to respond to families’ complex needs. And when services are struggling, their responses can add to the distress of children and parents who are already finding life difficult.

For families, this can mean reaching a crisis and then having to demonstrate just how bad things have become before support is available.

Burnham’s words were powerful because they acknowledged care workers whose contribution is too often overlooked. But they also invite a wider conversation about what society recognises as care in the first place.

Care can come with a uniform and a job title. It can also mean a parent staying close to a child whose earliest relationships taught them that the adults they depend on may not always be safe or able to stay.

Helping a child learn to trust those relationships can take years, and the emotional demands on parents can be considerable. That work deserves recognition and support.

Care should not become less deserving of either simply because we call it parenting.

*Claire Agius does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Adoptive parents can spend years helping children feel safe after early trauma, often while struggling to find support for their own mental health.

title: When parents don’t see eye to eye: are differences in parenting styles a bad thing?
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Trevor Mazzucchelli, Associate Professor of Clinical Psychology, Curtin University
content:
Sometimes it can be hard for parents to agree on how to raise children.

One parent might insist their child’s homework has to be finished before they’re allowed to use devices. The other may think a bit of screen time before study is perfectly reasonable. Rules and consequences might be the preferred strategy of one parent while the other favours a more flexible approach.

Parents may also differ in how much independence they’re comfortable giving their children. Is it OK for a child to play on their own at the park without an adult nearby, or should they always be supervised?

Parents bring different personalities, experiences and beliefs to raising children, so it’s hardly surprising these disagreements arise.

But what can parents do when they’re not on the same page?

## What are the different parenting styles?

Psychologists traditionally describe [four broad parenting styles](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10826-018-1242-x):

1. **Authoritative parents** are warm and supportive while setting clear expectations and boundaries. They listen to their children, explain rules, and encourage independence.
2. **Authoritarian parents** place greater emphasis on obedience and discipline, often expecting children to follow rules without questioning them.
3. **Permissive parents** are warm and accepting, but tend to set fewer limits or expectations.
4. **Uninvolved parents** provide relatively little emotional support, guidance or supervision.

Research generally finds authoritative parenting is associated with better outcomes for children, including fewer [emotional](https://doi.org/10.1080/01494929.2016.1247761) and [behavioural](https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0000295) difficulties.

But these categories are only a guide. Most parents don’t fit neatly into one style. For example, a parent might be strict about bedtime, but relaxed about household chores.

## Are different parenting approaches a problem?

Research [suggests](https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2012.651997) that differences in how parents approach raising children aren’t necessarily associated with behavioural or emotional difficulties in children.

Different approaches can also have advantages. One parent might be more playful and spontaneous, while another provides greater structure and routine. Both can contribute positively to children’s development.

What may matter more is how parents manage their differences. Disagreements aren’t necessarily a problem if parents handle them constructively. When children see adults listen respectfully, compromise and resolve differences, they can learn [useful ways of managing disagreements](https://doi.org/10.1111/sode.12015) themselves.

## When it becomes a problem

Problems can arise when parents disagree on important rules (such as, no screens before bed) or they respond very differently to a child’s challenging behaviour.

For example, when a child refuses to turn off the television, one parent might insist on following through with a consequence, while the other allows more screen time to avoid an argument.

When parents respond inconsistently, children may find it harder to understand what’s expected of them. They may also learn that behaviour which doesn’t work with one parent is more likely to succeed with the other.

Signs that disagreements about parenting have become a problem include:

- frequent or ongoing conflict between parents over parenting decisions
- parents undermining each other
- children feeling caught in the middle or becoming distressed by their parents’ disagreement
- increasing behavioural difficulties in the child.

[Research](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph191610346) has linked these problematic patterns of co-parenting with greater emotional and behavioural difficulties in children and adolescents.

So what are some ways parents can manage differences?

## 1. Start with shared goals

Rather than arguing about who’s right, parents can start by discussing what they want their child to learn.

For example, instead of debating punishments for a child when they refuse to turn off the television, parents could agree they want their child to learn how to follow instructions better.

## 2. Agree on practical strategies

When parents respond to their child’s behaviour in reasonably predictable ways, children learn what’s expected of them. Giving clear instructions, praising desirable behaviour, and following through calmly with reasonable limits are [good starting points](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaac.2018.07.900).

For example, if parents disagree about screen time, they could start by agreeing on the goal of helping their child develop healthy screen habits. They might then agree on a reasonable daily limit and how they’ll respond when it’s time to turn devices off.

## 3. Discuss difficult disagreements privately

Parents should avoid criticising or undermining each other [in front of their children](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijerph191610346). This can leave children feeling pressured to take sides or unsure about what’s expected of them.

Instead, they should find a calm moment to explain their concerns to each other, listen to the other person’s perspectives and work towards a solution.

## 4. Consider a parenting program

[Evidence-based parenting programs](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jaac.2018.07.900) can help parents learn effective strategies for encouraging positive behaviour and managing challenging situations.

Participating together can also help parents develop a shared approach, although [families can still benefit when only one parent participates](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10578-019-00934-0).

## 5. Keep reviewing and adapting

Parenting isn’t a set-and-forget exercise. As children grow, they develop new abilities and need increasing independence. This means parents [need to adjust their expectations](https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13526), rules and strategies.

Regular conversations about what’s working, what isn’t and what needs to change can help parents maintain a consistent, positive approach.

If disagreements continue to cause significant conflict, or children’s difficulties persist, consider seeking additional support from [a parenting practitioner or psychologist](https://doi.org/10.64628/AA.k7e9dm7jc).

However, working together doesn’t mean compromising on children’s safety or accepting harmful parenting practices. If you’re concerned about a child’s safety, seek advice from an appropriate health professional or specialist support service.

Ultimately, good parenting doesn’t require parents to do everything identically, or even [perfectly](https://doi.org/10.64628/AA.fhnn9rvp4). What matters is using effective strategies, working together where possible and adapting as children grow.

*For parenting advice and support, visit the [Raising Children Network](https://raisingchildren.net.au/) to find services in your state or territory.*

*Trevor Mazzucchelli is a co-author of Stepping Stones Triple P – Positive Parenting Program and a consultant to Triple P International. The Parenting and Family Support Centre is partly funded by royalties stemming from published resources of the Triple P, which is developed and owned by The University of Queensland (UQ). Royalties are also distributed to the Faculty of Health and Behavioural Sciences at UQ and contributory authors of published Triple P resources. Triple P International (TPI) is a private company licensed by UniQuest on behalf of UQ, to publish and disseminate Triple P worldwide. The author has no share or ownership of TPI, but has received, and may in the future, receive royalties and/or consultancy fees from TPI. TPI had no involvement in writing of this article.*
description: When parents have different approaches to raising children, who’s right? Research suggests the answer matters less than how they handle their disagreements.

title: When Chinese parents outsource control over their adult children
topic: Gia đình và nuôi dạy con
authors: Lina Ma · Global Voices
content:
*Parents whose children have reached adulthood are outsourcing coercion to private institutions*

On a Sunday morning in March, a 21-year-old music student arrived at an apartment complex in Beijing to teach a piano lesson — a side job she did to earn money to fund her studies. Her father, her aunt, and two employees of a private disciplinary institution were waiting for her.

Her relatives claimed that the strangers were police officers investigating a family member. They forced her into a van, confiscated her phone, and drove her hundreds of miles away to a closed institution in Henan province, China, supposedly for “internet addiction rehabilitation.”

She remained there for 11 days.

Her internet use had little to do with her confinement. According to [an investigation by Southern People Weekly](https://news.qq.com/rain/a/20260526A0AGXA00), her parents disapproved of her boyfriend and believed their previously obedient daughter had stopped listening to them. They paid the institution to isolate her, control her daily life, and pressure her to end the relationship. [Public reporting indicates](https://news.china.com/socialgd/10000169/20260602/49527148_all.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com) that this institution charged 26,800 yuan (USD 3,970) for six months or CNY 36,800 (USD 5,451) for a year, including room and board.

Staff told her that she could leave after she had forgotten her boyfriend. She was legally an adult and fully independent at the time.

Her case is part of a wider pattern.

### A marketplace of control

[A July 2026 investigation by China Newsweek](https://www.inewsweek.cn/society/2026-07-14/31097.shtml) documented several adults placed in similar institutions by their families. A 21-year-old shop worker said employees restrained him and transported him hundreds of miles after his parents paid them to correct his sleeping habits. A 25-year-old woman living alone said three people entered her home, seized her phone, and took her from Jiangxi to a disciplinary school in Hubei.

In another case, an institution advised a mother to lure her 26-year-old son to Chongqing by promising him a vacation. He spent 82 days inside the facility.

Several former detainees later reported the institutions for unlawful detention or restriction of personal liberty. Their complaints did not result in criminal cases.

For many readers outside China, “[internet addiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internet_addiction_camp)” camps feel like a remnant of the early 2000s. These institutions became notorious for military drills, physical punishment, forced confinement, and electroshock treatment during this time. In 2009, [China’s Ministry of Health ordered](https://www.nhc.gov.cn/zwgkzt/pyzgl1/200907/41730.shtml) medical institutions to stop using electrical stimulation to treat internet addiction, citing insufficient evidence of its safety and effectiveness.

The industry survived the public backlash. It changed its messaging and continued operating.

Today, “internet addiction” functions as a flexible label for behavior families reject. It can encompass gaming, romantic relationships, unconventional employment, irregular sleeping hours, and resistance to parental demands.

While internet addiction is not recognized under the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision ([ICD-11](https://icd.who.int/)), the global benchmark for mental health diagnoses, [China has recognized](https://en.nhc.gov.cn/2018-10/05/c_73812.htm) internet addiction as a clinical issue since 2008. This official terminology allows families to justify their actions. A disagreement becomes a disorder. Parental disapproval becomes a concern. Confinement becomes treatment.

Some institutions now call themselves specialized training schools, family education centers, behavioral-correction programs, psychological counseling centers, or youth-development organizations. These labels give forced confinement and coercive practices the guise of education and care.

The basic transaction remains clear. Families pay private organizations to discipline children they consider unmanageable.

The industry now applies this model to adults.

### A gap in enforcement

Parents have no general legal authority over adult children who possess full civil capacity. They cannot legally decide where those adult children live, whom they date, what work they pursue, or how they organize their daily lives. However, emotional pressure, financial dependence, and family obligation can preserve parental influence, even where legal control has ended.

Private disciplinary institutions offer families a way to override that boundary.

The institutions provide transportation, surveillance, confinement, isolation, forced routines, and psychological pressure. They confiscate phones, restrict movement, control communication, and demand obedience. Parents purchase forms of control they can no longer lawfully impose themselves.

These institutions extend parental authority beyond its legal endpoint. They turn coercion into a commercial service.

The recent cases also reveal an enforcement gap.

[Article 238 of China’s Criminal Law](https://www.stats.gov.cn/gk/tjfg/xgfxfg/202503/t20250311_1958931.html) prohibits unlawfully detaining another person or otherwise depriving them of personal liberty.

In the case of the Beijing music student, police issued a written non-filing notice stating that there were “no criminal facts,” and that they would not be pursuing a case. The published reporting discloses no further reasoning. It does not explain how police assessed the family’s false identification of institution employees as police officers, the abduction and transport of an adult, the confiscation of her phone, or her eleven-day forced confinement.

The notice records a conclusion while leaving the central legal question unanswered: Why wasn’t her report enough to establish grounds for a criminal investigation?

Other cases reveal fragments of the reasoning used in practice. One parent was reportedly told that the placement counted as voluntary because the family had authorized it. Other complaints stalled over jurisdiction and difficulties preserving evidence. These explanations center the parents’ decision and leave the adult detainee’s lack of consent unresolved.

### Confinement as protection

[A separate investigation by Jiemian News](https://www.jiemian.com/article/14667792.html?) in June 2026 found adults as old as 33 inside such institutions and reported that, at one location, adults and minors were present in almost equal numbers.

There is no official count for how many adults have been forced into such facilities, or of how many facilities exist throughout the country. One Chongqing institution was reported to have nearly 100 adults as of late June 2026. These institutions are scattered across cities and provinces throughout China, meaning there could be hundreds — if not thousands — of adults held against their will because their family disagrees with their life choices.

Parents describe confinement as protection. Institutions present it as education, counseling, or behavioral intervention. Police encounter families who insist that they are acting in their adult child’s best interests.

The confined person may have no phone, no access to independent legal assistance, and no opportunity to contradict the family’s account. Both investigations describe institutions using controlled recordings to shape the account presented to families or police. Detainees were asked to say that they were safe, grateful to their parents, or ready to end the relationships their families opposed.

Familial language softens the appearance of coercion. Conduct that would immediately raise alarm between strangers can be treated as a private disagreement when organized by a parent.

This response allows private institutions to operate between educational services and unlawful deprivation of liberty.

The institutions also rely on vague definitions of “misconduct” that can warrant people’s detention. The recent cases involved a romantic relationship, irregular sleeping hours, so-called excessive gaming, work habits, unemployment, and career choices that parents considered improper. None required a clear medical diagnosis.

In effect, this industry sells families the power to suspend adulthood. For a fee, they provide transportation, isolation, surveillance, forced routines, and obedience under the language of education.

Their continued existence reflects more than a regulatory failure. It also exposes the persistence of a family ideal in which parental authority is expected to outlast adulthood, and obedience remains a moral obligation rather than a legal choice.

As long as that expectation continues to blur the boundary between parental concern and personal liberty, there will be a market for companies willing to sell control over adults who are legally free.

**Written by [Lina Ma](https://globalvoices.org/author/lina-ma/)**
description: China's rebranded “internet addiction” industry now helps families confine legally independent adult children, exposing how parental coercion survives through private institutions and weak enforcement.

title: Constantly on edge at work? It could be anticipatory stress
authors: Sabrina Fitzsimons, Co-Director of DCU CREATE (Centre for Collaborative Research Across Teacher Education), Lecturer in Education, Dublin City University
content:
In [Nosferatu](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Nosferatu-film-by-Murnau-1922) (1922), one of cinema’s most haunting images arrives before the vampire himself: his shadow. Something is approaching, but we don’t know exactly what it is, or what will happen when it arrives. The fear lies in the anticipation.

This is called [anticipatory stress](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0305764X.2025.2451280), and it can affect us in our work lives. An event may be months away, yet psychologically it has already entered the room, casting a shadow on the present.

In my [research](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0305764X.2025.2451280), I explored the wellbeing at work of university education academics working within high-stakes inspection and accountability systems in the UK and Ireland.

In England, all initial teacher education providers are inspected by [Ofsted](https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/68b8762fcc8356c3c882aa4c/Independent_wellbeing_impact_assessment_of_the_revised_Ofsted_framework.pdf). In other nations, accreditation inspections may be conducted by professional regulatory bodies, such as the [Teaching Council of Ireland](https://www.teachingcouncil.ie/professional-learning/initial-teacher-education/). Across these different systems, many academics described feeling anticipatory stress while waiting for an inspection.

Participants in England described living in “constant anticipation”, on “constant red alert” and “on a knife edge” while waiting for the call from [Ofsted](https://www.educationsupport.org.uk/news-and-events/news/independent-ofsted-wellbeing-assessment-published/).

The inspection had not begun, but the expectation of it was already shaping how they worked, where they directed their attention and even how confidently they could make plans outside work. As one participant said, “every family plan is prefaced with, ‘but I could get the call’”.

[Anticipation](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RnJAtztON84) itself is not the problem. It’s a normal [psychological function](https://dictionary.apa.org/anticipation) that allows us to prepare for what is coming. The difficulty arises when we know something important is approaching, but our personal control is limited, and we don’t have enough information to decide what useful preparation actually looks like.

Under those conditions, the mind keeps working on the problem. We forecast possible outcomes, we revisit conversations we have had and we can become more attentive to potential signals.

An unexpected request for a meeting or a delayed email response can suddenly acquire particular significance, not necessarily because it means anything, but because uncertainty can make us more vigilant for information that might help predict what comes next.

[Psychologists](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16439263/) use the term “perseverative cognition” to describe how worry and rumination can keep a potential stressor mentally active when it is not actually present. In simple terms, the stressful event may be absent, but the mind keeps bringing it back into the present.

As one of my interviewees explained: “My mind has already gone into overdrive with worry – even though the inspection might not take place until next year.” Another said: “It’s the ‘not knowing’ that I find so stressful.” Indeed, [research](https://www.nature.com/articles/nrn3524) into uncertain threat suggests that unpredictability can sustain vigilance, partly because there is no clear point at which we know we can safely stand down.

## Stressful events at work

Many of the events we anticipate at work also carry an element of evaluation. An inspection, promotion process or performance review can place our competence directly under scrutiny, while restructuring may raise a broader question about our [future value](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0305764X.2026.2729309?scroll=top&needAccess=true#d1e113) within an organisation.

Research on [social-evaluative](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15122924/) threat – the stress we feel when we think we are being judged by others – suggests that these situations can provoke particularly strong stress responses. This was apparent in my own research. “It’s my name up front,” one participant said. “I have led the team so I feel a deep sense of personal responsibility that this goes well for everyone.”

Anticipation is often not only tethered to uncertainty, but to professional identity and the [consequences](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03054985.2017.1352499) of feeling judged.

My research also showed how the period of anticipation can generate [additional work](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0305764X.2026.2729309). Many participants noted the gap between official advice and the reality of preparing for a high-stakes event, such as an inspection. Professional bodies might say: “Don’t do anything special for us coming,” but participants felt that, in practice, preparation was unavoidable.

Some described how preparation “almost doubles your workload because you are doing your job and making sure you can demonstrate you are doing the job as well – which is very stressful”. This may be familiar to those in other [work contexts](https://www.rte.ie/brainstorm/2026/1005/1590902-work-measurements-targets-reviews-occupational-wellbeing/). Employees often have to deliver their work while documenting, checking and preparing to [account](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0305764X.2026.2729309) for it. When this preparation takes place in the light of a high-stakes event, it can easily be accompanied by anticipatory stress.

This kind of uncertainty is becoming a familiar feature of organisational life. [Restructures](https://www.independent.ie/business/technology/ebay-tells-government-it-is-restructuring-irish-base-as-workers-wait-for-news-of-potential-job-cuts/a/137911280.html) are announced before new roles are settled; [mergers](https://www.rte.ie/news/business/2026/0112/1552606-ccpc-saw-10-increase-in-mergers-notifications-in-2025/) begin to reshape teams while reporting lines remain unclear.

More recently, new technologies, such as [AI](https://www.image.ie/agenda/ask-aine-what-ai-really-means-for-work-in-2026-984834), have been introduced while employees are still trying to understand what they will mean for their [day-to-day work](https://www.image.ie/agenda/rustout-the-work-around-the-work-that-is-wearing-high-achievers-down-992050).

The difficulty isn’t change itself, nor the assumption that the change will necessarily end badly. It is the long period in which people know enough to realise that something important is shifting, but don’t have enough information to make informed decisions or understand their future with any degree of confidence.

Organisations cannot remove all uncertainty from the workplace, and leaders cannot provide answers they do not yet have. They can, however, give uncertainty some boundaries [by being clear](https://podcasts.apple.com/gb/podcast/how-can-i-stop-treating-employee-mental-health-as-a/id1839807801?i=1000793936997) about what is known, what aspects remain unresolved and when people can expect to know more. Without those boundaries, the period before an important event can fill with [worry](https://www.who.int/news-room/fact-sheets/detail/mental-health-at-work), rumination and attempts to make sense of incomplete information.

*Sabrina Fitzsimons does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: An event may be months away, yet psychologically it has already entered the room, casting a shadow on the present.

title: Remote work made these colleagues more open with each other, not less
authors: Vanessa M. Conzon, Assistant Professor of Management and Organizations, Boston College
content:
If you need to participate in video meetings for work, you’ve probably experienced more than one disruption, whether it’s kids darting around or home renovation noise.

Meetings that use Zoom and similar software are a fixture of remote work, which [surged during the COVID-19 pandemic](https://www.census.gov/library/publications/2023/acs/acs-52.html) and remains prevalent. As of August 2026, [36% of American workers](https://www.bls.gov/web/empsit/cpseea42.htm) in management, professional and related occupations did at least some of their work from home, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

I’m a management scholar who studies [how, when and where people work](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=3I0eCFcAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao). Before the pandemic began, I was studying a professional services company. That made it possible for me to follow how its staff transitioned from primarily working in person to mostly remote through 2024, which gave me more insight into how remote work has changed people’s lives.

The study included 275 interviews and about 330 hours of observation. Most people in the groups I followed ended up working from home four or five days a week, joining meetings by video. What I found was the opposite of what I expected.

## Learning more about colleagues

Rather than pulling colleagues apart, remote work brought them closer and made them more willing to be open with one another. The findings were peer-reviewed and will be [published in an upcoming issue](https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2024.19818) of the management journal Organization Science.

Before the shift to remote work, I assumed – consistent with the predictions made by many prominent [researchers of workplace relationships](https://hbr.org/2021/04/what-psychological-safety-looks-like-in-a-hybrid-workplace) – that moving people out of the office would break down social connections. But I was wrong.

In the office, before the shift to remote work, I found that people primarily viewed one another as work colleagues rather than whole people. Reflecting this relationship, workers sometimes said they felt uncomfortable sharing with one another aspects of their lives that might limit their ability to do work.

For example, one worker I interviewed, Patrick, was afraid to tell his colleagues he could not work late one night because he was helping his mom. All the names I’m mentioning are pseudonyms to protect the privacy of the people involved and their employer.

“Even though you didn’t sleep last night, you’re expected to show up and smile and be fine,” said Tamara, an exhausted parent with two young children, when she was still commuting regularly to the office.

Surprisingly, people told me that they learned a lot more about one another once they began to work remotely instead of being together in an office. During my research, I heard about children yelling in the background and pets wandering in front of cameras. A spouse arriving home from work stopped to say hello on screen.

In team chat channels, people posted photos of their children, their animals and the meals they had cooked.

“Everyone has noises in the background, or they have something going on or whatever, and so we get to know each other quicker and on a deeper level than we would otherwise,” Tamara told me. In some cases, this increased sense of closeness happened to people who had known each other for years prior to switching to remote work.

## Growing psychological safety

[Psychological safety](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-031413-091305) is the sense that you can take an interpersonal risk at work, such as admitting a mistake, asking for help or raising a problem, without being judged negatively.

Decades of management research tie psychological safety to important outcomes for both workers and organizations, including [learning, creativity and speaking up](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-orgpsych-120920-055217).

Over time, working remotely seemed to improve psychological safety for many of these co-workers.

People became “less afraid to talk about the interface of their personal and professional lives,” Leah said. Before, she added, no one would have volunteered that a breakup was affecting them and that they needed a day off to decompress.

After the company went remote, people told me they felt more comfortable sharing their own challenges as they tried to juggle their work and the challenges they faced in their personal lives.

## Supporting work and nonwork activities

And as people started sharing these problems with their co-workers, they also told me they felt as if they could then better support one another.

When one worker’s father fell ill, his colleague, Brooke, took over the tasks the two had planned to do together.

“I’m just going to take this over for you right now,” Brooke told him. “And then, whenever you can, come back and swoop in.”

The colleague was able to dedicate time to caring for his father. And importantly, because help circulated this way, Brooke said, a task no longer “stopped dead in the water” when one person could not get to it.

This deeper collaboration did not seem to come at the expense of getting tasks completed. As an employee I’m calling Charles explained, having co-workers sharing details about their personal lives has “helped us to work more effectively in a lot of ways.”

Crucially, these improvements were experienced by people with many different living arrangements – young and old, those with and without kids or partners, men and women. And these benefits were positively reinforcing. For instance, sharing more meant learning more about others, which further reinforced psychological safety.

My findings suggest that remote work can be a benefit that employers and employees may overlook. Rather than treating time out of the office as a cost to social connection among employees, they might treat it as a way to grow personally and get to know co-workers better.

*Vanessa M. Conzon does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Remote work does not necessarily mean that social connections break down. Instead, it can provide the spark for stronger and better relationships between co-workers.

title: Why your boss matters more than remote or hybrid work when it comes to burnout and job satisfaction
authors: Christos Makridis, Associate Research Professor of Information Systems, Arizona State University; Institute for Humane Studies
content:
The post-pandemic push to bring workers back to the office has left many nostalgic for more [flexible arrangements](https://theconversation.com/hybrid-work-is-not-always-the-golden-compromise-employees-expect-even-as-more-companies-implement-it-283015), such as hybrid or remote work.

But a wealth of data since the pandemic now suggests that [workplace factors](https://theconversation.com/how-employers-can-make-good-decisions-about-remote-work-before-the-next-crisis-strikes-282671) like feeling appreciated and having a good relationship with your manager are much more tied to job satisfaction than the actual time spent in the office.

To understand this insight, it’s important to recognize that a return to the office can mean very different things to different workers. Someone who values uninterrupted time at home may resent the commute. A younger trainee struggling to learn the job may welcome easier access to colleagues. An employee who dislikes their manager may lament having to see them in person.

These differences help explain why the return-to-office debate often produces conflicting answers.

[As a researcher](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=KKQXJ_8AAAAJ&hl=en) of the ways technology is changing the workplace, I co-authored a study with business and accounting scholar [Jason Schloetzer](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=D1lDcKYAAAAJ&hl=en) that [analyzed responses](https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07017) from nearly 165,000 U.S. employees between 2020 and 2023 from the database Payscale. These surveys let us look beyond location to ask whether employees felt appreciated; considered pay fair and transparent; received useful communication; had chances to develop; and enjoyed a good relationship with their manager.

Once we accounted for these and other job-specific variables, we found that the edge in satisfaction for fully or mostly remote workers disappears. The only group of employees who felt more satisfied on the job were those who sometimes worked remotely – and that difference was modest.

In other words, long-standing factors shaping job satisfaction outweighed workplace format when it came to making employees happy.

## The workplace behind the work arrangement

Semi- or fully remote workers [may appear more satisfied](https://www.wsj.com/lifestyle/careers/remote-work-happiness-evidence-153351d8). But other factors, such as having better pay or more supportive workplace practices, need to be taken into account, we argue.

Employees’ relationships with their managers is one of those variables. We asked employees to rate the statement “I have a great relationship with my direct manager” on a 5-point scale, with 4 or 5 indicating favorable. The measure reflects the employee’s own assessment rather than a checklist of managerial skills; questions about communication, appreciation and development opportunities were asked separately.

A favorable manager relationship was tied to higher job satisfaction across work arrangements, we found. But that association was stronger among employees working on-site than among those who always or sometimes worked remotely. One possible explanation is that working together gives employees more opportunities to benefit from a supportive manager who mentors and offers development opportunities, while distance can offer some relief when the relationship is less favorable.

We also used data from the Gallup Workplace Panel to study the same workers over time. These results reinforced our findings: It’s important to consider the workplace as a whole when evaluating remote or hybrid work.

## Burnout and happiness are different questions

Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can like their job while feeling exhausted, or they may appreciate working at home while feeling socially disconnected. That’s why we treat job satisfaction, burnout and happiness as separate values, and why we distinguish stress on a particular day from persistent work exhaustion.

Looking at stress, for example, we found that it’s common across work arrangements. According to [Gallup’s 2026 State of the Global Workplace report](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/697904/state-of-the-global-workplace-global-data.aspx), 41% of fully remote employees reported substantial stress the previous day, compared with 46% of hybrid employees, as well as 46% of on-site employees whose jobs could be done remotely.

Feeling satisfied with a job, however, doesn’t necessarily mean feeling well overall. Someone can value their work while finding its demands exhausting. Job satisfaction, daily stress and burnout capture different aspects of that experience.

Physicians are one example. Among physicians whose organizations participated in an [American Medical Association survey](https://www.ama-assn.org/practice-management/physician-health/us-physician-burnout-hits-lowest-rate-covid-19) in 2024, about three-quarters reporting being satisfied with their job, while almost half reported feeling a great deal of stress because of their job, such as from burdensome paperwork or staff shortages.

The published summary doesn’t identify exactly how many doctors reported both, but it shows that satisfaction and widespread stress can coexist within a profession.

Meanwhile, separate [Gallup research on nearly 7,500 full-time U.S. employees](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/237059/employee-burnout-part-main-causes.aspx) helps explain why working conditions deserve attention. The factors most closely tied to burnout included unfair treatment, crushing workloads, unclear expectations, poor communication and support from managers, and unreasonable deadlines.

Work location may ease some pressures while introducing others. Working from home can remove a draining commute, for example, while making it harder to get timely help from colleagues. But neither arrangement automatically resolves an excessive workload or uncertainty about manager expectations.

Those problems require attention wherever employees work.

## Working apart can carry social costs

The expression “work-life balance” implies that [it’s healthy to engage](https://theconversation.com/when-workers-lives-outside-work-are-more-fulfilling-it-benefits-employers-too-260772) in social activity with friends and family outside work.

But as [other research](http://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5386372) of mine shows, more flexibility for office work doesn’t necessarily translate into more time with other people. Among younger workers in occupations that can readily be done remotely, I found that the share of leisure time spent alone rose from about 25% to 40% from 2017 to 2024. For workers who also spend their workday alone, that means fewer opportunities for socializing both on and off the job.

Time alone doesn’t have to lead to loneliness. But the finding raises a concern: Just because you gain more control over your schedule doesn’t mean that friends, family or colleagues will be available to share that time – or that you’ll make the effort to see them.

Related research suggests that these concerns about social connection deserve more attention. The expansion of remote work has been tied to increases in isolation and mental distress, [according to new research](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec7671) published by economists Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais. In a nonrandomized experiment covering almost 600,000 people, they compared changes in mental health before and after the pandemic in jobs that could and could not readily be done remotely, excluding 2020 and 2021. Remote workers living alone fared the worst.

## The next steps

These findings raise a practical question for employers: How can time together at work become more useful?

For employers considering a return to the office, a useful starting point is to first [identify what employees gain](https://theconversation.com/remote-work-has-made-developing-relationships-with-colleagues-harder-heres-what-workers-and-bosses-need-now-194883) from being together and then organize office time around it. Teams that depend on frequent collaboration need overlapping schedules. Newer employees need access to colleagues who can teach them. Managers need to provide useful feedback and address workload issues wherever people work, and employees need to be responsive to managerial efforts to engage them.

Employee preferences and job requirements differ across organizations, so managers need to determine which arrangements suit their teams. But regular, useful feedback matters across on-site, hybrid and remote settings. That means discussing priorities, recognizing employees’ contributions and helping them work effectively with colleagues.

As Gallup workplace researcher Jim Harter [has suggested](https://www.gallup.com/workplace/700718/span-control-optimal-team-size-managers.aspx), this kind of feedback should become a weekly habit.

“These conversations don’t have to be long; 15 to 30 minutes, done consistently, is enough,” he wrote.

*Christos Makridis is also a senior researcher in Gallup, receives funding from foundations to study remote work and organizations, and is affiliated with other nonprofit education and thinktank institutions.*
description: A return to the office can mean very different things to different workers, which is why this debate often produces conflicting answers.

title: An iced coffee won’t predict job performance  — but it might reveal hiring bias
authors: Eddy Ng, Smith Professor of Equity and Inclusion in Business, Queen's University, Ontario
content:
Imagine two candidates with identical qualifications interviewing for the same job. One arrives carrying a bottle of water, while the other walks in with an iced coffee. Should that difference matter?

A [recent TikTok from an American recruiter](https://www.tiktok.com/@caitlinrecruiter/video/7686166507759455501) argued that it can. Discussing Gen Z candidates, Wehniainen said arriving at a corporate interview with an iced coffee can make someone appear too casual, as though the interview were simply one more errand in the day.

The video prompted a lively online debate. Some users agreed wholeheartedly, while others called the advice outdated and arbitrary. The discussion quickly became another round of the familiar [“Gen Z versus everyone else” debate](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/gen-z-stare-1.7584710).

But the real question isn’t whether bringing a coffee to an interview is good etiquette; it’s why something so trivial can influence how we judge a candidate in the first place. Do these snap judgments actually help employers identify candidates who will perform well on the job?

## The coffee is not the real issue

Nobody wants a spilled latte on the boardroom table. Slurping, rattling ice cubes or juggling a drink during a handshake can be distracting. But some reactions to interview coffee go beyond these practical concerns.

Most interviewers would probably think little of a candidate carrying a bottle of water. Many employers even offer coffee to candidates when they arrive. But bringing an iced coffee from elsewhere can evoke a different response.

The “offence” may be symbolic rather than practical. An interviewer might interpret an iced coffee as a sign that a candidate is too casual or not taking the interview seriously. Another might see the same behaviour as a sign of confidence or comfort.

The important point is that these interpretations are subjective. They may tell us more about an interviewer’s expectations about what professionalism should look like than the candidate themselves.

## First impressions can mislead

Research suggests interviewers can form impressions of candidates very quickly. A [2010 study](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0019918), for example, found that interviewers often form impressions during the first few minutes of an encounter, sometimes before any substantive interview questions have been asked.

Those early impressions can shape how the rest of the interview unfolds. But there is an important difference between predicting interview outcomes and predicting job performance.

A review of [research on job interviews](https://doi.org/10.1037/a0016532) found that candidates’ appearances, self-presentation and non-verbal behaviours influence interview ratings more strongly than they predict future job performance.

In other words, candidates who make favourable first impressions may receive better interview without necessarily being the people who will be the most effective employee later on.

This is one reason why hiring experts generally recommend [structured interviews](https://doi.org/10.1037/apl0000994), in which candidates are asked the same questions and evaluated using consistent criteria.

Structured interviews are among the more reliable ways of predicting future job performance, in part because they reduce the influence of subjective impressions and personal preferences.

## It’s not really about Gen Z

It didn’t take long for an iced coffee to become a story about Gen Z. Generational labels are an easy way to explain behaviour that seems unfamiliar or inconsistent with our own expectations.

Ironically, many of the managers now judging Gen Z applicants are millennials, [the generation once labelled “entitled](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10869-010-9159-4).” Many young job seekers feel they are being judged on minor signals and unwritten rules in an increasingly competitive entry-level market.

Meanwhile, some managers and older workers are navigating more [flexible and remote workplaces](https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/public-employment-and-management-2023_5b378e11-en/full-report/component-5.html) that have disrupted traditional workplace norms since the COVID-19 pandemic.

Social media can turn these differences into “everyone versus Gen Z” narratives because [conflict attracts attention online](https://doi.org/10.1093/workar/waw009). But many of these disagreements are really about differing assumptions about professionalism and respect.

In my study of [Gen Z’s workplace expectations and behaviours with colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1108/PR-02-2022-0101), we found them to be cautious and security-focused. So what one generation considers obvious interview etiquette, another may never have been taught.

From my experience as a professor, the COVID-19 pandemic also disrupted how many young adults learned expectations in the classroom and workplace.

## The problem with unwritten rules

There is another reason employers should be cautious about evaluating candidates based on small behavioural cues: standards of professionalism are rarely applied equally.

Research shows that seemingly neutral judgments about “polish,” “fit” and professionalism can be influenced [by age](https://doi.org/10.1111/peps.12003), [race](https://doi.org/10.1177/1948550620937937), [gender](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11199-019-01111-2) and [social class](https://doi.org/10.1002/smj.70113).

A senior executive carrying a cold brew might look as though he is deliberately breaking a rule — the “[red sneakers effect”](https://doi.org/10.1086/674870) — while a 22-year-old first-time applicant may be seen as someone who simply doesn’t know the rules. The same behaviour that is interpreted as confidence in one person can be interpreted as carelessness in another.

When hiring decisions rely heavily on unwritten rules, candidates with access to professional networks and insider knowledge also gain an advantage. First-generation professionals, newcomers or individuals unfamiliar with particular workplace cultures may be unfairly disadvantaged.

## Hire for the job, not the etiquette

For job seekers, my advice is simple: if you’re worried that an interviewer might judge you for bringing an iced coffee, finish it beforehand. Leaving it outside costs nothing, while bringing it in risks creating a negative impression that has little to do with your talents or ability.

But the larger issue is for employers. It’s natural for interviewers to pick up on small cues, but making hiring decisions based on them is unfair and misses the point.

The goal of interviews is to find who can do the job, not who already knows every unwritten social rule about iced coffee. The less hiring depends on knowing a particular set of unwritten social rules, the more likely it is that candidates will be evaluated on the qualities that actually matter.

*Eddy Ng receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.*
description: A recruiter’s advice that candidates should leave their iced coffee at home has sparked a familiar Gen Z workplace debate.

title: Does increased childcare funding help mothers into work?
authors: Eva Lloyd, Emeritus Professor of Early Childhood, School of Childhood and Social Care, University of East London; Sung-Hee Lee, Senior Lecturer in Sociology and Social Policy, University of Derby
content:
Since Labour won the 2024 general election, policy focused on children in the early years – from birth to school age – and their parents has moved sharply up the political agenda.

The government’s most expensive [early years](https://theconversation.com/topics/early-years-2299) commitment so far has been its decision to honour the previous administration’s pledge to provide 30 [funded hours of childcare](https://researchbriefings.files.parliament.uk/documents/CBP-8052/CBP-8052.pdf) for children aged from nine months to school age whose parents are in work. This was implemented in September 2025.

If parents require their children to be in childcare for more than 30 hours a week (they might need over 50 hours to cover full-time employment), they pay the excess. Childcare providers may also charge for services on top of the funded hours, such as meals, nappies and optional activities. However, such charges cannot be mandatory conditions of accessing the funded hours.

The £9 billion allocated to this provision represents a doubling of childcare funding since [2024](https://ifs.org.uk/sites/default/files/2026-01/IFS-annual-report-on-education-spending-in-England-2025%E2%80%9326.pdf). [The policy’s central aim](https://www.nao.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/preparations-to-extend-early-years-entitlements-for-working-parents-in-england.pdf) is to make childcare more affordable for working parents and to increase mothers’ employment rates. It is also intended to support children’s development and educational outcomes.

We [set out to explore](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/journal-of-international-and-comparative-social-policy/article/comparing-the-english-and-korean-marketised-childcare-systems-in-the-context-of-promoting-maternal-employment/729534C9D301B8194C344D16234D679E) whether increasing the funding for this system would increase mothers’ employment.

We compared England with South Korea, where a fairly similar arrangement has been on offer for a number of years. In Korea, though, early childhood education and care receives significantly higher funding. It stands at 0.9% of GDP, compared with 0.5% in the UK.

Korea has offered a universal entitlement of 35 hours of funded childcare weekly for children aged from birth to age two since 2012. This was extended to children aged three to five the following year.

Our study found systemic problems in both countries. Our findings suggest that the [design of funding systems](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/0001699311433428), and how they interact with labour market and parental leave policies, may matter more than [funding levels](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0927537121001354) alone.

## Exploring similarities

England and Korea share similar early years policy goals. Both aim to support children’s development while helping mothers into work. Both also rely heavily on [marketised childcare systems](https://www.tcpress.com/products/the-early-advantage-1early-childhood-systems-that-lead-by-example_9780807777152), meaning that different childcare providers compete to offer care. Both systems combine public, [private for-profit](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10142357/7/Childcare%20Main%20Report%20010222.pdf) and not-for-profit providers.

Public spending on early childhood education and care is proportionally much higher in Korea. Yet full-time maternal employment rates in Korea (56.2% in 2021) remain well below both UK (74.2% in 2021) and [OECD averages](https://www.oecd.org/en/data/datasets/oecd-family-database.html) (71.4% in 2021).

Possible explanations for the relatively low maternal employment levels may be found beyond the childcare funding model, in wider social and labour market conditions. In Korea, [traditional gender norms](https://pureadmin.qub.ac.uk/ws/portalfiles/portal/148005820/Women_s_experiences_of_Balancing_Work_and_Family_Care_in_South_Korea_Continuity_and_Change.pdf) and limited access to [flexible, family-friendly employment practices](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2019/10/rejuvenating-korea-policies-for-a-changing-society_fa737e99/c5eed747-en.pdf) such as paid maternity leave and flexible hours, continue to create major barriers to mothers returning to work. These issues are coupled with a wider gender pay gap.

At the same time, the childcare system itself faces structural weaknesses. Childcare provision [hasn’t expanded](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17516234.2021.1955644) enough to allow all children access to high-quality care, particularly in the private for-profit sectors.

In England, [family-friendly employment policies](https://www.leavenetwork.org/fileadmin/user_upload/k_leavenetwork/annual_reviews/2025/Dobrotic_et_al__LPRN_2025.pdf), including maternity, paternity and parental leave, provide stronger support for maternal employment. But England’s childcare system also faces serious challenges.

Access and affordability problems persist. In some disadvantaged areas, [“childcare deserts”](https://content.vu.edu.au/sites/default/files/documents/2024-09/childcare-deserts-international-report.pdf) mean families have no local access to good-quality childcare. With [Korea](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/support-materials/2025/01/reducing-inequalities-by-investing-in-early-childhood-education-and-care_a0fd3f31/Korea-country-note-25Feb.pdf), England shares the problems of limited provision for [disadvantaged children](https://www.nuffieldfoundation.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/02/Early-education-for-disadvantagted-children-How-Local-action-can-support-take-up-of-the-15-hours-entitlement.pdf), especially those with [special educational needs and disabilities](https://www.nao.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/improving-educational-outcomes-for-disadvantaged-children-1.pdf). In both countries, there is a problem of low pay and high staff turnover in the private-for-profit childcare sector.

Quality in England also varies considerably. The dominance of private for-profit provision, notably [large childcare corporations](https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10142357/7/Childcare%20Main%20Report%20010222.pdf), shapes staff pay, qualifications and working conditions.

The early years sector [has problems](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/646ca30371a2ef6a657e9309/t/65482050ded6710668b8b62a/1699225681784/Retention+and+Return.pdf) recruiting workers and keeping them in the profession. Between 2018 and 2025, the number of registered childcare providers [dropped by nearly 20%](https://explore-education-statistics.service.gov.uk/find-statistics/childcare-and-early-years-provider-survey/2025#section-section-1-childcare-providers-and-their-characteristics). Complex governance arrangements often [leave parents confused](https://www.coram.org.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/Childcare-Survey-2026.pdf) about eligibility and access to subsidies.

These barriers affect English mothers’ ability to participate in paid work, [particularly full-time work](https://www.fawcettsociety.org.uk/Handlers/Download.ashx?IDMF=d73d0c92-19af-479c-a206-0807ec008bf1).

In both England and Korea, despite the funded hours, families may not be able to access high-quality childcare.

## Looking elsewhere

A 2025 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) [report](https://www.oecd.org/content/dam/oecd/en/publications/reports/2025/01/reducing-inequalities-by-investing-in-early-childhood-education-and-care_a0fd3f31/b78f8b25-en.pdf) argues that investment in early childhood education and care can reduce social inequalities of the kind seen in both England and Korea. But it also stresses that how governments allocate funding matters.

[Earlier comparative research](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/13501763.2017.1401108) reached similar conclusions. This research found that the distribution of childcare support can be as important as the scale of spending itself if disadvantaged children are to benefit.

In countries where reforms have combined affordability with guaranteed access to childcare, increases in mothers’ employment have been more evident.

From the 1970s, childcare expansion in Norway has had [a demonstrable effect](https://docs.iza.org/dp12146.pdf) on mothers’ employment and working patterns. [Germany’s](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0927537119301125) more recent childcare expansion policies achieved similar outcomes. Both countries have streamlined systems of integrated early education and childcare, while parents pay income related fees. In some German states [all places are free](https://eurydice.eacea.ec.europa.eu/eurypedia/germany/early-childhood-and-school-education-funding), [while in Norway](https://eurydice.eacea.ec.europa.eu/eurypedia/norway/early-childhood-and-school-education-funding) they are free for low-income families. In both countries children have a legal right to a nursery place from the age of one, whether or not their parents are in work.

Both England and Korea now appear close to important childcare policy [“tipping points”](https://www.e-elgar.com/shop/gbp/complexity-institutions-and-public-policy-9780857932631.html?srsltid=AfmBOopma3X9bE5KJY6aMtGMWsfzydl5KVbDHG5_MNWFIKl49Rnu06nB) where radical intervention is indicated.

[In England](https://www.local.gov.uk/publications/early-education-and-childcare-changes-and-challenges-future), further progress is likely to depend on extending 30-hours childcare support beyond working families, simplifying complex subsidy arrangements, and strengthening regulation of childcare markets.

[In Korea](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17516234.2021.1955644#abstract), improvements in maternal employment rates will primarily require the development of stronger family-friendly employment policies, and wider efforts to challenge persistent gender inequalities in both the workplace and family life.

The wider lesson is clear. Increased spending alone is unlikely to raise maternal employment if labour market structures, gender norms and childcare market dynamics remain unchanged. Both countries illustrate the limitations of heavily marketised childcare systems in delivering high-quality and sustainable early years provision that is accessible to all. Increasing childcare funding cannot be separated from employment policy, gender equality policies, or the organisation of care itself.

*Eva Lloyd received funding from the British Academy, the Department for Education, the National Centre for Social Research, the Nuffield Foundation, and the Joseph Rowntree Foundation. She is a trustee of Foundation Years Information and Research, a charity that promotes the importance of children's earliest years to their development and wellbeing. In recent years Eva Lloyd was a member of an Expert Group advising the Irish Government's Department of Children, Disability and Equality on a funding model for its early learning and care and school-age childcare system, and of a Programme Oversight Board overseeing the work required to design a National Agency for Early Learning and Childcare.*

*Sung-Hee Lee has received funding from the British Academy, UKRI’s Economic and Social Research Council (ESRC), NHS England, the Social Policy Association (SPA), and the Academy of Korean Studies. She is Treasurer of the East Asian Social Policy (EASP) Network and a member of the SPA Family Policy Group. She also sits on the Overseas Intelligence Committee of the Korea Institute for Health and Social Affairs (KIHSA), and most recently served as an International Committee Member of the Korean Academy of Family and Social Work.*
description: The design of funding systems may matter more than funding levels.

title: The ‘dream job’ myth: Why a fulfilling career does not have to define your life
authors: Valerie Onyia Babatope, Assistant Professor of Human Resource Management, MacEwan University
content:
At some point, most of us have heard the same advice about work: find a job you love, and you’ll never work a day in your life.

The idea of a “[dream job](https://www.refinery29.com/en-gb/dream-job-backlash)” sounds inspiring, even noble; it suggests that work can be a source of meaning, identity and personal fulfillment. But this ideal can also create a significant amount of pressure, especially for those just entering the workforce.

If your career does not feel like a calling — or if your interests change over time and your work no longer feels like a perfect fit — it can feel like a personal failure.
