But research on careers and motivation suggests the challenge may not be that we’re struggling to find purpose, but that we’ve been taught to expect one job to provide everything: meaning, identity, financial security and personal fulfillment.

Meaningful work can be an important part of a satisfying life. But the relentless pursuit of a single “dream job” can lead to burnout, financial strain and a fragile sense of identity. A more sustainable approach is to view work as one part of a fulfilling life rather than the whole picture.

***No one’s 20s and 30s look the same.** You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our [Quarter Life series](https://tcnv.link/RYTudJL) has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.*

**Read more from Quarter Life:**

- *[Getting outside despite your 9‑to‑5 job can improve your mental health – here’s how to spend time in nature during and around working hours](https://theconversation.com/getting-outside-despite-your-9-to-5-job-can-improve-your-mental-health-heres-how-to-spend-time-in-nature-during-and-around-working-hours-286619)*
- *[You have more ways to connect than ever, but deep friendship feels hard to find – here’s how to build better connections](https://theconversation.com/you-have-more-ways-to-connect-than-ever-but-deep-friendship-feels-hard-to-find-heres-how-to-build-better-connections-285022)*
- *[What everyone gets wrong about the modern job search — and what actually works](https://theconversation.com/what-everyone-gets-wrong-about-the-modern-job-search-and-what-actually-works-285582)*

## When loving your job comes at a cost

One challenge with the dream-job ideal is that passion can sometimes create difficult workplace trade-offs.

[Research by psychologist Aaron Kay and colleagues](https://www.fuqua.duke.edu/duke-fuqua-insights/kay-passion-exploitation) suggests that people are more likely to view it as acceptable to place extra demands on passionate workers — including unpaid work, tasks outside their job description and sacrifices of personal time because they assume the work itself provides a form of reward.

This dynamic may be particularly relevant in fields often associated with passion, such as media, fashion, entertainment and the arts, where workers frequently describe their jobs as closely tied to personal identity and creative fulfillment.

Passion can be a source of motivation and satisfaction, but when work is treated as a calling, it can become easier to justify blurred boundaries and unrealistic expectations.

## Tying your identity to work

The second challenge is psychological. The person you are at 22 is unlikely to be the same person you become at 32 or 42. [Career development researchers have long argued](https://doi.org/10.1016/0001-8791(80%2990056-1) that occupational identity is not fixed; it develops over time as people’s interests, values and life circumstances change.

But when we build a large part of our identity around a single occupation, career changes can become more difficult. Research on career identity suggests that [having a more flexible sense of self can help people navigate transitions](https://doi.org/10.1177/0018726708100358), while a narrowly defined professional identity may make change feel more disruptive.

Finally, there is [the risk of burnout](https://doi.org/10.1186/s43093-023-00219-y). When a hobby or personal interest becomes a profession, the activity that once provided relaxation can become tied to deadlines, client and patient feedback, and revenue targets.

When work is also your passion, a difficult day can feel like a personal failure. The pressure to maintain enthusiasm and constantly demonstrate commitment can gradually undermine the motivation that brought someone into the field in the first place.

## A new definition of career success

A growing body of research suggests that many workers are rethinking the traditional idea that career success means finding one perfect occupation.

This shift is particularly visible among Generation Z, the cohort currently entering the workforce. While younger workers are sometimes criticized as being “lazy” or “uncommitted,” they may instead be challenging older assumptions about what a successful career should provide.

A 2025 survey found that [financial stability and work-life balance rank among the most important factors](https://www.deloitte.com/global/en/issues/work/genz-millennial-survey.html) for Gen Z and millennials, alongside opportunities for growth and meaningful work. It’s a mindset of “peace over promotion.”

Recruiter and career coach [Emily Durham argues we should seek work that meets three core needs](https://shows.acast.com/fixable/episodes/finding-purpose-emily-the-recruiter): validation (feeling seen and appreciated), purpose (finding meaning) and lifestyle (meeting your financial and personal needs).

Crucially, these needs do not all have to be met by one “dream job.” By looking at the entirety of our lives, we can create more stability and resilience, especially in a world of economic uncertainty and AI-driven change.

## Build a career that can adapt

If the dream-job model is limiting, what should replace it? One alternative is to focus less on finding the perfect job title and more on developing a portfolio of transferable skills.

Instead of anchoring your identity to being a “marketing director,” for example, you could set a goal to master a portfolio of skills like persuasive writing, data analysis and project management.

A skill portfolio is adaptable, allowing you to apply your toolkit to different industries and roles as your passions evolve. It gives you the freedom to pivot without starting over.

Another important part of career development is mentorship. Mentorship is one of the most effective strategies for navigating career decisions and building confidence. My own research shows [effective mentoring](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-01813-7) helps build awareness of career paths and clarify options.

Psychosocial mentoring, meanwhile, provides emotional support and helps individuals decouple their sense of worth from their job titles. This kind of support is invaluable when you are trying to figure out what you want, not just what you can get.

## Work is only one part of a fulfilling life

The relentless pursuit of a “dream job” isn’t the only path to a successful career. In a world where the nature of work is changing faster than ever, the most resilient and fulfilling career path is one that is adaptable.

It starts with building a portfolio of skills, is guided by mentors and is measured not by finding a single perfect job title, but by how well your work fits into a life you are passionate about living.

A fulfilling career does not have to provide every source of purpose and identity. Sometimes, the healthiest relationship with work comes from allowing it to be one meaningful part of a larger, richer life.

*Valerie Onyia Babatope does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: A more sustainable approach sees careers as one part of a meaningful life, not the entire foundation of it.

title: Greater job security can make inventors less creative
authors: David Wehrheim, Associate Professor of Strategic Management, IESE Business School (Universidad de Navarra); Eduardo Melero, Associate Professor of Management, Universidad Carlos III; Neus Palomeras, Associate Professor, Universidad Carlos III
content:
When Apple recently presented its ([rather pricey](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/clyjd1jnd03o)) new folding phone, one of the questions hovering over the launch – [and in particular its new CEO, John Ternus](https://theconversation.com/apple-chief-executive-tim-cook-resigns-after-15-years-whats-next-for-the-tech-giant-281122) – was whether the technology giant can recover its famously innovative magic touch.

Apple remains extraordinarily profitable, but the company that revolutionised consumer electronics in the 2000s has been dogged by concerns over its dependency on a single, decades-old product – the iPhone – and its associated services. There is [intense speculation](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/09/apple-product-showcase-ceo-john-ternus) around whether Ternus will reinvigorate the culture of radical innovation that drove Apple’s growth, as well as the development of the smartphone itself.

But concerns around innovation are not confined to one tech company. Over the last few months, figures like [Gordon Brown](https://www.ft.com/content/53d6b648-ea21-43a9-ba89-f1102462ff9b) and [Ursula von der Leyen](https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_26_1718) have underscored its vital economic importance, as well as its glaring absence from European industry in particular.

Our research looks at the origins of innovation, but pinpointing the forces that drive it can be tricky. We have studied innovation from many angles, from how [competition from Chinese imports spurred innovation in the US electronics market](https://www.iese.edu/insight/articles/trade-war-us-china-innovation/), to how [knowledgeable generalist inventors contribute to innovation teams](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.respol.2014.07.005).

[Our most recent study](https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2025.21133) looks at the ways job security factors into the innovation process. The core question we set out to answer was: are people who don’t worry about getting fired more innovative, or less?

***Leer más: [Will AI accelerate or undermine the way humans have always innovated?](https://theconversation.com/will-ai-accelerate-or-undermine-the-way-humans-have-always-innovated-272246)***

## Are safe jobs innovative jobs?

Conventional wisdom dictates that, yes, job security provides innovators with a safety net. It allows them to test the sorts of new ideas that innovation requires, without the fear that failure will get them fired.

This seems to hold true in many settings. Studies of [managers](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.1120.1683) and [academic scientists](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/j.1756-2171.2011.00140.x), for example, suggest that greater job security or tolerance for failure can encourage experimentation, exploration and innovation.

But corporate Research and Development (R&D) introduces another dimension. When choosing new projects, these in-house inventors often have to decide what knowledge to build on: do they deepen expertise in technologies specific to their employer, or develop broader knowledge that will benefit the wider industry?

***Leer más: [China’s AI and tech breakthroughs are built on decades of work. Here’s what other nations can learn](https://theconversation.com/chinas-ai-and-tech-breakthroughs-are-built-on-decades-of-work-heres-what-other-nations-can-learn-289989)***

Our study looked at 82,000 R&D professionals who secured patents at US-based publicly traded firms. We focused on established companies because this allowed us to clearly link inventors’ patents to their employers.

The study looks at data from the 1970s through to the 1990s. We chose this period because it was a time when employee-friendly “wrongful discharge laws” were being gradually passed in many states, allowing us to see the change one state at a time.

Wrongful discharge laws make it harder for firms to fire employees without a valid reason. Since different states adopted these protections at different times, we were able to compare inventors’ outputs before and after their job security increased, as well as with inventors in states where the law had not changed.

## Job security turns innovators inward

We found that greater job security impacts the innovation chain, from what sorts of projects innovators take on, to how novel their innovations are, to how much firm-specific value an innovation creates for employers.

Almost immediately after each state passed wrongful discharge laws, the resulting increase in job security meant innovators turned more inward. They overwhelmingly pursued patents for projects linked to their company’s proprietary equipment, internal know-how or existing products.

In short, employees immersed themselves in mastering the specific technologies of the firm, rather than looking outward.

This, in turn, produced innovations that were less novel, but often more valuable to the employer because they were more closely aligned with the firm’s existing technologies and needs.

***Leer más: [Cannabis legalization spurs innovation, but not always in ways that benefit patients or public health](https://theconversation.com/cannabis-legalization-spurs-innovation-but-not-always-in-ways-that-benefit-patients-or-public-health-277422)***

In contrast, those who were less protected were more likely to rely on broad, general-use technologies and think more outside of their corporate box. Our analysis of patents showed that these less stable settings produced more novel or disruptive creations.

This might seem counterintuitive: why would less secure workers not want to prove themselves as relevant as possible to their employer? The dynamic seems to be that less secure employees were aware that they needed innovations that would stand out in the broader market – including the job market.

Neither outcome is necessarily better, as incremental and disruptive innovation each have their own benefits. But it is useful for managers to know that stable employment may encourage employees to play it safe, and use firm-specific information to innovate within the firm’s needs.

Those seeking breakthrough innovations in places with strong workplace protections may need to counter those effects. Importantly, this does not mean putting all R&D employees on notice.

Rather, leaders seeking more radical developments might consider complementary measures – such as job rotations, external collaboration, or incentives that explicitly reward novelty – to counterbalance the tendency toward more inward-looking innovation.

It provides an introduction to the diversity of research coming out of the continent and considers some of the key issues facing European countries. [Get the newsletter!](https://theconversation.com/europe/newsletters?promoted=europe-newsletter-116)*

description: When worker protection laws were passed across the US, in-house R&D staff began to take fewer risks.

title: AI is creating jobs as well as erasing them – but how rewarding are they?
authors: Akhil Bhardwaj, Associate Professor (Strategy and Organisation), School of Management, University of Bath
content:
Don’t believe the hype about AI taking over all forms of [work](https://theconversation.com/topics/work-401). Most of the evidence to date suggests large-scale job losses are [limited](https://www.ilo.org/publications/impact-genai-jobs-productivity-and-work-organization-review-empirical). But what is changing is the way work is organised.

One area of [increased employment](https://www.upwork.com/research/ai-generated-work-is-creating-more-work-for-humans?afsrc=1&irclickid=zP3VJpTstxyZU55XVM2UVQJnUkrzN2wVm0uezI0&irgwc=1&utm_campaign=10078_Skimbit+Ltd.&utm_medium=affiliate&utm_source=Impact) is in people [“cleaning up”](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/02/ai-jobs-freelance-cleanup) after large language models (LLMs), or [quality controlling](https://www.indeed.com/q-ai-quality-control-jobs.html?vjk=bb40c4898fd54869) them.

The sales pitch is that these AI systems can program code, write reports, analyse data and automate routine decisions faster and better than humans, all at negligible marginal cost. In theory, this should free people to focus on higher-level thinking, and leisure.

In practice, AI agents produce vast amounts of “almost right” output – but there are still errors, hallucinations and odd gaps in judgment that a real person has to catch.

The resulting jobs, often known as [AI remediation](https://www.reddit.com/r/ExperiencedDevs/comments/1vm2r31/how_many_of_you_are_already_employed_in_ai_code/), vary in their skill and remuneration levels. Some AI companies are now hiring experienced professionals in many different fields to ensure their agents are producing work of requisite quality – and to help them change that if not.

But there is also a more subtle shift in job responsibilities within many organisations. Some white-collar workers in industries such as finance, tech and retail are suggesting that AI can add to, rather than reduce, their workload, because of the [need to monitor so-called “workslop”](https://www.linkedin.com/posts/mspilley_ai-generated-workslop-is-destroying-productivity-share-7398660242957365248-Zy4v/). This can also undermine trust in colleagues who are using AI agents.

A 2025 [Harvard Business Review report](https://hbr.org/2025/09/ai-generated-workslop-is-destroying-productivity) quoted a retail director who lamented spending “more time following up on the information \[provided by AI\] and checking it with my own research. I then had to waste even more time setting up meetings with other supervisors to address the issue.”

## Public sector slop

The public sector risks being drawn into this “AI repair” logic. The UK government (among many others) is [experimenting](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/guidance-to-civil-servants-on-use-of-generative-ai/guidance-to-civil-servants-on-use-of-generative-ai) with AI for tasks such as summarising consultation responses, drafting correspondence and analysing sentiment in citizen feedback. Official guidance for civil servants encourages [cautious](https://publications.parliament.uk/pa/cm5901/cmselect/cmpubacc/356/report.html) use of generative AI, while warning that its outputs can be misleading and must be independently verified.

This means, if public services start producing large volumes of AI-generated analysis and letters, they will also have to create new positions whose main responsibility is to monitor, check and correct that output before it reaches citizens or feeds into policy.

How much of the apparent AI efficiency gain will be consumed by people silently tidying up after systems that are sold as automatic?

We already know what can happen when AI automation goes wrong in government. In the Netherlands, tax authorities used algorithms to generate risk scores for supposed fraud and automatically flag families for investigation. Tens of thousands of parents – many from minorities – were [wrongly accused of fraud](https://www.vice.com/en/article/how-a-discriminatory-algorithm-wrongly-accused-thousands-of-families-of-fraud/), forced to repay benefits they did not owe, and pushed into debt or bankruptcy.

Here, the problem was not just the output but the absence of robust human supervision, able to question the machine’s verdict before lives were destroyed. Any public-sector wave of generative AI adoption will have to invest heavily in exactly that kind of [supervision](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41599-025-05749-0.pdf), to avoid repeating the same harms at a larger scale.

There is a deeper trap here. The [tokens](https://www.techradar.com/pro/what-is-a-token-in-ai-and-why-is-it-so-important) (the basic building blocks of data processed by LLMs) that generate all this output are heavily [subsidised](https://aitechmodel.com/are-ai-companies-subsidizing-heavy-users-subscription-economics-explained/) by debt-laden AI companies – but the human time needed to check and fix it is not.

Many companies are deliberately pricing access below cost to [build dependence](https://theconversation.com/governments-are-rushing-to-embrace-ai-they-should-think-twice-272455) on their systems. Once enough organisations have reoriented their workflows and services around a particular AI model, the company behind it can start to raise prices, limit free tiers, change terms or segment features. So the cost-benefit analysis of AI today may look very different in the future.

## Hidden humans

There has already long been a global dimension to the [“hidden humans”](https://www.polytechnique-insights.com/en/columns/digital/ai-the-invisible-yet-very-real-work-of-data-workers/) underpinning AI. Some of the most unpleasant aspects of AI work – chatbot moderation, data labelling, low-level annotation of images – has been [outsourced](https://yalebooks.co.uk/book/9780300264630/atlas-of-ai/) to low-wage countries for many years.

This work has been found to take a [substantial mental toll](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2023/aug/02/ai-chatbot-training-human-toll-content-moderator-meta-openai) on some of these workers, because of the disturbing nature of graphic text and images of violence, self-harm and the like. Employees in such sectors and geographies also [often lack any legal protection](https://yalebooks.yale.edu/book/9780300264630/atlas-of-ai/).

If AI workslop becomes the norm inside organisations, it is easy to imagine a second wave of outsourcing: the routine checking and correction of AI-generated text shipped to offshore centres – packaged as quality control, but experienced on the ground as endless, underpaid digital piecework.

We can already see the work-reorganisation side of this in [translation services](https://theconversation.com/ai-translators-are-getting-more-fluent-but-communication-is-never-just-a-matter-of-words-288739). In many agencies, the main workflow is now machine translation plus “post-editing”. The AI does a first pass; freelance human translators are paid less money to correct its mistakes.

[Research](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0907676X.2025.2604026) suggests that post-editing is often [paid worse](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0907676X.2023.2292572) than traditional translation, requires similar or greater cognitive effort, and is widely perceived as [tedious](https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/sep/02/ai-jobs-freelance-cleanup) and deskilling. Yet those doing this role simultaneously [raise concerns about even that position being replaced](https://aclanthology.org/2025.mtsummit-1.32.pdf) in the longer term.

## How to push back

Popular culture shows how workers can try to resist being pushed into low-status AI clean-up roles. In 2023, Hollywood writers [went on strike](https://apnews.com/article/hollywood-ai-strike-wga-artificial-intelligence-39ab72582c3a15f77510c9c30a45ffc8) partly because they feared studios would use AI tools to generate first drafts and then hire humans to polish them on the cheap.

The resulting agreement with the Writers Guild of America set [guardrails](https://www.ign.com/articles/what-the-writers-new-deal-means-for-ai-and-what-it-can-and-cant-do-to-hollywoods-scripts): AI cannot be credited as a writer, cannot be forced on writers, and cannot be used in ways that undercut human pay and recognition. In effect, the union fought to stop a slide into AI-janitor work, where creative professionals would spend most of their time tidying up after algorithms rather than originating stories themselves,

However, [translators, freelancers working in fields such as video-gaming](https://www.penguin.co.uk/books/462159/we-are-not-machines-by-oconnor-sarah/9780241704226), and other workers have far less collective bargaining power, which makes it easier for AI-driven business models to quietly make repair work as the new normal.

In my view, the problem is not only economic – it is also about [meaning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.03344). Most people would like to feel their work actually contributes something in the world. They want to believe they are [solving problems](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00146-025-02328-4), helping people, or contributing to making something that would not exist without them.

But for at least as long as access to powerful AI systems remains cheap (and heavily subsidised), more and more people will be diverted to cleaning up the mess these systems inevitably create. How meaningful these jobs are is, I believe, a question we cannot afford to dodge.

*Akhil Bhardwaj does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: One area of burgeoning employment is in people cleaning up ‘workslop’.

title: Living with chronic pain at work: Supportive managers can help, but they can’t solve everything
authors: Nick Turner, Professor and Ken Croft Chair in Management, Haskayne School of Business, University of Calgary; Duygu Biricik Gulseren, Associate Professor, School of Human Resource Management, York University, Canada; Fırat K Sayın, Associate Professor of Management, Saint Mary’s University
content:
“I don’t want the pain to define me. I want me to define me.”

This was how one employee described working with chronic pain in interviews [conducted in 2021 by one of us, Duygu Biricik Gulseren, and co-researcher Kevin Kelloway](https://doi.org/10.1007/s41542-020-00078-x). The employee wanted colleagues to understand their experience without pain becoming the centre of every conversation.

For many workers living with chronic pain, disclosure is complicated. Some interviewees worried that revealing their pain would make them seem less capable or put their jobs at risk. Yet keeping it hidden can make it harder to explain why previously manageable tasks suddenly become difficult.

When pain persists or recurs for [longer than three months](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12875-024-02667-z), it’s generally considered chronic pain. Many people continue working while experiencing it, and may have chronic pain-related needs. As [Duygu’s earlier work argues](https://doi.org/10.1080/24740527.2021.2010023), understanding these needs requires looking at how employees experience their jobs and what they need to participate fully.

Our [new research](https://doi.org/10.1111/joop.70148) examines the role supervisors play in shaping that experience. The findings suggest supportive leadership may help employees’ psychological well-being, but this pathway weakens as pain becomes more intense.

## Pain is not only about intensity

Two concepts are key to understanding our results. Pain intensity describes how much pain hurts, while pain interference describes how much pain disrupts activities. At work, interference can mean difficulty concentrating, completing physical tasks or interacting with others.

The distinction is important because working conditions can affect how the pain limits activities, even when its intensity changes little.

In Duygu’s earlier interviews mentioned above, employees described adjusting their pace, rescheduling meetings or changing tasks to reduce pain’s impact. But those options depended on how much control their jobs allowed.

The interviews also showed why standard solutions may miss the mark. Employees all have different needs, even when they have similar conditions. Sitting aggravated one person’s back pain, while standing was difficult for another. Understanding what helps requires listening to the person doing the job.

## How supervisors affect experiences

For our recent study, we followed 195 full-time employees in the United Kingdom who were living with chronic pain. Participants worked in occupations ranging from nursing and construction to office management and information technology, and completed three surveys one month apart.

We asked about pain intensity, psychological well-being, pain interference at work and supervisors’ transformational leadership behaviours. This type of leadership includes taking employees’ needs seriously, expressing confidence in employees and encouraging them to approach problems in new ways.

Employees who reported more of these leadership behaviours tended to report better psychological well-being a month later. Better well-being, in turn, predicted less pain interference at the final survey. The analyses accounted for initial well-being and pain interference, as well as age.

However, this pattern depended on pain intensity. We found evidence of this pathway among employees reporting lower and average levels of pain intensity within our sample, but not higher intensity. That does not establish that leadership is unhelpful for people experiencing severe pain; it suggests this pathway has limits.

## Supportive leadership has limits

We did not find evidence that supervisors’ leadership behaviours directly predicted less pain interference later, once psychological well-being and other factors in the model were taken into account.

Instead, the pattern we observed was indirect: supportive leadership was associated with better psychological well-being, which in turn predicted less interference from pain at work.

Because this was a survey study, it cannot establish cause and effect. Other working conditions, such as flexibility, could help explain the pattern. The findings therefore suggest a possible pathway through psychological well-being, rather than showing that managers’ actions directly reduce pain interference.

One possible explanation is that supportive relationships help people maintain the emotional resources needed to handle work alongside pain. When pain is more intense, those resources may be harder to sustain.

## Support requires action

For managers, the findings highlight the importance of everyday interactions. Showing employees their contributions are important, taking their needs seriously and inviting ideas about problems can help sustain well-being while they manage pain.

However, these behaviours should accompany [practical workplace support](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.orgdyn.2022.100926). An encouraging conversation cannot make an unsuitable workstation comfortable or create recovery time in a rigid schedule.

We recommend asking employees what would make their work more manageable. Depending on the job and person, this might involve adjusting tasks, hours, duties or equipment. Managers should revisit arrangements as needs change.

We also recommend responding to requests without judgment. An employee’s ability to complete a task one day should not become grounds for dismissing difficulties on another. Fluctuating needs call for ongoing conversations.

Flexibility also needs to extend beyond office jobs. Working from home is rarely an option on a construction site or hospital ward. Employers should consider adjusting tasks, staffing or breaks.

Organizations need to give supervisors the resources and authority to respond. Access to accommodations, leave and health benefits should be part of the broader response, including when needs exceed what a supervisor can address alone.

The goal should be to make work more manageable for people living with pain. Encouraging employees to feel positive while leaving avoidable barriers in place would miss that goal. Supportive leadership should be part of a workplace prepared to act on what employees need.

*Duygu Biricik Gulseren has received funding from SSHRC and Canadian Centre for Advanced Leadership in Business for this study.*

*Fırat K Sayın does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: New research shows supportive supervisors may help protect employees’ psychological well-being, but meaningful support requires workplaces that can adapt to changing needs.

title: As AI reshapes jobs and workers change industries, employers need to be more flexible too
authors: Marzena Baker, Senior Lecturer and Head of Discipline - HRM & Management & OHSE, Australian Catholic University
content:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the tasks people do at work and the skills they need. As work changes, being able to move between jobs, and sometimes industries, may become increasingly important.

For women, the pressure to adapt may be particularly significant. Jobs and Skills Australia [has found](https://www.jobsandskills.gov.au/publications/our-gen-ai-transition-final-release?) women have greater exposure than men to automation and AI changes, largely because of the industries and occupations in which they work.

And while it doesn’t mean that jobs will just disappear, it does mean AI is likely to change how the jobs are conducted. Many workers will need to learn new skills and adapt; others may need to move into different jobs or industries altogether.

Much of this discussion about transition currently focuses on workers – they need to reskill, retrain and become more adaptable.

But there’s another side to this story. Employers across industries may also need to become more flexible in how they decide what experience really matters.

## Changing industries doesn’t mean starting again

Our research with women who successfully moved into construction from other unrelated industries suggests employers will also need to adapt, particularly in how they recognise experience gained in other sectors and industries. Changing industries does not mean starting from zero.

We [studied 655 women working](https://ascelibrary.org/doi/10.1061/JCEMD4.COENG-15382) in Australian construction companies. Some had started their careers in construction, while others had moved there from health care, education, transport, finance, hospitality or manufacturing.

Those career changers brought many skills developed over the years, including management, communication, collaboration, coordination and experience. One woman who previously worked as a commercial pilot and later in engineering consulting told us:

> I do have a lot of experience, and I do have lot of relevant skills that I think I bring to the table too.

But having these skills from diverse professional backgrounds and getting the employer to recognise them are two different things.

Australian construction industry is already struggling to find enough workers. Around [20,000 construction jobs](https://masterbuilders.com.au/abs-labour-data-a-reminder-that-construction-workforce-shortfall-continues/) remain unfilled, while women make up just [13% of the industry’s 1.37 million workers](https://www.jobsandskills.gov.au/data/occupation-and-industry-profiles/industries/construction).

Attracting more women could help. BuildSkills Australia estimates that increasing women’s participation in residential construction could [add 51,000 workers by 2029](https://cdn.sanity.io/files/7v56p0it/production/f61240319e437c5ee9f723dd653a4fd46eff9730.pdf), reducing its projected workforce gap by 44%.

## Getting through the door

In fact, most of the career changers in the study entered construction through informal channels, often using personal networks rather than conventional recruitment.

One woman explained how important these connections had been for her:

> If I \[…\] didn’t have access to this network, I’m not sure how I’d even go about starting. I’d find it intimidating, and would presume my qualifications wouldn’t marry with the expectations.

Networks might help with people getting a foot in the door, but they also reveal a bigger problem. What if people moving between industries don’t have the industry contacts, and they don’t know where opportunities are? They may assume that their skills and experience are not what the employers want.

Our research showed this may also happen via formal recruitment. Hiring managers recognised that the problem was not simply with the candidates, but with how the industry viewed career changers. One told us:

> I don’t believe the obstacle is with the candidate; I think it’s us not being creative enough to create roles or positions that would suit the skill set of those candidates or provide them with a platform where they can transition into the industry.

This creates a paradox – we are asking workers to become more mobile and more adaptive, while employers may still struggle to recognise experience gained in another industry.

## Who really needs industry experience?

This does not mean employers should ignore industry experience, of course. It takes time to learn those critical skills.

The hiring managers we interviewed said specialist roles require specialist training in construction or engineering. But they also saw much more scope for people to move across industries into roles such as administration, finance, safety and environmental work. In these jobs, skills developed elsewhere could be very useful, while industry experience could sometimes be learned.

That suggests a different way of thinking about career changers.

Instead of asking only whether this candidate has worked in our industry before, employers could ask:

- what existing skills could the person bring to the role?
- what can they learn?
- and what genuinely requires specialist training or experience?

Adaptation may need to work both ways. Employers will have to get better at recognising transferable skills.

## Focus on the skills

This matters beyond construction. As AI changes the jobs and the skills needed, workers will increasingly be told they need to adapt.

But career mobility and adaptation depend on more than workers being willing to change. If we expect workers to become more adaptable as AI changes the work we do, employers may need to become more adaptable too.

They can do that by getting better at recognising what skills people already bring, what they can learn, and what really requires previous industry experience.

***Read more: [These 3 charts show female-dominated jobs are actually the most exposed to AI](https://theconversation.com/these-3-charts-show-female-dominated-jobs-are-actually-the-most-exposed-to-ai-288103)***

*Marzena Baker does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Most career changers rely on their networks to move to a new industry, new research shows.

title: The autonomy paradox: how more freedom at work can leave you feeling powerless
authors: Andreana Drencheva, Senior Lecturer in Entrepreneurship, King's College London
content:
You may know the feeling. You’re supposed to have finished work for the day, but later, during your evening meal, you start mentally preparing for tomorrow’s meeting. Or just having a quick check of your emails while you half watch TV.

You might not mean to, or even want to. It’s just something that you end up doing as part of the price of enjoying some autonomy at [work](https://theconversation.com/topics/work-401).

For a while now, research has claimed that professional autonomy was [a good thing](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0149206316632058?casa_token=rRd0dOwKZaYAAAAA%3AWMZk3OgEW6jtymNQyWKHNMPWMuZhThlcLjMbX8xmjwX3jY6DHuovtF93dEOtlmbfpZOsVoCsXzI). Being able to decide how, where and when you worked was considered a major plus in terms of [motivation, job satisfaction](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17845089/) and [overall health](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/001872678603901104).

And although those benefits still exist, we now know that more autonomy can often also mean more work and less downtime.

Research shows that workers with a high degree of autonomy [struggle to leave work behind](https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/joop.70087) at the end of the day. When you have control over your job, it can stay on your mind as you run through decisions and ponder unresolved problems. Switching off becomes difficult.

But the capacity to stop thinking about work during personal time, what’s known as “psychological detachment”, is a form of [emotional and cognitive recovery](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001879109000803?casa_token=rtV-biSQNfgAAAAA:diPxJB07YxgeQwK7cxjw2ZqF21ENnfo_3sk8r5aFdM6dQxtHir-QatOcS60XPvnC6a0pjDL1). Without it, resources are never fully replenished. The person who cannot switch off does not just feel tired – they go back to work the next day already running on empty.

Autonomy can make this detachment harder precisely because of the sense of [ownership it brings](https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.13169/workorgalaboglob.10.2.0027?seq=1). Responsibility does not respect working hours, and the person who controls their own job carries it home in a way that the person purely following instructions does not.

Research my colleague and I [conducted with 40 entrepreneurs](https://bpspsychub.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/joop.70107) – people whose working lives are especially autonomous – reveals another problem arrives when your [work and identity](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001879125000971?via%3Dihub) are entwined. When work becomes bound up in who you are, detachment becomes virtually impossible.

One woman in her 20s told us that she would regularly lie awake at night, unable to stop thinking about her work. She explained: “I feel the pressure. I am still struggling with \[what it means\] to be an entrepreneur.”

“Sometimes, I feel I am not giving enough to the company. Like \[at\] 11pm, should I just work an extra hour and a half?”

She understood that this was unsustainable, but she could not stop. For her, the work and the self had become the same thing – the result of a working life in which she alone was responsible for every outcome. No changes to her evening routine could help her separate the two.

Another told us that she felt guilty if she separated her business from the rest of her life.

## Working from everywhere

Separate research confirms that workers who have a high degree of autonomy over their schedules and tasks end up [working more, not less](https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.13169/workorgalaboglob.10.2.0027?seq=1). When people have autonomy, they repay the trust with [extra effort](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/00221856251315859).

This is especially the case in situations where autonomy removes visibility, such as when people work from home.

Being seen less in the workplace can mean having more to prove. In these situations, some workers end up showing their commitment by replying quickly, being online late or taking on extra projects.

The shift to working from home and the technology which allows it, has brought a big change in what it means to stop working for the day. When work requires being in a specific place, the end of the day has a physical logic to it. You leave that place and the day’s work is done.

***Read more: [How AI could make us work even harder](https://theconversation.com/how-ai-could-make-us-work-even-harder-286688)***

But for many that shift has gone and been replaced with [constant availability](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/abs/10.1287/orsc.1120.0806). Being reachable shows commitment. Not being reachable requires explanation and justification.

And that problem cannot really be solved with legislation. Things like the [“right-to-disconnect”](https://theconversation.com/what-a-right-to-disconnect-from-work-could-look-like-in-the-uk-235061) or flexible working policies tend to address intrusions from outside – the manager who emails at 9pm, or the meeting which clashes with the school run.

Laws can do nothing about the work pressures inside employees’ own minds. Because in many cases, organisations have not simply given workers more freedom, they have also given the job of managing that work onto the worker themselves.

While autonomy is still worth having, it often comes at a personal cost. It can mean less power and more work – which is unacknowledged and unpaid.

*Andreana Drencheva received funding from Arts and Humanities Research Council and the Leverhulme Trust to support some of the research cited in this article.*
description: Feeling in control is not always good for us.

title: Qualified but overlooked: How bias keeps Indigenous job seekers from getting hired
authors: Andrew Stevens, Associate Professor, Faculty of Business Administration, University of Regina; Catherine E. Connelly, Distinguished Business Research Professor of Organizational Behaviour, McMaster University
content:
Indigenous workers in Canada [experience higher unemployment rates and lower rates of labour market participation](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=1410036501) than non-Indigenous workers. [Policy discussions about closing this gap](https://www.sac-isc.gc.ca/eng/1690909773300/1690909797208) have often highlighted education, training and skills development as important pathways to employment.

But what happens when people acquire the necessary qualifications, submit applications and still don’t receive a response?

[Our new research on hiring practices in the food services industry](https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/saskatchewan/hiring-bias-exists-in-the-food-service-industry-a-study-finds-1.7284109) suggests that improving access to skills and education alone doesn’t fully address employment disparities. Instead, we must also consider what happens after people acquire these qualifications: how employers evaluate, select and ultimately reject or advance job applicants.

Our findings reveal that Indigenous job seekers can face barriers at the very point of entry into the workforce, where decisions are shaped not only by qualifications and experience but also by perceptions of identity and workplace fit.

## Discrimination in the hiring process

Public debates about Canada’s labour market often focus on labour supply: [migrant worker programs](https://www.canada.ca/en/employment-social-development/services/foreign-workers/temporary-measures.html), immigration and [the challenges](https://cdhowe.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Commentary_718-2.pdf) facing [young workers](https://www.statcan.gc.ca/o1/en/plus/8640-youth-faced-challenging-labour-market-summer-and-september). Less attention is paid to the experiences of Indigenous people seeking employment.

To examine these experiences, [we conducted a large-scale resumé audit study of employer hiring preferences in the food services sector](https://doi.org/10.1108/EDI-12-2025-0854). We submitted more than 6,000 fictitious but realistic resumés to actual job postings for servers, hosts and bartenders in Ontario and Saskatchewan.

Each resumé contained equivalent levels of education, work experience, certifications and availability. The resumés differed only in signals of identity, including names, gender, citizenship status and indicators of ethnicity or Indigenous identity.

To signal an Indigenous background, some resumés included volunteer experience with Indigenous community organizations, fluency in an Indigenous language or credentials from an Indigenous college or university. These were compared against resumés representing other common groups in the food service workforce: white Canadian-born, Canadian-born Filipino and Filipino permanent resident applicants.

Restaurant industry groups have [consistently pointed to a labour shortage](https://www.restaurantscanada.org/ceo-note/workforce-challenges-are-growing-and-heres-how-were-responding/) as the reason so many positions go unfilled. But in our study, employers responded to only 11.4 per cent of applications.

The low callback rate suggests that employers’ difficulties filling positions cannot be explained solely by a shortage of available workers; hiring practices also influence who receives opportunities.

More importantly, the findings revealed unequal treatment. Indigenous applicants received callbacks at a lower rate than non-Indigenous applicants: 9.9 per cent compared with 11.9 per cent.

## Regional differences and bias

The patterns varied significantly by region. In Ontario, callback rates for Indigenous and non-Indigenous applicants were nearly identical. In Saskatchewan, however, the gap was much larger: non-Indigenous applicants received callbacks 13.2 per cent of the time, compared with 8.1 per cent for Indigenous applicants.

To better understand these differences, we conducted interviews with hiring managers and workers in both provinces. These interviews suggested that hiring decisions involved more than formal qualifications and experience.

Instead, it was governed by an unwritten standard of “fit” — one shaped by racialized and gendered expectations about who represents an ideal hospitality worker.

Our quantitative findings showed that Indigenous women received more callbacks than Indigenous men (11.6 per cent compared with 8.3 per cent), reflecting broader patterns in hospitality hiring in which [women are perceived as being especially suited to customer-facing roles](https://doi.org/10.1017/elr.2024.31).

However, this apparent advantage does not necessarily represent greater equality. Our interviews showed that women workers were expected to be “Instagram ready” and were often sexualized. Women in the food service industry also [earn less than their male counterparts](https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/wonk/wp/2014/08/28/chart-the-troubling-gender-pay-gap-in-the-american-restaurant-industry/), and are less likely to land managerial roles.

For Indigenous applicants, these expectations collide with longstanding racial stereotypes. Hiring managers and workers described biases associating Indigenous people with social issues such as poverty and addiction. These assumptions, [shaped by broader patterns of anti-Indigenous racism](https://doi.org/10.15402/esj.v10i1.70848), can influence how employers interpret applicants before they have any opportunity to demonstrate their skills.

## Addressing structural barriers

Conventional economic theories, [namely labour market segmentation theory](https://www.oxfordreference.com/display/10.1093/oi/authority.20110803100046432), suggest that marginalized groups are funnelled into lower-paid precarious jobs because they lack paths to corporate careers.

But our research shows that Indigenous workers can face exclusion even from entry-level positions. Because early jobs provide opportunities to gain experience, build professional networks and establish pathways for future employment, barriers at this stage [can have long-term consequences](https://doi.org/10.1093/jleo/ewag008).

When policymakers examine Indigenous employment disparities, they must recognize that the Canadian labour market doesn’t provide equal opportunities for all workers. Education and experience matter, but they do not operate independently from the social and institutional factors that shape hiring decisions.

If Canada is committed to advancing the [Truth and Reconciliation Commission’s Call to Action No. 92 on economic reconciliation](https://www.rcaanc-cirnac.gc.ca/eng/1100100015576/1571581687074), employment gaps cannot continue to be framed primarily as failures of education, training or individual effort.

Addressing these disparities requires confronting [the structural barriers and racialized assumptions](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40719-022-00225-5) that continue to influence marginalized people’s access to work.

*Andrew Stevens receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.*

*Catherine E. Connelly receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.*
description: New research shows that Indigenous applicants can face discrimination at the hiring stage, even when they have the same qualifications and experience as other candidates.

title: How to prepare your online life for your death
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Jenny Tang, Ph.D. Student in Societal Computing, Carnegie Mellon University; Xiaoyuan (Owen) Wu, Ph.D. Student in Societal Computing, Carnegie Mellon University
content:
What happens to all of your online accounts – credit cards, merchants, news subscriptions, social media, streaming services – after you die? How will your heirs know how to access these accounts or understand what you want done with them? Most people haven’t considered these questions, and this lack of planning can create significant headaches for next of kin.

We [studied challenges older adults encounter](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791633) when thinking about what should happen to their online accounts after they die. We interviewed 21 American adults over age 60 to learn about their concerns, needs and practices for their online accounts, as well as what would make planning for these accounts easier.

Most of the people we interviewed had hired lawyers or estate planners to draft wills specifying how their money and physical property should be handled after their deaths. They wanted to make sure that heirs had easy access to the money and assets left behind.

People also wanted their relatives to have easy access to their digital estates, but they had not done any formal planning and didn’t know how to plan for transitioning or shutting down online accounts, such as email, social media and accounts for online bills. Some told us they hadn’t thought about their online accounts at all. Others said they assumed heirs would know what to do, or they assumed that giving heirs the passwords to accounts would be enough to grant access to their digital estates.

Unfortunately, more planning is typically necessary to smoothly transition a digital estate.

## Passing down a list of passwords

The older adults we interviewed mainly kept track of their passwords by hand: They wrote their passwords down on paper, or they stored them in a digital file. Almost everyone had already shared some of their passwords with family members who help them manage their accounts. Everyone also believed that their heirs would be able to find their list of passwords after their death.

The people we interviewed weren’t always happy with their current systems for keeping track of their passwords. Some people complained that when accounts required frequent password changes, it was [difficult to keep their password lists up to date](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/soups2019-pearman.pdf). As a result, they weren’t sure their heirs would get the latest version of all their passwords.

[Password managers](https://www.pcmag.com/picks/the-best-password-managers) can be a good way to make sure passwords are up to date and, if set up appropriately, accessible to a designated heir. While most of the people we interviewed used password managers, some said they didn’t save important passwords in them because [they didn’t know whether they were secure](https://www.usenix.org/system/files/sec21summer_ray.pdf). However, using a password manager is the [most frequent security recommendation from experts](https://www.usenix.org/conference/soups2025/presentation/ortloff), who typically use them to store passwords for all of their accounts.

By using a password manager, you can make sure your designated heir has access to all your latest passwords. Some password managers provide access for survivors by default, such as through [time-delayed](https://support.nordpass.com/hc/en-us/articles/5691777958929-How-to-give-Emergency-Access-in-NordPass) [emergency access features](https://bitwarden.com/help/emergency-access/). You can also write the master password down somewhere safe to pass to your heir. Instead of making sure dozens of account passwords are up to date, you only have to manage one.

## Passwords alone cannot unlock all accounts

Unfortunately, just handing someone your passwords doesn’t always mean they can log in and manage your account. If the account asks for two-factor authentication, such as through a code sent to a phone or email, a password alone won’t grant access. And if the email account is closed or the phone number is no longer active after you die, then [they might be out of luck](https://www.cnn.com/2024/02/26/tech/digital-legacy-planning-personal-technology/index.html).

To make sure your heirs aren’t locked out, identify the devices and accounts that can act as keys for heirs to unlock the rest of your online accounts, and direct your heirs to keep them open until other accounts have been settled. This not only makes sure that heirs can get authentication codes, but also lets heirs reset passwords to your other accounts if they can’t find the password.

In some cases, passwords might not be necessary. Some online services, such as [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/help/103897939701143/) and [Google](https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/3036546?ai1hc=1), have features that let you choose someone to manage your account or get your data after you die. However, not all platforms offer this option, and few of the older adults we interviewed were aware of these features.

## Online accounts don’t automatically die with you

Like many of the people we interviewed, you might also assume that heirs will properly deal with accounts with money and important data, while unimportant accounts can be ignored. But even if there is nothing important in an account, it can still be [used by hackers for identity theft, spam or fraudulent activities](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/technology/safety-security/updating-our-inactive-account-policies/). Automatic monthly charges, to cover the cost of streaming services or annual billing for magazine subscriptions, for example, might also continue for a long time.

Without instructions, the people managing your online accounts after you die might not think to close those accounts. They might also find it hard to guess your intentions.

You can leave instructions for your heirs by going through your accounts and noting which ones can be closed outright, which ones require final payments before closure, and which ones might require other actions. You can also periodically tidy up and close accounts you are no longer using to keep your list of accounts more manageable.

## Planning ahead for you and your heirs

While it seems simple to just let your heirs handle your important online accounts and let the others slowly fade into nonexistence after you die, the reality is often more complex.

Your online accounts will live on after you die. Planning ahead for what happens to those accounts can reduce the stress on your heirs and ensure your digital accounts are handled according to your wishes.

*[Lujo Bauer](https://www.cylab.cmu.edu/directory/bios/bauer-lujo.html), [Nicolas Christin](https://engineering.cmu.edu/directory/bios/christin-nicolas.html) and [Lorrie Cranor](https://s3d.cmu.edu/people/core-faculty/cranor-lorrie.html) contributed to this article.*

description: Handing your heirs a list of passwords is only the first step in ensuring they can access and manage your digital affairs after you die.

title: Why it could be a bad idea to get AI to flirt for you
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Ten-Herng Lai, Lecturer in Philosophy, University of Stirling; Alfred Archer, Assistant Professor, School of Humanities and Digital Sciences, Tilburg University
content:
You finally started an online conversation with a stranger you find attractive, yet you don’t really know what to say. They seem happy to talk, but you struggle to find the correct responses. You worry that their patience is growing thin. You pray for some guidance. Luckily, the solution could be just a few clicks away.

After all, you have the power of [AI](https://theconversation.com/topics/artificial-intelligence-ai-90) at your fingertips. Why not use it to come up with something fun and interesting to say?

Yet many of us might hesitate in this scenario. Researchers have already warned of [“cognitive debt”](https://www.media.mit.edu/publications/your-brain-on-chatgpt/) – students can use AI to write excellent assignments, but then [fail miserably](https://cepr.org/publications/dp21577) in final exams because they remember nothing. No one would want to show up to a date unable to recall anything they had copied and pasted into an online conversation.

Flirting online, like many other emotionally loaded tasks such as writing an apology, a eulogy or a message of congratulations, reflects how you feel about the person. The philosopher [Talbot Brewer](https://academic.oup.com/book/34596/chapter/294250266) wrote that a person’s efforts to make sense of their emotions through articulating them can reveal what they value.

For example, suppose someone thought she didn’t especially care about her work. But then she found herself feeling pride when she was promoted. Her emotion may reveal to her that she does in fact care about workplace success.

## How your emotions reveal yourself to you

In our [recent research](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13347-026-01203-4), we contend that using AI to flirt – or for any other task where personal connection is valuable – risks bypassing those moments where emotions can reveal important self-knowledge.

Perhaps in flirting online, a person may not read what their date says carefully. Instead, they might quickly copy the text into ChatGPT and then equally quickly paste the response back into the chat.

Alternatively, perhaps an AI wingman is already integrated into the dating app, allowing people to simply click and send the suggested text. They don’t pay attention to what the date says, maybe overlooking potential deal-breakers, things that might be odd, or small stylistic details that would otherwise give them some pause.

By outsourcing this emotional task to ChatGPT, it’s possible for a person to deprive themselves of the opportunity to really let the moments affect them. They could miss the chance to properly consider whether they would be happy to make compromises for their date. They may not even know whether they are genuinely excited about the date.

Instead of slowly articulating their feelings and, in so doing, working out what they value in a relationship, they are authorising AI to say whatever might impress their date.

There’s also the issue of [privacy](https://www.ethicaldatingonline.com/open-letter) – the flirty exchanges could find their way into training data. And is the AI wingman even trustworthy? It could misrepresent the person using it – and the other party might feel they’d suffered a deception. Even before AI, researchers have questioned whether lying on dating platforms [invalidates consent](https://doi.org/10.1086/670249).

At the end of the day, it just feels a bit disrespectful. The output of AI has little to do with how someone feels about their date, but [draws more from the training data](https://doi.org/10.1093/pq/pqag043). This data has nothing to do with the person or their date.

But maybe some people are less careless. Plenty of daters would make sure to scrutinise the AI output before sending it.

Yet humans have a tendency to overly trust AI. [Another study](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s13347-025-00932-2) found that when people regularly let AI produce their first draft, they tend to accept the output uncritically. The study also found that people can easily adopt the biases of large language models (LLMs), even if they know those biases exist.

From our own study, one worry that emerged was that instead of being true to their own feelings, over-reliance on AI may give the LLMs too much say in shaping what a person values.

We are not suggesting that people should never outsource emotional tasks to AI. Sometimes, there’s no other option but to interact with emotionally manipulative or difficult people – perhaps a relative or an ex-partner. If you are already certain about your feelings towards this person, it may be better to refuse to let them [get to you](https://www.theatlantic.com/family/2026/10/ai-family-text/688962/). AI may provide some breathing space.

But if as humans we want to get to know other people, have or repair meaningful relations, or make sure that what we communicate truly reflects how we feel, we should consider resisting the temptation to outsource our emotions to AI. After all, our emotions have the power to reveal to us what we deeply value.
