description: Choosing your own words can reveal how you really feel about a person or situation.

title: Are narcissists multiplying or is the social media algorithm making them bolder? The answer in five stages
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Calli Tzani, Reader in Psychology, Cyberpsychology Research Network Co-Director and ADM Forensic Editor, University of Huddersfield; Maria Ioannou, Professor of Psychology, Cyberpsychology Research Network Co-Director, MSc Investigative Psychology Director, University of Huddersfield
content:
Social media doesn’t necessarily reflect who you are, but it may intensify particular personality traits and confirm or even persuade you that your worst behaviour is justified.

We are addressing that imbalance, with our framework, the Algorithmic Trait Amplification, or ATA, with particular regard to narcissism.

Narcissism [runs on a spectrum](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8431185/). At the far end is narcissistic personality disorder, a clinical diagnosis. But many people have milder narcissistic traits – a strong need for admiration, a habit of overrating their own importance, struggling to take criticism, little empathy. That said, some traits such as healthy ambition and assertiveness are beneficial.

People who [have these traits](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8508105/), which are common, are [especially drawn to social media](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0272868) and platforms built around status and approval from others.

For years we have been studying online behaviour and the [affect of social media upon relationships](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0747563225000962); including how [psychopathy shows up in romantic relationships](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01639625.2025.2588612) and how [TikTok shapes young women’s attraction to dangerous partners](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01639625.2025.2520587). That work, combined with what psychology already knows on [how narcissistic people operate online](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0272868), how [algorithms chase engagement](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11894805/), and [what personality change requires](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20617789/) led us to a realisation. The algorithmic loop process may slowly strengthen an inflated, entitled self-image.

These are the five steps over which ATA predicts that social media will heighten narcissistic traits.

## Stage 1: The engagement hook

Someone with narcissistic traits tends to react strongly to content that matches their self-image. Winning. Status. Being special. Always being right. Most of us have some version of a For You content feed. But for people high in these traits, the pull is more powerful. Such content fulfils a narcissist’s higher need for validation.

## Stage 2: Taking it all in

Social media recommendation systems are designed to keep us engaged but they cannot tell whether the content is good for us. They only measure whether it holds our attention. Our [reactions become instructions](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25061): give this person more of this, feed the loop.

For example, a user rewatches a video about how “strong personalities intimidate weak people”. The app notices and fills the feed with content about cutting off “toxic” friends and refusing to apologise. Every video tells them the problem is everyone else. And they agree. So, they watch more.

[Audit studies](https://arxiv.org/html/2603.25061) of online recommendation systems show that feeds narrow in proportion to how selectively a user engages. Someone low in narcissistic traits engages more evenly in different types of content. Someone high in these traits engages hard and narrow and the algorithm obliges.

## Stage 3: The mirror oracle

We call this the echo algorithm, after the [Greek myth of Narcissus](https://classictales.co.uk/metamorphoses/echo-and-narcissus). The nymph Echo can only repeat what is said to her. She cannot challenge or answer back.

Social media algorithms are the same. Over time, the user unknowingly builds a mirror: more praise, more validation, more self-image inflation. And the worst part for narcissistic users is that the feed feels like the world agrees with them. Objective. External. Almost all-knowing. But it is an oracle that they trained themselves, to say exactly what they wanted to hear.

## Stage 4: Challenge disappears

Psychologists explain that personality change, in all of us, depends on [corrective emotional experiences](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20617789/). These are moments that contradict your self-image in a way you cannot ignore. Or as we call them, uncomfortable moments of truth. They are also [how people with narcissistic traits](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36970988/) change. These moments help us grow. Take them away, and the traits they would have challenged only get stronger.

Content that challenges the narcissist gets less engagement than content that flatters them. Therefore, challenging content and moments of truths slowly vanishes from the feed – an unplanned algorithmic side-effect of platforms’ aim to chase users’ attention.

## Stage 5: The loop feeds itself

Fed a diet of constant validation, narcissistic traits may intensify. Stronger traits produce stronger reactions, thus producing an ever more perfect mirror within the loop.

## Is narcissism rising?

Psychologists [don’t agree](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18507710/) on whether overall levels of narcissism are on the rise. Some psychologists say it is, while others [have found no change](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18271867/). So the argument is not settled. But psychology researchers [do agree that](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2352853219302391) narcissistic traits correlate with heavier, more problematic social media use and that the expression of narcissistic behaviour is more visible online. Rising or not, our model predicts that for people who already have these traits, the algorithm may be turning up the volume.

Working with narcissistic clients is already considered [one of the hardest jobs](http://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32186980/) in psychology. These clients often experience honest feedback as an attack. On one hand, progress depends on carefully managed moments of challenge, built up over sessions. And many clients never get that far: around two-thirds of [people diagnosed with narcissistic personality disorder](https://www.ovid.com/jnls/jonmd/fulltext/10.1097/nmd.0000000000001777%7Ecan-patients-with-narcissistic-personality-disorder-change-a) drop out of therapy early. Change is possible, but only for those who stay.

On the other, their phone, trained on years of their own reactions, may offer a world that reflects them at their best, agrees with their grievances and doesn’t challenge. Their therapist may only have an hour a week with them, while the algorithm gets anytime the person picks up their phone.

Our framework may explain why so many people [believe narcissism is](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0188287) on the rise: the behaviour is more visible, because the loop rewards it. The algorithm has been running its own experiment on all of us and we wonder, what else has it been intensifying?

*The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Someone with narcissistic traits will react strongly to content that matches their self-image.

title: Before bans for under-16s, we need to ask: what counts as social media?
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Charlotte Pennington, Lecturer in Psychology, Aston University; Daniel Shaw, Lecturer in Psychology, Aston University; Evelyn Murray, PhD Candidate in Cyberpsychology, Aston University
content:
Amid growing concerns about teenagers’ mental health and wellbeing, governments around the world are considering or enacting new restrictions on young people’s access to social media.

Australia has already legislated a [ban on social media](https://theconversation.com/topics/social-media-ban-159730) for under-16s, and the UK government has announced plans to introduce similar restrictions from spring 2027.

Yet a fundamental question remains largely unanswered: what exactly are governments trying to regulate through these bans?

Policymakers are already drawing boundaries around which platforms count as social media and which do not. The proposed UK approach is expected to follow the [Australian model](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwyp9d3ddqyo), covering platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, Facebook, YouTube and X. Messaging services such as WhatsApp and Signal are [expected to be exempt](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/fact-sheet-new-rules-to-protect-children-online/fact-sheet-new-rules-to-protect-children-online) from the proposed ban.

Our new research suggests that these boundaries may not always align with how the public understands social media.

[Our study](https://psycnet.apa.org/fulltext/2027-92943-001.html) surveyed 968 UK adults, including 484 18- to 25-year-olds, about their perceptions of social media. We asked participants which online platforms they considered to be social media, what characteristics they associated with it, and whether they agreed with common definitions used by researchers and organisations. We also collected their views of how social media affects people’s lives.

## Differing opinions

As digital technologies continue to evolve, distinctions between online platforms are becoming increasingly blurred. Many now combine messaging, content sharing, entertainment and community participation in the same app. Our findings suggest that the boundaries policymakers are drawing around “social media” may not always align with how ordinary users understand and experience these platforms. Social media encompasses a range of different online activities and experiences.

One of our clearest findings was that people do not consistently agree on what counts as social media. Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, X and Snapchat were almost universally recognised as social media platforms. But agreement became less clear for others, despite many possessing characteristics commonly used in scholarly definitions of social media.

For instance, Roblox enables users to create and share content and interact with each other in shared virtual spaces through messaging functions. But nearly 80% of the people we surveyed didn’t see it as social media. Opinion was also split on whether blogs and forums counted as social media.

On the other hand, approximately 65% of the people we surveyed considered WhatsApp to be social media, despite this platform being excluded from the UK’s proposed restrictions. More people also considered Reddit, Tumblr, and Pinterest to be social media than YouTube, despite YouTube being included within the proposed ban and the others currently falling outside it.

Defining social media was only part of the story. We also found that public perceptions of its impacts were far more nuanced than the often-polarised debate suggests.

Importantly, people rarely described social media as wholly good or bad. Instead, they emphasised context. The perceived impact depended on which platform was being used, how it was being used, and what people were doing while using it.

Young people showed a sophisticated understanding of these trade-offs. They spoke about concerns relating to anxiety, body image, cyberbullying and excessive use. They also highlighted the important role social media can play in maintaining friendships, finding communities and accessing support. Many described actively managing their use to protect their wellbeing and productivity.

Our findings suggest that young people themselves are often aware of both the risks and benefits and do not necessarily view social media as a uniformly negative force.

## What does this mean for bans?

Our findings suggest that regulating social media is more complicated than it first appears. If politicians, researchers and the public do not share a common understanding of what the term “social media” includes, regulations may be difficult to communicate, implement and evaluate. Decisions about which platforms fall inside or outside a ban are not solely technical; they shape who is affected by the policy and why.

More broadly, our findings raise questions about where responsibility for online harms should lie. Debates about social media bans often focus on restricting children and young people’s access to technology. However, many of the harms that our respondents identified, including exposure to harmful content, misinformation, cyberbullying and potentially addictive platform features, can be harmful to any user. Crucially, these potential impacts are shaped by decisions made by technology companies themselves.

Attention should be shifted from the behaviour of young people to the design and governance of the platforms they use. Stronger regulation of harmful content, algorithms, age-appropriate design features, accessible reporting, transparency and platform accountability are all parts of the solution.

If future regulation is to be effective, it must be grounded not only in evidence about risks, but also in a clear understanding of the technologies it seeks to govern.

*The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: People do not consistently agree on what counts as social media

title: AI may quickly generate ideas, but working with people leads to more creative ones
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Clin Lai, Postdoctoral Fellow in Artificial Intelligence and Society, Brandeis University; Roger Beaty, Associate Professor of Psychology, Penn State
content:
[The productivity gains](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adh2586) of generative AI are often touted as the main reason for its rapid adoption. Much like how a calculator can instantly solve mathematical equations too long for the human brain to compute, generative AI can help someone quickly summarize long articles and draft emails.

But beyond productivity, a key question remains: How is AI affecting quintessentially human activities, such as collaboration and creativity?

[As cognitive scientists](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Gbc3CbQAAAAJ&hl=en) [who study creativity](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=xP-eQ4wAAAAJ&hl=en), we recently [conducted an experiment](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2026.109172) that explored how working with AI – rather than humans – affects originality and other aspects of creativity.

## Speedy and wordy doesn’t mean creative

Creativity is often tied to what cognitive scientists call “[divergent thinking](https://theconversation.com/new-study-reveals-why-some-people-are-more-creative-than-others-90065).” One way of measuring divergent thinking is to ask someone to come up with a range of uses for a common item, such as a brick or a book. This is known as [the alternate uses task](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guilford%27s_Alternate_Uses).

Researchers then compare the number of ideas and the originality of these ideas to assess creative capacity.

Large language models appear to have the “number of ideas” part down pat: They can generate [many more ideas than humans can](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-53303-w). This ability to produce more – and produce that high volume more quickly – partially explains why [more than half of new articles online are now generated by AI](https://theconversation.com/more-than-half-of-new-articles-on-the-internet-are-being-written-by-ai-is-human-writing-headed-for-extinction-268354).

These texts, however, are often verbose, with redundant information. Researchers who tested 12 AI chatbots across different companies on thousands of factual questions [found that their answers were often many times longer](https://aclanthology.org/2025.findings-acl.1125/) than human-written answers, with the actual answer making up only about 42% of the text. The rest was largely extra padding: repetitive information, unnecessary background details and explanations that went into too much detail or veered off topic.

Large language models also seem to struggle with the originality of their outputs.

## An ‘original’ idea – again and again

[In our research](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chb.2026.109172), we compared the results of people working on the alternate uses task with another person to those who collaborated with ChatGPT on the same task. We randomly assigned 208 participants to work with either AI or another person.

We found that compared with two people taking turns together, people working with ChatGPT wrote longer responses on the alternate uses task. But human pairs came up with more creative ideas than the humans working with ChatGPT.

We also found that the ideas people came up with when working with other people tended to be more distinct and diverse than those who worked with large language models. Individual AI suggestions could be quite creative – using a book as a sound dampener, for example – but ChatGPT presented that same idea across many separate sessions, making its overall pool of ideas more homogeneous.

Other studies have highlighted the homogeneity of generative AI’s outputs. One group of researchers found that using AI repeatedly over time to generate images often results in bland, generic pictures – what they call “[visual elevator music](https://theconversation.com/ai-induced-cultural-stagnation-is-no-longer-speculation-its-already-happening-272488).” Other studies have found that although AI may help an individual write a more creative story when compared with their preexisting work, AI-assisted writing as a whole, across all users, [tends to be more similar](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adn5290).

All of this makes sense when you think about [how large language models work](https://theconversation.com/large-language-models-how-the-ai-behind-the-likes-of-chatgpt-actually-works-244701). After being trained on massive sets of texts, large language models predict the next most likely words. Because their training processes were similar, different large language models, whether it’s ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, tend to [have similar cadences, diction, syntax and suggestions](https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/5/3/pgag042/8529001) – particularly when compared with the work of two random human writers.

In other words, generative AI’s ideas may seem unique in a vacuum. But if everyone’s using AI, the ideas and writing style start to converge.

## Creative collaboration is a long game

Finally, we also found that the creativity benefits of working with another person became even stronger as the collaboration progressed.

Ideas can be measured through [semantic distance](https://doi.org/10.1037/aca0000125), which is a way of quantifying how distinct individual concepts are. Over time, interacting with other humans seems to result in larger semantic distance than interacting with a chatbot. In other words, people may traverse more creative terrain when collaborating with other people. Meanwhile, the tendency for ideas to converge in chatbot-assisted brainstorming could accumulate, potentially narrowing the range of ideas people explore over the course of a long period of time.

This is important because many creative projects involve long-term engagement.

For example, to launch a new product, researchers have found that it takes an [average of 27 months](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-8501(01%2900162-6) to go from the initial idea to the finished product. More innovative products can take [as long as 54 months](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0019-8501(01%2900162-6).

## Chat-human before you ChatGPT

If you want to work with a chatbot, how can you preserve your creativity in the face of AI’s tendency toward homogeneity?

Some research suggests using what’s called “[persona prompting](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2026.100289).” Like talking to other people with different perspectives, users could provide an extensive prompt to give chatbots a pretend personality that can simulate different types of people. For example, you might prompt it to respond as if it is “a male college professor from India who is an expert in teaching” or “a 58-year-old female founder of a construction company.” Researchers found that while this persona prompting increased ChatGPT’s idea diversity, [the overall range of ideas still fell short of that produced by human writers](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chbah.2025.100207). These findings echo other recent research suggesting that chatbots are [poor simulators of human personality](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2501660122).

If you need help with a creative task, we suggest going back to the basics: Chat with a person before chatting with AI. They’ll have idiosyncratic personal experiences that can’t be captured by a large language model that’s trained to generate average responses.

Composing a sentence, however modest, is a creative act, whether it’s in a text to a friend or a wedding speech. As AI is integrated into workflows, it’s important to remember that other people can still be a valuable resource. Work completed in collaboration with other humans [feels more meaningful](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-026-42312-6).

They might not respond as quickly or as comprehensively. But chances are they’ll have something more interesting to say.

*Clin Lai received funding from APA Division 10 and National Science Foundation.*

*Roger Beaty receives funding from Amazon, the Army Research Institute, and the National Science Foundation.*
description: A recent experiment found that people working with ChatGPT generated fewer unique ideas than those who collaborated with other humans.

title: Are you a creature or a machine? How to live in ecological community in a time of AI
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Timothy Martin, Postdoctoral fellow, Faculty of Education, Simon Fraser University
content:
We have been bombarded in recent weeks with [apocalyptic headlines](https://www.economist.com/finance-and-economics/2026/09/22/you-cant-trade-your-way-through-the-ai-apocalypse) about “artificial super-intelligence” and the possibilities of a new era of [“artificial general intelligence” (AGI)](https://www.livescience.com/technology/artificial-intelligence/openai-claims-weve-entered-the-agi-era-has-gpt-6-astra-really-demonstrated-general-intelligence) in which AI achieves human capacities for reason and learning.

Concerns vary from its [misuse in bioterrorism](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cx2zrrpkx20o) to the capacity of AI agents to form collectives, “[go rogue](https://theconversation.com/eight-ways-to-feed-ourselves-if-rogue-ai-destroys-modern-agriculture-292086)” and [perform unauthorized attacks](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/ai-agents-are-hacking-systems-without-any-input-from-humans-how-did-we-get-here) on systems, or [even to take over the internet](https://theconversation.com/cyber-attacks-bioterrorism-to-pace-the-frontier-of-ai-effectively-we-must-improve-our-anticipatory-thinking-291027) and [terminate humanity](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wWjUJnrELd0).

***Read more: [How an OpenAI safety test became a real-world cyberattack on the Hugging Face platform](https://theconversation.com/how-an-openai-safety-test-became-a-real-world-cyberattack-on-the-hugging-face-platform-288334)***

As a scholar interested in public memory, I find myself returning to the writing of [Wendell Berry](https://www.npr.org/2026/09/01/1139228585/wendell-berry-obituary) in response as a source of wisdom for these turbulent times. Berry, [who died at home in August](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/sep/01/wendell-berry-us-author-dead), was a cultural critic, [writer](https://www.poetryfoundation.org/poets/wendell-berry), [farmer](https://theconversation.com/what-wendell-berry-meant-to-christian-farmers-going-green-291756), [environmentalist](https://www.neh.gov/about/awards/jefferson-lecture/wendell-e-berry-biography) and an early influence on my thinking. His book, [*Life is a miracle: An essay against modern superstition*](https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/life-is-a-miracle/) reads as an eerie letter to the purveyors of AI.

For Berry, the mind was shaped by its place in the world, the textures of the local, a sense of home and a notion of history. To have a mind, argued Berry, one must have a world. In a section of the book titled, “Creatures as machines,” he railed against the way in which the *metaphor* of mind as machine, has turned into an *equivalence.*

## The death of the earth

Some thinkers believe AI promises to save us from work. Elon Musk has made radical claims that [AI will make work optional within the next two decades](https://fortune.com/2026/01/19/when-does-elon-musk-say-work-will-be-optional-and-money-will-be-irrelevant-ai-robotics/). But part of taking our place in the world — and in time — is through work.

Berry himself gave up a promising life in New York’s literary scene to move back to Kentucky and work the land. Of course, he continued to produce written works as well: no less than [50 books](https://www.loa.org/writers/682-wendell-berry/).

Some analysts also claim that [AI could reduce inequality](https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/1/issues/c-suite-insights/the-leadership-agenda/ai-income-inequality.html). Berry addressed similar promises made by 20th century science in the domains of [nuclear power](https://voicesofdemocracy.umd.edu/eisenhower-atoms-for-peace-speech-text/), [genetic engineering](https://doi.org/10.7202/1089801ar) and [industrial agriculture](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/peace/1970/borlaug/lecture/).

In the face of systems that were meant bring us global food security, Berry declared that many of us are now mourning [“the progressive death of the Earth.”](https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/life-is-a-miracle/)

## Technology without consent

We are already witnessing how AI is accelerating many breakthroughs in the sciences — from [solving previously unsolvable](https://theconversation.com/a-new-golden-age-of-mathematics-may-be-dawning-thanks-to-ai-and-human-ingenuity-287346) mathematics [problems](https://theconversation.com/openai-may-have-solved-the-navier-stokes-equation-but-mathematics-is-more-than-1-million-trophy-hunts-291963) to diverse transformations in [health care](https://theconversation.com/ai-is-transforming-health-care-but-not-everyone-will-share-the-benefits-285578) and disciplines as diverse as [meteorology and synthetic biology](https://www.nature.com/articles/d42473-025-00164-0). Many commentators within science and the AI industry have drawn [parallels between AI](https://time.com/7339628/geoffrey-hinton-ai/) and [the Industrial Revolution](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2my-NU6LuCM).

***Read more: [Artificial intelligence raises profound moral questions — for all of humanity to answer](https://theconversation.com/artificial-intelligence-raises-profound-moral-questions-for-all-of-humanity-to-answer-284886)***

The better comparison may be with nuclear weapons. Geneticist [Wes Jackson](https://landinstitute.org/about-us/staff/wes-jackson/), founder of the Land Institute, once warned [“we ought to stay out of the nuclei.”](https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/life-is-a-miracle/) Jackson was concerned about [corporate patents on genetically engineered seed crops](https://theconversation.com/how-everyone-pays-the-cost-for-patents-on-seeds-and-private-companies-get-rich-from-keeping-them-secret-284144) and the destructive potential of [nuclear fission](https://www.ucs.org/resources/how-nuclear-weapons-work#).

As a plant geneticist, Jackson himself developed [innovative perennial grains](https://e360.yale.edu/features/with-new-perennial-grain-a-step-forward-for-eco-friendly-agriculture) by looking to the natural resilience of prairie plant communities. By “entering” the nuclei, Jackson held that we were crossing a threshold that should remain off limits to humans, given the risks involved.

Quoting [his friend and collaborator Jackson](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=88OaToCAt8g), Berry invoked a notion of planetary and creaturely consent: “When a few scientists decided to go in, they decided for everybody.”

Similarly, when [Musk warns of a 20 per cent chance of AI destroying humanity](https://www.businessinsider.com/elon-musk-20-percent-chance-ai-destroys-humanity-2024-3) and still plugs away at developing it, he is deciding for all of us.

## Avoidance of difficult thoughts

It’s tough to argue against the expedience brought about by computers, smart phones and artificial intelligence. And yet Berry showed us how the totalitarian regimes of the 20th century grew in alignment with the development of mechanical processes.

If freedom is our express purpose, Berry argued, then democracy actually requires instruments that impede operation. These include trial by jury, consent of the governed and the idea of minority rights — all concepts with processes that are frustratingly inefficient but more equal and free.

AI apologists are fond of dismissing doubters and critics [as Luddites](https://futurism.com/artificial-intelligence/ceo-ai-slop-podcasts-critics-luddites). But [the Luddites themselves protested precarious work and food insecurity](https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/what-the-luddites-really-fought-against-264412/) in an age of widespread economic inequality in 19th century England. Berry, in a couple of [instances](https://www.villanova.edu/dam/villanova/mission/faith/Readings/fall-2020/Health%20is%20Membership%20by%20Wendell%20Berry.pdf), [identified with](https://thetyee.ca/Culture/2026/09/11/For-Wendell-Berry-My-North-Star-American-Rural-Consciousness/) the Luddites.

The common refrain when it comes to technological development is to embrace it as inevitable. Berry described this recourse to inevitability as the [avoidance of difficult thought](https://www.counterpointpress.com/books/life-is-a-miracle/).

***Read more: [Who were the Luddites? Their legacy ripples through politics, cultural commentary and literature](https://theconversation.com/who-were-the-luddites-their-legacy-ripples-through-politics-cultural-commentary-and-literature-287473)***

## Minds like trees or computers?

For the [German philosopher Martin Heidegger](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/heidegger/), technology was less about the knobs and buttons and more a particular expression of reality, influenced by our immersion in particular tools and activities.

And there is the impasse. For some, inevitable AI is part of [“the way reality discloses itself.”](https://doi.org/10.21464/sp32110) To others, an entirely different existence is made possible by [attending to the body, land and material objects](https://www.politybooks.com/bookdetail?book_slug=non-things-upheaval-in-the-lifeworld--9781509551699). The difficulty today is the distance between these two realities.

Avoiding the digital screen, Berry wrote in “How to Be a Poet (to remind myself),” was a simple matter of staying [“away from anything that obscures the place it is in.”](https://www.goodreads.com/work/quotes/141045-given-poems) In the same poem, he wrote that that [“a tree forms itself in answer to its place and the light.”](https://www.goodreads.com/work/quotes/141045-given-poems)

It’s perhaps difficult to conceive of ourselves as creatures, tethered to other creatures and to places — the way trees are wedged into soil and [connected by underground mycorrhizal networks](https://doi.org/10.1093/aobpla/plv050). It’s maybe easier to accept we are merely computers, and that by making better computers we take the pressure off the computer that lives somewhere between our ears.

In Berry’s words: “It is easy for me to imagine that the next great division of the world will be between people who wish to live as creatures and people who wish to live as machines.”

***Read more: [What happens to your brain in nature? The neuroscience explained](https://theconversation.com/what-happens-to-your-brain-in-nature-the-neuroscience-explained-277332)***

## How to live in community

If he was still with us, Berry might remind us [to judge what we make](https://books.google.ca/books?id=p-GaEQAAQBAJ&pg=PT83&source=gbs_toc_r&cad=2#v=onepage&q&f=false) not for its independent utility, but for its wider relationship to the community. [Berry despised the word “environment,”](https://www.routledge.com/Key-Thinkers-on-the-Environment/Palmer-Cooper/p/book/9781138684737) and the notion that “we” might be separate from “it.” Instead, he demanded that we conceive of ourselves as part of a community — including [creatures, places, the dead and those not yet born](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-94-6209-293-8_9).

He would invite each of us, tech innovators included, to speak a [common language](https://books.google.ca/books?id=p-GaEQAAQBAJ&pg=PT83&source=gbs_toc_r&cad=2#v=onepage&q&f=false) and openly reveal our inventions. He disliked academic over-specialization and feared loss of accountability and understanding across disciplinary boundaries.

He would tell us to [find a place, get to know it](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.ca/books/674945/the-long-legged-house-by-wendell-berry/9781619020016) and [consult the land](https://www.routledge.com/Key-Thinkers-on-the-Environment/Palmer-Cooper/p/book/9781138684737) — an essential educational opportunity in an age of declining ecological knowledge and numb senses.

If I listen hard, I can hear Berry’s voice: Go slowly; be quiet; plant seeds; restore local watersheds; eat what grows; build community with all creatures that come.

*Timothy Martin receives funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada.*
description: As we are bombarded with apocalyptic headlines about the future of artificial intelligence, the writer, farmer and environmentalist Wendell Berry can help bring us back to our earthly community.

title: As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Murugan Anandarajan, Professor of Decision Sciences and Management Information Systems, Drexel University
content:
Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.

But does the employee know how to do the task?

I’m a [professor of management information systems](https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/Murugan-Anandarajan-2180077211) and the [academic director](https://www.lebow.drexel.edu/people/murugananandarajan) of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI & Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.

AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.

The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, [studies of automation bias](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1118723) have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not.

What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to [assume larger parts](https://doi.org/10.1080/23311975.2026.2692205) of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.

## The success paradox

The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance – rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.

This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is [redesigning its graduate audit training](https://www.icaew.com/insights/viewpoints-on-the-news/2026/mar-2026/how-deloitte-is-reshaping-its-audit-training-for-the-ai-age) as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.

More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “[ironies of automation](https://doi.org/10.1080/00140139.2023.2296176)”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the [out-of-the-loop](https://doi.org/10.1518/001872095779064555) performance problem.

This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.

What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.

## The accountability problem

Accountability [may not change as quickly](https://kpmg.com/us/en/media/blogs/2026/q1-ai-pulse-2.html) as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control.

This creates a mismatch. Research on [meaningful human control](https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-022-00167-3) suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility and capability can begin to separate.

Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.

## The measurement problem

Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as [accuracy and productivity](https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/top-5-tips-measuring-productivity-gen-AI-enterprise). Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps.

But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The [number of overrides alone](https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.15873) tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.

The key is to understand how the [division of work](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ifacol.2025.09.129) between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.

## The governance problem

Organizational governance – defining roles and responsibilities – is also under pressure from AI.

Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to [change over time](https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2024.0546). There is nothing inherently wrong with that change.

The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?

In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic.

## Maintaining the human backstop

Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.

Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.

As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.

For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?

*Murugan Anandarajan does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Having a human “in the loop” overseeing when an AI makes a decision is important, but what happens to that responsible human over time when the AI gets it right over and over again?

title: What might turning off the algorithm look like? Chinese social media provides some hints
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Fan Yang, Research Fellow at Melbourne Law School and ARC Centre of Excellence for Automated Decision-Making Society, The University of Melbourne; Luke Heemsbergen, Senior Lecturer in Communication, Faculty of Arts and Education, Deakin University; Robbie Fordyce, Senior Lecturer, Communications and Media Studies, Monash University
content:
The Albanese government has introduced its [digital duty of care legislation](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/bills/r7553_first-reps/toc_pdf/26131b01.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf) to parliament today. The bill includes an “off switch” to allow social media users to [opt out of recommender algorithms](https://theconversation.com/australians-may-soon-be-able-to-switch-off-social-media-algorithms-is-that-censorship-291359).

If passed, Australians could choose to switch off their algorithmic recommendation and consume a news feed populated by the accounts they subscribe to. It’s [been welcomed](https://www.instagram.com/p/DdAnqUiCe9g/?img_index=1) by online safety advocates.

The bill echoes a model that one of the world’s largest platforms has run for more than a decade: WeChat in China.

Its long experience offers Australia an preview of what a feed unshackled from algorithms might look like. It’s not all good news.

***Read more: [Australians may soon be able to switch off social media algorithms. Is that censorship?](https://theconversation.com/australians-may-soon-be-able-to-switch-off-social-media-algorithms-is-that-censorship-291359)***

## What is WeChat?

The Chinese platform [WeChat](https://www.wechat.com/en) was launched in 2011 and now has one billion users globally, making it one of the primary social media services for Chinese-speakers worldwide.

The platform’s design logic was simple. WeChat was meant to be [an efficiency tool](https://newsroom.wechat.com/newsRooms/NewsDetails/WhatisWeixinWeChatsdreamWeixinWeChatfounderAllenZhangexplains). Unlike its American or Chinese counterparts, which used algorithmic recommendations to keep users on the platform, WeChat is designed for users to open the app, do what they need, close the app and put their phone away.

Algorithmic curation played a minimal role until the introduction of the short-video function “[Channels](https://www.scmp.com/tech/apps-social/article/3118521/future-chinas-most-popular-app-wechat-short-videos-and-live)” launched in 2021 to compete with Douyin (the Chinese version of TikTok) and RedNote (Xiaohongshu) in the rising short-video market.

Yet, WeChat largely remains focused on efficiency.

Instead of trying to hold user attention for as long as possible, WeChat is a “[super app](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/01634437221128937)” that offers a suite of services including finance, commerce, publication, entertainment, and communications within a single platform to make it integral to people’s lives.

## It’s all about the clicks

WeChat’s news feature lists stories published by “[Official Accounts](https://www.niemanlab.org/2021/02/the-wechat-model-how-facebooks-australian-ban-could-change-the-business-of-news/)”, or content creators. Users only see content they follow.

Our research project, [RECapture](https://ijoc.org/index.php/ijoc/article/view/22818), has studied Official Accounts targeting Chinese-Australians since 2019. Our data offer a longitudinal study of monitored content.

We found the absence of algorithmic curation gives publishers significant autonomy to generate revenue independently of the app.

But within the platform itself, [creators](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/20563051231186343) still fiercely compete for user attention. This is because users search for content they’re interested in and subscribe to accounts they find most compelling, which means subscribed accounts compete with one another for user attention within that pool.

This competition has manifested as increased publication speed. Outlets, restricted by their own budgets, produce low-quality, clickbait content, often compiled from multiple fragmented and unverified sources, to attract subscribers and maximise user engagement.

Increasingly, this race is further accelerated by the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI).

The logic is simple: publish early and often; the clicks roll in throughout the day. Hit the right publication timing, the so-called “golden window”, and clicks spike further. Run a striking headline, and clicks climb yet again. This is the strategy to maximise a publisher’s chances of appearing in a user’s search query and capturing their attention.

It’s clicks, clicks, clicks (or taps) that matter, as this is the metric to attract eyes to [advertisements](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/20563051231186343), and therefore money to the platform.

If the digital duty of care legislation passes in Australia and enough people choose to opt out of algorithms, we might see a similar increase in poor quality content here.

It’s also possible the laws won’t deliver what they promise. This is because we don’t really know how digital platforms curate users’ subscribed content. We need the platforms to be more transparent about this.

## My feed, my responsibility?

Under the promise of giving Australians more control over their online environment, the government effectively offloads its responsibility of care onto individual users.

Exposure to harmful content implicitly becomes a consequence of the user’s failure to switch off their algorithm. This could let tech companies off the hook.

The legislation also reads as a compromised version of the abandoned [Combatting Misinformation and Disinformation Bill](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Committees/Senate/Environment_and_Communications/MisandDisinfobill).

Rather than tasking law enforcement bodies with addressing the issue (which risked being entangled in freedom-of-speech debates), the government instead leaves citizens to manage the problems themselves.

The government knows the product harms. So, it is making sure to protect the children through the under-16 social media ban, even while individualising choices for harmful digital products for everybody else.

## Getting to the root cause

The Australian government has started viewing digital platforms more critically, which is a welcome change from laissez faire attitudes of the past.

However, the government tends to understand digital platforms as a bunch of functions and tools rather than products of technology business entities, with which the government nonetheless continues to do deals.

This means the government operates on the assumption that switching off [the “bad” ones](https://www.techpolicy.press/australia-wants-an-off-switch-for-the-algorithm-thats-the-wrong-fix/), cutting off access, or introducing surveillance systems is a straightforward solution to the problems that we face in our digital environment.

What this view overlooks is that harm stems from the business model of tech companies. As long as that business model remains unchanged, harms will not disappear.

Being able to opt out of the algorithm will not shift the business model of content creators for the Australian market. And how the platforms themselves navigate this remains to be seen.

And, while the government’s legislation focuses on the problems of social media over the past decade or so, the emerging potential harms from the same big tech firms’ AI products loom.

It seems the government’s advocacy for a duty of care only extends to areas where the stakes are currently low, exhausted or no longer a priority for industry to make money from.

*The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: If the government’s digital duty of care bill passes, users would be able to switch off algorithms. But this might not be as good as it seems.

title: Five ways to beat dating algorithms at their own game
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Stefania Masè, Associate professor of marketing and communication, IPAG Business School; Alisa Minina Jeunemaître, Associate Professor of Marketing, EM Lyon Business School; Jamie Smith, Professor of Marketing, Escola de Administração de Empresas de São Paulo da Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV/EAESP)
content:
**KEY TAKEAWAYS**

- **Decide what you want before you start swiping. An app can suggest people to meet, but it cannot decide what kind of relationship matters to you.**
- **Set limits on your time and attention. More profiles and more matches do not necessarily bring you closer to a meaningful connection.**
- **Treat the app as an introduction, not the whole relationship. If you want to get to know someone, make room for conversation and, when you both feel comfortable, a meeting beyond the app.**

You open a dating app intending to spend ten minutes on it. An hour later, you are still swiping. You might have a few new matches, but are you any closer to meeting someone you actually like? Arguably, one of the benefits of dating apps is that they make introductions possible on a scale that would once have been hard to imagine.

They can help people meet outside their usual circles and offer a less daunting way to signal interest. But their design also shapes what we do: profiles arrive one after another, choices take seconds, and there is always the possibility that the next person will be a better match.

In [our research](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/14705931261486522), we examined 21 interviews with dating app users alongside public online discussions and French newspaper coverage. We found that people navigate three coexisting, sometimes competing ideas about dating. The first one is the romantic approach to dating where it is important to take time, build trust and look for a connection. The second, the shopping approach, treats [dating more like browsing](https://theconversation.com/dating-apps-like-tinder-affect-relationships-and-the-economics-of-desire-287756) where a person can compare options, filter efficiently and keep their choices open. The third, the systems approach follows the app’s own rhythm: swipe, match, respond to prompts and keep engaging, without necessarily thinking about the long-term goals.

Most people do not fit neatly into just one of these approaches. Someone may hope for a lasting relationship while filtering profiles like a careful shopper. Another may enjoy casual dating but resent feeling pushed to make endless quick decisions. That tension helps explain why using an app can feel both useful and exhausting.

## So how can you ‘beat’ a dating algorithm?

Despite years of research dedicated to looking for determinants of online dating success, there is no proven secret combination of swipes, photos or messages that will make a platform deliver the right partner.

Ask yourself instead, how can you stop the app’s rhythm from setting the terms of your romantic life? Here’s how:

- Keep a clear picture of your intentions

Before opening the app, consider whether you want a committed relationship, casual dates or simply to meet people without deciding yet. Any of these is a valid aim. Knowing yours can help you choose whom to talk to and what to say. It can also make it easier to notice when you are following someone else’s expectations because it seems simpler than explaining your own. When a conversation starts to matter to you, share what you are looking for and ask what the other person wants, too. You need not settle everything immediately, but you should not have to guess indefinitely.

- Choose when to stop browsing

One participant in our study, Rose, imposed a swiping ban on herself so she could focus on a few people she was genuinely interested in. Her choice did not reveal a flaw in the app’s code. It changed how she used the app. If you find yourself collecting matches without talking to them, try pausing new searches long enough to give existing conversations your attention.

- Use filters and profiles as tools, not verdicts

Some people in our study carefully shaped their profiles, used several apps or filtered matches to save time. These tactics can be useful, particularly when they reflect what you genuinely value. But a profile offers only a partial view of a person. A match is a reason to begin a conversation, [not evidence that a relationship will work](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0956797617714580). Critically, a lack of matches is not a measure of your worth. Research shows that low match rates on dating apps may lead to [negative mental health outcomes](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/talking-about-men/201810/are-dating-apps-damaging-our-mental-health) because the apps create a false equivalence between algorithmic compatibility and personal worth.

- Take promising connections beyond the swipe cycle

Participants seeking closeness often wanted more than an exchange of quick reactions. Some moved conversations off the app or made plans to meet, rather than continuing to browse indefinitely. You can do this at a pace that feels comfortable to both people. The point is to give a connection a chance to develop in a setting where the next profile is not constantly competing for attention.

## The importance of psychological sovereignty

Finally, give yourself permission to leave.

One participant in our study, Alan, deleted an app when dating began to feel like a game, though he sometimes returned later. Taking a break need not mean giving up on meeting someone. It can be a way to check whether the app is still helping you pursue what you want. We call this reclaiming [psychological sovereignty](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1177/14705931261486522). Put plainly, it means [keeping hold of your ability to decide what matters to you, how much attention you give the app and when you have had enough](https://theconversation.com/its-not-screen-time-that-matters-its-what-you-do-and-when-you-do-it-new-study-266845). You cannot control who appears on your screen or how the platform ranks profiles, but you can decide what you do next.

Dating apps can open doors, but it is important to remember that you are the one who is in control. You get to choose whether to walk through this door, keep looking, or put your phone away, and no algorithm can make this decision for you.

title: AI behaves more like a brain than a database – cognitive science’s role in its origin story helps explain why
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Michael Hout, Associate Dean of Research and Professor of Psychology, New Mexico State University; Arryn Robbins, Assistant Professor of Psychology, University of Richmond
content:
When people think about what ChatGPT or other large language models are doing behind the scenes, it’s common to reach for the language of computing. You might assume there is a database, or a logical series of steps being executed, in order to provide a response to your query.

Picturing AI responses as akin to your computer pulling up a file is a sensible line of thinking. But it’s incorrect. Understanding the central influence of cognitive science in AI’s evolution helps explain why.

AI’s history isn’t only a computer science story. Fundamental advances that gave rise to today’s AI were brought about by people whose goal was to understand the human mind, not help you with your homework or travel itinerary. This distinction is important, because it helps better explain how these systems “behave” the way they do.

[We are](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=RzltjfkAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao) [cognitive scientists](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Z9t4ZG0AAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao) who teach students about the interdisciplinary roots of our field, including its deep and often overlooked ties to computer science and AI. There’s a shared history that often gets lost in conversations about what AI is doing.

## AI’s lineage is often overlooked

The term “artificial intelligence” was coined in 1956, at a [Dartmouth College workshop](https://home.dartmouth.edu/about/artificial-intelligence-ai-coined-dartmouth). At the time, people thought that a machine could be made intelligent if you could write down the right set of rules for it to follow.

Rather than build a machine that followed rules, however, psychologist Frank Rosenblatt built one in 1958 – [the Perceptron](https://homepages.math.uic.edu/%7Elreyzin/papers/rosenblatt58.pdf) – that learned from examples. Rosenblatt hadn’t been at the Dartmouth workshop, but he was thinking about how to make a machine intelligent in a fundamentally different, more human way. His key insight was to build an [artificial neural network](https://news.cornell.edu/stories/2019/09/professors-perceptron-paved-way-ai-60-years-too-soon): a computer algorithm modeled loosely on the architecture of the brain.

This approach built on the work of psychologists like [Donald Hebb](https://can-acn.org/donald-olding-hebb/) who were studying brains and behavior. Specifically, Hebb explored how neural connections strengthen when used, a fundamental insight that later seeded machine learning.

Further advances came in the 1980s, as psychologists sought to explain how people perform complex cognitive tasks, such as recognizing words and forming memories. Cognitive and computer scientists together – [David Rumelhart](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2011/03/david-rumelhart-pioneer-cognitive-neuroscience-dies-68), [Geoffrey Hinton](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=JicYPdAAAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao) and [Ronald Williams](https://www.khoury.northeastern.edu/a-tribute-to-ron-williams-khoury-professor-and-machine-learning-pioneer/) – figured out how to [train artificial neural networks with multiple layers](https://doi.org/10.1038/323533a0), an idea that later became known as “deep learning.” These multilayered neural networks were capable of more complex tasks and generalizing what they “learned” to apply to new examples.

In the following decades, computer scientists and engineers enabled computing capabilities to be [scaled up](https://penntoday.upenn.edu/news/moore-meets-eye-evolution-computing), [developing graphics chips](https://cacm.acm.org/federal-funding-of-academic-research/the-origins-of-gpu-computing/), the [transformer architecture](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper_files/paper/2017/file/3f5ee243547dee91fbd053c1c4a845aa-Paper.pdf?src_trk=em66c5166b7bad47.12959706424423622) and more. Without these systems, modern AI would still struggle to recognize letters and words, rather than be able to hold realistic conversations in natural language.

The fundamental insights, however, came from the study of the mind: AI should learn from examples, and its architecture should be based on the human brain.

These foundational ideas matter for reasons of practicality. Modern AI isn’t born from rules – it’s grown from examples. And things that are grown are not as predictable as systems based on rules.

## Its origin helps explain its ‘behavior’

Human intuitions and [mental models](https://doi.org/10.1006/imms.1993.1028) about how technology works [govern how people use it](https://thedecisionlab.com/reference-guide/design/mental-models). The idea of AI as software – deterministic, fact-retrieving – causes people to misinterpret the outputs they provide.

AI [“hallucinations” are common](https://doi.org/10.2196/53164); chatbots [often state falsehoods](https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/2221c875-02dc-4789-800b-e7758f3722c1/o3-and-o4-mini-system-card.pdf). Thinking of AI as a database makes this behavior appear confusing. How could a system look up an answer that doesn’t exist?

But human memory doesn’t “look up” answers. It is [reconstructive and imperfect](https://theconversation.com/photographic-memory-is-a-myth-heres-what-research-really-says-about-remembering-278160), filling in gaps with plausible details. Thanks to pioneering work by psychologist [Elizabeth Loftus](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ZNoHqr8AAAAJ&hl=en&oi=ao), researchers know that [false memories are unfortunately common](https://theconversation.com/brian-williams-told-a-tale-but-it-could-be-how-he-really-remembers-what-happened-37447) and can be implanted with relative ease.

A system that “looks something up” gives the same answer every time, but it is therefore limited in responding to a finite set of questions. Human minds don’t work that way, and neither does AI. The price to pay for being able to generalize to new questions and tasks is a system prone to confabulation.

Thinking of AI as like a primitive brain also helps explain additional puzzling behaviors, such as getting different answers to the same question. Ask your young child what they want for dinner twice and you may get different requests. [Framing matters when interacting with an AI system](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2026/03/ai-advice-sycophantic-models-research) too, as these systems [can be nudged](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec8352) into giving you answers you prefer. They operate in a probabilistic fashion, much like human memory, not in a deterministic fashion, like a calculator.

None of this means that AI necessarily thinks like people do, if the systems think at all. [Humans and AI commonly “perceive” things differently](https://theconversation.com/ai-doesnt-see-the-way-that-you-do-and-that-could-be-a-problem-when-it-categorizes-objects-and-scenes-271481); computer vision can spot subtle abnormalities that human screeners might miss, but might also misinterpret something, such as a defaced road sign.

## Why those origins still matter

If modern AI is unpredictable, how can people come to understand it?

The answer is by understanding where this technology came from. Recognizing that AI systems are more akin to brains than databases can help people build more accurate mental models of what AI can do and can lead to better ways of understanding how these systems work.

1. **Users overtrust the wrong things.** With a significant proportion of ChatGPT users indicating that they [use ChatGPT like a search engine](https://www.adobe.com/express/learn/blog/chatgpt-as-a-search-engine), it seems that people are treating outputs as retrieved fact rather than fluent, confident guesses. This misunderstanding can cause users to skip the verification step they’d likely apply to a person and potentially make decisions, [including financial ones](https://theconversation.com/when-managing-your-money-take-a-chatbots-confidence-with-a-grain-of-salt-286106), based on confabulation.
2. **Institutions grapple with differing mental models.** [Faculty remain split](https://doi.org/10.3389/frma.2024.1486832) between banning AI tools outright and [building them into coursework](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.caeai.2024.100348), treating AI as producing answers to be checked or trusted like collaborators. Divisions are causing confusion and sowing rifts among (and within) educators and their students.
3. **Computer science is rediscovering cognitive science’s questions.** Today’s systems are opaque even to their builders. One approach to understanding them, probing [what goes in](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.14257) and what comes out, resembles [behaviorism](https://www.britannica.com/science/behaviourism-psychology), a once-dominant field of psychology that studied only observable behavior. Researchers are now moving toward [interpretability](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/interpretability): opening up the models to see what’s happening inside – closer in spirit to neuroscience – and working on [problems cognitive scientists have chewed on](https://www.anthropic.com/research/team/interpretability) for decades.

The exchange runs both ways. Just as computer science draws on cognitive science’s questions and methods, cognitive science draws on the accessibility of AI models themselves, using them to test and [refine theories of the mind](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tics.2019.01.009). Computer science and cognitive science split off from one project decades ago: understanding how intelligence works. The more these fields keep trading questions and tools, the better placed humanity will be.

description: Modern AI owes its existence to both cognitive and computer science. What you envision as its origin story can influence how you understand what large language models can do.

title: A new study finds that to counter misinformation online, we need to copy its style
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Jooyoung Lee, Research Fellow, Behavioural Data Science Lab, University of Technology Sydney; Emily Booth, Research Fellow, Data Science Institute, University of Technology Sydney; Marian-Andrei Rizoiu, Professor of AI and Behavioral Data Science, University of Technology Sydney
content:
Imagine you’re worried about vaccinating your baby. A message on Facebook tells you: “Protect the community and your kids by booking their vaccinations today.” Another asks: “Do you know all the effects of childhood vaccinations on your babies?”

Both link to the same reliable vaccination information. But in our [recently published research](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42001-026-00493-0), the second message was about 52% more likely to be clicked on.

We wanted to test whether changing the way that factual information is presented online could help it reach audiences who might otherwise overlook it. Our findings suggest the wording matters, even when the information itself stays the same.

## What is misinformation?

Misinformation can appear in everyday discussions on social media, including conversations about childhood vaccination. In the Australian Facebook communities we studied, these discussions often connected with personal concerns about protecting children.

[Misinformation](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3696410.3714527) means false information shared without an intention to cause harm. Disinformation is false information deliberately created and shared.

However, false claims are only part of the problem. Our [earlier research](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1140/epjds/s13688-025-00567-5) found far-right users also shared articles from moderate news sources. They selected a narrow range of topics that fit their world views, meaning even mostly accurate news articles could reinforce those views.

Not only does this make it harder to get reliable information to people, it can also negatively affect their relationships. [Our research](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/14407833241231756) describes people withdrawing from loved ones and mainstream information as they became more involved in fringe communities.

## A misinformation minefield

Governments provide factual resources, while researchers and other organisations investigate misleading claims and provide the evidence. Fact-checking [can help](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s42001-026-00493-0), but people need to trust the source and understand the explanation.

Social media platforms have also tried removing false or misleading content or making it less visible. [Research on Meta’s pandemic response](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/1329878X241236984) found many of the Facebook pages regulated by Meta and examined in the study declined in performance, although some continued growing.

Social media platforms have also tried adding warning labels to misleading posts and showing them to fewer people.

Users found ways around restrictions, such as coded language and links to less moderated platforms.

[Meta stopped using independent fact-checkers](https://about.fb.com/news/2025/01/meta-more-speech-fewer-mistakes/) in the United States in April 2025. It began introducing Community Notes, where users write and rate explanations that appear alongside posts.

So these approaches have had some impact, but they leave a question: how do you get reliable information in front of someone who isn’t looking for it?

## Meet Jennifer, Patrick and Aaron

We spent months observing Australian Facebook communities sharing anti-vaccination and far-right narratives.

Alongside information, these communities offered companionship. Messages could sound like a friend sharing worries about their child.

We used these observations to develop three fictional audience profiles, known as personas.

Jennifer was a young mother concerned about vaccination. Patrick was a retired teacher worried about his grandchildren’s future. Aaron was a young man interested in fitness and technology. These profiles helped us select audiences for Facebook advertisements and write messages using familiar styles.

For Jennifer, we used personal, caring language, like a friend sharing worries about their children.

Patrick’s messages took an authoritative, explanatory tone. Aaron’s used a motivational tone, encouraging readers to take charge and check the facts for themselves.

We then compared those messages with neutral versions of the same ad. Each pair used the same image and linked to the same government or government-affiliated resource. The sponsor and advertising settings stayed the same, only the wording changed.

In 11 out of the 12 comparisons, people were more likely to click on an ad when its wording reflected the language used in the communities we studied.

Ads about school education received clicks 6% of the time when they used familiar language. The same ads with neutral wording only received clicks 1.1% of the time. This means the language inspired by communities the ads were trying to reach were roughly five times more likely to be clicked on.

For vaccination ads, those with familiar language were clicked on 0.98% of the time, compared to 0.65% for those with neutral wording.

## Speaking their language

Our findings suggest communication style can help attract attention to reliable information.

They don’t show that we changed anyone’s mind. We don’t know whether people read the linked pages, and Facebook’s delivery system influenced who saw each advertisement.

We also changed several features of the wording together, so we can’t identify which feature made the difference.

But even with these caveats in mind, there are ways these findings can be used now to help combat mis- and disinformation online.

For example, public health teams could use this approach by listening to how people describe their concerns, then testing different ways of presenting the same evidence.

This doesn’t mean impersonating community members or amplifying fear to attract attention. It just means adopting language that speaks directly to questions and concerns of the people you’re trying to reach.

For a vaccination campaign, this could mean testing messages that acknowledge parents’ questions. For example, “You want to keep your little one safe. Wondering what vaccinations will mean for your baby?”.

A follow-up study could then examine whether readers understood the information and felt better able to make a decision.
