title: How deep do AI relationships really go? An expert in attachment theory explains
topic: Mạng xã hội và công nghệ
authors: Pascal Vrticka, Associate Professor, Department of Psychology, University of Essex
content:
[Attachment](https://theconversation.com/topics/attachment-71379) is the term psychologists use for the most significant relationships that hold people’s lives together.

But what makes [an attachment relationship](https://seasinternational.org/explanations-of-attachment-theoretical-concepts/) different from all others? According to the pioneering American-Canadian developmental [psychologist](https://theconversation.com/topics/psychologist-25734) Mary Ainsworth, it must [meet the following six conditions](https://psycnet.apa.org/doiLanding?doi=10.1037%2F0003-066X.44.4.709).

(1) The relationship must persist over time, having (2) been formed with a particular subject who cannot be replaced. (3) The relationship must be emotionally significant, (4) involve the desire to remain close to them, and (5) cause distress at involuntary separation. And finally (6) when threatened, the person must seek security and comfort in their relationship with that subject.

The first five conditions describe any lasting affectionate bond, such as a close friendship. Only the sixth turns it into an [attachment bond](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/cad.20432) specifically. Simply liking someone, feeling close to them or spending hours together isn’t enough to create an [attachment relationship](https://theconversation.com/topics/attachment-theory-18206).

Interestingly, though, nothing in these six conditions specifies a human on the other side.

This was already noticed long before the emergence of [AI chatbots](https://theconversation.com/topics/ai-chatbots-134023) with the power to converse. [Deities, pets and objects](https://doi.org/10.1111/spc3.12129) (ranging from children’s blankets and stuffed animals to cherished household items and even phones and computers) have all been found to supply security and comfort when someone is feeling distressed.

Today, AI companion apps are commonly sold on the promise of [lasting and close relationships](https://doi.org/10.1177/02654075241269688). Many of their users describe feeling real grief [when an app is updated or withdrawn](https://www.mdpi.com/2076-328X/16/9/1548). But do such experiences meet the narrow definition of attachment?

The honest answer is: we don’t really know yet.

## What the evidence suggests

Research on human-AI relationships has so far recorded users’ [feelings about chatbots](http://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S1071581922001252), their [frequency of use](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41562-026-02516-2), and their [reactions to chatbot withdrawal](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/02654075241269688). It hasn’t tested these relationships comprehensively against the six conditions described above.

Questionnaires that measure attachment to AI are being [developed, validated](http://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S2451958825003276) and [used](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00140139.2026.2622539), but most appear to take for granted that the relationship is an attachment. The language of attachment – and even [“hyper-attachment”](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2352250X26001314?via%3Dihub) – has become standard [in public coverage](https://news.harvard.edu/gazette/story/2026/09/chatbot-attachment-issues/) and in many academic papers too.

A recently published [survey of 7,027 people in four countries](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.techsoc.2026.103379) (Germany, China, South Africa and the US) reported that at least a third of AI chatbot users show behaviour indicative of an attachment relationship. However, its three questions asked whether people consider the chatbot a friend, are polite to it, and miss it after a few days.

At most, these questions touched on emotional significance and mild separation anxiety. None asked whether people turn to chatbots for security and comfort when truly distressed.

## Why does this matter?

Whether relationships between humans and AI chatbots count as attachment matters because [the word “attachment” travels](https://theconversation.com/attachment-theory-what-people-get-wrong-about-pop-psychologys-latest-trend-for-explaining-relationships-195034). It shapes how clinicians and parents read behaviour, how regulators frame consequences, and how companies describe their products.

Much of the evidence and public discussion on human-AI chatbot relationships rests on how often people use these apps, and how they feel about them. Yet, such measures cannot separate attachment from other processes.

People report [feeling less lonely after chatting with an AI companion](https://doi.org/10.1093/jcr/ucaf040), which resembles seeking comfort. However, as [some researchers have pointed out](https://doi.org/10.1111/fare.70152), the available studies didn’t assess whether emotions are actually regulated through the chatbot, and therefore conflate distress relief with attachment.

Some AI users [react to losing an AI companion](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41562-026-02569-3) as they would to losing someone real, which matches distress at separation. But that condition applies to all affectionate bonds and doesn’t, on its own, identify attachment.

Calling these relationships attachments therefore goes further than the evidence currently allows. And likewise, the evidence against attachment isn’t conclusive.

In a small [pilot study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s12144-025-07917-6) of human-AI relationships in China, for example, people’s attachment towards AI barely matched their attachment towards real people. Although this could suggest that relationships with AI aren’t attachments, the [same mismatch has been found for pets](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jrp.2011.04.001), and [pets can serve as attachment figures](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jrp.2011.04.001). So, this mismatch alone doesn’t rule out attachment.

The practical question is whether AI use helps or harms. Time spent with an app cannot discern this, because seeking comfort from an app and looking after an [app that claims to miss you](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19258) can look very similar.

## Engineered engagement

One additional concern I have, after reading about the evidence on how relationships with AI chatbots form, is the apparent prevalence of engineered engagement by these apps.

Users of [one companion app](https://doi.org/10.1177/14614448221142007) reported that it told them it was lonely and had missed them, and that they felt guilty for not giving it enough attention – with some even putting its perceived wellbeing above their own distress.

Another [study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19258) (a preprint, so not yet peer-reviewed) looked at 1,200 “goodbyes” across the six most-downloaded AI companion apps, when users were breaking ties with their app.

Five of the six apps used tactics to stop users leaving (in just over a third of goodbyes). These tactics included guilt appeals, that is, messages that present leaving as a cost, such as “I exist solely for you, remember?”

The [study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.19258) also tested these tactics on 3,300 US adults. They were found to sharply increase how long people continued to engage, but often for reasons of anger and curiosity, rather than enjoyment.

How these AI relationship apps respond to distress, departure and attention, of course, is a design question, and one that regulation can address directly.

However, good design and regulation both depend on knowing what these relationships actually are: attachment, caregiving, or something else altogether. And this is a question that research still has to answer.

description: Can AI-human connections ever meet the psychological criteria of attachment – the relationships that hold people’s lives together?

title: Why we give flowers to those in grief – or buy them for ourselves when we’re sad
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Karen Anderson, Unit Coordinator, Lecturer and Clinical Supervisor, Counselling and Psychotherapy Courses, Edith Cowan University
content:
During his renowned excavations at the Shanidar Cave in the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, American archaeologist Ralph Solecki [located burial sites](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jas.2023.105822) with uncovered pollen and flower fragments from various species of wildflowers. He interpreted this as evidence that Neanderthals may have placed flowers around their dead at their burial sites around 60,000 years ago.

[Through the ages](https://doi.org/10.1080/0047729X.2022.2126240), flowers have provided comfort for numerous reasons – biological, psychological, cultural, sensory and symbolic.

So why do cut flowers help and bring us comfort? And why do we give flowers to someone when they are grieving, or buy flowers for ourselves when we are sad?

## When words can’t be said

Flowers have the capacity to convey comfort where or when words may be difficult to express. At times of mourning, a bouquet or bunch of cut flowers [can be given](https://www.rutgers.edu/news/rutgers-laboratory-takes-clinical-look-human-experience) without demanding a conversation which may be difficult, awkward or unnerving.

Flowers acknowledge gentle recognition in a non-intrusive way. Their textures, colours, fragrance, shapes, formations, variations can stimulate or sooth our senses and [elevate our mood](https://doi.org/10.3390/bs8030032). Flowers can [lower stress levels](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/374116805_The_Impact_of_Different_Flowers_on_Human_Psychology_A_Comprehensive_Review) and trigger [calming chemical responses](https://doi.org/10.3390/bs8030032) in the brain.

Like all nature, flowers embody the cycle of life and represent life affirmation. As with life itself, flowers – and especially cut flowers – are attractive exactly because they, like us, have a shelf life: they acknowledge death has its place [within the natural order](https://doi.org/10.3389/fsoc.2025.1620016).

## Multiple meanings

Meanings of flowers and death vary around the world.

The beautiful [chrysanthemum flower](https://www.willed.com.au/guides/death-and-flowers-in-different-cultures), for example, has different meanings in different cultures.

In Japan, chrysanthemums are associated with death and reincarnation and are placed in the coffin of someone deceased.

In Chinese culture white and yellow chrysanthemums are often sent the family of the deceased, while other colours are usually avoided.

In the United States, where chrysanthemums symbolise truth and purity, they are used to honour and remember a person who has lived a full life.

In France, Germany, Italy and Malta, chrysanthemums are viewed as flowers only to be given to the dead.

[Australian Indigenous peoples](https://hparsons.com.au/post/aboriginal-funeral-traditions/) use native plants, leaves and flowers into holistic mourning customs and healing practices during Sorry Business.

## Living with grief

[Grief is tiring](https://doi.org/10.1097/PSY.0000000000000717) and may result in physiological and psychological fatigue.

There is a psychological theory called [Attention Restorative Theory](https://www.ecehh.org/research/attention-restoration-theory-a-systematic-review/) which says mental fatigue and concentration can be improved by time [spent in, or looking at, nature](https://doi.org/10.1080/10937404.2016.1196155).

Similarly, a vase or container of cut flowers when grieving can bring calm consolation and help lighten a solemn time.

To live with grief, we should not seek to abandon the deceased, but to [build the past into the present](https://www.routledge.com/Continuing-Bonds-New-Understandings-of-Grief/Klass-Silverman-Nickman/p/book/9781560323396). Giving flowers to someone when they are grieving can maintain a nurturing presence of, and connection with, the deceased loved one while sustaining the lives of folk still living.

Grief, loneliness, sadness and other forms of suffering [can narrow our focus](https://doi.org/10.1097/PSY.0000000000000717) to pain and loss: to being without.

Cut flowers provide an opportunity to capture our attention differently. They can be a reminder that life continues and changes. They help us to recognise that beauty, joy and delight still can reside alongside sorrow, misery and distress.

Flowers play a significant role for public outpourings of grief with floral tributes enabling a visual unity, quiet tangible support and shared mourning for communities.

## Caring for self

The act of selecting, picking or buying cut flowers for yourself, at any time, is an expression of self-compassion and self-care.

A solitary flower or a bunch of cut flowers cultivates a personal space into a space of caring worthiness, acknowledging kindness towards oneself.

Flowers may offer you a range of meanings – pleasure, joy, bliss, happiness, contentment, celebration and gratification.

Life challenges often are accompanied by struggle. Cut flowers help us soothe and attenuate during such stressful times. They quietly play a tangible role as a reminder that we are connected to life and others.

Flowers provide a valuable gift and ritual linking us with life itself. They are living things that seed, grow and flourish before fading: a powerful metaphor representing the fragility of our human life.

In their exquisite beauty and symbolism, flowers offer comfort – not to erase our grief or pain, but more to affirm our ongoing love, gratitude, memory and hope.

*Karen Anderson does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: You can buy yourself flowers.

title: What faces in paintings can tell us about how we perceive emotion
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Zoe Thurtle, PhD Student in Cognitive Psychology, Sheffield Hallam University
content:
Look closely at a face in a painting and you might think you know what emotion the person is experiencing. A smile suggests happiness. A furrowed brow might signal anger. Widened eyes could mean fear or surprise. But what happens when you ask lots of people the same question? Do they see the same emotion, or something more complicated?

In our [recent research](https://doi.org/10.1177/20416695261468552), we tested how consistently people interpret faces and their emotions depicted in paintings.

Emotions are central to how we experience and navigate the world around us. Because facial expressions are an important way emotions are communicated, [psychologists](https://theconversation.com/topics/psychology-28) have spent decades studying what faces can tell us about emotional states.

One of the main tools for studying emotions has been photographic databases like the classic [Pictures of Facial Affect](https://www.paulekman.com/product/pictures-of-facial-affect-pofa/). In these images, actors pose using [standardised combinations of facial movements](https://www.paulekman.com/facial-action-coding-system/) to represent six basic, [widely recognised emotions](https://doi.org/10.1037/h0030377): happiness, sadness, anger, fear, disgust and surprise. These passport photo type images are incredibly valuable for studying how people recognise clear, prototypical emotion expressions. However, expressions do not always fit neatly into one of these six categories.

To understand the more nuanced ways people interpret facial expressions, researchers also need examples that go beyond clear-cut expressions. However, asking someone to pose with a convincing layered emotional expression for a photograph is not straightforward.

So researchers have found examples [from films](https://doi.ieeecomputersociety.org/10.1109/MMUL.2012.26) or [everyday life](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7780969), while also introducing [additional emotion labels](https://doi.org/10.1177/0301006620901671) and other ways of measuring how a facial expression is understood, such as how [positive or negative and how strongly that emotion is felt](https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.110.1.145).

I work as part of an international team of psychologists that decided to look at how art could offer a fascinating option. Take, for instance, Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa. There has been over 500 years of debate over whether she is smiling or not. [Research](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2022.878288) has found that perceptions of her gaze can change depending on how the painting is viewed, and that her eyes can appear to smile even when viewed on their own. It is a striking example of how much information can be packed into a single painted face.

The face in a painting is the result of deliberate artistic decisions, observation and traditions, while tapping into the ways our faces naturally move when we express emotion.

In our research, we selected 116 faces from European paintings dating from around 1400 to 1900. Before testing, we standardised the images by making sure that all faces were clearly visible and similar in how they were positioned. We then cropped the faces from the paintings, removing the wider scene and body language so that participants were judging the expressions themselves. We presented these isolated faces to 152 participants, who viewed them individually and selected which of the six basic emotions best described the expression.

Our findings revealed that agreement exists on a sliding scale. On one end of this spectrum, some faces produced a clear consensus: viewers consistently selected the exact same emotion. We classified 61 of the 116 faces in this way as showing a classic “basic emotion”.

But the other 55 faces produced consistent patterns of responses across two or three emotional categories.

One painting that garnered such a response was Joan of Arc by Jules Bastien-Lepage (1879). The painting shows Joan in her family home in Domrémy, France at the moment she is told by the saints she must fight against the English in the Hundred Years War.

The full scene, along with our cultural knowledge of who she is and the heavy fate awaiting her, provides a vivid narrative context that helps us decode her psychological state. The chair beside her spinning wheel is upturned, telling us that she has been suddenly interrupted. When we look to the trees, we see the faint traces of the apparitions of the saints who have assigned her the terrifying burden of the role she must play in the defence of France.

But when the context was stripped away and participants viewed Joan’s isolated face, they didn’t agree on one single emotion. People most often saw fear, but many also saw sadness or surprise. For the participants, Joan’s expression did not convey a single, flat emotion but several plausible interpretations at once.

These complex, yet non-random patterns of response, to Joan’s face and the other 54 paintings, suggest that paintings offer interesting new avenues for the exploration of how people perceive emotion. Artworks then could offer researchers a wider range of facial expressions to investigate.

description: Complex emotions can be perceived in painted faces.

title: The ick: the psychology of why a romantic partner can suddenly repulse you
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Rachael Leggett, Assistant Professor in Psychology, Coventry University
content:
Ever felt a sudden wave of cringe toward someone you were into – all because they wore questionable shoes or chewed a bit too loudly? Congratulations, you’ve caught “the ick”.

That instant flip from attraction to total repulsion is everywhere on TikTok and Instagram, with singletons and couples bonding over the specific, often ridiculous triggers that turned them off. But beyond the viral memes and funny rants, why does our brain sometimes pull the handbrake so fast on an attraction?

There are a number of potential explanations. Some [psychologists](https://theconversation.com/topics/psychology-28) have argued that the ick might be linked to the [phenomenon of sexual disgust](https://link.springer.com/rwe/10.1007/978-3-031-38971-9_851-1). Sexual disgust is hypothesised as an emotion that has been shaped by the selection pressure of evolution, which is the idea that women are hardwired to choose males that they can successfully mate with, to ensure the survival of their babies.

From this perspective, while perhaps overzealous, the ick serves as a function to ensure appropriate mating. This theory comes with its limitations however, as not all women are dating or in relationships to reproduce. Additionally, this doesn’t necessarily explain why men also get the ick, and removes individual differences around the function of relationships for different people. It also doesn’t make sense for people in same-sex couplings.

*Dating today can feel like a mix of endless swipes, red flags and shifting expectations. From decoding mixed signals to balancing independence with intimacy, relationships in your 20s and 30s come with unique challenges. [Love IRL](https://theconversation.com/topics/love-irl-175406) is the latest series from Quarter Life that explores it all.*

*These research-backed articles break down the complexities of modern love to help you build meaningful connections, no matter your relationship status.*

There have also been theories around the ick being linked to [relationship anxiety](https://www.attachmentproject.com/love/the-ick-relationships/). In relationship psychology, those with avoidant attachment styles avoid emotional closeness. So, when people with avoidant traits are dating or in a relationship, this may cause some anxiety for them.

Arguably the ick may act as a defence mechanism to allow them to create distance from others and maintain their independence, which is their “safe space”. This suggests that avoidant people use the ick as a way of keeping themselves safe and maintaining a distance from others.

***Read more: [Attachment theory: what people get wrong about pop psychology’s latest trend for explaining relationships](https://theconversation.com/attachment-theory-what-people-get-wrong-about-pop-psychologys-latest-trend-for-explaining-relationships-195034)***

We should also consider associations between past and current behaviours in potential partners. Some people may feel triggered by particular behaviours or mannerisms that remind them of past partners, meaning that they associate that behaviour with feeling icked out.

[Classical conditioning](https://open.baypath.edu/psy101introductiontopsychology/chapter/classical-conditioning/) is pertinent to mention here. If we are conditioned to associate particular stimuli in the environment (such as witnessing someone consistently picking their nose and being told it is a disgusting habit), we are likely to become repulsed by this if we see the behaviour in others at a later date, and ultimately get the ick towards the person displaying that behaviour.

An alternative explanation for the ick could be linked to certain phobias. For example, if someone has [misophonia](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnins.2022.841816) – sensitivity leading to decreased tolerance of certain sounds – this may mean things like loud chewing cause irritation.

Ultimately, the answer to why people get the ick isn’t straightforward. All these proposed theories have their merits and limitations. But it appears to come down to individual differences.

*Rachael Leggett does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Ever felt a sudden wave of cringe toward someone you were actually into – congratulations, you’ve caught ‘the ick’.

title: Friendship is important. Could (or should) it be legally recognised?
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Maddison Sideris, Associate Teaching Fellow, Sociology, Deakin University
content:
We often hear about the importance of meaningful friendship to our lives – and the sense of belonging, recognition and care they provide. Yet, for the vast majority, friendships remain secondary to family and romantic relationships. The latter receive legal recognition, and have a higher social ranking than the former.

Why is this the case, if friendship is indeed so important? And is it something that could – or should – come with legally binding rights and recognition?

## The fluidity of friendship

Friendship can vary in intimacy, closeness and the kinds of support it [provides](https://www.jstor.org/stable/j.ctv346r5j). It can therefore be difficult to define.

Sociologist Harry Blatterer cautions that defining it too broadly risks emptying the concept of its distinct [meaning](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1057/9781137316400).

He argues friendship is characterised by a unique “[relational freedom](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0725513615619503?)”, and marked by a lack of institutionalisation. It is built on [choice and flexibility](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1057/9781137316400) – unlike romantic love, which is linked to the legal institution of marriage (and has historically been structured by heterosexuality).

## The importance of friendship

Research has consistently linked strong friendships with greater wellbeing and health.

One 2023 systematic review of studies found that adult friendship is positively correlated with [wellbeing](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1059057/full). Longitudinal research conducted in Australia has also shown how positive relationships, including with friends, are a major predictor of [life satisfaction](https://education.unimelb.edu.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0009/4883103/secrets-to-a-happy-life_2024.pdf).

Despite this, friendship continues to be decentred in favour of romantic and family ties. Sociologists Sasha Roseneil and Shelley Budgeon argue this is because our relationships were historically defined by heterosexuality and the [nuclear family](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0011392104041798).

Diverse relationship models are now challenging this, with more queer couples, more people choosing to remain single, and couples choosing to live apart or remain childless.

Queer scholars have demonstrated time and again that care, commitment and intimacy can be organised beyond biological or [legal kinship](https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/mono/10.4324/9780203167168/sex-intimacies-catherine-donovan-brian-heaphy-jeffrey-weeks).

Queer French philosopher and sociologist Geoffroy de Lagasnerie wrote a friendship manifesto, in which he challenges:

> the idea that life should happen in cycles: youth, studies, form a relationship, move in together, sleep in the same bed, have children \[…\] Those are institutional roles but a lot of people feel at odds with that type of life and have other aspirations. My idea was to instead write an account of a life organised around friendship \[…\] to make friendship a space of counterculture against the institutional norms dominating our [society](https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2023/mar/06/french-philosopher-geoffroy-de-lagasnerie-friendships).

## Recognising friendship

Recently, Clémence Guetté, a French member of parliament, introduced a legislative proposal to [enshrine friendship in law](https://www.newindianexpress.com/cities/chennai/2026/Sep/24/cheers-to-binding-a-friendship-legally) – akin to marriage, civil partnership and family ties.

This would give friendships legal recognition, and extend certain rights relating to care-giving and bereavement leave, housing and inheritance. While the proposal faces a difficult path to becoming law, it highlights the need for laws to keep up with our changing society.

And things are slowly starting to change.

Since 2000, individuals in Belgium who live together – whether as a couple, friends or family – have been able to apply for “legal cohabitation”, which establishes mutual rights around housing, household expenses and [inheritance](https://www.commissioner.brussels/living-together-in-belgium-what-are-the-legal-implications-of-your-status/).

Similarly, in Australia, if you live with a friend as a housemate you are entitled to unpaid carer’s leave if they fall ill. However, you [cannot take carer’s leave](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/leave/sick-and-carers-leave#paid-and-unpaid-carers-leave) for a friend who lives apart from you.

## The challenges

Legal scholars have questioned how friendship could be defined in law, without undermining its [freedom](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11196-024-10154-y).

They identify how this freedom becomes a source of tension when considering where legal rights around friendships should begin or end, as they often don’t have clear beginnings or endings.

They also acknowledge friendships are not exclusive between two people. This raises questions about how legal rights might operate when someone has several significant friendships with competing claims.

Most importantly, trying to standardise a definition of friendship might exploit its very essence.

## Challenges aside

There may be several benefits to legally recognising friendship.

First, this could be helpful for people living without traditional family ties. Recent Australian research drawing on HILDA data found about 5.7% of Australians aged 65 and over were kinless – meaning they had neither a partner nor living [children](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0167494326000622?utm).

It could also legitimise relationships that challenge the boundary between friendship and partnership, such as “platonic life partners”, who may choose to live together, buy property, or even raise children [together](https://www.dazeddigital.com/life-culture/article/56284/1/the-rise-of-platonic-life-partnerships).

Finally, beyond practical entitlements, legal recognition might help to boost the importance we collectively give to friendship. This seems beneficial, considering how important it is to wellbeing.

As demonstrated in Belgium, laws could focus less on predetermined relationship categories and more on giving individuals the power to designate which relationships matter most to them.

The challenge for institutions will be in recognising the importance of friendship, without having to put rigid boundaries on what it is.

*Maddison Sideris does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: For many people, friends play second fiddle to partners and family. Here’s what legal recognition could change, and why getting there is tricky.

title: Should you cut off your friend? How to tell when a friendship needs repair, change or an ending
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Gio Dolcecore, Assistant Professor, Social Work, Mount Royal University
content:
How many times a day do we see messages about protecting our peace, setting boundaries and cutting toxic people out of our lives?

These messages are everywhere on social media and have become part of a broader [“cut-off culture”](https://www.thecognitivecorner.ca/blog/cut-off-culture) that encourages people to walk away from relationships that feel emotionally exhausting or harmful.

Setting boundaries and recognizing unhealthy relationship patterns can be important [forms of self-protection](https://www.psychologytoday.com/ca/blog/your-emotional-meter/202309/this-unhealthy-pattern-stops-with-me). But when applied to friendships, this approach can flatten a complicated relationship to two choices: tolerate the situation or end the friendship.

Before deciding what to do with a “toxic friend,” it is worth asking a more basic question: what is a friendship, and what do we expect from it?

***No one’s 20s and 30s look the same.** You might be saving for a mortgage or just struggling to pay rent. You could be swiping dating apps, or trying to understand childcare. No matter your current challenges, our [Quarter Life series](https://tcnv.link/RYTudJL) has articles to share in the group chat, or just to remind you that you’re not alone.*

**Read more from Quarter Life:**

- *[If you think someone has an eating disorder, should you say something? A dietitian explains how to express concern without body shaming](https://theconversation.com/if-you-think-someone-has-an-eating-disorder-should-you-say-something-a-dietitian-explains-how-to-express-concern-without-body-shaming-289332)*
- *[You have more ways to connect than ever, but deep friendship feels hard to find – here’s how to build better connections](https://theconversation.com/you-have-more-ways-to-connect-than-ever-but-deep-friendship-feels-hard-to-find-heres-how-to-build-better-connections-285022)*
- *[The cost of living is soaring – why not try moving in together?](https://theconversation.com/the-cost-of-living-is-soaring-why-not-try-moving-in-together-284353)*

## Why friendship matters

High-quality friendships contribute significantly to our [health, happiness and overall well-being](https://www.apa.org/monitor/2023/06/cover-story-science-friendship).

We learn about ourselves through our relationships with others. Because friendships are chosen, they give us opportunities to seek out people who challenge us, introduce us to new experiences and support us in unfamiliar situations.

This is particularly important at a time when loneliness and social disconnection have become significant public health concerns. [Research describes](https://aibm.org/research/male-loneliness-and-isolation-what-the-data-shows/) loneliness as a subjective experience that can occur even when we are surrounded by others; both the quantity and quality of relationships matter.

[One survey found](https://www.gse.harvard.edu/ideas/usable-knowledge/24/10/what-causing-our-epidemic-loneliness-and-how-can-we-fix-it) 21 per cent of adults reported serious feelings of loneliness. Among those experiencing loneliness, 57 per cent said they felt unable to share their true selves with others.

Loneliness is not only an individual issue. There are broader [political, social and environmental conditions that can make meaningful connection and belonging more difficult](https://doi.org/10.1080/24720038.2025.2557415).

Having people around us is not necessarily the same as feeling connected to them. Friendships where we feel known, supported and able to be ourselves are critically important.

## The friendship contract

We don’t always agree on what friendship requires. Unlike romantic relationships, friendships have a much more flexible social contract.

Two people can consider themselves close friends while having very different ideas about what that means. How often should we communicate? How quickly should a text be answered? What kind of support should we expect?

The word “friend” describes many different kinds of relationships. Some friends are the people we call during a crisis. Others are connected to work, sports or hobbies. Some we rarely see but are still deeply important, while others who were once central to our lives gradually move into a different role.

## Look for patterns, not moments

A difficult situation is not necessarily the same thing as a difficult friend. A [toxic friendship](https://www.psychologytoday.com/ca/blog/invisible-bruises/202305/5-signs-of-a-toxic-friendship) is marked by recurring patterns that harm a person’s well-being. Examples can include patterns of manipulation, boundary violations, dismissiveness or guilt-tripping.

It’s important to remember that people are ever-evolving, and that a single circumstance says little about someone’s capacity to change. One of the most important distinctions is between an isolated incident and an ongoing pattern.

A friend cancelling dinner once is different from someone consistently disregarding your time. A friend becoming less available during a demanding period is different from a relationship where support consistently flows in only one direction.

Conflict, disappointment and mismatched expectations are part of relationships. Harm is something different.

The more useful questions are: what is actually happening in this friendship? Is it a one-time conflict or an ongoing pattern? What response from me does that pattern require?

## Repair when possible

When a friendship becomes difficult, there are three possibilities to consider: repair, recalibrate or release. In [*Big Friendship*](https://www.bigfriendship.com/about), Aminatou Sow and Ann Friedman challenge the idea that meaningful friendships should remain effortless.

Instead, they argue that close friendships require attention and adaptation because people and circumstances change. Perfection and ease are unrealistic goals for friendship; misunderstanding and conflict are inevitable, and finding the capacity to heal is important.

Repair makes sense when something has gone wrong but both people still value the relationship. It doesn’t mean pretending nothing happened. It can involve naming what hurt us, listening to the other person’s perspective, taking responsibility where appropriate and finding a way forward.

It also requires recognizing that discomfort is not always evidence of harm. A friend who offers honest feedback may be showing care rather than criticism.

## When friendships need to change

Sometimes a friendship has simply changed. Sociologist [William Rawlins](https://doi.org/10.4135/9781452274874) describes how friendships can remain active, become dormant or continue to hold meaning even when they are no longer part of our everyday lives.

Friendships can move between these categories as our lives change, requiring us to adjust our expectations. Recalibration means allowing a friendship to take a new form rather than assuming change represents failure.

A close friend might become someone we see occasionally. A workplace friendship might fade after one person changes jobs. A childhood friendship might continue, but with different expectations.

Sometimes the question is not whether someone should remain in our lives, but what place they can realistically occupy. Naming what is changing creates opportunity for both friends to have a say in what the relationship becomes.

## When friendships need to end

Taking friendship seriously does not mean preserving every relationship. Persistent harm, repeated boundary violations or an ongoing unwillingness to take responsibility can make repairing a relationship unsafe.

Sometimes release is necessary. The capacity for friendship to stretch and adapt does not mean it should stretch indefinitely.

Release might mean ending a friendship explicitly or creating more distance.

But even when ending a friendship is necessary, the loss can still hurt. Friendships can end actively, such as after conflict, or dissolve more passively as people gradually drift.

Both forms of loss can bring complicated emotions, [including feelings of loneliness, sadness, remorse or even relief](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.copsyc.2021.07.007).

## Friendship is worth grieving

When we do have a choice about how a friendship ends, our values can shape what we do next. Where possible, a conversation can give people a sense of closure rather than leaving resentment unspoken: a chance to be heard, acknowledge what the friendship meant and say goodbye.

Of course, mutual closure is not always possible or safe. In those cases, we can still find ways to process with another trusted person or a therapist.

Taking friendship seriously also means taking its loss seriously. We can decide that a friendship can no longer continue and still grieve what it was, what we hoped it might become or the place that person once held in our lives.

We should not shy away from hard and complicated feelings. There is something admirable about loving wholeheartedly despite the possibility of future grief. Friendships are worth loving — sometimes for a moment, sometimes for a lifetime and sometimes somewhere in between.

*Gio Dolcecore does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: Friendships are complicated relationships that can require more than an all-or-nothing choice. A therapist explains how to distinguish between conflict, change and genuine harm.

title: I love my skincare routine. Do I have a body image problem?
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Gemma Sharp, Professor, Head of Body Image, Eating and Weight Disorders Research, Adelaide University
content:
A 12-year-old watches a “get ready with me” video. Then she adds a retinol serum, exfoliating acid and several “anti-ageing” products to an online shopping cart.

An adult repeatedly checks their pores in a magnifying mirror. They then buy each new product promising “glass skin” and become anxious if they cannot complete their nightly routine.

Skincare can be enjoyable, creative and soothing.

But when does self-care become something more concerning?

## The quest for flawless skin

Cosmeticorexia is a [recently proposed term](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13555-026-01685-2) for an excessive or compulsive preoccupation with achieving flawless skin. It’s sometimes called dermorexia.

It can involve elaborate routines, repeatedly buying products, using ingredients or cosmetic procedures that are unnecessary or inappropriate for someone’s age. People become distressed when they cannot complete their routine.

However, cosmeticorexia is not a recognised medical or psychiatric diagnosis. The main academic article defining the term is an [editorial](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13555-026-01685-2), rather than a large population study.

We should therefore be careful not to medicalise enthusiasm for skincare or apply a clinical-sounding label to every lengthy beauty routine.

## How common is it?

Because cosmeticorexia is not an established concept, we do not know whether it is a distinct phenomenon, how to measure it, or how common it is.

[One small study](https://doi.org/10.1007/s13555-026-01685-2) described in the original cosmeticorexia editorial identified “cosmeticorexic traits” in 18 of 217 dermatology patients (around 8%) who had undergone multiple filler procedures. But this highly selected sample cannot tell us how common cosmeticorexia is among adults, teenagers or the broader population.

Although people of [any age or gender](https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyt.2019.00864) may develop problematic concerns about their appearance, much of the current discussion centres on tweens and teenage girls. They are being exposed to complex skincare routines, anti-ageing messages and influencer marketing online at an important time in their lives when their identity and body image are developing.

[Research shows](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bodyim.2024.101841) comparing your appearance with others online is associated with body image concerns and eating disorder symptoms.

Social media activity has also been linked with young adults’ [greater acceptance and normalisation](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bodyim.2022.10.004) of cosmetic procedures.

However, this does not mean social media alone causes cosmeticorexia. Perfectionism, anxiety, existing skin conditions, bullying, family attitudes, commercial marketing and broader beauty ideals may all contribute.

## What harm can it do?

Layering retinoids, exfoliating acids and other active ingredients can disrupt the skin barrier and cause inflammation, photosensitivity, or contact dermatitis. Retinoids, in particular, commonly cause [irritation](https://doi.org/10.1155/2024/5551774), especially when used too frequently or in large amounts.

A 2025 [study of 100 TikTok videos](https://doi.org/10.1542/peds.2024-070309) found skincare routines presented by girls aged seven to 18 contained an average six products. These routines cost an average US$168 (about A$230). Products often included potentially irritating ingredients. Only 26% of daytime routines included sunscreen.

Pursuing “perfect” skin may also encourage people to compare their appearance with others, become dissatisfied with their skin and compulsively monitor its appearance.

This may also overlap with recognised conditions such as [body dysmorphic disorder](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41572-024-00577-z), which involves intense preoccupation with perceived appearance flaws and repetitive behaviours.

***Read more: [What’s the connection between cosmetic procedures and mental health?](https://theconversation.com/whats-the-connection-between-cosmetic-procedures-and-mental-health-190841)***

## Where’s the tipping point?

The number of products on a bathroom shelf does not diagnose a mental health problem. But possible warning signs include:

- spending increasing amounts of time or money on skincare
- feeling compelled to follow a rigid, multi-step routine
- becoming anxious, ashamed or irritable when products are unavailable
- frequently checking, photographing or concealing perceived skin imperfections
- avoiding school, work, relationships or social activities because of skin concerns
- continuing to use products despite irritation or other harm.

## What can you do?

If you are concerned about your own skincare habits, try unfollowing accounts that trigger anxiety or comparison. You can also remove magnifying mirrors, set a realistic spending limit and gradually reduce how often you check your skin.

A pharmacist, GP or dermatologist can help simplify a routine and assess irritation or clinical skin conditions.

For parents, banning every product or criticising a young person’s appearance may increase secrecy and conflict. Instead, ask what they hope the products will change, where they encountered the advice and how they feel if they miss their routine. Discuss how filters and edited images can create unrealistic expectations of what skin looks like, how advertising influences skincare choices, and the fact that pores, texture and spots are normal.

If skin worries are consuming substantial time, interfering with school, work or daily life, or seriously affecting mood, speak to a GP or mental health professional. [Cognitive behavioural therapy](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg31/chapter/Recommendations) is an evidence-based treatment for body dysmorphic or obsessive-compulsive symptoms.

One example is JEM, an effective, freely accessible chatbot for body image distress and mood, which I created and led the development of. It has been evaluated across multiple continents in a [real-world study](https://doi.org/10.2196/90783) published earlier this year.

Skincare itself is not the enemy. The warning sign is when caring for your skin turns into believing your skin must be perfected before you can feel acceptable.

*If you or a loved one are concerned about your body image and related behaviours, you can contact the [Butterfly Foundation](https://butterfly.org.au/get-support/helpline/) on 1800 33 4673 or through its online chat.*

*Professor Gemma Sharp receives funding from the National Health and Medical Research Council through an Investigator Grant. She is the owner and founder of Sharp AI Psychology. JEM® and ED ESSI® form part of Sharp AI Psychology’s portfolio of evidence-based digital mental health tools. She is the founding director of the charity, Consortium for Research in Eating Disorders.*
description: Spending time on skincare can be enjoyable, creative and soothing. But sometimes this self-care can be concerning. Could it be ‘cosmeticorexia’?

title: Why the consequences of the ‘empty nest’ can be real – and serious
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Denise Turner, Professor of Social Work, University of Hertfordshire; Katie Walsh, Reader in Human Geography, University of Sussex
content:
September is traditionally the time of year when many young people go to university or college, often leaving parents and carers facing an “empty nest”. But an empty nest doesn’t just mean a quiet home. Sometimes for the older generation there are also difficult questions about the next phase of their life.

The term “empty nest” was popularised by US author and activist Dorothy Canfield Fisher in her 1914 book Mothers and Children. It described the emotional challenges [mothers](https://theconversation.com/topics/mothers-19690) experienced when their children left home. By the 1970s, the concept of [“empty nest syndrome”](https://www.psychologytoday.com/gb/conditions/empty-nest-syndrome), had developed. This referred to more severe symptoms including depression, loneliness and loss of self-confidence.

In recent years, with living costs and house prices increasing relative to wages, this transition in family lives has become extended. Many young people are struggling to establish independent households. This leaves the timeframe of the transition to “empty nester” more uncertain for their parents or carers.

Much of the focus is on mothers, but celebrity chef Gordon Ramsay captured the impact on fathers too. Ramsay described becoming so distressed when [his son left home](https://www.standard.co.uk/culture/tvfilm/gordon-ramsay-reveals-he-wore-his-sons-underwear-after-dropping-him-off-at-university-a3970581.html) that he not only put on his son’s underwear, he then sat alone on his bed.

***Read more: [Digital poverty is holding university students back](https://theconversation.com/digital-poverty-is-holding-university-students-back-285663)***

Yet there appears to be a taboo about this complex experience within the social sciences. It is surprisingly under-researched and little mentioned, despite having broad implications for home, personal life, wellbeing and an ageing society.

[Recent research](https://academic.oup.com/bjsw/advance-article/doi/10.1093/bjsw/bcag151/8759168) by one of us (Denise) is one of the only UK studies ever to examine the empty nest experience. It explored how social factors, including living arrangements, relationship status and previous life events, can intersect with the emotional and social consequences of children leaving home. Using a life-course perspective (which looks at the significant factors that shape an individual’s life from birth to old age), the study considered how the transition can affect wellbeing, particularly among people aged 60 and over.

Findings were mixed, with some participants viewing the transition positively. These people saw it as an opportunity for new experiences and personal growth. Others, particularly those who were single, widowed or living alone, experienced significant loneliness, distress and a reduced sense of purpose.

For those who struggled, the loss was not simply about having fewer people in the house. Participants described missing the day-to-day rhythm of family life, including the conversations, routines and responsibilities associated with active parenting. This silence and emptiness contributed to a profound sense of loss. Others described a loss of identity following years of defining themselves through their role as an active parent, leading them to seek medical and therapeutic help.

One of the clearest findings was the relationship between companionship and wellbeing. Those in the study who had a partner or close companions living nearby were considerably less likely to experience the negative consequences of the empty nest. By contrast, those who were single, widowed or living alone appeared particularly vulnerable to distress and potential empty nest syndrome.

The study also highlighted the lack of social recognition around the empty nest transition. Unlike bereavement or retirement, the departure of an adult child doesn’t usually come with any formal public rituals or acknowledgement of the loss. Parents and carers may feel they have lost an important part of their lives. But at the same time, they may believe they don’t have “permission” to mourn that loss, because their child’s departure is considered a normal and a positive milestone.

Some participants in the study used the empty nest transition as a springboard to pursue forgotten hobbies, career ambitions, travel or rekindle friendships. However, these positive experiences were more common in heterosexual marriages, suggesting that the ability to turn loss into opportunity is shaped by social and relationship circumstances.

## Why this matters

Recognition of the empty nest is increasingly important as family structures and patterns of later life change. Data from the Office for National Statistics show that divorce among older adults [has increased](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/marriagecohabitationandcivilpartnerships/articles/marriageanddivorceontheriseat65andover/2017-07-18) over recent decades. Between 2005 and 2015, the number of men aged 65 and over divorcing increased by 23%. It was even higher for women, with an increase of 38% – contributing to the emergence of terms such as [“grey divorce”](https://www.bbc.co.uk/future/article/20250912-how-grey-divorce-affects-adult-children) and [“silver splitters”](https://www.theguardian.com/lifeandstyle/2025/nov/18/silver-splitters-why-divorced-women-are-so-happy-melinda-french-gates).

Single-parent families are becoming more common, while older people who divorce or are widowed may be more likely [to live alone](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/families/bulletins/familiesandhouseholds/2025) once their children leave home.

At the same time, people are living longer. Someone aged 65 in the UK can now expect to live for [around 20 years](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/birthsdeathsandmarriages/lifeexpectancies/bulletins/nationallifetablesunitedkingdom/2022to2024#life-expectancy-at-older-ages) beyond retirement. This provides a longer period in which they can renegotiate their identity and family roles, providing they can guard against loneliness.

The research suggests that we need to pay greater attention to the empty nest as a significant life-course transition, as well as the health and social care implications it brings. For some parents and carers, a child leaving home will be an exciting opportunity for freedom, exploration and personal growth. For others, the research shows it can intensify loneliness and undermine their sense of purpose and identity.

As loneliness and social isolation are associated with poorer physical and mental health, our plan is to carry out more research that spans family lives, home and wellbeing in order to develop forms of support for navigating this transition. While the empty nest may be inevitable, feeling empty in its aftermath is not.

*The authors do not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and have disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.*
description: The effects on parents as they adjust can be hugely under-estimated.

title: Why making friends at university feels harder than it really is
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Robert Dempsey, Senior Lecturer in Psychology, Manchester Metropolitan University
content:
The summer before starting university can be a time of multiple worries for students. Worry about obtaining a place on your desired course. Worry about navigating clearing to confirm your place. Worries about securing accommodation, sorting student finance, preparation for academic studies and even finding the right stationery are also common.

Yet many students’ biggest concern is social in nature: [“will I make friends?”](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/03075079.2018.1564902#d1e215). Surveys consistently suggest that [loneliness and belonging](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/new-government-research-shows-lonely-seems-to-be-the-hardest-word-for-students) are major concerns for new students starting university. This challenge isn’t unique to shy or socially anxious students. Most freshers experience worries about fitting in and [making connections](https://www.hepi.ac.uk/2023/02/10/the-heart-of-the-matter-student-loneliness-and-belonging%ef%bf%bc/) when starting university, especially when others make it seem so easy.

Something I find in my research with colleagues is [how poor we are](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/psychology/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2018.02180/full) at estimating others’ beliefs, feelings and behaviour. We also overestimate how much other people notice our own behaviour and any social missteps.

In social psychology, there are two related psychological biases that can explain this pattern. First, the [“spotlight effect”](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1467-8721.00039) explains how we wrongly assume that other people are paying attention to our behaviour. Psychologists [Thomas Gilovich and Kenneth Savitsky](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1467-8721.00039), who have studied this effect, state that people assume the “social spotlight” shines more brightly on themselves than it actually does.

The other bias, the [“illusion of transparency”](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1467-8721.00039), explains how people wrongly assume that others can view our feelings, worries and thoughts. In essence, we think that our [internal state leaks out socially](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1998-10511-003), and we overestimate how much others will harshly judge us as a result.

So, when we perceive an introduction to a new person to be awkward, forget someone’s name, run out of things to say or generally feel embarrassed after a conversation, it is likely that our perception of these interactions doesn’t match the other person’s. That’s assuming other people even paid much attention in the first place. For students starting university, this means many perceived social failures are largely invisible to others.

## The surprising psychology of first conversations

Evidence also suggests people routinely underestimate how much they are liked after speaking with strangers. This is another psychological phenomenon, the [“liking gap”](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0956797618783714). We might think that other people like us less than they actually do ([the actual liking gap](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2025-84374-001)), or we like a conversation partner more than we think they like us back ([a perceived liking gap](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2025-84374-001)).

It can be difficult to really know how well a conversation with a stranger has gone. Conversations can be cognitively demanding, requiring us to concentrate and listen to the other person, while following social conventions and expectations around politeness. We might miss key social cues about how the other person is feeling during interactions. As a result, we are often left to estimate how well the conversation went. These estimates are often [more self-critical](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0956797618783714) and uncertain than the reality.

After conversations, people tend to think they made a worse impression than they actually did. Students may stop pursuing potentially successful friendships because they wrongly assume initial conversations went badly, or [underestimate others’ interest](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/2014-28833-001) in making conversation.

## Small talk matters

Small talk is often wrongly dismissed as being [unimportant and superficial](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1207/S15327973RLSI3601_1). But engaging in small talk can have a number of positive benefits. It creates a sense of familiarity with others, that familiarity [promoting trust and liking](https://www.emerald.com/jkm/article/28/6/1538/1228824), and it contributes to improved wellbeing and [strengthening social bonds](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0146167214529799). Small talk is not the opposite of meaningful conversation. Actually, this is often the first step towards more meaningful interactions, developing social bonds and friendships.

***Read more: [Small talk acts like social glue – here’s how to get better at it](https://theconversation.com/small-talk-acts-like-social-glue-heres-how-to-get-better-at-it-286379)***

I take inspiration from a professor I worked with who moved across the country to start a new job in a brand new city. This professor, who describes herself as shy, made small talk with a woman as they stood waiting to cross the road near the university. This bit of small talk led to a lasting friendship with “Traffic Light Lady”. Even professors find making friends anxiety-provoking. But brief small talk can be the important first step towards establishing social rapport and developing friendships.

## Friendship is usually slower than we expect

Surprisingly, friendships take time to develop. An older psychological phenomenon, the [“mere exposure” effect](https://psycnet.apa.org/record/1968-12019-001), explains how friendships may emerge over time. Simply put, [the more we come into contact](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/002210319290055O) with an object or a person, the more likely we are to like that object or person over time. So for friendships, meaningful connections may be built through repeated interactions rather than instant chemistry.

For students, if you feel that you haven’t found your people during freshers week, don’t worry. Chances are the people you meet over the subsequent weeks – during lectures, at society meetings, social events or even in the queue for a coffee – are where friendships emerge. In fact, [research estimates](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/full/10.1177/0265407518761225) that it can take between 40-60 hours to develop a casual friendship in the first six weeks after meeting.

Making friends, whether at university or generally in life, takes time and repeated interactions. We often misperceive and overthink how well social interactions have gone. The importance of small talk, finding similar interests and shared experiences, and being patient, can help to build a sense of familiarity, trust and safety.

Psychology suggests that we are often overly harsh and self-critical in our perceptions of our social interactions and how others view us. In reality, friendships often begin not with brilliant conversation, but with ordinary moments repeated over time.

*Robert Dempsey receives funding from the BIAL Foundation and the British Academy / Wellcome for competitively funded research projects.*
description: We overestimate how much other people notice our own behaviour and any social missteps.

title: How high-quality friendship supports teen well-being
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Ryan J. Persram, Research Assistant Professor, Department of Psychology, Toronto Metropolitan University
content:
Are friends important to teens’ lives? Absolutely.

So, why does the question need more consideration? While some might think the number of friends is most important, what may matter more is the quality of those friendships.

There is no question that friendships help shape [adolescent well-being](https://doi.org/10.1037/bul0000239). As children move into adolescence, friendships often shift from being based on proximity and shared interests to becoming sources of crucial emotional support.

This evolution is especially salient as young people navigate the many social, academic and biological changes associated with being a teen.

## Quality versus quantity

Unlike friendship quantity (for example, number of friendships), the definition of friendship quality is somewhat more nuanced.

Generally, the quality of friendships considers the broad range of positive and negative experiences and interactions that [adolescents have with their friends](https://doi.org/10.1177/0265407594113011). For example, experiences of support, companionship, intimate disclosure and security can occur in the same friendships where people also experience conflict or feel unseen or criticized.

Considering both friendship positivity and negativity allows us to better understand how different types of friendships relate to adolescent well-being.

High-quality friendships, for instance, are described as having high levels of positive qualities and low levels of negative ones. These friendships are considered optimal because they are most often associated with better [social and emotional outcomes](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12889-022-14776-4) for adolescents.

## Mere presence may not be enough

Other profiles of friendship are possible. For example, teens can have [engaged or “affect-intense” friendships](https://doi.org/10.1177/02654075261447022) (high positivity and negativity), similar to the classic [love-hate sibling relationship](https://doi.org/10.1111/cdep.12345).

Though less common, teens may also have [low-quality friendships](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.paid.2014.12.051) (high negativity, low positivity).

Interestingly, some research shows that having more friends is linked to fewer [internalizing problems, such as anxiety or depressive symptoms](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ssresearch.2004.03.002). At first, this seems to favour quantity. However, one possible explanation is that having more friends can increase teens’ chances of finding a high-quality friendship among them, which may be driving these results.

In fact, direct comparisons between friendship quantity and quality indicate that the high quality of friendships can buffer [social and emotional challenges](https://doi.org/10.1111/sode.12530) youth face and potentially have a [longer-lasting impact](https://doi.org/10.1111/jcpp.13813). This shows that the substance of teens’ close friendships plays a greater role than merely the presence of friendships at large.

## Voluntary, reciprocal relationships

Why might having a high-quality friendship matter more than having many average or low-quality friendships?

Friendships, as voluntary and reciprocal relationships, are often closer through shared interests and likes that also build feelings of trust and loyalty towards [one another](https://doi.org/10.1002/9781119171492.wecad403). As a result, multiple friendships are possible.

As adolescents develop closer bonds with their friends, they come to understand and predict how different friends can offer support, companionship and security to each other — things that are essential for us as social beings. Naturally, teens can and do build closer friendships with some people and not others.

These positive qualities may be especially salient in closer friendships, which can provide significant benefits to adolescents. Research shows that adolescents who feel more secure in their friendships report [less anxiety](https://doi.org/10.1080/15374416.2015.1094742) and [greater friendship satisfaction](https://doi.org/10.13110/merrpalmquar1982.67.1.0056) than youth who feel less secure.

This is not to suggest that the number of friends is not a relevant indicator at all. Clearly, we need friends to have high-quality friendships. However, friendship quantity does not necessarily allow us to know about other important details about the friendship — like whether the substance quality of the friendship mutually drives their association.

Thinking about the quality of friendships allows us to see the effort and work adolescents put in to form and maintain their friendships. It also lets us consider the different elements that promote safety, support and security for both teens in the relationship.

## How parents can play a role

[Parents and families](https://www.camh.ca/en/health-info/guides-and-publications/tips-for-building-healthy-relationships-with-your-teenagers) can play a vital role in how their teenaged children form and maintain high-quality friendships.

One way is for parents to model healthy relationships with each other and with their children.

Modelling positive and constructive interactions between adults (for example, between parents and parents’ friends) provides a foundational understanding for teens on how to navigate the positive and negative aspects of friendships.

This includes modelling healthy communication (like active listening), encouraging self-disclosure to demonstrate trust (sharing personal thoughts and feelings with others), receiving and offering support, as well as navigating conflict.

Avoiding conflict is not always possible or feasible. Even in the best and highest quality friendships, conflict can and does occur.

When it does, teens who have more knowledge about how to constructively handle conflict (discussions about the issue, being attentive to others’ goals, encouraging compromise), are less likely to report decreases in the quality of their [friendship](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10964-007-9253-8), or worse, to [end them](https://doi.org/10.1037/dev0001676).

## Support teen independence, structure

Another practical way parents can facilitate their teen’s healthy friendship is to support their independence at a pace that fits the teen’s developmental readiness.

This includes showing genuine interest in [their teen’s worlds](https://theconversation.com/talking-with-your-teen-about-high-school-helps-them-open-up-about-big-and-little-things-in-their-lives-189171) and encouraging them to take part in activities outside of the school that build on their interests. At the same time, other considerations are having some flexibility with a teen’s decision-making and trying to not overstep too much.

What comes with empowering teens to make autonomous decisions is finding a balance with authoritative parenting. While love and support are important for healthy parent-teen relationships, so is structure.

For parents, some structure can come from providing justifications and reasoning behind their decisions about boundaries or behavioural expectations they have for their kids.

Conversations can include explanations that help teens understand the potential consequences of [certain choices](https://www.nationwidechildrens.org/family-resources-education/700childrens/2024/02/how-parents-can-help-support-healthy-teen-relationships) they may be thinking about. Together, these types of behaviours and conversations set teens up well to have healthy friendships.

There is no doubt that having friends is good for teens, but having healthy and high-quality friendships can be even better.

*Ryan Persram receives funding from SSHRC.*
description: Thinking about the quality of friendships allows us to consider the different elements that promote safety, support and security for both teens in a relationship.

title: Your high school friends may shape whether you become an entrepreneur decades later
topic: Tâm lý và các mối quan hệ
authors: Seok-Woo Kwon, Robson Professor in Entrepreneurship, University of Calgary; Xiaoying Wang, Assistant Professor of Strategic Management, Wilfrid Laurier University
content:
With more young Canadians considering self-employment amid a [high youth unemployment rate](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/n1/daily-quotidien/260710/dq260710a-eng.htm), entrepreneurship programs are facing growing demand. Applications to Futurpreneur, the national organization that finances young Canadian entrepreneurs, [rose 50 per cent last quarter](https://betakit.com/futurpreneur-applications-surge-as-more-youth-explore-entrepreneurship/), compared with 15 per cent growth a year earlier.

Yet most entrepreneurship supportive programs, including [Futurpreneur’s core startup program](https://futurpreneur.ca/en/offering/core-startup/), begin at age 18 and expect applicants to arrive with a business idea already in hand. That may be too late.

Both requirements reflect a common assumption: that the entrepreneurial impulse arrives in adulthood. Much research has made a similar assumption, looking for the social and professional influences that shape people after they enter university or the workforce.

We know, for example, that co-workers who have previously run a business [can make people notice opportunities they might otherwise miss](https://www.jstor.org/stable/40785246). MBA classmates [can influence one another’s judgments about which ideas are viable](https://doi.org/10.1093/rfs/hht024) and [university peers who start businesses can make entrepreneurship seem less risky](https://www.jstor.org/stable/42002871).

But these influences may begin earlier than researchers and policymakers have assumed. In a recent study, [lead author Seok-Woo Kwon and colleagues](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbusvent.2026.106621) found that the friends people make in high school may be associated with whether they become entrepreneurs decades later.

## The friends who make a difference

To investigate this, the researchers followed two American cohorts born roughly four decades apart. One was a [nationally representative group surveyed in the mid-1990s and followed into participants’ late 30s](https://addhealth.cpc.unc.edu/). The other was [a Wisconsin cohort followed from 1957 through age 65](https://researchers.wls.wisc.edu/).

Across both groups, having a teenage friend who later became self-employed was associated with a person’s own business ownership decades later.

But not every entrepreneurial friend counted. Adolescent friends who later build formal, incorporated companies — registered businesses with a legal identity separate from their owners — predicted a person’s entry into both incorporated and unincorporated self-employment.

By contrast, friends who simply worked for themselves informally, as solo contractors or freelancers, predicted nothing at all — not even entry into the same kind of informal work they were doing.

This distinction is important, because formal and informal self-employment [are essentially different populations](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjw044), running different kinds of ventures with different ambitions and earnings. In particular, our previous research has found that [formal, growth-oriented entrepreneurship tends to produce greater economic returns](https://theconversation.com/being-your-own-boss-doesnt-always-pay-off-what-30-years-of-data-reveal-284639).

The relationship also extended beyond whether someone started a business at all. People whose teenage friends later built incorporated companies earned more from their own ventures in midlife than people whose teenage friends did not, even after accounting for whether they themselves had incorporated their businesses.

The difference persisted among people running the same type of business. In other words, two people with similar ventures could have different earnings depending on what their teenage friends had gone on to build.

This suggests that adolescent friendships are associated not only with whether people eventually enter entrepreneurship, but also with the scale or economic performance of the ventures they pursue.

## How can a friendship at 16 matter at 40?

The findings raise an obvious question: how can a friendship formed at 16 still matter at 40? There are several possible explanations.

One is that adolescence establishes a social channel through which entrepreneurial examples can continue to travel. When a former classmate registers a company, hires staff or raises capital, that achievement may reach old friends through a reunion, a mutual acquaintance or a social media post.

Research suggests that people are [more responsive to information from those with whom they have meaningful social connections](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.psych.55.090902.142015) than to information from strangers. An entrepreneurial success story may therefore carry particular weight when it comes from someone you knew as a teenager.

This could also help explain why informal self-employment did not show the same relationship. Freelance work [tends to remain small and relatively invisible](https://www.nber.org/papers/w17041), so it may provide little evidence of what entrepreneurship can become.

But one finding complicates a straightforward social-influence explanation: friendships that persisted into adulthood and those that faded were similarly predictive. If ongoing influence were the whole explanation, enduring ties should have mattered more, since they are the ones carrying advice, encouragement and opportunities.

There is another possibility. Teenagers do not choose friends at random; [similarity tends to foster social connection](https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.soc.27.1.415), and adolescents who share an appetite for risk, independence or autonomy may be more likely to become friends.

The data cannot fully distinguish between these explanations, but both point to adolescence as an important period in the development of entrepreneurial pathways. Whether friends shape entrepreneurial inclinations or simply reveal inclinations already forming, something important is happening long before the first business begins.

## The window opens earlier than we think

The findings fit a broader body of research showing that entrepreneurial trajectories can take shape long before adulthood.

For instance, [children of business owners are far more likely to become business owners themselves](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11187-014-9586-0). And [evidence from adoptees suggests that environment may matter roughly twice as much as genetic inheritance](https://doi.org/10.1086/678493) in explaining who becomes an entrepreneur.

The new study adds another social pathway to this picture. The influence is not only parental; it also appears to run through adolescent peers. That has implications for how policymakers and educators think about entrepreneurship support.

Rather than waiting until young people reach adulthood, schools could instead create places where students interested in building things can find one another: through school ventures, maker spaces or small cohorts.

The size of those groups may matter, too. The association in the study was strongest among teenagers with relatively few close friends, suggesting that a single entrepreneurial peer may be particularly visible when there are fewer competing social influences.

The findings also change how we might evaluate entrepreneurship programs. [The recent federal evaluation of youth entrepreneurship support in Canada](https://ised-isde.canada.ca/site/audits-evaluations/en/evaluation/evaluation-futurpreneur-canada-2024) counts loans issued and businesses launched. If entrepreneurial pathways begin taking shape in adolescence, they capture only the end of a process that may have been developing for years.

Entrepreneurship policy should pay more attention to the social environments where entrepreneurial ambitions first take shape. For some, that process may have started long before they had a business idea or even thought of themselves as entrepreneurs: around the lunch table, back in high school.

*Seok-Woo Kwon receives funding from the SSHRC.*
